2.810: But thou O Father, I forewarn thee, shun
2.811: His deadly arrow; neither vainly hope
2.812: To be invulnerable in those bright Arms,
2.813: Though temper'd heav'nly, for that mortal dint,
2.814: Save he who reigns above, none can resist.
2.815: She finish'd, and the suttle Fiend his lore
2.816: Soon learnd, now milder, and thus answerd smooth.
2.817: Dear Daughter, since thou claim'st me for thy Sire,
2.818: And my fair Son here showst me, the dear pledge
2.819: Of dalliance had with thee in Heav'n, and joys
2.820: Then sweet, now sad to mention, through dire change
2.821: Befalln us unforeseen, unthought of, know
2.822: I come no enemie, but to set free
2.823: From out this dark and dismal house of pain,
2.824: Both him and thee, and all the heav'nly Host
2.825: Of Spirits that in our just pretenses arm'd
2.826: Fell with us from on high: from them I go
2.827: This uncouth errand sole, and one for all
2.828: My self expose, with lonely steps to tread
2.829: Th' unfounded deep, & through the void immense
2.830: To search with wandring quest a place foretold
2.831: Should be, and, by concurring signs, ere now
2.832: Created vast and round, a place of bliss
2.833: In the Pourlieues of Heav'n, and therein plac't
2.834: A race of upstart Creatures, to supply
2.835: Perhaps our vacant room, though more remov'd,
2.836: Least Heav'n surcharg'd with potent multitude
2.837: Might hap to move new broiles: Be this or aught
2.838: Then this more secret now design'd, I haste
2.839: To know, and this once known, shall soon return,
2.840: And bring ye to the place where Thou and Death
2.841: Shall dwell at ease, and up and down unseen
2.842: Wing silently the buxom Air, imbalm'd
2.843: With odours; there ye shall be fed and fill'd
2.844: Immeasurably, all things shall be your prey.
2.845: He ceas'd, for both seemd highly pleasd, and Death
2.846: Grinnd horrible a gastly smile, to hear
2.847: His famine should be fill'd, and blest his mawe
2.848: Destin'd to that good hour: no less rejoyc'd
2.849: His mother bad, and thus bespake her Sire.
2.850: The key of this infernal Pit by due,
2.851: And by command of Heav'ns all-powerful King
2.852: I keep, by him forbidden to unlock
2.853: These Adamantine Gates; against all force
2.854: Death ready stands to interpose his dart,
2.855: Fearless to be o'rematcht by living might.
2.856: But what ow I to his commands above
2.857: Who hates me, and hath hither thrust me down
2.858: Into this gloom of Tartarus profound,
2.859: To sit in hateful Office here confin'd,
2.861: Here in perpetual agonie and pain,
2.862: With terrors and with clamors compasst round
2.863: Of mine own brood, that on my bowels feed:
2.864: Thou art my Father, thou my Author, thou
2.865: My being gav'st me; whom should I obey
2.866: But thee, whom follow? thou wilt bring me soon
2.867: To that new world of light and bliss, among
2.868: The Gods who live at ease, where I shall Reign
2.869: At thy right hand voluptuous, as beseems
2.870: Thy daughter and thy darling, without end.
2.871: Thus saying, from her side the fatal Key,
2.872: Sad instrument of all our woe, she took;
2.873: And towards the Gate rouling her bestial train,
2.874: Forthwith the huge Portcullis high up drew,
2.875: Which but her self not all the Stygian powers
2.876: Could once have mov'd; then in the key-hole turns
2.877: Th' intricate wards, and every Bolt and Bar
2.878: Of massie Iron or sollid Rock with ease
2.879: Unfast'ns: on a sudden op'n flie
2.880: With impetuous recoile and jarring sound
2.881: Th' infernal dores, and on thir hinges great
2.882: Harsh Thunder, that the lowest bottom shook
2.883: Of Erebus. She op'nd, but to shut
2.884: Excel'd her power; the Gates wide op'n stood,
2.885: That with extended wings a Bannerd Host
2.886: Under spread Ensigns marching might pass through
2.887: With Horse and Chariots rankt in loose array;
2.888: So wide they stood, and like a Furnace mouth
2.889: Cast forth redounding smoak and ruddy flame.
2.890: Before thir eyes in sudden view appear
2.891: The secrets of the hoarie deep, a dark
2.893: Without dimension, where length, breadth, and highth,
2.894: And time and place are lost; where eldest Night
2.895: And Chaos, Ancestors of Nature, hold
2.897: Of endless warrs and by confusion stand.
2.898: For hot, cold, moist, and dry, four Champions fierce
2.899: Strive here for Maistrie, and to Battel bring
2.900: Thir embryon Atoms; they around the flag
2.901: Of each his faction, in thir several Clanns,
2.902: Light-arm'd or heavy, sharp, smooth, swift or slow,
2.903: Swarm populous, unnumber'd as the Sands
2.904: Of Barca or Cyrene's torrid soil,
2.905: Levied to side with warring Winds, and poise
2.906: Thir lighter wings. To whom these most adhere,
2.907: Hee rules a moment; Chaos Umpire sits,
2.908: And by decision more imbroiles the fray
2.909: By which he Reigns: next him high Arbiter
2.910: Chance governs all. Into this wilde Abyss,
2.911: The Womb of nature and perhaps her Grave,
2.912: Of neither Sea, nor Shore, nor Air, nor Fire,
2.913: But all these in thir pregnant causes mixt
2.914: Confus'dly, and which thus must ever fight,
2.915: Unless th' Almighty Maker them ordain
2.916: His dark materials to create more Worlds,
2.917: Into this wilde Abyss the warie fiend
2.918: Stood on the brink of Hell and look'd a while,
2.919: Pondering his Voyage; for no narrow frith
2.920: He had to cross. Nor was his eare less peal'd
2.921: With noises loud and ruinous (to compare
2.922: Great things with small) then when Bellona storms,
2.923: With all her battering Engines bent to rase
2.924: Som Capital City, or less then if this frame
2.925: Of Heav'n were falling, and these Elements
2.926: In mutinie had from her Axle torn
2.927: The stedfast Earth. At last his Sail-broad Vannes
2.928: He spreads for flight, and in the surging smoak
2.929: Uplifted spurns the ground, thence many a League
2.930: As in a cloudy Chair ascending rides
2.931: Audacious, but that seat soon failing, meets
2.933: Fluttring his pennons vain plumb down he drops
2.934: Ten thousand fadom deep, and to this hour
2.935: Down had been falling, had not by ill chance
2.936: The strong rebuff of som tumultuous cloud
2.937: Instinct with Fire and Nitre hurried him
2.938: As many miles aloft: that furie stay'd,
2.939: Quencht in a Boggie Syrtis, neither Sea,
2.940: Nor good dry Land: nigh founderd on he fares,
2.941: Treading the crude consistence, half on foot,
2.942: Half flying; behoves him now both Oare and Saile.
2.943: As when a Gryfon through the Wilderness
2.944: With winged course ore Hill or moarie Dale,
2.945: Pursues the Arimaspian, who by stelth
2.946: Had from his wakeful custody purloind
2.947: The guarded Gold: So eagerly the fiend
2.948: Ore bog or steep, through strait, rough, dense, or rare,
2.949: With head, hands, wings, or feet pursues his way,
2.950: And swims or sinks, or wades, or creeps, or flyes:
2.951: At length a universal hubbub wilde
2.952: Of stunning sounds and voices all confus'd
2.953: Born through the hollow dark assaults his eare
2.954: With loudest vehemence: thither he plyes,
2.955: Undaunted to meet there what ever power
2.956: Or Spirit of the nethermost Abyss
2.957: Might in that noise reside, of whom to ask
2.958: Which way the neerest coast of darkness lyes
2.959: Bordering on light; when strait behold the Throne
2.960: Of Chaos, and his dark Pavilion spread
2.961: Wide on the wasteful Deep; with him Enthron'd
2.962: Sat Sable-vested Night, eldest of things,
2.963: The consort of his Reign; and by them stood
2.964: Orcus and Ades, and the dreaded name
2.965: Of Demogorgon; Rumor next and Chance,
2.966: And Tumult and Confusion all imbroild,
2.967: And Discord with a thousand various mouths.
2.968: T' whom Satan turning boldly, thus. Ye Powers
2.969: And Spirits of this nethermost Abyss,
2.970: Chaos and Ancient Night, I come no Spie,
2.971: With purpose to explore or to disturb
2.972: The secrets of your Realm, but by constraint
2.973: Wandring this darksome desart, as my way
2.974: Lies through your spacious Empire up to light,
2.975: Alone, and without guide, half lost, I seek
2.976: What readiest path leads where your gloomie bounds
2.977: Confine with Heav'n; or if som other place
2.978: From your Dominion won, th' Ethereal King
2.980: I travel this profound, direct my course;
2.981: Directed, no mean recompence it brings
2.982: To your behoof, if I that Region lost,
2.984: To her original darkness and your sway
2.985: (Which is my present journey) and once more
2.986: Erect the Standerd there of Ancient Night;
2.987: Yours be th' advantage all, mine the revenge.
2.988: Thus Satan; and him thus the Anarch old
2.989: With faultring speech and visage incompos'd
2.990: Answer'd. I know thee, stranger, who thou art,
2.991: That mighty leading Angel, who of late
2.992: Made head against Heav'ns King, though overthrown.
2.993: I saw and heard, for such a numerous host
2.994: Fled not in silence through the frighted deep
2.995: With ruin upon ruin, rout on rout,
2.996: Confusion worse confounded; and Heav'n Gates
2.997: Pourd out by millions her victorious Bands
2.998: Pursuing. I upon my Frontieres here
2.999: Keep residence; if all I can will serve,
2.1000: That little which is left so to defend
2.1001: Encroacht on still through our intestine broiles
2.1002: Weakning the Scepter of old Night: first Hell
2.1003: Your dungeon stretching far and wide beneath;
2.1004: Now lately Heaven and Earth, another World
2.1005: Hung ore my Realm, link'd in a golden Chain
2.1006: To that side Heav'n from whence your Legions fell:
2.1007: If that way be your walk, you have not farr;
2.1008: So much the neerer danger; goe and speed;
2.1009: Havock and spoil and ruin are my gain.
2.1010: He ceas'd; and Satan staid not to reply,
2.1011: But glad that now his Sea should find a shore,
2.1012: With fresh alacritie and force renew'd
2.1013: Springs upward like a Pyramid of fire
2.1014: Into the wilde expanse, and through the shock
2.1015: Of fighting Elements, on all sides round
2.1016: Environ'd wins his way; harder beset
2.1017: And more endanger'd, then when Argo pass'd
2.1018: Through Bosporus betwixt the justling Rocks:
2.1019: Or when Ulysses on the Larbord shunnd
2.1020: Charybdis, and by th' other whirlpool steard.
2.1021: So he with difficulty and labour hard
2.1022: Mov'd on, with difficulty and labour hee;
2.1023: But hee once past, soon after when man fell,
2.1024: Strange alteration! Sin and Death amain
2.1025: Following his track, such was the will of Heav'n,
2.1026: Pav'd after him a broad and beat'n way
2.1027: Over the dark Abyss, whose boiling Gulf
2.1028: Tamely endur'd a Bridge of wondrous length
2.1029: From Hell continu'd reaching th' utmost Orbe
2.1030: Of this frail World; by which the Spirits perverse
2.1031: With easie intercourse pass to and fro
2.1032: To tempt or punish mortals, except whom
2.1033: God and good Angels guard by special grace.
2.1034: But now at last the sacred influence
2.1035: Of light appears, and from the walls of Heav'n
2.1036: Shoots farr into the bosom of dim Night
2.1037: A glimmering dawn; here Nature first begins
2.1038: Her fardest verge, and Chaos to retire
2.1039: As from her outmost works a brok'n foe
2.1040: With tumult less and with less hostile din,
2.1041: That Satan with less toil, and now with ease
2.1042: Wafts on the calmer wave by dubious light
2.1043: And like a weather-beaten Vessel holds
2.1044: Gladly the Port, though Shrouds and Tackle torn;
2.1045: Or in the emptier waste, resembling Air,
2.1046: Weighs his spread wings, at leasure to behold
2.1047: Farr off th' Empyreal Heav'n, extended wide
2.1048: In circuit, undetermind square or round,
2.1049: With Opal Towrs and Battlements adorn'd
2.1050: Of living Saphire, once his native Seat;
2.1051: And fast by hanging in a golden Chain
2.1052: This pendant world, in bigness as a Starr
2.1053: Of smallest Magnitude close by the Moon.
2.1054: Thither full fraught with mischievous revenge,
2.1055: Accurst, and in a cursed hour he hies.

3.0:
*The Argument*
God sitting on his Throne sees Satan flying towards this world, then newly created; shews him to the Son who sat at his right hand; foretells the success of Satan in perverting mankind; clears his own Justice and Wisdom from all imputation, having created Man free and able enough to have withstood his Tempter; yet declares his purpose of grace towards him, in regard he fell not of his own malice, as did Satan, but by him seduc't.  The Son of God renders praises to his father for the manifestation of his gracious purpose towards Man; God again declares, that Grace cannot be extended towards Man without the satisfaction of divine Justice; Man hath offended the majesty of God by aspiring to Godhead, and therefore with all his progeny devoted to death must dye, unless some one can be found sufficient to answer for his offence, and undergoe his Punishment. The Son of God freely offers himself a Ransome for Man: the Father accepts him, ordains his incarnation, pronounces his exaltation above all in Heaven and Earth, commands all the Angels to adore him; they obey, amid hymning to their Harps in full Quire, celebrate the Father and the Son.. Mean while Satan alights upon the bare convex of this Worlds outermost Orb; where wandring he first finds a place since call'd The Lymbo of Vanity, what persons and things fly up thither; thence comes to the Gate of Heaven, describ'd ascending by stairs and the waters above the Firmament that flow about it: His passage thence to the Orb of the Sun; he finds there Uriel the Regent of that Orb, but first changes himself into the shape of a meaner Angel; and pretending a zealous desire to behold the new Creation and Man whom God had plac't here, inquires of him the place of his habitation, and is directed; alights first on Mount Niphates.
3.1: Hail holy light, ofspring of Heav'n first-born,
3.2: Or of th' Eternal Coeternal beam
3.3: May I express thee unblam'd? since God is light,
3.4: And never but in unapproached light
3.5: Dwelt from Eternitie, dwelt then in thee,
3.6: Bright effluence of bright essence increate.
3.7: Or hear'st thou rather pure Ethereal stream,
3.8: Whose Fountain who shall tell? before the Sun,
3.9: Before the Heavens thou wert, and at the voice
3.10: Of God, as with a Mantle didst invest
3.11: The rising world of waters dark and deep,
3.12: Won from the void and formless infinite.
3.13: Thee I re-visit now with bolder wing,
3.14: Escap't the Stygian Pool, though long detain'd
3.15: In that obscure sojourn, while in my flight
3.16: Through utter and through middle darkness borne
3.17: With other notes then to th' Orphean Lyre
3.18: I sung of Chaos and Eternal Night,
3.19: Taught by the heav'nly Muse to venture down
3.20: The dark descent, and up to reascend,
3.21: Though hard and rare: thee I revisit safe,
3.22: And feel thy sovran vital Lamp; but thou
3.23: Revisit'st not these eyes, that rowle in vain
3.24: To find thy piercing ray, and find no dawn;
3.25: So thick a drop serene hath quencht thir Orbs,
3.26: Or dim suffusion veild. Yet not the more
3.27: Cease I to wander where the Muses haunt
3.28: Cleer Spring, or shadie Grove, or Sunnie Hill,
3.29: Smit with the love of sacred song; but chief
3.30: Thee Sion and the flowrie Brooks beneath
3.31: That wash thy hallowd feet, and warbling flow,
3.32: Nightly I visit: nor somtimes forget
3.33: Those other two equal'd with me in Fate,
3.34: So were I equal'd with them in renown,
3.36: And Tiresias and Phineus Prophets old.
3.37: Then feed on thoughts, that voluntarie move
3.38: Harmonious numbers; as the wakeful Bird
3.39: Sings darkling, and in shadiest Covert hid
3.40: Tunes her nocturnal Note. Thus with the Year
3.41: Seasons return, but not to me returns
3.42: Day, or the sweet approach of Ev'n or Morn,
3.43: Or sight of vernal bloom, or Summers Rose,
3.44: Or flocks, or herds, or human face divine;
3.45: But cloud in stead, and ever-during dark
3.46: Surrounds me, from the chearful waies of men
3.47: Cut off, and for the book of knowledg fair
3.49: Of Natures works to mee expung'd and ras'd,
3.50: And wisdome at one entrance quite shut out.
3.51: So much the rather thou Celestial light
3.52: Shine inward, and the mind through all her powers
3.53: Irradiate, there plant eyes, all mist from thence
3.54: Purge and disperse, that I may see and tell
3.55: Of things invisible to mortal sight.
3.56: Now had the Almighty Father from above,
3.57: From the pure Empyrean where he sits
3.58: High Thron'd above all highth, bent down his eye,
3.59: His own works and their works at once to view:
3.60: About him all the Sanctities of Heaven
3.61: Stood thick as Starrs, and from his sight receiv'd
3.62: Beatitude past utterance; on his right
3.63: The radiant image of his Glory sat,
3.64: His onely Son; On Earth he first beheld
3.65: Our two first Parents, yet the onely two
3.66: Of mankind, in the happie Garden plac't,
3.67: Reaping immortal fruits of joy and love,
3.69: In blissful solitude; he then survey'd
3.70: Hell and the Gulf between, and Satan there
3.71: Coasting the wall of Heav'n on this side Night
3.72: In the dun Air sublime, and ready now
3.73: To stoop with wearied wings, and willing feet
3.74: On the bare outside of this World, that seem'd
3.76: Uncertain which, in Ocean or in Air.
3.77: Him God beholding from his prospect high,
3.78: Wherein past, present, future he beholds,
3.79: Thus to his onely Son foreseeing spake.
3.80: Onely begotten Son, seest thou what rage
3.81: Transports our adversarie, whom no bounds
3.82: Prescrib'd, no barrs of Hell, nor all the chains
3.83: Heapt on him there, nor yet the main Abyss
3.84: Wide interrupt can hold; so bent he seems
3.85: On desperat revenge, that shall redound
3.86: Upon his own rebellious head. And now
3.87: Through all restraint broke loose he wings his way
3.88: Not farr off Heav'n, in the Precincts of light,
3.89: Directly towards the new created World,
3.90: And Man there plac't, with purpose to assay
3.91: If him by force he can destroy, or worse,
3.92: By som false guile pervert; and shall pervert;
3.93: For man will heark'n to his glozing lyes,
3.94: And easily transgress the sole Command,
3.95: Sole pledge of his obedience: So will fall
3.96: Hee and his faithless Progenie: whose fault?
3.97: Whose but his own? ingrate, he had of mee
3.98: All he could have; I made him just and right,
3.99: Sufficient to have stood, though free to fall.
3.100: Such I created all th' Ethereal Powers
3.101: And Spirits, both them who stood & them who faild;
3.102: Freely they stood who stood, and fell who fell.
3.103: Not free, what proof could they have givn sincere
3.104: Of true allegiance, constant Faith or Love,
3.105: Where onely what they needs must do, appeard,
3.106: Not what they would? what praise could they receive?
3.107: What pleasure I from such obedience paid,
3.108: When Will and Reason (Reason also is choice)
3.109: Useless and vain, of freedom both despoild,
3.110: Made passive both, had servd necessitie,
3.111: Not mee. They therefore as to right belongd,
3.112: So were created, nor can justly accuse
3.113: Thir maker, or thir making, or thir Fate;
3.115: Thir will, dispos'd by absolute Decree
3.116: Or high foreknowledge; they themselves decreed
3.117: Thir own revolt, not I: if I foreknew,
3.118: Foreknowledge had no influence on their fault,
3.119: Which had no less prov'd certain unforeknown.
3.120: So without least impulse or shadow of Fate,
3.121: Or aught by me immutablie foreseen,
3.122: They trespass, Authors to themselves in all
3.123: Both what they judge and what they choose; for so
3.124: I formd them free, and free they must remain,
3.125: Till they enthrall themselves: I else must change
3.126: Thir nature, and revoke the high Decree
3.128: Thir freedom, they themselves ordain'd thir fall.
3.129: The first sort by thir own suggestion fell,
3.131: By the other first: Man therefore shall find grace,
3.132: The other none: in Mercy and Justice both,
3.133: Through Heav'n and Earth, so shall my glorie excel,
3.134: But Mercy first and last shall brightest shine.
3.135: Thus while God spake, ambrosial fragrance fill'd
3.136: All Heav'n, and in the blessed Spirits elect
3.137: Sense of new joy ineffable diffus'd:
3.138: Beyond compare the Son of God was seen
3.139: Most glorious, in him all his Father shon
3.140: Substantially express'd, and in his face
3.142: Love without end, and without measure Grace,
3.143: Which uttering thus he to his Father spake.
3.144: O Father, gracious was that word which clos'd
3.145: Thy sovran sentence, that Man should find grace;
3.146: For which both Heav'n and Earth shall high extoll
3.147: Thy praises, with th' innumerable sound
3.148: Of Hymns and sacred Songs, wherewith thy Throne
3.149: Encompass'd shall resound thee ever blest.
3.150: For should Man finally be lost, should Man
3.151: Thy creature late so lov'd, thy youngest Son
3.152: Fall circumvented thus by fraud, though joynd
3.153: With his own folly? that be from thee farr,
3.154: That farr be from thee, Father, who art Judge
3.155: Of all things made, and judgest onely right.
3.156: Or shall the Adversarie thus obtain
3.157: His end, and frustrate thine, shall he fulfill
3.158: His malice, and thy goodness bring to naught,
3.159: Or proud return though to his heavier doom,
3.160: Yet with revenge accomplish't and to Hell
3.161: Draw after him the whole Race of mankind,
3.162: By him corrupted? or wilt thou thy self
3.164: For him, what for thy glorie thou hast made?
3.165: So should thy goodness and thy greatness both
3.166: Be questiond and blaspheam'd without defence.
3.167: To whom the great Creatour thus reply'd.
3.168: O Son, in whom my Soul hath chief delight,
3.169: Son of my bosom, Son who art alone
3.170: My word, my wisdom, and effectual might,
3.171: All hast thou spok'n as my thoughts are, all
3.172: As my Eternal purpose hath decreed:
3.173: Man shall not quite be lost, but sav'd who will,
3.174: Yet not of will in him, but grace in me
3.175: Freely voutsaft; once more I will renew
3.176: His lapsed powers, though forfeit and enthrall'd
3.177: By sin to foul exorbitant desires;
3.178: Upheld by me, yet once more he shall stand
3.179: On even ground against his mortal foe,
3.180: By me upheld, that he may know how frail
3.181: His fall'n condition is, and to me ow
3.182: All his deliv'rance, and to none but me.
3.183: Some I have chosen of peculiar grace
3.184: Elect above the rest; so is my will:
3.185: The rest shall hear me call, and oft be warnd
3.186: Thir sinful state, and to appease betimes
3.187: Th' incensed Deitie, while offerd grace
3.188: Invites; for I will cleer thir senses dark,
3.189: What may suffice, and soft'n stonie hearts
3.190: To pray, repent, and bring obedience due.
3.191: To prayer, repentance, and obedience due,
3.192: Though but endevord with sincere intent,
3.193: Mine eare shall not be slow, mine eye not shut.
3.194: And I will place within them as a guide
3.195: My Umpire Conscience, whom if they will hear,
3.196: Light after light well us'd they shall attain,
3.197: And to the end persisting, safe arrive.
3.198: This my long sufferance and my day of grace
3.199: They who neglect and scorn, shall never taste;
3.200: But hard be hard'nd, blind be blinded more,
3.201: That they may stumble on, and deeper fall;
3.202: And none but such from mercy I exclude.
3.203: But yet all is not don; Man disobeying,
3.204: Disloyal breaks his fealtie, and sinns
3.205: Against the high Supremacie of Heav'n,
3.206: Affecting God-head, and so loosing all,
3.207: To expiate his Treason hath naught left,
3.208: But to destruction sacred and devote,
3.209: He with his whole posteritie must die,
3.210: Die hee or Justice must; unless for him
3.211: Som other able, and as willing, pay
3.212: The rigid satisfaction, death for death.
3.213: Say Heav'nly Powers, where shall we find such love,
3.214: Which of ye will be mortal to redeem
3.215: Mans mortal crime, and just th' unjust to save,
3.216: Dwels in all Heaven charitie so deare?
3.217: He ask'd, but all the Heav'nly Quire stood mute,
3.218: And silence was in Heav'n: on mans behalf
3.220: Much less that durst upon his own head draw
3.221: The deadly forfeiture, and ransom set.
3.222: And now without redemption all mankind
3.223: Must have bin lost, adjudg'd to Death and Hell
3.224: By doom severe, had not the Son of God,
3.225: In whom the fulness dwels of love divine,
3.227: Father, thy word is past, man shall find grace;
3.228: And shall grace not find means, that finds her way,
3.229: The speediest of thy winged messengers,
3.230: To visit all thy creatures, and to all
3.232: Happie for man, so coming; be her aide
3.233: Can never seek, once dead in sins and lost;
3.234: Attonement for himself or offering meet,
3.235: Indebted and undon, hath none to bring:
3.236: Behold mee then, mee for him, life for life
3.237: I offer, on mee let thine anger fall;
3.238: Account mee man; I for his sake will leave
3.239: Thy bosom, and this glorie next to thee
3.240: Freely put off, and for him lastly die
3.241: Well pleas'd, on me let Death wreck all his rage;
3.242: Under his gloomie power I shall not long
3.243: Lie vanquisht; thou hast givn me to possess
3.244: Life in my self for ever, by thee I live,
3.245: Though now to Death I yeild, and am his due
3.246: All that of me can die, yet that debt paid,
3.247: Thou wilt not leave me in the loathsom grave
3.248: His prey, nor suffer my unspotted Soule
3.249: For ever with corruption there to dwell;
3.250: But I shall rise Victorious, and subdue
3.251: My Vanquisher, spoild of his vanted spoile;
3.252: Death his deaths wound shall then receive, & stoop
3.253: Inglorious, of his mortall sting disarm'd.
3.254: I through the ample Air in Triumph high
3.255: Shall lead Hell Captive maugre Hell, and show
3.256: The powers of darkness bound. Thou at the sight
3.257: Pleas'd, out of Heaven shalt look down and smile,
3.258: While by thee rais'd I ruin all my Foes,
3.259: Death last, and with his Carcass glut the Grave:
3.260: Then with the multitude of my redeemd
3.261: Shall enter Heaven long absent, and returne,
3.262: Father, to see thy face, wherein no cloud
3.263: Of anger shall remain, but peace assur'd,
3.264: And reconcilement; wrauth shall be no more
3.265: Thenceforth, but in thy presence Joy entire.
3.266: His words here ended, but his meek aspect
3.267: Silent yet spake, and breath'd immortal love
3.268: To mortal men, above which only shon
3.270: Glad to be offer'd, he attends the will
3.271: Of his great Father. Admiration seis'd
3.272: All Heav'n, what this might mean, & whither tend
3.273: Wondring; but soon th' Almighty thus reply'd:
3.274: O thou in Heav'n and Earth the only peace
3.275: Found out for mankind under wrauth, O thou
3.276: My sole complacence! well thou know'st how dear,
3.277: To me are all my works, nor Man the least
3.278: Though last created, that for him I spare
3.279: Thee from my bosom and right hand, to save,
3.280: By loosing thee a while, the whole Race lost.
3.281: Thou therefore whom thou only canst redeeme,
3.282: Thir Nature also to thy Nature joyne;
3.283: And be thy self Man among men on Earth,
3.284: Made flesh, when time shall be, of Virgin seed,
3.285: By wondrous birth: Be thou in Adams room
3.286: The Head of all mankind, though Adams Son.
3.287: As in him perish all men, so in thee
3.288: As from a second root shall be restor'd,
3.289: As many as are restor'd, without thee none.
3.290: His crime makes guiltie all his Sons, thy merit
3.291: Imputed shall absolve them who renounce
3.292: Thir own both righteous and unrighteous deeds,
3.293: And live in thee transplanted, and from thee
3.294: Receive new life. So Man, as is most just,
3.295: Shall satisfie for Man, be judg'd and die,
3.296: And dying rise, and rising with him raise
3.297: His Brethren, ransomd with his own dear life.
3.298: So Heav'nly love shal outdoo Hellish hate,
3.299: Giving to death, and dying to redeeme,
3.300: So dearly to redeem what Hellish hate
3.301: So easily destroy'd, and still destroyes
3.302: In those who, when they may, accept not grace.
3.303: Nor shalt thou by descending to assume
3.304: Mans Nature, less'n or degrade thine owne.
3.305: Because thou hast, though Thron'd in highest bliss
3.306: Equal to God, and equally enjoying
3.307: God-like fruition, quitted all to save
3.308: A World from utter loss, and hast been found
3.309: By Merit more then Birthright Son of God,
3.310: Found worthiest to be so by being Good,
3.311: Farr more then Great or High; because in thee
3.312: Love hath abounded more then Glory abounds,
3.314: With thee thy Manhood also to this Throne;
3.315: Here shalt thou sit incarnate, here shalt Reigne
3.316: Both God and Man, Son both of God and Man,
3.318: I give thee, reign for ever, and assume
3.319: Thy Merits; under thee as Head Supream
3.320: Thrones, Princedoms, Powers, Dominions I reduce:
3.321: All knees to thee shall bow, of them that bide
3.322: In Heaven, or Earth, or under Earth in Hell;
3.323: When thou attended gloriously from Heav'n
3.324: Shalt in the Skie appeer, and from thee send
3.326: Thy dread Tribunal: forthwith from all Windes
3.327: The living, and forthwith the cited dead
3.328: Of all past Ages to the general Doom
3.329: Shall hast'n, such a peal shall rouse thir sleep.
3.330: Then all thy Saints assembl'd, thou shalt judge
3.331: Bad men and Angels, they arraignd shall sink
3.332: Beneath thy Sentence; Hell, her numbers full,
3.333: Thenceforth shall be for ever shut. Mean while
3.334: The World shall burn, and from her ashes spring
3.335: New Heav'n and Earth, wherein the just shall dwell
3.336: And after all thir tribulations long
3.337: See golden days, fruitful of golden deeds,
3.338: With Joy and Love triumphing, and fair Truth.
3.339: Then thou thy regal Scepter shalt lay by,
3.340: For regal Scepter then no more shall need,
3.341: God shall be All in All. But all ye Gods,
3.342: Adore him, who to compass all this dies,
3.343: Adore the Son, and honour him as mee.
3.344: No sooner had th' Almighty ceas't, but all
3.345: The multitude of Angels with a shout
3.346: Loud as from numbers without number, sweet
3.347: As from blest voices, uttering joy, Heav'n rung
3.348: With Jubilee, and loud Hosanna's fill'd
3.350: Towards either Throne they bow, & to the ground
3.351: With solemn adoration down they cast
3.352: Thir Crowns inwove with Amarant and Gold,
3.353: Immortal Amarant, a Flour which once
3.354: In Paradise, fast by the Tree of Life
3.355: Began to bloom, but soon for mans offence
3.356: To Heav'n remov'd where first it grew, there grows,
3.357: And flours aloft shading the Fount of Life,
3.358: And where the river of Bliss through midst of Heavn
3.359: Rowls o're Elisian Flours her Amber stream;
3.360: With these that never fade the Spirits Elect
3.361: Bind thir resplendent locks inwreath'd with beams,
3.362: Now in loose Garlands thick thrown off, the bright
3.363: Pavement that like a Sea of Jasper shon
3.365: Then Crown'd again thir gold'n Harps they took,
3.366: Harps ever tun'd, that glittering by their side
3.367: Like Quivers hung, and with Praeamble sweet
3.369: Thir sacred Song, and waken raptures high;
3.370: No voice exempt, no voice but well could joine
3.371: Melodious part, such concord is in Heav'n.
3.372: Thee Father first they sung Omnipotent,
3.374: Eternal King; thee Author of all being,
3.375: Fountain of Light, thy self invisible
3.376: Amidst the glorious brightness where thou sit'st
3.377: Thron'd inaccessible, but when thou shad'st
3.378: The full blaze of thy beams, and through a cloud
3.379: Drawn round about thee like a radiant Shrine,
3.380: Dark with excessive bright thy skirts appeer,
3.381: Yet dazle Heav'n, that brightest Seraphim
3.382: Approach not, but with both wings veil thir eyes.
3.383: Thee next they sang of all Creation first,
3.385: In whose conspicuous count'nance, without cloud
3.386: Made visible, th' Almighty Father shines,
3.387: Whom else no Creature can behold; on thee
3.388: Impresst the effulgence of his Glorie abides,
3.389: Transfus'd on thee his ample Spirit rests.
3.390: Hee Heav'n of Heavens and all the Powers therein
3.391: By thee created, and by thee threw down
3.392: Th' aspiring Dominations: thou that day
3.393: Thy Fathers dreadful Thunder didst not spare,
3.394: Nor stop thy flaming Chariot wheels, that shook
3.395: Heav'ns everlasting Frame, while o're the necks
3.396: Thou drov'st of warring Angels disarraid.
3.397: Back from pursuit thy Powers with loud acclaime
3.398: Thee only extold, Son of thy Fathers might,
3.399: To execute fierce vengeance on his foes,
3.400: Not so on Man; him through their malice fall'n,
3.401: Father of Mercie and Grace, thou didst not doome
3.402: So strictly, but much more to pitie encline:
3.403: No sooner did thy dear and onely Son
3.404: Perceive thee purpos'd not to doom frail Man
3.405: So strictly, but much more to pitie enclin'd,
3.406: He to appease thy wrauth, and end the strife
3.407: Of Mercy and Justice in thy face discern'd,
3.408: Regardless of the Bliss wherein hee sat
3.409: Second to thee, offerd himself to die
3.410: For mans offence. O unexampl'd love,
3.411: Love no where to be found less then Divine!
3.412: Hail Son of God, Saviour of Men, thy Name
3.413: Shall be the copious matter of my Song
3.414: Henceforth, and never shall my Harp thy praise
3.415: Forget, nor from thy Fathers praise disjoine.
3.416: Thus they in Heav'n, above the starry Sphear,
3.417: Thir happie hours in joy and hymning spent.
3.418: Mean while upon the firm opacous Globe
3.419: Of this round World, whose first convex divides
3.421: From Chaos and th' inroad of Darkness old,
3.422: Satan alighted walks: a Globe farr off
3.423: It seem'd, now seems a boundless Continent
3.424: Dark, waste, and wild, under the frown of Night
3.426: Of Chaos blustring round, inclement skie;
3.427: Save on that side which from the wall of Heav'n
3.428: Though distant farr som small reflection gaines
3.429: Of glimmering air less vext with tempest loud:
3.430: Here walk'd the Fiend at large in spacious field.
3.431: As when a Vultur on Imaus bred,
3.432: Whose snowie ridge the roving Tartar bounds,
3.433: Dislodging from a Region scarce of prey
3.434: To gorge the flesh of Lambs or yeanling Kids
3.435: On Hills where Flocks are fed, flies toward the Springs
3.436: Of Ganges or Hydaspes, Indian streams;
3.437: But in his way lights on the barren plaines
3.439: With Sails and Wind thir canie Waggons light:
3.440: So on this windie Sea of Land, the Fiend
3.441: Walk'd up and down alone bent on his prey,
3.442: Alone, for other Creature in this place
3.443: Living or liveless to be found was none,
3.444: None yet, but store hereafter from the earth
3.445: Up hither like Aereal vapours flew
3.446: Of all things transitorie and vain, when Sin
3.447: With vanity had filld the works of men:
3.448: Both all things vain, and all who in vain things
3.449: Built thir fond hopes of Glorie or lasting fame,
3.450: Or happiness in this or th' other life;
3.451: All who have thir reward on Earth, the fruits
3.452: Of painful Superstition and blind Zeal,
3.453: Naught seeking but the praise of men, here find
3.454: Fit retribution, emptie as thir deeds;
3.455: All th' unaccomplisht works of Natures hand,
3.457: Dissolvd on earth, fleet hither, and in vain,
3.459: Not in the neighbouring Moon, as some have dreamd;
3.460: Those argent Fields more likely habitants,
3.461: Translated Saints, or middle Spirits hold
3.462: Betwixt th' Angelical and Human kinde:
3.463: Hither of ill-joynd Sons and Daughters born
3.464: First from the ancient World those Giants came
3.465: With many a vain exploit, though then renownd:
3.466: The builders next of Babel on the Plain
3.467: Of Sennaar, and still with vain designe
3.468: New Babels, had they wherewithall, would build:
3.469: Others came single; hee who to be deemd
3.470: A God, leap'd fondly into Aetna flames,
3.471: Empedocles, and hee who to enjoy
3.472: Plato's Elysium, leap'd into the Sea,
3.473: Cleombrotus, and many more too long,
3.474: Embryo's and Idiots, Eremits and Friers
3.475: White, Black and Grey, with all thir trumperie.
3.476: Here Pilgrims roam, that stray'd so farr to seek
3.477: In Golgotha him dead, who lives in Heav'n;
3.478: And they who to be sure of Paradise
3.479: Dying put on the weeds of Dominic,
3.480: Or in Franciscan think to pass disguis'd;
3.481: They pass the Planets seven, and pass the fixt,
3.482: And that Crystalline Sphear whose ballance weighs
3.483: The Trepidation talkt, and that first mov'd;
3.484: And now Saint Peter at Heav'ns Wicket seems
3.485: To wait them with his Keys, and now at foot
3.486: Of Heav'ns ascent they lift thir Feet, when loe
3.487: A violent cross wind from either Coast
3.488: Blows them transverse ten thousand Leagues awry
3.489: Into the devious Air; then might ye see
3.490: Cowles, Hoods and Habits with thir wearers tost
3.491: And flutterd into Raggs, then Reliques, Beads,
3.493: The sport of Winds: all these upwhirld aloft
3.494: Fly o're the backside of the World farr off
3.495: Into a Limbo large and broad, since calld
3.496: The Paradise of Fools, to few unknown
3.497: Long after, now unpeopl'd, and untrod;
3.498: All this dark Globe the Fiend found as he pass'd,
3.499: And long he wanderd, till at last a gleame
3.500: Of dawning light turnd thither-ward in haste
3.501: His travell'd steps; farr distant hee descries
3.503: Up to the wall of Heaven a Structure high,
3.504: At top whereof, but farr more rich appeerd
3.505: The work as of a Kingly Palace Gate
3.506: With Frontispice of Diamond and Gold
3.507: Imbellisht, thick with sparkling orient Gemmes
3.508: The Portal shon, inimitable on Earth
3.509: By Model, or by shading Pencil drawn.
3.510: The Stairs were such as whereon Jacob saw
3.512: Of Guardians bright, when he from Esau fled
3.513: To Padan-aram in the field of Luz,
3.514: Dreaming by night under the open Skie,
3.515: And waking cri'd, This is the Gate of Heav'n.
3.516: Each Stair mysteriously was meant, nor stood
3.517: There alwaies, but drawn up to Heav'n somtimes
3.518: Viewless, and underneath a bright Sea flow'd
3.519: Of Jasper, or of liquid Pearle, whereon
3.520: Who after came from Earth, sayling arriv'd,
3.521: Wafted by Angels, or flew o're the Lake
3.522: Rapt in a Chariot drawn by fiery Steeds.
3.523: The Stairs were then let down, whether to dare
3.524: The Fiend by easie ascent, or aggravate
3.525: His sad exclusion from the dores of Bliss.
3.526: Direct against which op'nd from beneath,
3.527: Just o're the blissful seat of Paradise,
3.528: A passage down to th' Earth, a passage wide,
3.529: Wider by farr then that of after-times
3.530: Over Mount Sion, and, though that were large,
3.531: Over the Promis'd Land to God so dear,
3.532: By which, to visit oft those happy Tribes,
3.533: On high behests his Angels to and fro
3.534: Pass'd frequent, and his eye with choice regard
3.535: From Paneas the fount of Jordans flood
3.536: To Beersaba, where the Holy Land
3.537: Borders on Aegypt and the Arabian shoare;
3.538: So wide the op'ning seemd, where bounds were set
3.539: To darkness, such as bound the Ocean wave.
3.540: Satan from hence now on the lower stair
3.541: That scal'd by steps of Gold to Heav'n Gate
3.542: Looks down with wonder at the sudden view
3.543: Of all this World at once. As when a Scout
3.544: Through dark and desart wayes with peril gone
3.545: All night; at last by break of chearful dawne
3.546: Obtains the brow of some high-climbing Hill,
3.547: Which to his eye discovers unaware
3.548: The goodly prospect of some forein land
3.550: With glistering Spires and Pinnacles adornd,
3.551: Which now the Rising Sun guilds with his beams.
3.552: Such wonder seis'd, though after Heaven seen,
3.553: The Spirit maligne, but much more envy seis'd
3.554: At sight of all this World beheld so faire.
3.555: Round he surveys, and well might, where he stood
3.556: So high above the circling Canopie
3.557: Of Nights extended shade; from Eastern Point
3.558: Of Libra to the fleecie Starr that bears
3.560: Beyond th' Horizon; then from Pole to Pole
3.561: He views in bredth, and without longer pause
3.562: Down right into the Worlds first Region throws
3.563: His flight precipitant, and windes with ease
3.564: Through the pure marble Air his oblique way
3.566: Stars distant, but nigh hand seemd other Worlds,
3.567: Or other Worlds they seemd, or happy Iles,
3.568: Like those Hesperian Gardens fam'd of old,
3.569: Fortunate Fields, and Groves and flourie Vales,
3.570: Thrice happy Iles, but who dwelt happy there
3.571: He stayd not to enquire: above them all
3.572: The golden Sun in splendor likest Heaven
3.573: Allur'd his eye: Thither his course he bends
3.574: Through the calm Firmament; but up or downe
3.575: By center, or eccentric, hard to tell,
3.576: Or Longitude, where the great Luminarie
3.578: That from his Lordly eye keep distance due,
3.579: Dispenses Light from farr; they as they move
3.580: Thir Starry dance in numbers that compute
3.581: Days, months, and years, towards his all-chearing Lamp
3.582: Turn swift their various motions, or are turnd
3.583: By his Magnetic beam, that gently warms
3.584: The Univers, and to each inward part
3.586: Shoots invisible vertue even to the deep:
3.587: So wondrously was set his Station bright.
3.588: There lands the Fiend, a spot like which perhaps
3.589: Astronomer in the Sun's lucent Orbe
3.590: Through his glaz'd Optic Tube yet never saw.
3.591: The place he found beyond expression bright,
3.592: Compar'd with aught on Earth, Medal or Stone;
3.593: Not all parts like, but all alike informd
3.594: With radiant light, as glowing Iron with fire;
3.595: If mettal, part seemd Gold, part Silver cleer;
3.596: If stone, Carbuncle most or Chrysolite,
3.597: Rubie or Topaz, to the Twelve that shon
3.598: In Aarons Brest-plate, and a stone besides
3.599: Imagind rather oft then elsewhere seen,
3.600: That stone, or like to that which here below
3.601: Philosophers in vain so long have sought,
3.602: In vain, though by thir powerful Art they binde
3.603: Volatil Hermes, and call up unbound
3.604: In various shapes old Proteus from the Sea,
3.605: Draind through a Limbec to his Native forme.
3.606: What wonder then if fields and regions here
3.607: Breathe forth Elixir pure, and Rivers run
3.608: Potable Gold, when with one vertuous touch
3.609: Th' Arch-chimic Sun so farr from us remote
3.611: Here in the dark so many precious things
3.612: Of colour glorious and effect so rare?
3.613: Here matter new to gaze the Devil met
3.614: Undazl'd, farr and wide his eye commands,
3.615: For sight no obstacle found here, nor shade,
3.616: But all Sun-shine, as when his Beams at Noon
3.617: Culminate from th' Aequator, as they now
3.618: Shot upward still direct, whence no way round
3.619: Shadow from body opaque can fall, and the Aire,
3.620: No where so cleer, sharp'nd his visual ray
3.621: To objects distant farr, whereby he soon
3.622: Saw within kenn a glorious Angel stand,
3.623: The same whom John saw also in the Sun:
3.624: His back was turnd, but not his brightness hid;
3.625: Of beaming sunnie Raies, a golden tiar
3.626: Circl'd his Head, nor less his Locks behind
3.627: Illustrious on his Shoulders fledge with wings
3.628: Lay waving round; on som great charge imploy'd
3.629: Hee seemd, or fixt in cogitation deep.
3.630: Glad was the Spirit impure as now in hope
3.631: To find who might direct his wandring flight
3.632: To Paradise the happie seat of Man,
3.633: His journies end and our beginning woe.
3.634: But first he casts to change his proper shape,
3.635: Which else might work him danger or delay:
3.636: And now a stripling Cherube he appeers,
3.637: Not of the prime, yet such as in his face
3.638: Youth smil'd Celestial, and to every Limb
3.639: Sutable grace diffus'd, so well he feignd;
3.640: Under a Coronet his flowing haire
3.641: In curles on either cheek plaid, wings he wore
3.642: Of many a colourd plume sprinkl'd with Gold,
3.643: His habit fit for speed succinct, and held
3.644: Before his decent steps a Silver wand.
3.645: He drew not nigh unheard, the Angel bright,
3.646: Ere he drew nigh, his radiant visage turnd,
3.647: Admonisht by his eare, and strait was known
3.648: Th' Arch-Angel Uriel, one of the seav'n
3.649: Who in Gods presence, neerest to his Throne
3.650: Stand ready at command, and are his Eyes
3.651: That run through all the Heav'ns, or down to th' Earth
3.652: Bear his swift errands over moist and dry,
3.653: O're Sea and Land: him Satan thus accostes;
3.654: Uriel, for thou of those seav'n Spirits that stand
3.655: In sight of God's high Throne, gloriously bright,
3.656: The first art wont his great authentic will
3.657: Interpreter through highest Heav'n to bring,
3.658: Where all his Sons thy Embassie attend;
3.659: And here art likeliest by supream decree
3.660: Like honour to obtain, and as his Eye
3.661: To visit oft this new Creation round;
3.662: Unspeakable desire to see, and know
3.663: All these his wondrous works, but chiefly Man,
3.664: His chief delight and favour, him for whom
3.665: All these his works so wondrous he ordaind,
3.666: Hath brought me from the Quires of Cherubim
3.667: Alone thus wandring. Brightest Seraph tell
3.668: In which of all these shining Orbes hath Man
3.669: His fixed seat, or fixed seat hath none,
3.670: But all these shining Orbes his choice to dwell;
3.671: That I may find him, and with secret gaze,
3.673: On whom the great Creator hath bestowd
3.674: Worlds, and on whom hath all these graces powrd;
3.675: That both in him and all things, as is meet,
3.676: The Universal Maker we may praise;
3.677: Who justly hath drivn out his Rebell Foes
3.678: To deepest Hell, and to repair that loss
3.679: Created this new happie Race of Men
3.680: To serve him better: wise are all his wayes.
3.681: So spake the false dissembler unperceivd;
3.682: For neither Man nor Angel can discern
3.683: Hypocrisie, the only evil that walks
3.685: By his permissive will, through Heav'n and Earth:
3.686: And oft though wisdom wake, suspicion sleeps
3.687: At wisdoms Gate, and to simplicitie
3.688: Resigns her charge, while goodness thinks no ill
3.689: Where no ill seems: Which now for once beguil'd
3.690: Uriel, though Regent of the Sun, and held
3.691: The sharpest sighted Spirit of all in Heav'n;
3.692: Who to the fraudulent Impostor foule
3.693: In his uprightness answer thus returnd.
3.694: Faire Angel, thy desire which tends to know
3.695: The works of God, thereby to glorifie
3.696: The great Work-Maister, leads to no excess
3.697: That reaches blame, but rather merits praise
3.698: The more it seems excess, that led thee hither
3.699: From thy Empyreal Mansion thus alone,
3.700: To witness with thine eyes what some perhaps
3.701: Contented with report heare onely in heav'n:
3.702: For wonderful indeed are all his works,
3.703: Pleasant to know, and worthiest to be all
3.704: Had in remembrance alwayes with delight;
3.705: But what created mind can comprehend
3.706: Thir number, or the wisdom infinite
3.707: That brought them forth, but hid thir causes deep.
3.708: I saw when at his Word the formless Mass,
3.709: This worlds material mould, came to a heap:
3.710: Confusion heard his voice, and wilde uproar
3.711: Stood rul'd, stood vast infinitude confin'd;
3.712: Till at his second bidding darkness fled,
3.713: Light shon, and order from disorder sprung:
3.714: Swift to thir several Quarters hasted then
3.715: The cumbrous Elements, Earth, Flood, Aire, Fire,
3.716: And this Ethereal quintessence of Heav'n
3.717: Flew upward, spirited with various forms,
3.718: That rowld orbicular, and turnd to Starrs
3.719: Numberless, as thou seest, and how they move;
3.720: Each had his place appointed, each his course,
3.721: The rest in circuit walles this Universe.
3.722: Look downward on that Globe whose hither side
3.723: With light from hence, though but reflected, shines;
3.724: That place is Earth the seat of Man, that light
3.725: His day, which else as th' other Hemisphere
3.726: Night would invade, but there the neighbouring Moon
3.727: (So call that opposite fair Starr) her aide
3.728: Timely interposes, and her monthly round
3.729: Still ending, still renewing, through mid Heav'n;
3.730: With borrowd light her countenance triform
3.731: Hence fills and empties to enlighten th' Earth,
3.732: And in her pale dominion checks the night.
3.733: That spot to which I point is Paradise,
3.734: Adams abode, those loftie shades his Bowre.
3.735: Thy way thou canst not miss, me mine requires.
3.736: Thus said, he turnd, and Satan bowing low,
3.737: As to superior Spirits is wont in Heaven,
3.738: Where honour due and reverence none neglects,
3.739: Took leave, and toward the coast of Earth beneath,
3.740: Down from th' Ecliptic, sped with hop'd success,
3.741: Throws his steep flight with many an Aerie wheele,
3.742: Nor staid, till on Niphates top he lights.

4.0:
*The Argument*
Satan now in prospect of Eden, and nigh the place where he must now attempt the bold enterprize which he undertook alone against God and Man, falls into many doubts with himself, and many passions, fear, envy, and despare; but at length confirms himself in evil,  journeys on to Paradise, whose outward prospect and scituation is described, overleaps the bounds, sits in the shape of a Cormorant on the tree of life, as highest in the Garden to look about him.  The Garden describ'd; Satans first sight of Adam and Eve; his wonder at thir excellent form and happy state but with resolution to work thir fall; overhears thir discourse, thence gathers that the Tree of knowledge was forbidden them to eat of, under penalty of death; and thereon intends to found his temptation, by seducing them to transgress: then leaves them a while to know further of thir state by some other means. Mean while Uriel descending on a Sunbeam warns Gabriel, who had in charge the Gate of Paradise, that some evil spirit had escap'd the Deep, and past at Noon by his Sphere in the shape of a good Angel down to Paradise, discovered after by his furious gestures in the Mount. Gabriel promises to find him out ere morning. Night coming on, Adam and Eve discourse of going to thir rest: thir Bower describ'd; thir Evening worship. Gabriel drawing forth his Bands of Night-watch to walk the round of Paradise, appoints two strong Angels to Adams Bower, least the evill spirit should be there doing some harm to Adam or Eve sleeping; there they find him at the ear of Eve, tempting her in a dream, and bring him, though unwilling, to Gabriel; by whom question'd he scornfully answers, prepares resistance, but hinder'd by a Sign from Heaven, flies out of Paradise.
4.1: O For that warning voice, which he who saw
4.2: Th' Apocalyps, heard cry in Heaven aloud,
4.3: Then when the Dragon, put to second rout,
4.4: Came furious down to be reveng'd on men,
4.5: Wo To The Inhabitants On Earth! that now,
4.6: While time was, our first Parents had bin warnd
4.7: The coming of thir secret foe, and scap'd
4.8: Haply so scap'd his mortal snare; for now
4.9: Satan, now first inflam'd with rage, came down,
4.10: The Tempter ere th' Accuser of man-kind,
4.11: To wreck on innocent frail man his loss
4.12: Of that first Battel, and his flight to Hell:
4.13: Yet not rejoycing in his speed, though bold,
4.14: Far off and fearless, nor with cause to boast,
4.15: Begins his dire attempt, which nigh the birth
4.16: Now rowling, boiles in his tumultuous brest,
4.17: And like a devillish Engine back recoiles
4.18: Upon himself; horror and doubt distract
4.19: His troubl'd thoughts, and from the bottom stirr
4.20: The Hell within him, for within him Hell
4.21: He brings, and round about him, nor from Hell
4.22: One step no more then from himself can fly
4.23: By change of place: Now conscience wakes despair
4.24: That slumberd, wakes the bitter memorie
4.25: Of what he was, what is, and what must be
4.26: Worse; of worse deeds worse sufferings must ensue.
4.27: Sometimes towards Eden which now in his view
4.28: Lay pleasant, his grievd look he fixes sad,
4.29: Sometimes towards Heav'n and the full-blazing Sun,
4.30: Which now sat high in his Meridian Towre:
4.31: Then much revolving, thus in sighs began.
4.32: O thou that with surpassing Glory crownd,
4.33: Look'st from thy sole Dominion like the God
4.34: Of this new World; at whose sight all the Starrs
4.35: Hide thir diminisht heads; to thee I call,
4.36: But with no friendly voice, and add thy name
4.37: O Sun, to tell thee how I hate thy beams
4.38: That bring to my remembrance from what state
4.39: I fell, how glorious once above thy Spheare;
4.40: Till Pride and worse Ambition threw me down
4.41: Warring in Heav'n against Heav'ns matchless King:
4.42: Ah wherefore! he deservd no such return
4.43: From me, whom he created what I was
4.44: In that bright eminence, and with his good
4.45: Upbraided none; nor was his service hard.
4.46: What could be less then to afford him praise,
4.47: The easiest recompence, and pay him thanks,
4.48: How due! yet all his good prov'd ill in me,
4.49: And wrought but malice; lifted up so high
4.50: I sdeind subjection, and thought one step higher
4.51: Would set me highest, and in a moment quit
4.52: The debt immense of endless gratitude,
4.53: So burthensome, still paying, still to ow;
4.54: Forgetful what from him I still receivd,
4.55: And understood not that a grateful mind
4.56: By owing owes not, but still pays, at once
4.57: Indebted and dischargd; what burden then?
4.58: O had his powerful Destiny ordaind
4.59: Me some inferiour Angel, I had stood
4.60: Then happie; no unbounded hope had rais'd
4.61: Ambition. Yet why not? som other Power
4.62: As great might have aspir'd, and me though mean
4.63: Drawn to his part; but other Powers as great
4.64: Fell not, but stand unshak'n, from within
4.65: Or from without, to all temptations arm'd.
4.66: Hadst thou the same free Will and Power to stand?
4.67: Thou hadst: whom hast thou then or what to accuse,
4.68: But Heav'ns free Love dealt equally to all?
4.69: Be then his Love accurst, since love or hate,
4.70: To me alike, it deals eternal woe.
4.71: Nay curs'd be thou; since against his thy will
4.72: Chose freely what it now so justly rues.
4.73: Me miserable! which way shall I flie
4.75: Which way I flie is Hell; my self am Hell;
4.76: And in the lowest deep a lower deep
4.77: Still threatning to devour me opens wide,
4.78: To which the Hell I suffer seems a Heav'n.
4.79: O then at last relent: is there no place
4.80: Left for Repentance, none for Pardon left?
4.81: None left but by submission; and that word
4.82: Disdain forbids me, and my dread of shame
4.83: Among the spirits beneath, whom I seduc'd
4.84: With other promises and other vaunts
4.85: Then to submit, boasting I could subdue
4.86: Th' Omnipotent. Ay me, they little know
4.87: How dearly I abide that boast so vaine,
4.88: Under what torments inwardly I groane;
4.89: While they adore me on the Throne of Hell,
4.90: With Diadem and Scepter high advanc'd
4.91: The lower still I fall, onely Supream
4.92: In miserie; such joy Ambition findes.
4.93: But say I could repent and could obtaine
4.94: By Act of Grace my former state; how soon
4.95: Would highth recal high thoughts, how soon unsay
4.96: What feign'd submission swore: ease would recant
4.97: Vows made in pain, as violent and void.
4.98: For never can true reconcilement grow
4.99: Where wounds of deadly hate have peirc'd so deep:
4.100: Which would but lead me to a worse relapse
4.101: And heavier fall: so should I purchase deare
4.102: Short intermission bought with double smart.
4.103: This knows my punisher; therefore as farr
4.104: From granting hee, as I from begging peace:
4.105: All hope excluded thus, behold in stead
4.106: Of us out-cast, exil'd, his new delight,
4.107: Mankind created, and for him this World.
4.108: So farwel Hope, and with Hope farwel Fear,
4.109: Farwel Remorse: all Good to me is lost;
4.110: Evil be thou my Good; by thee at least
4.111: Divided Empire with Heav'ns King I hold
4.112: By thee, and more then half perhaps will reigne;
4.113: As Man ere long, and this new World shall know.
4.114: Thus while he spake, each passion dimm'd his face
4.115: Thrice chang'd with pale, ire, envie and despair,
4.116: Which marrd his borrow'd visage, and betraid
4.117: Him counterfet, if any eye beheld.
4.118: For heav'nly mindes from such distempers foule
4.119: Are ever cleer. Whereof hee soon aware,
4.120: Each perturbation smooth'd with outward calme,
4.121: Artificer of fraud; and was the first
4.122: That practisd falshood under saintly shew,
4.123: Deep malice to conceale, couch't with revenge:
4.124: Yet not anough had practisd to deceive
4.125: Uriel once warnd; whose eye pursu'd him down
4.126: The way he went, and on th' Assyrian mount
4.127: Saw him disfigur'd, more then could befall
4.128: Spirit of happie sort: his gestures fierce
4.129: He markd and mad demeanour, then alone,
4.130: As he suppos'd, all unobserv'd, unseen.
4.131: So on he fares, and to the border comes
4.133: Now nearer, Crowns with her enclosure green,
4.134: As with a rural mound the champain head
4.135: Of a steep wilderness, whose hairie sides
4.136: With thicket overgrown, grottesque and wilde,
4.137: Access deni'd; and over head up grew
4.139: Cedar, and Pine, and Firr, and branching Palm,
4.140: A Silvan Scene, and as the ranks ascend
4.141: Shade above shade, a woodie Theatre
4.142: Of stateliest view. Yet higher then thir tops
4.143: The verdurous wall of Paradise up sprung:
4.144: Which to our general Sire gave prospect large
4.145: Into his neather Empire neighbouring round.
4.146: And higher then that Wall a circling row
4.147: Of goodliest Trees loaden with fairest Fruit,
4.148: Blossoms and Fruits at once of golden hue
4.149: Appeerd, with gay enameld colours mixt:
4.150: On which the Sun more glad impress'd his beams
4.151: Then in fair Evening Cloud, or humid Bow,
4.152: When God hath showrd the earth; so lovely seemd
4.153: That Lantskip: And of pure now purer aire
4.154: Meets his approach, and to the heart inspires
4.155: Vernal delight and joy, able to drive
4.156: All sadness but despair: now gentle gales
4.158: Native perfumes, and whisper whence they stole
4.159: Those balmie spoiles. As when to them who saile
4.160: Beyond the Cape Of Hope, and now are past
4.161: Mozambic, off at Sea North-East windes blow
4.162: Sabean Odours from the spicie shoare
4.163: Of Arabie the blest, with such delay
4.164: Well pleas'd they slack thir course, and many a League
4.165: Cheard with the grateful smell old Ocean smiles.
4.166: So entertaind those odorous sweets the Fiend
4.167: Who came thir bane, though with them better pleas'd
4.168: Then Asmodeus with the fishie fume,
4.169: That drove him, though enamourd, from the Spouse
4.170: Of Tobits Son, and with a vengeance sent
4.171: From Media post to Aegypt, there fast bound.
4.172: Now to th' ascent of that steep savage Hill
4.173: Satan had journied on, pensive and slow;
4.174: But further way found none, so thick entwin'd,
4.175: As one continu'd brake, the undergrowth
4.176: Of shrubs and tangling bushes had perplext
4.177: All path of Man or Beast that past that way:
4.178: One Gate there onely was, and that look'd East
4.179: On th' other side: which when th' arch-fellon saw
4.180: Due entrance he disdaind, and in contempt,
4.181: At one slight bound high overleap'd all bound
4.182: Of Hill or highest Wall, and sheer within
4.183: Lights on his feet. As when a prowling Wolfe,
4.184: Whom hunger drives to seek new haunt for prey,
4.185: Watching where Shepherds pen thir Flocks at eeve
4.186: In hurdl'd Cotes amid the field secure,
4.187: Leaps o're the fence with ease into the Fould:
4.188: Or as a Thief bent to unhoord the cash
4.189: Of some rich Burgher, whose substantial dores,
4.190: Cross-barrd and bolted fast, fear no assault,
4.191: In at the window climbes, or o're the tiles;
4.192: So clomb this first grand Thief into Gods Fould:
4.193: So since into his Church lewd Hirelings climbe.
4.194: Thence up he flew, and on the Tree of Life,
4.195: The middle Tree and highest there that grew,
4.196: Sat like a Cormorant; yet not true Life
4.197: Thereby regaind, but sat devising Death
4.198: To them who liv'd; nor on the vertue thought
4.199: Of that life-giving Plant, but only us'd
4.200: For prospect, what well us'd had bin the pledge
4.202: Any, but God alone, to value right
4.203: The good before him, but perverts best things
4.204: To worst abuse, or to thir meanest use.
4.205: Beneath him with new wonder now he views
4.206: To all delight of human sense expos'd
4.207: In narrow room Natures whole wealth, yea more,
4.208: A Heaven on Earth, for blissful Paradise
4.209: Of God the Garden was, by him in the East
4.210: Of Eden planted; Eden stretchd her Line
4.211: From Auran Eastward to the Royal Towrs
4.212: Of great Seleucia, built by Grecian Kings,
4.213: Or where the Sons of Eden long before
4.214: Dwelt in Telassar: in this pleasant soile
4.215: His farr more pleasant Garden God ordaind;
4.216: Out of the fertil ground he caus'd to grow
4.217: All Trees of noblest kind for sight, smell, taste;
4.218: And all amid them stood the Tree of Life,
4.220: Of vegetable Gold; and next to Life
4.221: Our Death the Tree of Knowledge grew fast by,
4.222: Knowledge of Good bought dear by knowing ill.
4.223: Southward through Eden went a River large,
4.224: Nor chang'd his course, but through the shaggie hill
4.225: Pass'd underneath ingulft, for God had thrown
4.226: That Mountain as his Garden mould high rais'd
4.227: Upon the rapid current, which through veins
4.228: Of porous Earth with kindly thirst up drawn,
4.229: Rose a fresh Fountain, and with many a rill
4.230: Waterd the Garden; thence united fell
4.231: Down the steep glade, and met the neather Flood,
4.232: Which from his darksom passage now appeers,
4.233: And now divided into four main Streams,
4.234: Runs divers, wandring many a famous Realme
4.235: And Country whereof here needs no account,
4.236: But rather to tell how, if Art could tell,
4.237: How from that Saphire Fount the crisped Brooks,
4.238: Rowling on Orient Pearl and sands of Gold,
4.239: With mazie error under pendant shades
4.240: Ran Nectar, visiting each plant, and fed
4.241: Flours worthy of Paradise which not nice Art
4.242: In Beds and curious Knots, but Nature boon
4.243: Powrd forth profuse on Hill and Dale and Plaine,
4.244: Both where the morning Sun first warmly smote
4.245: The open field, and where the unpierc't shade
4.246: Imbround the noontide Bowrs: Thus was this place,
4.247: A happy rural seat of various view;
4.248: Groves whose rich Trees wept odorous Gumms and Balme,
4.249: Others whose fruit burnisht with Golden Rinde
4.251: If true, here onely, and of delicious taste:
4.252: Betwixt them Lawns, or level Downs, and Flocks
4.253: Grasing the tender herb, were interpos'd,
4.254: Or palmie hilloc, or the flourie lap
4.255: Of som irriguous Valley spread her store,
4.256: Flours of all hue, and without Thorn the Rose:
4.257: Another side, umbrageous Grots and Caves
4.258: Of coole recess, o're which the mantling Vine
4.259: Layes forth her purple Grape, and gently creeps
4.260: Luxuriant; mean while murmuring waters fall
4.261: Down the slope hills, disperst, or in a Lake,
4.262: That to the fringed Bank with Myrtle crownd,
4.263: Her chrystall mirror holds, unite thir streams.
4.264: The Birds thir quire apply; aires, vernal aires,
4.265: Breathing the smell of field and grove, attune
4.266: The trembling leaves, while Universal Pan
4.267: Knit with the Graces and the Hours in dance
4.268: Led on th' Eternal Spring. Not that faire field
4.269: Of Enna, where Proserpin gathring flours
4.270: Her self a fairer Floure by gloomie Dis
4.271: Was gatherd, which cost Ceres all that pain
4.272: To seek her through the world; nor that sweet Grove
4.273: Of Daphne by Orontes, and th' inspir'd
4.274: Castalian Spring might with this Paradise
4.275: Of Eden strive; nor that Nyseian Ile
4.276: Girt with the River Triton, where old Cham,
4.277: Whom Gentiles Ammon call and Libyan Jove,
4.278: Hid Amalthea and her Florid Son
4.279: Young Bacchus from his Stepdame Rhea's eye;
4.280: Nor where Abassin Kings thir issue Guard,
4.281: Mount Amara, though this by som suppos'd
4.282: True Paradise under the Ethiop Line
4.283: By Nilus head, enclos'd with shining Rock,
4.284: A whole dayes journey high, but wide remote
4.285: From this Assyrian Garden, where the Fiend
4.286: Saw undelighted all delight, all kind
4.287: Of living Creatures new to sight and strange:
4.288: Two of far nobler shape erect and tall,
4.289: Godlike erect, with native Honour clad
4.290: In naked Majestie seemd Lords of all,
4.291: And worthie seemd, for in thir looks Divine
4.292: The image of thir glorious Maker shon,
4.293: Truth, Wisdome, Sanctitude severe and pure,
4.294: Severe, but in true filial freedom plac't;
4.295: Whence true autoritie in men; though both
4.296: Not equal, as thir sex not equal seemd;
4.297: For contemplation hee and valour formd,
4.298: For softness shee and sweet attractive Grace,
4.299: Hee for God only, shee for God in him:
4.300: His fair large Front and Eye sublime declar'd
4.302: Round from his parted forelock manly hung
4.303: Clustring, but not beneath his shoulders broad:
4.304: Shee as a vail down to the slender waste
4.306: Dissheveld, but in wanton ringlets wav'd
4.307: As the Vine curles her tendrils, which impli'd
4.308: Subjection, but requir'd with gentle sway,
4.309: And by her yeilded, by him best receivd,
4.310: Yeilded with coy submission, modest pride,
4.312: Nor those mysterious parts were then conceald,
4.313: Then was not guiltie shame, dishonest shame
4.315: Sin-bred, how have ye troubl'd all mankind
4.316: With shews instead, meer shews of seeming pure,
4.317: And banisht from mans life his happiest life,
4.319: So passd they naked on, nor shund the sight
4.320: Of God or Angel, for they thought no ill:
4.321: So hand in hand they passd, the lovliest pair
4.322: That ever since in loves imbraces met,
4.323: Adam the goodliest man of men since borne
4.324: His Sons, the fairest of her Daughters Eve.
4.325: Under a tuft of shade that on a green
4.326: Stood whispering soft, by a fresh Fountain side
4.327: They sat them down, and after no more toil
4.328: Of thir sweet Gardning labour then suffic'd
4.329: To recommend coole Zephyr, and made ease
4.330: More easie, wholsom thirst and appetite
4.331: More grateful, to thir Supper Fruits they fell,
4.332: Nectarine Fruits which the compliant boughes
4.333: Yeilded them, side-long as they sat recline
4.334: On the soft downie Bank damaskt with flours:
4.335: The savourie pulp they chew, and in the rinde
4.336: Still as they thirsted scoop the brimming stream;
4.337: Nor gentle purpose, nor endearing smiles
4.338: Wanted, nor youthful dalliance as beseems
4.339: Fair couple, linkt in happie nuptial League,
4.340: Alone as they. About them frisking playd
4.341: All Beasts of th' Earth, since wilde, and of all chase
4.342: In Wood or Wilderness, Forrest or Den;
4.343: Sporting the Lion rampd, and in his paw
4.344: Dandl'd the Kid; Bears, Tygers, Ounces, Pards
4.345: Gambold before them, th' unwieldy Elephant
4.346: To make them mirth us'd all his might, and wreathd
4.347: His Lithe Proboscis; close the Serpent sly
4.349: His breaded train, and of his fatal guile
4.350: Gave proof unheeded; others on the grass
4.351: Coucht, and now fild with pasture gazing sat,
4.352: Or Bedward ruminating: for the Sun
4.353: Declin'd was hasting now with prone carreer
4.354: To th' Ocean Iles, and in th' ascending Scale
4.355: Of Heav'n the Starrs that usher Evening rose:
4.356: When Satan still in gaze, as first he stood,
4.357: Scarce thus at length faild speech recoverd sad.
4.358: O Hell! what doe mine eyes with grief behold,
4.359: Into our room of bliss thus high advanc't
4.360: Creatures of other mould, earth-born perhaps,
4.361: Not Spirits, yet to heav'nly Spirits bright
4.362: Little inferior; whom my thoughts pursue
4.363: With wonder, and could love, so lively shines
4.364: In them Divine resemblance, and such grace
4.365: The hand that formd them on thir shape hath pourd.
4.366: Ah gentle pair, yee little think how nigh
4.367: Your change approaches, when all these delights
4.368: Will vanish and deliver ye to woe,
4.369: More woe, the more your taste is now of joy;
4.370: Happie, but for so happie ill secur'd
4.371: Long to continue, and this high seat your Heav'n
4.372: Ill fenc't for Heav'n to keep out such a foe
4.373: As now is enterd; yet no purpos'd foe
4.374: To you whom I could pittie thus forlorne
4.375: Though I unpittied: League with you I seek,
4.376: And mutual amitie so streight, so close,
4.377: That I with you must dwell, or you with me
4.378: Henceforth; my dwelling haply may not please
4.379: Like this fair Paradise, your sense, yet such
4.380: Accept your Makers work; he gave it me,
4.381: Which I as freely give; Hell shall unfould,
4.382: To entertain you two, her widest Gates,
4.383: And send forth all her Kings; there will be room,
4.384: Not like these narrow limits, to receive
4.385: Your numerous ofspring; if no better place,
4.386: Thank him who puts me loath to this revenge
4.387: On you who wrong me not for him who wrongd.
4.388: And should I at your harmless innocence
4.389: Melt, as I doe, yet public reason just,
4.390: Honour and Empire with revenge enlarg'd,
4.391: By conquering this new World, compels me now
4.392: To do what else though damnd I should abhorre.
4.393: So spake the Fiend, and with necessitie,
4.394: The Tyrants plea, excus'd his devilish deeds.
4.395: Then from his loftie stand on that high Tree
4.396: Down he alights among the sportful Herd
4.397: Of those fourfooted kindes, himself now one,
4.398: Now other, as thir shape servd best his end
4.399: Neerer to view his prey, and unespi'd
4.400: To mark what of thir state he more might learn
4.401: By word or action markt: about them round
4.402: A Lion now he stalkes with fierie glare,
4.403: Then as a Tiger, who by chance hath spi'd
4.404: In some Purlieu two gentle Fawnes at play,
4.405: Strait couches close, then rising changes oft
4.406: His couchant watch, as one who chose his ground
4.407: Whence rushing he might surest seise them both
4.408: Grip't in each paw: when Adam first of men
4.409: To first of women Eve thus moving speech,
4.410: Turnd him all eare to heare new utterance flow.
4.411: Sole partner and sole part of all these joyes,
4.412: Dearer thy self then all; needs must the Power
4.413: That made us, and for us this ample World
4.414: Be infinitly good, and of his good
4.415: As liberal and free as infinite,
4.416: That rais'd us from the dust and plac't us here
4.417: In all this happiness, who at his hand
4.418: Have nothing merited, nor can performe
4.419: Aught whereof hee hath need, hee who requires
4.420: From us no other service then to keep
4.421: This one, this easie charge, of all the Trees
4.422: In Paradise that beare delicious fruit
4.423: So various, not to taste that onely Tree
4.424: Of knowledge, planted by the Tree of Life,
4.425: So neer grows Death to Life, what ere Death is,
4.426: Som dreadful thing no doubt; for well thou knowst
4.427: God hath pronounc't it death to taste that Tree,
4.428: The only sign of our obedience left
4.429: Among so many signes of power and rule
4.430: Conferrd upon us, and Dominion giv'n
4.431: Over all other Creatures that possesse
4.432: Earth, Aire, and Sea. Then let us not think hard
4.434: Free leave so large to all things else, and choice
4.436: But let us ever praise him, and extoll
4.437: His bountie, following our delightful task
4.438: To prune these growing Plants, & tend these Flours,
4.439: Which were it toilsom, yet with thee were sweet.
4.440: To whom thus Eve repli'd. O thou for whom
4.441: And from whom I was formd flesh of thy flesh,
4.442: And without whom am to no end, my Guide
4.443: And Head, what thou hast said is just and right.
4.444: For wee to him indeed all praises owe,
4.445: And daily thanks, I chiefly who enjoy
4.446: So farr the happier Lot, enjoying thee
4.447: Preeminent by so much odds, while thou
4.448: Like consort to thy self canst no where find.
4.449: That day I oft remember, when from sleep
4.450: I first awak't, and found my self repos'd
4.451: Under a shade on flours, much wondring where
4.452: And what I was, whence thither brought, and how.
4.453: Not distant far from thence a murmuring sound
4.454: Of waters issu'd from a Cave and spread
4.455: Into a liquid Plain, then stood unmov'd
4.456: Pure as th' expanse of Heav'n; I thither went
4.457: With unexperienc't thought, and laid me downe
4.458: On the green bank, to look into the cleer
4.459: Smooth Lake, that to me seemd another Skie.
4.460: As I bent down to look, just opposite,
4.461: A Shape within the watry gleam appeerd
4.462: Bending to look on me, I started back,
4.463: It started back, but pleasd I soon returnd,
4.464: Pleas'd it returnd as soon with answering looks
4.465: Of sympathie and love, there I had fixt
4.466: Mine eyes till now, and pin'd with vain desire,
4.467: Had not a voice thus warnd me, What thou seest,
4.468: What there thou seest fair Creature is thy self,
4.469: With thee it came and goes: but follow me,
4.470: And I will bring thee where no shadow staies
4.471: Thy coming, and thy soft imbraces, hee
4.472: Whose image thou art, him thou shall enjoy
4.473: Inseparablie thine, to him shalt beare
4.474: Multitudes like thy self, and thence be call'd
4.475: Mother of human Race: what could I doe,
4.476: But follow strait, invisibly thus led?
4.477: Till I espi'd thee, fair indeed and tall,
4.478: Under a Platan, yet methought less faire,
4.479: Less winning soft, less amiablie milde,
4.480: Then that smooth watry image; back I turnd,
4.481: Thou following cryd'st aloud, Return fair Eve,
4.482: Whom fli'st thou? whom thou fli'st, of him thou art,
4.483: His flesh, his bone; to give thee being I lent
4.484: Out of my side to thee, neerest my heart
4.485: Substantial Life, to have thee by my side
4.487: Part of my Soul I seek thee, and thee claim
4.488: My other half: with that thy gentle hand
4.489: Seisd mine, I yeilded, and from that time see
4.490: How beauty is excelld by manly grace
4.491: And wisdom, which alone is truly fair.
4.492: So spake our general Mother, and with eyes
4.494: And meek surrender, half imbracing leand
4.495: On our first Father, half her swelling Breast
4.496: Naked met his under the flowing Gold
4.497: Of her loose tresses hid: he in delight
4.498: Both of her Beauty and submissive Charms
4.499: Smil'd with superior Love, as Jupiter
4.500: On Juno smiles, when he impregns the Clouds
4.501: That shed May Flowers; and press'd her Matron lip
4.502: With kisses pure: aside the Devil turnd
4.503: For envie, yet with jealous leer maligne
4.504: Ey'd them askance, and to himself thus plaind.
4.505: Sight hateful, sight tormenting! thus these two
4.507: The happier Eden, shall enjoy thir fill
4.508: Of bliss on bliss, while I to Hell am thrust,
4.509: Where neither joy nor love, but fierce desire,
4.510: Among our other torments not the least,
4.511: Still unfulfill'd with pain of longing pines;
4.512: Yet let me not forget what I have gain'd
4.513: From thir own mouths; all is not theirs it seems:
4.514: One fatal Tree there stands of Knowledge call'd,
4.515: Forbidden them to taste: Knowledge forbidd'n?
4.516: Suspicious, reasonless. Why should thir Lord
4.517: Envie them that? can it be sin to know,
4.518: Can it be death? and do they onely stand
4.519: By Ignorance, is that thir happie state,
4.520: The proof of thir obedience and thir faith?
4.521: O fair foundation laid whereon to build
4.522: Thir ruine! Hence I will excite thir minds
4.523: With more desire to know, and to reject
4.525: To keep them low whom knowledge might exalt
4.526: Equal with Gods; aspiring to be such,
4.527: They taste and die: what likelier can ensue?
4.528: But first with narrow search I must walk round
4.529: This Garden, and no corner leave unspi'd;
4.530: A chance but chance may lead where I may meet
4.531: Some wandring Spirit of Heav'n, by Fountain side,
4.532: Or in thick shade retir'd, from him to draw
4.533: What further would be learnt. Live while ye may,
4.534: Yet happie pair; enjoy, till I return,
4.535: Short pleasures, for long woes are to succeed.
4.536: So saying, his proud step he scornful turn'd,
4.537: But with sly circumspection, and began
4.538: Through wood, through waste, o're hil, o're dale his roam.
4.539: Mean while in utmost Longitude, where Heav'n
4.540: With Earth and Ocean meets, the setting Sun
4.541: Slowly descended, and with right aspect
4.542: Against the eastern Gate of Paradise
4.543: Leveld his eevning Rayes: it was a Rock
4.544: Of Alablaster, pil'd up to the Clouds,
4.545: Conspicuous farr, winding with one ascent
4.546: Accessible from Earth, one entrance high;
4.547: The rest was craggie cliff, that overhung
4.548: Still as it rose, impossible to climbe.
4.549: Betwixt these rockie Pillars Gabriel sat
4.550: Chief of th' Angelic Guards, awaiting night;
4.552: Th' unarmed Youth of Heav'n, but nigh at hand
4.553: Celestial Armourie, Shields, Helmes, and Speares
4.554: Hung high with Diamond flaming, and with Gold.
4.555: Thither came Uriel, gliding through the Eeven
4.556: On a Sun beam, swift as a shooting Starr
4.557: In Autumn thwarts the night, when vapors fir'd
4.558: Impress the Air, and shews the Mariner
4.559: From what point of his Compass to beware
4.560: Impetuous winds: he thus began in haste.
4.561: Gabriel, to thee thy cours by Lot hath giv'n
4.562: Charge and strict watch that to this happie place
4.563: No evil thing approach or enter in;
4.564: This day at highth of Noon came to my Spheare
4.565: A Spirit, zealous, as he seem'd, to know
4.566: More of th' Almighties works, and chiefly Man
4.567: Gods latest Image: I describ'd his way
4.568: Bent all on speed, and markt his Aerie Gate;
4.569: But in the Mount that lies from Eden North,
4.570: Where he first lighted, soon discernd his looks
4.571: Alien from Heav'n, with passions foul obscur'd:
4.572: Mine eye pursu'd him still, but under shade
4.573: Lost sight of him; one of the banisht crew
4.574: I fear, hath ventur'd from the deep, to raise
4.575: New troubles; him thy care must be to find.
4.576: To whom the winged Warriour thus returnd:
4.577: Uriel, no wonder if thy perfet sight,
4.578: Amid the Suns bright circle where thou sitst,
4.579: See farr and wide: in at this Gate none pass
4.580: The vigilance here plac't, but such as come
4.581: Well known from Heav'n; and since Meridian hour
4.582: No Creature thence: if Spirit of other sort,
4.583: So minded, have oreleapt these earthie bounds
4.584: On purpose, hard thou knowst it to exclude
4.586: But if within the circuit of these walks
4.587: In whatsoever shape he lurk, of whom
4.588: Thou telst, by morrow dawning I shall know.
4.589: So promis'd hee, and Uriel to his charge
4.590: Returnd on that bright beam, whose point now raisd
4.591: Bore him slope downward to the Sun now fall'n
4.592: Beneath th' Azores; whither the prime Orb,
4.593: Incredible how swift, had thither rowl'd
4.594: Diurnal, or this less volubil Earth
4.595: By shorter flight to th' East, had left him there
4.596: Arraying with reflected Purple and Gold
4.597: The Clouds that on his Western Throne attend:
4.598: Now came still Eevning on, and Twilight gray
4.599: Had in her sober Liverie all things clad;
