4.600: Silence accompanied, for Beast and Bird,
4.601: They to thir grassie Couch, these to thir Nests
4.602: Were slunk, all but the wakeful Nightingale;
4.603: She all night long her amorous descant sung;
4.604: Silence was pleas'd: now glow'd the Firmament
4.605: With living Saphirs: Hesperus that led
4.606: The starrie Host, rode brightest, till the Moon
4.607: Rising in clouded Majestie, at length
4.608: Apparent Queen unvaild her peerless light,
4.609: And o're the dark her Silver Mantle threw.
4.610: When Adam thus to Eve: Fair Consort, th' hour
4.611: Of night, and all things now retir'd to rest
4.612: Mind us of like repose, since God hath set
4.613: Labour and rest, as day and night to men
4.614: Successive, and the timely dew of sleep
4.615: Now falling with soft slumbrous weight inclines
4.616: Our eye-lids; other Creatures all day long
4.617: Rove idle unimploid, and less need rest;
4.618: Man hath his daily work of body or mind
4.620: And the regard of Heav'n on all his waies;
4.622: And of thir doings God takes no account.
4.623: Tomorrow ere fresh Morning streak the East
4.624: With first approach of light, we must be ris'n,
4.625: And at our pleasant labour, to reform
4.626: Yon flourie Arbors, yonder Allies green,
4.627: Our walks at noon, with branches overgrown,
4.628: That mock our scant manuring, and require
4.629: More hands then ours to lop thir wanton growth:
4.630: Those Blossoms also, and those dropping Gumms,
4.631: That lie bestrowne unsightly and unsmooth,
4.632: Ask riddance, if we mean to tread with ease;
4.633: Mean while, as Nature wills, Night bids us rest.
4.634: To whom thus Eve with perfet beauty adornd.
4.635: My Author and Disposer, what thou bidst
4.636: Unargu'd I obey; so God ordains,
4.637: God is thy Law, thou mine: to know no more
4.638: Is womans happiest knowledge and her praise.
4.639: With thee conversing I forget all time,
4.640: All seasons and thir change, all please alike.
4.641: Sweet is the breath of morn, her rising sweet,
4.642: With charm of earliest Birds; pleasant the Sun
4.643: When first on this delightful Land he spreads
4.644: His orient Beams, on herb, tree, fruit, and flour,
4.645: Glistring with dew; fragrant the fertil earth
4.646: After soft showers; and sweet the coming on
4.647: Of grateful Eevning milde, then silent Night
4.648: With this her solemn Bird and this fair Moon,
4.649: And these the Gemms of Heav'n, her starrie train:
4.650: But neither breath of Morn when she ascends
4.651: With charm of earliest Birds, nor rising Sun
4.652: On this delightful land, nor herb, fruit, floure,
4.653: Glistring with dew, nor fragrance after showers,
4.654: Nor grateful Evening mild, nor silent Night
4.655: With this her solemn Bird, nor walk by Moon,
4.656: Or glittering Starr-light without thee is sweet.
4.657: But wherfore all night long shine these, for whom
4.658: This glorious sight, when sleep hath shut all eyes?
4.659: To whom our general Ancestor repli'd.
4.660: Daughter of God and Man, accomplisht Eve,
4.661: Those have thir course to finish, round the Earth,
4.662: By morrow Eevning, and from Land to Land
4.663: In order, though to Nations yet unborn,
4.664: Ministring light prepar'd, they set and rise;
4.665: Least total darkness should by Night regaine
4.666: Her old possession, and extinguish life
4.667: In Nature and all things, which these soft fires
4.668: Not only enlighten, but with kindly heate
4.669: Of various influence foment and warme,
4.670: Temper or nourish, or in part shed down
4.671: Thir stellar vertue on all kinds that grow
4.672: On Earth, made hereby apter to receive
4.673: Perfection from the Suns more potent Ray.
4.674: These then, though unbeheld in deep of night,
4.675: Shine not in vain, nor think, though men were none,
4.676: That heav'n would want spectators, God want praise;
4.677: Millions of spiritual Creatures walk the Earth
4.678: Unseen, both when we wake, and when we sleep:
4.679: All these with ceasless praise his works behold
4.680: Both day and night: how often from the steep
4.681: Of echoing Hill or Thicket have we heard
4.682: Celestial voices to the midnight air,
4.683: Sole, or responsive each to others note
4.684: Singing thir great Creator: oft in bands
4.685: While they keep watch, or nightly rounding walk
4.686: With Heav'nly touch of instrumental sounds
4.687: In full harmonic number joind, thir songs
4.688: Divide the night, and lift our thoughts to Heaven.
4.689: Thus talking hand in hand alone they pass'd
4.690: On to thir blissful Bower; it was a place
4.691: Chos'n by the sovran Planter, when he fram'd
4.692: All things to mans delightful use; the roofe
4.693: Of thickest covert was inwoven shade
4.694: Laurel and Mirtle, and what higher grew
4.695: Of firm and fragrant leaf; on either side
4.696: Acanthus, and each odorous bushie shrub
4.697: Fenc'd up the verdant wall; each beauteous flour,
4.698: Iris all hues, Roses, and Gessamin
4.699: Rear'd high thir flourisht heads between, and wrought
4.701: Crocus, and Hyacinth with rich inlay
4.702: Broiderd the ground, more colour'd then with stone
4.703: Of costliest Emblem: other Creature here
4.704: Beast, Bird, Insect, or Worm durst enter none;
4.705: Such was thir awe of man. In shadier Bower
4.706: More sacred and sequesterd, though but feignd,
4.707: Pan or Silvanus never slept, nor Nymph,
4.708: Nor Faunus haunted. Here in close recess
4.709: With Flowers, Garlands, and sweet-smelling Herbs
4.710: Espoused Eve deckt first her Nuptial Bed,
4.711: And heav'nly Quires the Hymenaean sung,
4.712: What day the genial Angel to our Sire
4.713: Brought her in naked beauty more adorn'd,
4.714: More lovely then Pandora, whom the Gods
4.715: Endowd with all thir gifts, and O too like
4.716: In sad event, when to the unwiser Son
4.717: Of Japhet brought by Hermes, she ensnar'd
4.718: Mankind with her faire looks, to be aveng'd
4.719: On him who had stole Joves authentic fire.
4.720: Thus at thir shadie Lodge arriv'd, both stood,
4.721: Both turnd, and under op'n Skie ador'd
4.722: The God that made both Skie, Air, Earth & Heav'n
4.723: Which they beheld, the Moons resplendent Globe
4.724: And starrie Pole: Thou also mad'st the Night,
4.725: Maker Omnipotent, and thou the Day,
4.726: Which we in our appointed work imployd
4.727: Have finisht happie in our mutual help
4.728: And mutual love, the Crown of all our bliss
4.729: Ordain'd by thee, and this delicious place
4.730: For us too large, where thy abundance wants
4.731: Partakers, and uncropt falls to the ground.
4.732: But thou hast promis'd from us two a Race
4.733: To fill the Earth, who shall with us extoll
4.734: Thy goodness infinite, both when we wake,
4.735: And when we seek, as now, thy gift of sleep.
4.736: This said unanimous, and other Rites
4.738: Which God likes best, into thir inmost bower
4.739: Handed they went; and eas'd the putting off
4.740: These troublesom disguises which wee wear,
4.741: Strait side by side were laid, nor turnd I weene
4.742: Adam from his fair Spouse, nor Eve the Rites
4.745: Of puritie and place and innocence,
4.746: Defaming as impure what God declares
4.747: Pure, and commands to som, leaves free to all.
4.748: Our Maker bids increase, who bids abstain
4.749: But our Destroyer, foe to God and Man?
4.750: Haile wedded Love, mysterious Law, true source
4.752: In Paradise of all things common else.
4.753: By thee adulterous lust was driv'n from men
4.754: Among the bestial herds to raunge, by thee
4.755: Founded in Reason, Loyal, Just, and Pure,
4.756: Relations dear, and all the Charities
4.757: Of Father, Son, and Brother first were known.
4.758: Farr be it, that I should write thee sin or blame,
4.759: Or think thee unbefitting holiest place,
4.761: Whose Bed is undefil'd and chast pronounc't,
4.762: Present, or past, as Saints and Patriarchs us'd.
4.763: Here Love his golden shafts imploies, here lights
4.764: His constant Lamp, and waves his purple wings,
4.765: Reigns here and revels; not in the bought smile
4.767: Casual fruition, nor in Court Amours
4.768: Mixt Dance, or wanton Mask, or Midnight Bal,
4.769: Or Serenate, which the starv'd Lover sings
4.770: To his proud fair, best quitted with disdain.
4.771: These lulld by Nightingales imbraceing slept,
4.772: And on thir naked limbs the flourie roof
4.773: Showrd Roses, which the Morn repair'd. Sleep on,
4.774: Blest pair; and O yet happiest if ye seek
4.775: No happier state, and know to know no more.
4.776: Now had night measur'd with her shaddowie Cone
4.777: Half way up Hill this vast Sublunar Vault,
4.778: And from thir Ivorie Port the Cherubim
4.779: Forth issuing at th' accustomd hour stood armd
4.780: To thir night watches in warlike Parade,
4.781: When Gabriel to his next in power thus spake.
4.782: Uzziel, half these draw off, and coast the South
4.783: With strictest watch; these other wheel the North,
4.784: Our circuit meets full West. As flame they part
4.785: Half wheeling to the Shield, half to the Spear.
4.786: From these, two strong and suttle Spirits he calld
4.787: That neer him stood, and gave them thus in charge.
4.788: Ithuriel and Zephon, with wingd speed
4.789: Search through this Garden, leav unsearcht no nook,
4.790: But chiefly where those two fair Creatures Lodge,
4.791: Now laid perhaps asleep secure of harme.
4.792: This Eevning from the Sun's decline arriv'd
4.793: Who tells of som infernal Spirit seen
4.794: Hitherward bent (who could have thought?) escap'd
4.795: The barrs of Hell, on errand bad no doubt:
4.796: Such where ye find, seise fast, and hither bring.
4.797: So saying, on he led his radiant Files,
4.798: Daz'ling the Moon; these to the Bower direct
4.799: In search of whom they sought: him there they found
4.800: Squat like a Toad, close at the eare of Eve;
4.801: Assaying by his Devilish art to reach
4.802: The Organs of her Fancie, and with them forge
4.803: Illusions as he list, Phantasms and Dreams,
4.804: Or if, inspiring venom, he might taint
4.805: Th' animal Spirits that from pure blood arise
4.806: Like gentle breaths from Rivers pure, thence raise
4.808: Vain hopes, vain aimes, inordinate desires
4.809: Blown up with high conceits ingendring pride.
4.810: Him thus intent Ithuriel with his Spear
4.811: Touch'd lightly; for no falshood can endure
4.812: Touch of Celestial temper, but returns
4.813: Of force to its own likeness: up he starts
4.814: Discoverd and surpriz'd. As when a spark
4.815: Lights on a heap of nitrous Powder, laid
4.816: Fit for the Tun som Magazin to store
4.817: Against a rumord Warr, the Smuttie graine
4.818: With sudden blaze diffus'd, inflames the Aire:
4.819: So started up in his own shape the Fiend.
4.820: Back stept those two fair Angels half amaz'd
4.821: So sudden to behold the grieslie King;
4.822: Yet thus, unmovd with fear, accost him soon.
4.823: Which of those rebell Spirits adjudg'd to Hell
4.824: Com'st thou, escap'd thy prison, and transform'd,
4.825: Why satst thou like an enemie in waite
4.826: Here watching at the head of these that sleep?
4.827: Know ye not then said Satan, filld with scorn,
4.828: Know ye not me? ye knew me once no mate
4.829: For you, there sitting where ye durst not soare;
4.830: Not to know mee argues your selves unknown,
4.831: The lowest of your throng; or if ye know,
4.832: Why ask ye, and superfluous begin
4.833: Your message, like to end as much in vain?
4.834: To whom thus Zephon, answering scorn with scorn.
4.835: Think not, revolted Spirit, thy shape the same,
4.836: Or undiminisht brightness, to be known
4.837: As when thou stoodst in Heav'n upright and pure;
4.838: That Glorie then, when thou no more wast good,
4.839: Departed from thee, and thou resembl'st now
4.840: Thy sin and place of doom obscure and foule.
4.841: But come, for thou, be sure, shalt give account
4.842: To him who sent us, whose charge is to keep
4.843: This place inviolable, and these from harm.
4.844: So spake the Cherube, and his grave rebuke
4.845: Severe in youthful beautie, added grace
4.847: And felt how awful goodness is, and saw
4.848: Vertue in her shape how lovly, saw, and pin'd
4.849: His loss; but chiefly to find here observd
4.850: His lustre visibly impar'd; yet seemd
4.851: Undaunted. If I must contend, said he,
4.852: Best with the best, the Sender not the sent,
4.853: Or all at once; more glorie will be wonn,
4.854: Or less be lost. Thy fear, said Zephon bold,
4.855: Will save us trial what the least can doe
4.856: Single against thee wicked, and thence weak.
4.857: The Fiend repli'd not, overcome with rage;
4.858: But like a proud Steed reind, went hautie on,
4.859: Chaumping his iron curb: to strive or flie
4.860: He held it vain; awe from above had quelld
4.861: His heart, not else dismai'd. Now drew they nigh
4.862: The western point, where those half-rounding guards
4.863: Just met, & closing stood in squadron joind
4.864: Awaiting next command. To whom thir Chief
4.865: Gabriel from the Front thus calld aloud.
4.866: O friends, I hear the tread of nimble feet
4.867: Hasting this way, and now by glimps discerne
4.868: Ithuriel and Zephon through the shade,
4.869: And with them comes a third of Regal port,
4.870: But faded splendor wan; who by his gate
4.871: And fierce demeanour seems the Prince of Hell,
4.872: Not likely to part hence without contest;
4.873: Stand firm, for in his look defiance lours.
4.874: He scarce had ended, when those two approachd
4.875: And brief related whom they brought, wher found,
4.876: How busied, in what form and posture coucht.
4.877: To whom with stern regard thus Gabriel spake.
4.878: Why hast thou, Satan, broke the bounds prescrib'd
4.879: To thy transgressions, and disturbd the charge
4.880: Of others, who approve not to transgress
4.881: By thy example, but have power and right
4.882: To question thy bold entrance on this place;
4.883: Imploi'd it seems to violate sleep, and those
4.884: Whose dwelling God hath planted here in bliss?
4.885: To whom thus Satan with contemptuous brow.
4.886: Gabriel, thou hadst in Heav'n th' esteem of wise,
4.887: And such I held thee; but this question askt
4.888: Puts me in doubt. Lives ther who loves his pain?
4.889: Who would not, finding way, break loose from Hell,
4.890: Though thither doomd? Thou wouldst thy self, no doubt,
4.891: And boldly venture to whatever place
4.892: Farthest from pain, where thou mightst hope to change
4.894: Dole with delight, which in this place I sought;
4.895: To thee no reason; who knowst only good,
4.896: But evil hast not tri'd: and wilt object
4.897: His will who bound us? let him surer barr
4.898: His Iron Gates, if he intends our stay
4.899: In that dark durance: thus much what was askt.
4.900: The rest is true, they found me where they say;
4.901: But that implies not violence or harme.
4.902: Thus hee in scorn. The warlike Angel mov'd,
4.904: O loss of one in Heav'n to judge of wise,
4.905: Since Satan fell, whom follie overthrew,
4.906: And now returns him from his prison scap't,
4.907: Gravely in doubt whether to hold them wise
4.908: Or not, who ask what boldness brought him hither
4.909: Unlicenc't from his bounds in Hell prescrib'd;
4.910: So wise he judges it to fly from pain
4.911: However, and to scape his punishment.
4.912: So judge thou still, presumptuous, till the wrauth,
4.913: Which thou incurr'st by flying, meet thy flight
4.914: Seavenfold, and scourge that wisdom back to Hell,
4.915: Which taught thee yet no better, that no pain
4.917: But wherefore thou alone? wherefore with thee
4.918: Came not all Hell broke loose? is pain to them
4.919: Less pain, less to be fled, or thou then they
4.920: Less hardie to endure? courageous Chief,
4.921: The first in flight from pain, had'st thou alleg'd
4.922: To thy deserted host this cause of flight,
4.923: Thou surely hadst not come sole fugitive.
4.924: To which the Fiend thus answerd frowning stern.
4.925: Not that I less endure, or shrink from pain,
4.926: Insulting Angel, well thou knowst I stood
4.927: Thy fiercest, when in Battel to thy aide
4.928: The blasting volied Thunder made all speed
4.929: And seconded thy else not dreaded Spear.
4.930: But still thy words at random, as before,
4.932: From hard assaies and ill successes past
4.933: A faithful Leader, not to hazard all
4.934: Through wayes of danger by himself untri'd.
4.935: I therefore, I alone first undertook
4.936: To wing the desolate Abyss, and spie
4.937: This new created World, whereof in Hell
4.938: Fame is not silent, here in hope to find
4.939: Better abode, and my afflicted Powers
4.940: To settle here on Earth, or in mid Aire;
4.941: Though for possession put to try once more
4.942: What thou and thy gay Legions dare against;
4.943: Whose easier business were to serve thir Lord
4.944: High up in Heav'n, with songs to hymne his Throne,
4.945: And practis'd distances to cringe, not fight.
4.946: To whom the warriour Angel soon repli'd.
4.947: To say and strait unsay, pretending first
4.948: Wise to flie pain, professing next the Spie,
4.949: Argues no Leader, but a lyar trac't,
4.950: Satan, and couldst thou faithful add? O name,
4.951: O sacred name of faithfulness profan'd!
4.952: Faithful to whom? to thy rebellious crew?
4.953: Armie of Fiends, fit body to fit head;
4.954: Was this your discipline and faith ingag'd,
4.956: Allegeance to th' acknowledg'd Power supream?
4.957: And thou sly hypocrite, who now wouldst seem
4.958: Patron of liberty, who more then thou
4.959: Once fawn'd, and cring'd, and servilly ador'd
4.960: Heav'ns awful Monarch? wherefore but in hope
4.961: To dispossess him, and thy self to reigne?
4.962: But mark what I arreede thee now, avant;
4.963: Flie thither whence thou fledst: if from this houre
4.964: Within these hallowd limits thou appeer,
4.965: Back to th' infernal pit I drag thee chaind,
4.966: And Seale thee so, as henceforth not to scorne
4.967: The facil gates of hell too slightly barrd.
4.968: So threatn'd hee, but Satan to no threats
4.969: Gave heed, but waxing more in rage repli'd.
4.970: Then when I am thy captive talk of chaines,
4.971: Proud limitarie Cherube, but ere then
4.972: Farr heavier load thy self expect to feel
4.973: From my prevailing arme, though Heavens King
4.974: Ride on thy wings, and thou with thy Compeers,
4.975: Us'd to the yoak, draw'st his triumphant wheels
4.976: In progress through the rode of Heav'n Star-pav'd.
4.977: While thus he spake, th' Angelic Squadron bright
4.978: Turnd fierie red, sharpning in mooned hornes
4.979: Thir Phalanx, and began to hemm him round
4.980: With ported Spears, as thick as when a field
4.981: Of Ceres ripe for harvest waving bends
4.982: Her bearded Grove of ears, which way the wind
4.983: Swayes them; the careful Plowman doubting stands
4.984: Least on the threshing floore his hopeful sheaves
4.985: Prove chaff. On th' other side Satan allarm'd
4.986: Collecting all his might dilated stood,
4.988: His stature reacht the Skie, and on his Crest
4.989: Sat horror Plum'd; nor wanted in his graspe
4.990: What seemd both Spear and Shield: now dreadful deeds
4.991: Might have ensu'd, nor onely Paradise
4.992: In this commotion, but the Starrie Cope
4.993: Of Heav'n perhaps, or all the Elements
4.994: At least had gon to rack, disturbd and torne
4.995: With violence of this conflict, had not soon
4.996: Th' Eternal to prevent such horrid fray
4.997: Hung forth in Heav'n his golden Scales, yet seen
4.998: Betwixt Astrea and the Scorpion signe,
4.999: Wherein all things created first he weighd,
4.1000: The pendulous round Earth with ballanc't Aire
4.1001: In counterpoise, now ponders all events,
4.1002: Battels and Realms: in these he put two weights
4.1003: The sequel each of parting and of fight;
4.1004: The latter quick up flew, and kickt the beam;
4.1005: Which Gabriel spying, thus bespake the Fiend.
4.1006: Satan, I know thy strength, and thou knowst mine,
4.1007: Neither our own but giv'n; what follie then
4.1008: To boast what Arms can doe, since thine no more
4.1009: Then Heav'n permits, nor mine, though doubld now
4.1010: To trample thee as mire: for proof look up,
4.1011: And read thy Lot in yon celestial Sign
4.1012: Where thou art weigh'd, & shown how light, how weak,
4.1013: If thou resist. The Fiend lookt up and knew
4.1014: His mounted scale aloft: nor more; but fled
4.1015: Murmuring, and with him fled the shades of night.

5.0:
*The Argument*
Morning approach't, Eve relates to Adam her troublesome dream: he likes it not, yet comforts her: They come forth to thir day labours: Their Morning Hymn  at the Door of their Bower. God to render Man inexcusable sends Raphael to admonish him of his obedience, of his free estate, of his enemy near at hand; who he is, and why his enemy, and whatever else may avail Adam to know. Raphael comes down to Paradise; his appearance describ'd, his coming discern'd by Adam afar off sitting at the door of his Bower; he goes out to meet him, brings him to his lodge, entertains him with the choycest fruits of Paradise got together by Eve;  their discourse at Table: Raphael performs his message, minds Adam of his state and of his enemy; relates at Adams request who that enemy is, and how he came to be so, beginning with his first revolt in Heaven and the occasion thereof; how he drew his Legions after him to the parts of the North, and there incited them to rebel with him, perswading all but only Abdiel a Seraph, who in Argument diswades and opposes him, then forsakes him.
5.1: Now Morn her rosie steps in th' Eastern Clime
5.2: Advancing, sow'd the Earth with Orient Pearle,
5.3: When Adam wak't, so customd, for his sleep
5.4: Was Aerie light, from pure digestion bred,
5.5: And temperat vapors bland, which th' only sound
5.6: Of leaves and fuming rills, Aurora's fan,
5.7: Lightly dispers'd, and the shrill Matin Song
5.8: Of Birds on every bough; so much the more
5.9: His wonder was to find unwak'nd Eve
5.10: With Tresses discompos'd, and glowing Cheek,
5.11: As through unquiet rest: he on his side
5.12: Leaning half-rais'd, with looks of cordial Love
5.13: Hung over her enamour'd, and beheld
5.14: Beautie, which whether waking or asleep,
5.15: Shot forth peculiar Graces; then with voice
5.16: Milde, as when Zephyrus on Flora breathes,
5.17: Her hand soft touching, whisperd thus. Awake
5.18: My fairest, my espous'd, my latest found,
5.19: Heav'ns last best gift, my ever new delight,
5.20: Awake, the morning shines, and the fresh field
5.21: Calls us, we lose the prime, to mark how spring
5.22: Our tended Plants, how blows the Citron Grove,
5.23: What drops the Myrrhe, & what the balmie Reed,
5.24: How Nature paints her colours, how the Bee
5.25: Sits on the Bloom extracting liquid sweet.
5.26: Such whispering wak'd her, but with startl'd eye
5.27: On Adam, whom imbracing, thus she spake.
5.28: O Sole in whom my thoughts find all repose,
5.29: My Glorie, my Perfection, glad I see
5.30: Thy face, and Morn return'd, for I this Night,
5.31: Such night till this I never pass'd, have dream'd,
5.32: If dream'd, not as I oft am wont, of thee,
5.33: Works of day pass't, or morrows next designe,
5.34: But of offence and trouble, which my mind
5.35: Knew never till this irksom night; methought
5.36: Close at mine ear one call'd me forth to walk
5.37: With gentle voice, I thought it thine; it said,
5.38: Why sleepst thou Eve? now is the pleasant time,
5.39: The cool, the silent, save where silence yields
5.40: To the night-warbling Bird, that now awake
5.41: Tunes sweetest his love-labor'd song; now reignes
5.42: Full Orb'd the Moon, and with more pleasing light
5.43: Shadowie sets off the face of things; in vain,
5.44: If none regard; Heav'n wakes with all his eyes,
5.45: Whom to behold but thee, Natures desire,
5.46: In whose sight all things joy, with ravishment
5.47: Attracted by thy beauty still to gaze.
5.48: I rose as at thy call, but found thee not;
5.49: To find thee I directed then my walk;
5.50: And on, methought, alone I pass'd through ways
5.51: That brought me on a sudden to the Tree
5.52: Of interdicted Knowledge: fair it seem'd,
5.53: Much fairer to my Fancie then by day:
5.54: And as I wondring lookt, beside it stood
5.55: One shap'd and wing'd like one of those from Heav'n
5.56: By us oft seen; his dewie locks distill'd
5.57: Ambrosia; on that Tree he also gaz'd;
5.58: And O fair Plant, said he, with fruit surcharg'd,
5.59: Deigns none to ease thy load and taste thy sweet,
5.60: Nor God, nor Man; is Knowledge so despis'd?
5.61: Or envie, or what reserve forbids to taste?
5.62: Forbid who will, none shall from me withhold
5.63: Longer thy offerd good, why else set here?
5.64: This said he paus'd not, but with ventrous Arme
5.65: He pluckt, he tasted; mee damp horror chil'd
5.66: At such bold words voucht with a deed so bold:
5.67: But he thus overjoy'd, O Fruit Divine,
5.68: Sweet of thy self, but much more sweet thus cropt,
5.69: Forbidd'n here, it seems, as onely fit
5.70: For Gods, yet able to make Gods of Men:
5.71: And why not Gods of Men, since good, the more
5.73: The Author not impair'd, but honourd more?
5.74: Here, happie Creature, fair Angelic Eve,
5.75: Partake thou also; happie though thou art,
5.76: Happier thou mayst be, worthier canst not be:
5.77: Taste this, and be henceforth among the Gods
5.78: Thy self a Goddess, not to Earth confind,
5.79: But somtimes in the Air, as wee, somtimes
5.80: Ascend to Heav'n, by merit thine, and see
5.81: What life the Gods live there, and such live thou.
5.82: So saying, he drew nigh, and to me held,
5.83: Even to my mouth of that same fruit held part
5.84: Which he had pluckt; the pleasant savourie smell
5.85: So quick'nd appetite, that I, methought,
5.86: Could not but taste. Forthwith up to the Clouds
5.87: With him I flew, and underneath beheld
5.88: The Earth outstretcht immense, a prospect wide
5.89: And various: wondring at my flight and change
5.91: My Guide was gon, and I, me thought, sunk down,
5.92: And fell asleep; but O how glad I wak'd
5.93: To find this but a dream! Thus Eve her Night
5.94: Related, and thus Adam answerd sad.
5.95: Best Image of my self and dearer half,
5.96: The trouble of thy thoughts this night in sleep
5.97: Affects me equally; nor can I like
5.98: This uncouth dream, of evil sprung I fear;
5.99: Yet evil whence? in thee can harbour none,
5.100: Created pure. But know that in the Soule
5.101: Are many lesser Faculties that serve
5.102: Reason as chief; among these Fansie next
5.103: Her office holds; of all external things,
5.104: Which the five watchful Senses represent,
5.106: Which Reason joyning or disjoyning, frames
5.107: All what we affirm or what deny, and call
5.108: Our knowledge or opinion; then retires
5.109: Into her private Cell when Nature rests.
5.110: Oft in her absence mimic Fansie wakes
5.111: To imitate her; but misjoyning shapes,
5.112: Wilde work produces oft, and most in dreams,
5.113: Ill matching words and deeds long past or late.
5.114: Som such resemblances methinks I find
5.115: Of our last Eevnings talk, in this thy dream,
5.116: But with addition strange; yet be not sad.
5.117: Evil into the mind of God or Man
5.118: May come and go, so unapprov'd, and leave
5.119: No spot or blame behind: Which gives me hope
5.120: That what in sleep thou didst abhorr to dream,
5.121: Waking thou never wilt consent to do.
5.122: Be not disheart'nd then, nor cloud those looks
5.123: That wont to be more chearful and serene
5.124: Then when fair Morning first smiles on the World,
5.125: And let us to our fresh imployments rise
5.126: Among the Groves, the Fountains, and the Flours
5.127: That open now thir choicest bosom'd smells
5.128: Reservd from night, and kept for thee in store.
5.129: So cheard he his fair Spouse, and she was cheard,
5.130: But silently a gentle tear let fall
5.131: From either eye, and wip'd them with her haire;
5.132: Two other precious drops that ready stood,
5.133: Each in thir chrystal sluce, hee ere they fell
5.134: Kiss'd as the gracious signs of sweet remorse
5.135: And pious awe, that feard to have offended.
5.136: So all was cleard, and to the Field they haste.
5.137: But first from under shadie arborous roof,
5.138: Soon as they forth were come to open sight
5.139: Of day-spring, and the Sun, who scarce up risen
5.140: With wheels yet hov'ring o're the Ocean brim,
5.141: Shot paralel to the earth his dewie ray,
5.142: Discovering in wide Lantskip all the East
5.143: Of Paradise and Edens happie Plains,
5.144: Lowly they bow'd adoring, and began
5.145: Thir Orisons, each Morning duly paid
5.146: In various style, for neither various style
5.147: Nor holy rapture wanted they to praise
5.148: Thir Maker, in fit strains pronounc't or sung
5.150: Flowd from thir lips, in Prose or numerous Verse,
5.151: More tuneable then needed Lute or Harp
5.152: To add more sweetness, and they thus began.
5.153: These are thy glorious works, Parent of good,
5.155: Thus wondrous fair; thy self how wondrous then!
5.156: Unspeakable, who sitst above these Heavens
5.157: To us invisible or dimly seen
5.158: In these thy lowest works, yet these declare
5.159: Thy goodness beyond thought, and Power Divine:
5.160: Speak yee who best can tell, ye Sons of light,
5.161: Angels, for yee behold him, and with songs
5.162: And choral symphonies, Day without Night,
5.163: Circle his Throne rejoycing, yee in Heav'n,
5.164: On Earth joyn all yee Creatures to extoll
5.165: Him first, him last, him midst, and without end.
5.166: Fairest of Starrs, last in the train of Night,
5.167: If better thou belong not to the dawn,
5.168: Sure pledge of day, that crownst the smiling Morn
5.169: With thy bright Circlet, praise him in thy Spheare
5.170: While day arises, that sweet hour of Prime.
5.171: Thou Sun, of this great World both Eye and Soule,
5.172: Acknowledge him thy Greater, sound his praise
5.173: In thy eternal course, both when thou climb'st,
5.174: And when high Noon hast gaind, & when thou fallst.
5.175: Moon, that now meetst the orient Sun, now fli'st
5.176: With the fixt Starrs, fixt in thir Orb that flies,
5.177: And yee five other wandring Fires that move
5.178: In mystic Dance not without Song, resound
5.179: His praise, who out of Darkness call'd up Light.
5.180: Aire, and ye Elements the eldest birth
5.181: Of Natures Womb, that in quaternion run
5.183: And nourish all things, let your ceasless change
5.184: Varie to our great Maker still new praise.
5.185: Ye Mists and Exhalations that now rise
5.186: From Hill or steaming Lake, duskie or grey,
5.187: Till the Sun paint your fleecie skirts with Gold,
5.188: In honour to the Worlds great Author rise,
5.189: Whether to deck with Clouds the uncolourd skie,
5.190: Or wet the thirstie Earth with falling showers,
5.191: Rising or falling still advance his praise.
5.192: His praise ye Winds, that from four Quarters blow,
5.193: Breath soft or loud; and wave your tops, ye Pines,
5.194: With every Plant, in sign of Worship wave.
5.195: Fountains and yee, that warble, as ye flow,
5.196: Melodious murmurs, warbling tune his praise.
5.197: Joyn voices all ye living Souls, ye Birds,
5.198: That singing up to Heaven Gate ascend,
5.199: Bear on your wings and in your notes his praise;
5.200: Yee that in Waters glide, and yee that walk
5.201: The Earth, and stately tread, or lowly creep;
5.202: Witness if I be silent, Morn or Eeven,
5.203: To Hill, or Valley, Fountain, or fresh shade
5.204: Made vocal by my Song, and taught his praise.
5.205: Hail universal Lord, be bounteous still
5.206: To give us onely good; and if the night
5.207: Have gathered aught of evil or conceald,
5.208: Disperse it, as now light dispels the dark.
5.209: So pray'd they innocent, and to thir thoughts
5.210: Firm peace recoverd soon and wonted calm.
5.211: On to thir mornings rural work they haste
5.212: Among sweet dewes and flours; where any row
5.213: Of Fruit-trees overwoodie reachd too farr
5.214: Thir pamperd boughes, and needed hands to check
5.215: Fruitless imbraces: or they led the Vine
5.216: To wed her Elm; she spous'd about him twines
5.217: Her mariageable arms, and with her brings
5.218: Her dowr th' adopted Clusters, to adorn
5.219: His barren leaves. Them thus imploid beheld
5.220: With pittie Heav'ns high King, and to him call'd
5.221: Raphael, the sociable Spirit, that deign'd
5.222: To travel with Tobias, and secur'd
5.223: His marriage with the seaventimes-wedded Maid.
5.224: Raphael, said hee, thou hear'st what stir on Earth
5.225: Satan from Hell scap't through the darksom Gulf
5.226: Hath raisd in Paradise, and how disturbd
5.227: This night the human pair, how he designes
5.228: In them at once to ruin all mankind.
5.229: Go therefore, half this day as friend with friend
5.230: Converse with Adam, in what Bowre or shade
5.231: Thou find'st him from the heat of Noon retir'd,
5.232: To respit his day-labour with repast,
5.233: Or with repose; and such discourse bring on,
5.234: As may advise him of his happie state,
5.235: Happiness in his power left free to will,
5.236: Left to his own free Will, his Will though free,
5.237: Yet mutable; whence warne him to beware
5.238: He swerve not too secure: tell him withall
5.239: His danger, and from whom, what enemie
5.240: Late falln himself from Heav'n, is plotting now
5.241: The fall of others from like state of bliss;
5.242: By violence, no, for that shall be withstood,
5.243: But by deceit and lies; this let him know,
5.246: So spake th' Eternal Father, and fulfilld
5.247: All Justice: nor delaid the winged Saint
5.248: After his charge receivd, but from among
5.249: Thousand Celestial Ardors, where he stood
5.250: Vaild with his gorgeous wings, up springing light
5.251: Flew through the midst of Heav'n; th' angelic Quires
5.252: On each hand parting, to his speed gave way
5.253: Through all th' Empyreal road; till at the Gate
5.254: Of Heav'n arriv'd, the gate self-opend wide
5.255: On golden Hinges turning, as by work
5.256: Divine the sov'ran Architect had fram'd.
5.257: From hence, no cloud, or, to obstruct his sight,
5.258: Starr interpos'd, however small he sees,
5.259: Not unconform to other shining Globes,
5.260: Earth and the Gard'n of God, with Cedars crownd
5.261: Above all Hills. As when by night the Glass
5.263: Imagind Lands and Regions in the Moon:
5.264: Or Pilot from amidst the Cyclades
5.265: Delos or Samos first appeering kenns
5.266: A cloudy spot. Down thither prone in flight
5.267: He speeds, and through the vast Ethereal Skie
5.268: Sailes between worlds & worlds, with steddie wing
5.269: Now on the polar windes, then with quick Fann
5.270: Winnows the buxom Air; till within soare
5.271: Of Towring Eagles, to all the Fowles he seems
5.272: A Phoenix, gaz'd by all, as that sole Bird
5.273: When to enshrine his reliques in the Sun's
5.274: Bright Temple, to Aegyptian Theb's he flies.
5.275: At once on th' Eastern cliff of Paradise
5.276: He lights, and to his proper shape returns
5.277: A Seraph wingd; six wings he wore, to shade
5.278: His lineaments Divine; the pair that clad
5.279: Each shoulder broad, came mantling o're his brest
5.280: With regal Ornament; the middle pair
5.281: Girt like a Starrie Zone his waste, and round
5.282: Skirted his loines and thighes with downie Gold
5.283: And colours dipt in Heav'n; the third his feet
5.284: Shaddowd from either heele with featherd maile
5.285: Skie-tinctur'd grain. Like Maia's son he stood,
5.286: And shook his Plumes, that Heav'nly fragrance filld
5.287: The circuit wide. Strait knew him all the bands
5.288: Of Angels under watch; and to his state,
5.289: And to his message high in honour rise;
5.290: For on som message high they guessd him bound.
5.291: Thir glittering Tents he passd, and now is come
5.292: Into the blissful field, through Groves of Myrrhe,
5.293: And flouring Odours, Cassia, Nard, and Balme;
5.294: A Wilderness of sweets; for Nature here
5.295: Wantond as in her prime, and plaid at will
5.296: Her Virgin Fancies, pouring forth more sweet,
5.297: Wilde above rule or art; enormous bliss.
5.298: Him through the spicie Forrest onward com
5.299: Adam discernd, as in the dore he sat
5.300: Of his coole Bowre, while now the mounted Sun
5.301: Shot down direct his fervid Raies, to warme
5.302: Earths inmost womb, more warmth then Adam needs;
5.303: And Eve within, due at her hour prepar'd
5.304: For dinner savourie fruits, of taste to please
5.305: True appetite, and not disrelish thirst
5.306: Of nectarous draughts between, from milkie stream,
5.307: Berrie or Grape: to whom thus Adam call'd.
5.308: Haste hither Eve, and worth thy sight behold
5.309: Eastward among those Trees, what glorious shape
5.310: Comes this way moving; seems another Morn
5.311: Ris'n on mid-noon; som great behest from Heav'n
5.312: To us perhaps he brings, and will voutsafe
5.313: This day to be our Guest. But goe with speed,
5.314: And what thy stores contain, bring forth and poure
5.315: Abundance, fit to honour and receive
5.316: Our Heav'nly stranger; well we may afford
5.317: Our givers thir own gifts, and large bestow
5.318: From large bestowd, where Nature multiplies
5.319: Her fertil growth, and by disburd'ning grows
5.320: More fruitful, which instructs us not to spare.
5.321: To whom thus Eve. Adam, earths hallowd mould,
5.322: Of God inspir'd, small store will serve, where store,
5.323: All seasons, ripe for use hangs on the stalk;
5.324: Save what by frugal storing firmness gains
5.325: To nourish, and superfluous moist consumes:
5.326: But I will haste and from each bough and break,
5.327: Each Plant & juciest Gourd will pluck such choice
5.328: To entertain our Angel guest, as hee
5.329: Beholding shall confess that here on Earth
5.330: God hath dispenst his bounties as in Heav'n.
5.331: So saying, with dispatchful looks in haste
5.332: She turns, on hospitable thoughts intent
5.333: What choice to chuse for delicacie best,
5.334: What order, so contriv'd as not to mix
5.335: Tastes, not well joynd, inelegant, but bring
5.336: Taste after taste upheld with kindliest change,
5.337: Bestirs her then, and from each tender stalk
5.339: In India East or West, or middle shoare
5.340: In Pontus or the Punic Coast, or where
5.341: Alcinous reign'd, fruit of all kindes, in coate,
5.342: Rough, or smooth rin'd, or bearded husk, or shell
5.343: She gathers, Tribute large, and on the board
5.344: Heaps with unsparing hand; for drink the Grape
5.345: She crushes, inoffensive moust, and meathes
5.346: From many a berrie, and from sweet kernels prest
5.347: She tempers dulcet creams, nor these to hold
5.348: Wants her fit vessels pure, then strews the ground
5.349: With Rose and Odours from the shrub unfum'd.
5.350: Mean while our Primitive great Sire, to meet
5.351: His god-like Guest, walks forth, without more train
5.352: Accompani'd then with his own compleat
5.353: Perfections, in himself was all his state,
5.354: More solemn then the tedious pomp that waits
5.355: On Princes, when thir rich Retinue long
5.356: Of Horses led, and Grooms besmeard with Gold
5.357: Dazles the croud, and sets them all agape.
5.358: Neerer his presence Adam though not awd,
5.359: Yet with submiss approach and reverence meek,
5.360: As to a superior Nature, bowing low,
5.361: Thus said. Native of Heav'n, for other place
5.362: None can then Heav'n such glorious shape contain;
5.363: Since by descending from the Thrones above,
5.364: Those happie places thou hast deignd a while
5.365: To want, and honour these, voutsafe with us
5.366: Two onely, who yet by sov'ran gift possess
5.367: This spacious ground, in yonder shadie Bowre
5.368: To rest, and what the Garden choicest bears
5.369: To sit and taste, till this meridian heat
5.370: Be over, and the Sun more coole decline.
5.371: Whom thus the Angelic Vertue answerd milde.
5.372: Adam, I therefore came, nor art thou such
5.373: Created, or such place hast here to dwell,
5.374: As may not oft invite, though Spirits of Heav'n
5.375: To visit thee; lead on then where thy Bowre
5.376: Oreshades; for these mid-hours, till Eevning rise
5.377: I have at will. So to the Silvan Lodge
5.378: They came, that like Pomona's Arbour smil'd
5.379: With flourets deck't and fragrant smells; but Eve
5.380: Undeckt, save with her self more lovely fair
5.381: Then Wood-Nymph, or the fairest Goddess feign'd
5.382: Of three that in Mount Ida naked strove,
5.383: Stood to entertain her guest from Heav'n; no vaile
5.384: Shee needed, Vertue-proof, no thought infirme
5.385: Alterd her cheek. On whom the Angel Haile
5.387: Long after to blest Marie, second Eve.
5.388: Haile Mother of Mankind, whose fruitful Womb
5.389: Shall fill the World more numerous with thy Sons
5.390: Then with these various fruits the Trees of God
5.391: Have heap'd this Table. Rais'd of grassie terf
5.392: Thir Table was, and mossie seats had round,
5.393: And on her ample Square from side to side
5.394: All Autumn pil'd, though Spring and Autumn here
5.395: Danc'd hand in hand. A while discourse they hold;
5.396: No fear lest Dinner coole; when thus began
5.397: Our Authour. Heav'nly stranger, please to taste
5.398: These bounties which our Nourisher, from whom
5.399: All perfet good unmeasur'd out, descends,
5.400: To us for food and for delight hath caus'd
5.401: The Earth to yeild; unsavourie food perhaps
5.402: To spiritual Natures; only this I know,
5.403: That one Celestial Father gives to all.
5.404: To whom the Angel. Therefore what he gives
5.405: (Whose praise be ever sung) to man in part
5.406: Spiritual, may of purest Spirits be found
5.407: No ingrateful food: and food alike those pure
5.409: As doth your Rational; and both contain
5.411: Of sense, whereby they hear, see, smell, touch, taste,
5.414: For know, whatever was created, needs
5.415: To be sustaind and fed; of Elements
5.416: The grosser feeds the purer, earth the sea,
5.417: Earth and the Sea feed Air, the Air those Fires
5.418: Ethereal, and as lowest first the Moon;
5.419: Whence in her visage round those spots, unpurg'd
5.420: Vapours not yet into her substance turnd.
5.421: Nor doth the Moon no nourishment exhale
5.422: From her moist Continent to higher Orbes.
5.423: The Sun that light imparts to all, receives
5.425: In humid exhalations, and at Even
5.426: Sups with the Ocean: though in Heav'n the Trees
5.427: Of life ambrosial frutage bear, and vines
5.428: Yeild Nectar, though from off the boughs each Morn
5.429: We brush mellifluous Dewes, and find the ground
5.430: Cover'd with pearly grain: yet God hath here
5.431: Varied his bounty so with new delights,
5.432: As may compare with Heaven; and to taste
5.433: Think not I shall be nice. So down they sat,
5.434: And to thir viands fell, nor seemingly
5.435: The Angel, nor in mist, the common gloss
5.436: Of Theologians, but with keen dispatch
5.437: Of real hunger, and concoctive heate
5.439: Through Spirits with ease; nor wonder; if by fire
5.440: Of sooty coal the Empiric Alchimist
5.441: Can turn, or holds it possible to turn
5.442: Metals of drossiest Ore to perfet Gold
5.443: As from the Mine. Mean while at Table Eve
5.444: Ministerd naked, and thir flowing cups
5.445: With pleasant liquors crown'd: O innocence
5.447: Then had the Sons of God excuse to have bin
5.448: Enamour'd at that sight; but in those hearts
5.450: Was understood, the injur'd Lovers Hell.
5.451: Thus when with meats & drinks they had suffic'd,
5.452: Not burd'nd Nature, sudden mind arose
5.453: In Adam, not to let th' occasion pass
5.454: Given him by this great Conference to know
5.455: Of things above his World, and of thir being
5.456: Who dwell in Heav'n, whose excellence he saw
5.457: Transcend his own so farr, whose radiant forms
5.458: Divine effulgence, whose high Power so far
5.459: Exceeded human, and his wary speech
5.460: Thus to th' Empyreal Minister he fram'd.
5.461: Inhabitant with God, now know I well
5.462: Thy favour, in this honour done to man,
5.463: Under whose lowly roof thou hast voutsaf't
5.464: To enter, and these earthly fruits to taste,
5.465: Food not of Angels, yet accepted so,
5.466: As that more willingly thou couldst not seem
5.467: At Heav'ns high feasts to have fed: yet what compare?
5.468: To whom the winged Hierarch repli'd.
5.469: O Adam, one Almightie is, from whom
5.470: All things proceed, and up to him return,
5.471: If not deprav'd from good, created all
5.472: Such to perfection, one first matter all,
5.473: Indu'd with various forms, various degrees
5.474: Of substance, and in things that live, of life;
5.475: But more refin'd, more spiritous, and pure,
5.476: As neerer to him plac't or neerer tending
5.477: Each in thir several active Sphears assignd,
5.478: Till body up to spirit work, in bounds
5.479: Proportiond to each kind. So from the root
5.480: Springs lighter the green stalk, from thence the leaves
5.481: More aerie, last the bright consummate floure
5.482: Spirits odorous breathes: flours and thir fruit
5.483: Mans nourishment, by gradual scale sublim'd
5.484: To vital Spirits aspire, to animal,
5.485: To intellectual, give both life and sense,
5.486: Fansie and understanding, whence the soule
5.487: Reason receives, and reason is her being,
5.489: Is oftest yours, the latter most is ours,
5.490: Differing but in degree, of kind the same.
5.491: Wonder not then, what God for you saw good
5.492: If I refuse not, but convert, as you,
5.493: To proper substance; time may come when men
5.494: With Angels may participate, and find
5.495: No inconvenient Diet, nor too light Fare:
5.496: And from these corporal nutriments perhaps
5.497: Your bodies may at last turn all to Spirit
5.498: Improv'd by tract of time, and wingd ascend
5.499: Ethereal, as wee, or may at choice
5.500: Here or in Heav'nly Paradises dwell;
5.501: If ye be found obedient, and retain
5.503: Whose progenie you are. Mean while enjoy
5.504: Your fill what happiness this happie state
5.506: To whom the Patriarch of mankind repli'd.
5.508: Well hast thou taught the way that might direct
5.509: Our knowledge, and the scale of Nature set
5.512: By steps we may ascend to God. But say,
5.513: What meant that caution joind, If Ye Be Found
5.514: Obedient? can wee want obedience then
5.515: To him, or possibly his love desert
5.516: Who formd us from the dust, and plac'd us here
5.517: Full to the utmost measure of what bliss
5.518: Human desires can seek or apprehend?
5.519: To whom the Angel. Son of Heav'n and Earth,
5.520: Attend: That thou art happie, owe to God;
5.521: That thou continu'st such, owe to thy self,
5.522: That is, to thy obedience; therein stand.
5.523: This was that caution giv'n thee; be advis'd.
5.524: God made thee perfet, not immutable;
5.525: And good he made thee, but to persevere
5.526: He left it in thy power, ordaind thy will
5.527: By nature free, not over-rul'd by Fate
5.530: Not our necessitated, such with him
5.531: Findes no acceptance, nor can find, for how
5.532: Can hearts, not free, be tri'd whether they serve
5.533: Willing or no, who will but what they must
5.534: By Destinie, and can no other choose?
5.535: My self and all th' Angelic Host that stand
5.536: In sight of God enthron'd, our happie state
5.537: Hold, as you yours, while our obedience holds;
5.538: On other surety none; freely we serve.
5.539: Because wee freely love, as in our will
5.540: To love or not; in this we stand or fall:
5.541: And som are fall'n, to disobedience fall'n,
5.542: And so from Heav'n to deepest Hell; O fall
5.543: From what high state of bliss into what woe!
5.544: To whom our great Progenitor. Thy words
5.545: Attentive, and with more delighted eare
5.546: Divine instructer, I have heard, then when
5.547: Cherubic Songs by night from neighbouring Hills
5.548: Aereal Music send: nor knew I not
5.549: To be both will and deed created free;
5.550: Yet that we never shall forget to love
5.551: Our maker, and obey him whose command
5.552: Single, is yet so just, my constant thoughts
5.553: Assur'd me and still assure: though what thou tellst
5.554: Hath past in Heav'n, som doubt within me move,
5.555: But more desire to hear, if thou consent,
5.556: The full relation, which must needs be strange,
5.557: Worthy of Sacred silence to be heard;
5.558: And we have yet large day, for scarce the Sun
5.559: Hath finisht half his journey, and scarce begins
5.560: His other half in the great Zone of Heav'n.
5.561: Thus Adam made request, and Raphael
5.562: After short pause assenting, thus began.
5.563: High matter thou injoinst me, O prime of men,
5.564: Sad task and hard, for how shall I relate
5.565: To human sense th' invisible exploits
5.566: Of warring Spirits; how without remorse
5.567: The ruin of so many glorious once
5.568: And perfet while they stood; how last unfould
5.569: The secrets of another world, perhaps
5.570: Not lawful to reveal? yet for thy good
5.571: This is dispenc't, and what surmounts the reach
5.572: Of human sense, I shall delineate so,
5.573: By lik'ning spiritual to corporal forms,
5.574: As may express them best, though what if Earth
5.575: Be but the shaddow of Heav'n, and things therein
5.576: Each to other like, more then on earth is thought?
5.577: As yet this world was not, and Chaos wilde
5.578: Reignd where these Heav'ns now rowl, where Earth now rests
5.579: Upon her Center pois'd, when on a day
5.581: To motion, measures all things durable
5.582: By present, past, and future) on such day
5.583: As Heav'ns great Year brings forth, th' Empyreal Host
5.584: Of Angels by Imperial summons call'd,
5.586: Forthwith from all the ends of Heav'n appeerd
5.587: Under thir Hierarchs in orders bright
5.588: Ten thousand thousand Ensignes high advanc'd,
5.589: Standards, and Gonfalons twixt Van and Reare
5.590: Streame in the Aire, and for distinction serve
5.591: Of Hierarchies, of Orders, and Degrees;
5.592: Or in thir glittering Tissues bear imblaz'd
5.593: Holy Memorials, acts of Zeale and Love
5.594: Recorded eminent. Thus when in Orbes
5.596: Orb within Orb, the Father infinite,
5.597: By whom in bliss imbosom'd sat the Son,
5.598: Amidst as from a flaming Mount, whose top
5.599: Brightness had made invisible, thus spake.
5.600: Hear all ye Angels, Progenie of Light,
5.602: Hear my Decree, which unrevok't shall stand.
5.603: This day I have begot whom I declare
5.604: My onely Son, and on this holy Hill
5.605: Him have anointed, whom ye now behold
5.606: At my right hand; your Head I him appoint;
5.607: And by my Self have sworn to him shall bow
5.608: All knees in Heav'n, and shall confess him Lord:
5.609: Under his great Vice-gerent Reign abide
5.611: For ever happie: him who disobeyes
5.612: Mee disobeyes, breaks union, and that day
5.613: Cast out from God and blessed vision, falls
5.614: Into utter darkness, deep ingulft, his place
5.616: So spake th' Omnipotent, and with his words
5.617: All seemd well pleas'd, all seem'd, but were not all.
5.618: That day, as other solem dayes, they spent
5.619: In song and dance about the sacred Hill,
5.620: Mystical dance, which yonder starrie Spheare
5.621: Of Planets and of fixt in all her Wheeles
5.624: Then most, when most irregular they seem:
5.625: And in thir motions harmonie Divine
5.626: So smooths her charming tones, that Gods own ear
5.628: (For we have also our Eevning and our Morn,
5.629: We ours for change delectable, not need)
5.630: Forthwith from dance to sweet repast they turn
5.631: Desirous, all in Circles as they stood,
5.632: Tables are set, and on a sudden pil'd
5.633: With Angels Food, and rubied Nectar flows:
5.634: In Pearl, in Diamond, and massie Gold,
5.635: Fruit of delicious Vines, the growth of Heav'n.
5.636: They eat, they drink, and with refection sweet
5.637: Are fill'd, before th' all bounteous King, who showrd
5.638: With copious hand, rejoycing in thir joy.
5.639: Now when ambrosial Night with Clouds exhal'd
5.640: From that high mount of God, whence light & shade
5.641: Spring both, the face of brightest Heav'n had changd
5.642: To grateful Twilight (for Night comes not there
5.643: In darker veile) and roseat Dews dispos'd
5.644: All but the unsleeping eyes of God to rest,
5.645: Wide over all the Plain, and wider farr
5.646: Then all this globous Earth in Plain outspred,
5.647: (Such are the Courts of God) Th' Angelic throng
5.648: Disperst in Bands and Files thir Camp extend
5.649: By living Streams among the Trees of Life,
5.652: Fannd with coole Winds, save those who in thir course
5.653: Melodious Hymns about the sovran Throne
5.654: Alternate all night long: but not so wak'd
5.655: Satan, so call him now, his former name
5.656: Is heard no more in Heav'n; he of the first,
5.657: If not the first Arch-Angel, great in Power,
5.658: In favour and praeeminence, yet fraught
5.659: With envie against the Son of God, that day
5.660: Honourd by his great Father, and proclaimd
5.661: Messiah King anointed, could not beare
5.662: Through pride that sight, and thought himself impaird.
5.664: Soon as midnight brought on the duskie houre
5.665: Friendliest to sleep and silence, he resolv'd
5.666: With all his Legions to dislodge, and leave
5.669: Awak'ning, thus to him in secret spake.
5.670: Sleepst thou Companion dear, what sleep can close
5.671: Thy eye-lids? and remembrest what Decree
5.672: Of yesterday, so late hath past the lips
5.673: Of Heav'ns Almightie. Thou to me thy thoughts
5.674: Wast wont, I mine to thee was wont to impart;
5.675: Both waking we were one; how then can now
5.676: Thy sleep dissent? new Laws thou seest impos'd;
5.677: New Laws from him who reigns, new minds may raise
5.678: In us who serve, new Counsels, to debate
5.679: What doubtful may ensue, more in this place
5.680: To utter is not safe. Assemble thou
5.681: Of all those Myriads which we lead the chief;
5.682: Tell them that by command, ere yet dim Night
5.683: Her shadowie Cloud withdraws, I am to haste,
5.684: And all who under me thir Banners wave,
5.685: Homeward with flying march where we possess
5.686: The Quarters of the North, there to prepare
5.687: Fit entertainment to receive our King
5.688: The great Messiah, and his new commands,
5.689: Who speedily through all the Hierarchies
5.690: Intends to pass triumphant, and give Laws.
5.691: So spake the false Arch-Angel, and infus'd
5.692: Bad influence into th' unwarie brest
5.693: Of his Associate; hee together calls,
5.694: Or several one by one, the Regent Powers,
5.695: Under him Regent, tells, as he was taught,
5.696: That the most High commanding, now ere Night,
5.697: Now ere dim Night had disincumberd Heav'n,
5.698: The great Hierarchal Standard was to move;
5.699: Tells the suggested cause, and casts between
5.700: Ambiguous words and jealousies, to sound
5.701: Or taint integritie; but all obey'd
5.702: The wonted signal, and superior voice
5.703: Of thir great Potentate; for great indeed
5.704: His name, and high was his degree in Heav'n;
5.705: His count'nance, as the Morning Starr that guides
5.706: The starrie flock, allur'd them, and with lyes
5.707: Drew after him the third part of Heav'ns Host:
5.708: Mean while th' Eternal eye, whose sight discernes
5.709: Abstrusest thoughts, from forth his holy Mount
5.710: And from within the golden Lamps that burne
5.711: Nightly before him, saw without thir light
5.712: Rebellion rising, saw in whom, how spred
5.713: Among the sons of Morn, what multitudes
5.714: Were banded to oppose his high Decree;
5.715: And smiling to his onely Son thus said.
5.716: Son, thou in whom my glory I behold
5.717: In full resplendence, Heir of all my might,
5.718: Neerly it now concernes us to be sure
5.719: Of our Omnipotence, and with what Arms
5.720: We mean to hold what anciently we claim
5.721: Of Deitie or Empire, such a foe
5.722: Is rising, who intends to erect his Throne
5.723: Equal to ours, throughout the spacious North;
5.724: Nor so content, hath in his thought to trie
5.725: In battel, what our Power is, or our right.
5.726: Let us advise, and to this hazard draw
5.727: With speed what force is left, and all imploy
5.728: In our defence, lest unawares we lose
5.729: This our high place, our Sanctuarie, our Hill.
5.730: To whom the Son with calm aspect and cleer
5.732: Made answer. Mightie Father, thou thy foes
5.733: Justly hast in derision, and secure
5.734: Laugh'st at thir vain designes and tumults vain,
5.735: Matter to mee of Glory, whom thir hate
5.736: Illustrates, when they see all Regal Power
5.737: Giv'n me to quell thir pride, and in event
5.738: Know whether I be dextrous to subdue
5.739: Thy Rebels, or be found the worst in Heav'n.
5.740: So spake the Son, but Satan with his Powers
5.741: Farr was advanc't on winged speed, an Host
5.742: Innumerable as the Starrs of Night,
5.743: Or Starrs of Morning, Dew-drops, which the Sun
5.744: Impearls on every leaf and every flouer.
5.745: Regions they pass'd, the mightie Regencies
5.746: Of Seraphim and Potentates and Thrones
5.747: In thir triple Degrees, Regions to which
5.748: All thy Dominion, Adam, is no more
5.749: Then what this Garden is to all the Earth,
5.750: And all the Sea, from one entire globose
5.751: Stretcht into Longitude; which having pass'd
5.752: At length into the limits of the North
5.753: They came, and Satan to his Royal seat
5.754: High on a Hill, far blazing, as a Mount
5.755: Rais'd on a Mount, with Pyramids and Towrs
5.756: From Diamond Quarries hew'n, & Rocks of Gold,
5.757: The Palace of great Lucifer, (so call
5.758: That Structure in the Dialect of men
5.759: Interpreted) which not long after, hee
5.761: In imitation of that Mount whereon
5.762: Messiah was declar'd in sight of Heav'n,
5.763: The Mountain of the Congregation call'd;
5.764: For thither he assembl'd all his Train,
5.766: About the great reception of thir King,
5.767: Thither to come, and with calumnious Art
5.768: Of counterfeted truth thus held thir ears.
5.770: If these magnific Titles yet remain
5.771: Not meerly titular, since by Decree
5.772: Another now hath to himself ingross't
5.773: All Power, and us eclipst under the name
5.774: Of King anointed, for whom all this haste
5.775: Of midnight march, and hurried meeting here,
5.776: This onely to consult how we may best
5.777: With what may be devis'd of honours new
5.778: Receive him coming to receive from us
5.780: Too much to one, but double how endur'd,
5.781: To one and to his image now proclaim'd?
5.782: But what if better counsels might erect
5.783: Our minds and teach us to cast off this Yoke?
5.784: Will ye submit your necks, and chuse to bend
5.785: The supple knee? ye will not, if I trust
5.786: To know ye right, or if ye know your selves
5.787: Natives and Sons of Heav'n possest before
5.788: By none, and if not equal all, yet free,
5.789: Equally free; for Orders and Degrees
5.790: Jarr not with liberty, but well consist.
5.791: Who can in reason then or right assume
5.792: Monarchie over such as live by right
5.793: His equals, if in power and splendor less,
5.794: In freedome equal? or can introduce
5.795: Law and Edict on us, who without law
5.796: Erre not, much less for this to be our Lord,
5.797: And look for adoration to th' abuse
5.798: Of those Imperial Titles which assert
5.799: Our being ordain'd to govern, not to serve?
5.800: Thus farr his bold discourse without controule
5.801: Had audience, when among the Seraphim
5.802: Abdiel, then whom none with more zeale ador'd
5.803: The Deitie, and divine commands obei'd,
5.804: Stood up, and in a flame of zeale severe
5.805: The current of his fury thus oppos'd.
5.806: O argument blasphemous, false and proud!
5.807: Words which no eare ever to hear in Heav'n
5.808: Expected, least of all from thee, ingrate
5.809: In place thy self so high above thy Peeres.
5.810: Canst thou with impious obloquie condemne
5.811: The just Decree of God, pronounc't and sworn,
5.812: That to his only Son by right endu'd
5.813: With Regal Scepter, every Soule in Heav'n
5.814: Shall bend the knee, and in that honour due
5.815: Confess him rightful King? unjust thou saist
5.816: Flatly unjust, to binde with Laws the free,
5.817: And equal over equals to let Reigne,
5.818: One over all with unsucceeded power.
5.819: Shalt thou give Law to God, shalt thou dispute
5.820: With him the points of libertie, who made
5.821: Thee what thou art, & formd the Pow'rs of Heav'n
5.822: Such as he pleasd, and circumscrib'd thir being?
5.823: Yet by experience taught we know how good,
5.824: And of our good, and of our dignitie
5.825: How provident he is, how farr from thought
5.826: To make us less, bent rather to exalt
5.827: Our happie state under one Head more neer
5.828: United. But to grant it thee unjust,
5.829: That equal over equals Monarch Reigne:
5.830: Thy self though great & glorious dost thou count,
5.831: Or all Angelic Nature joind in one,
5.832: Equal to him begotten Son, by whom
5.833: As by his Word the mighty Father made
5.834: All things, ev'n thee, and all the Spirits of Heav'n
5.835: By him created in thir bright degrees,
5.836: Crownd them with Glory, & to thir Glory nam'd
5.838: Essential Powers, nor by his Reign obscur'd,
5.839: But more illustrious made, since he the Head
5.840: One of our number thus reduc't becomes,
5.841: His Laws our Laws, all honour to him done
5.842: Returns our own. Cease then this impious rage,
5.843: And tempt not these; but hast'n to appease
5.844: Th' incensed Father, and th' incensed Son,
5.845: While Pardon may be found in time besought.
5.846: So spake the fervent Angel, but his zeale
5.847: None seconded, as out of season judg'd,
5.848: Or singular and rash, whereat rejoic'd
5.849: Th' Apostat, and more haughty thus repli'd.
5.850: That we were formd then saist thou? & the work
5.851: Of secondarie hands, by task transferd
5.852: From Father to his Son? strange point and new!
5.853: Doctrin which we would know whence learnt: who saw
5.854: When this creation was? rememberst thou
5.855: Thy making, while the Maker gave thee being?
5.856: We know no time when we were not as now;
5.857: Know none before us, self-begot, self-rais'd
5.858: By our own quick'ning power, when fatal course
5.859: Had circl'd his full Orbe, the birth mature
5.860: Of this our native Heav'n, Ethereal Sons.
5.861: Our puissance is our own, our own right hand
5.862: Shall teach us highest deeds, by proof to try
5.863: Who is our equal: then thou shalt behold
5.865: Address, and to begirt th' Almighty Throne
5.867: These tidings carrie to th' anointed King;
5.868: And fly, ere evil intercept thy flight.
5.869: He said, and as the sound of waters deep
5.870: Hoarce murmur echo'd to his words applause
5.871: Through the infinite Host, nor less for that
5.872: The flaming Seraph fearless, though alone
5.873: Encompass'd round with foes, thus answerd bold.
5.874: O alienate from God, O spirit accurst,
5.875: Forsak'n of all good; I see thy fall
5.876: Determind, and thy hapless crew involv'd
5.877: In this perfidious fraud, contagion spred
5.878: Both of thy crime and punishment: henceforth
5.879: No more be troubl'd how to quit the yoke
5.880: Of Gods Messiah; those indulgent Laws
5.881: Will not be now voutsaf't, other Decrees
5.882: Against thee are gon forth without recall;
5.883: That Golden Scepter which thou didst reject
5.884: Is now an Iron Rod to bruise and breake
5.885: Thy disobedience. Well thou didst advise,
5.886: Yet not for thy advise or threats I fly
5.887: These wicked Tents devoted, least the wrauth
5.889: Distinguish not: for soon expect to feel
5.890: His Thunder on thy head, devouring fire.
5.891: Then who created thee lamenting learne,
5.892: When who can uncreate thee thou shalt know.
5.893: So spake the Seraph Abdiel faithful found,
5.894: Among the faithless, faithful only hee;
5.897: His Loyaltie he kept, his Love, his Zeale;
5.898: Nor number, nor example with him wrought
5.899: To swerve from truth, or change his constant mind
5.900: Though single. From amidst them forth he passd,
5.901: Long way through hostile scorn, which he susteind
5.902: Superior, nor of violence fear'd aught;
5.903: And with retorted scorn his back he turn'd
5.904: On those proud Towrs to swift destruction doom'd.

6.0:
*The Argument*
Raphael continues to relate how Michael and Gabriel were sent forth to Battel against Satan and his Angels. The first Fight describ'd: Satan and his Powers retire under Night: he calls a Councel, invents devilish Engines, which in the second dayes Fight put Michael and his Angels to some disorder; But they at length pulling up Mountains overwhelm'd both the force and Machins of Satan: Yet the Tumult not so ending, God on the third day sends Messiah his Son, for whom he had reserv'd the glory of that Victory.  Hee in the Power of his Father coming to the place, and causing all his Legions to stand still on either side, with his Chariot and Thunder driving into the midst of his Enemies, pursues them unable to resist towards the wall of Heaven; which opening, they leap down with horror and confusion into the place of punishment prepar'd for them in the Deep: Messiah returns with triumph to his Father.
6.1: All night the dreadless Angel unpursu'd
6.2: Through Heav'ns wide Champain held his way, till Morn,
6.3: Wak't by the circling Hours, with rosie hand
6.4: Unbarr'd the gates of Light. There is a Cave
6.5: Within the Mount of God, fast by his Throne,
6.6: Where light and darkness in perpetual round
6.7: Lodge and dislodge by turns, which makes through Heav'n
6.8: Grateful vicissitude, like Day and Night;
6.9: Light issues forth, and at the other dore
6.10: Obsequious darkness enters, till her houre
6.11: To veile the Heav'n, though darkness there might well
6.12: Seem twilight here; and now went forth the Morn
6.13: Such as in highest Heav'n, arrayd in Gold
6.14: Empyreal, from before her vanisht Night,
6.15: Shot through with orient Beams: when all the Plain
6.16: Coverd with thick embatteld Squadrons bright,
6.17: Chariots and flaming Armes, and fierie Steeds
6.18: Reflecting blaze on blaze, first met his view:
6.19: Warr he perceav'd, warr in procinct, and found
6.20: Already known what he for news had thought
6.21: To have reported: gladly then he mixt
6.22: Among those friendly Powers who him receav'd
6.23: With joy and acclamations loud, that one
6.24: That of so many Myriads fall'n, yet one
6.25: Returnd not lost: On to the sacred hill
6.26: They led him high applauded, and present
6.27: Before the seat supream; from whence a voice
6.28: From midst a Golden Cloud thus milde was heard.
6.29: Servant of God, well done, well hast thou fought
6.30: The better fight, who single hast maintaind
6.32: Of Truth, in word mightier then they in Armes;
6.33: And for the testimonie of Truth hast born
6.34: Universal reproach, far worse to beare
6.35: Then violence: for this was all thy care
6.36: To stand approv'd in sight of God, though Worlds
6.37: Judg'd thee perverse: the easier conquest now
6.38: Remains thee, aided by this host of friends,
6.39: Back on thy foes more glorious to return
6.40: Then scornd thou didst depart, and to subdue
6.41: By force, who reason for thir Law refuse,
6.42: Right reason for thir Law, and for thir King
6.43: Messiah, who by right of merit Reigns.
6.44: Goe Michael of Celestial Armies Prince,
6.45: And thou in Military prowess next
6.46: Gabriel, lead forth to Battel these my Sons
6.47: Invincible, lead forth my armed Saints
6.48: By Thousands and by Millions rang'd for fight;
6.49: Equal in number to that Godless crew
6.50: Rebellious, them with Fire and hostile Arms
6.51: Fearless assault, and to the brow of Heav'n
6.52: Pursuing drive them out from God and bliss,
6.53: Into thir place of punishment, the Gulf
6.54: Of Tartarus, which ready opens wide
6.55: His fiery Chaos to receave thir fall.
6.56: So spake the Sovran voice, and Clouds began
6.57: To darken all the Hill, and smoak to rowl
6.58: In duskie wreathes, reluctant flames, the signe
6.59: Of wrauth awak't: nor with less dread the loud
6.60: Ethereal Trumpet from on high gan blow:
6.61: At which command the Powers Militant,
6.62: That stood for Heav'n, in mighty Quadrate joyn'd
6.64: In silence thir bright Legions, to the sound
6.67: Under thir God-like Leaders, in the Cause
6.68: Of God and his Messiah. On they move
6.70: Nor streit'ning Vale, nor Wood, nor Stream divides
6.71: Thir perfet ranks; for high above the ground
6.72: Thir march was, and the passive Air upbore
6.73: Thir nimble tread; as when the total kind
6.74: Of Birds in orderly array on wing
6.75: Came summond over Eden to receive
6.76: Thir names of thee; so over many a tract
6.77: Of Heav'n they march'd, and many a Province wide
6.78: Tenfold the length of this terrene: at last
6.79: Farr in th' Horizon to the North appeer'd
6.80: From skirt to skirt a fierie Region, stretcht
6.81: In battailous aspect, and neerer view
6.83: Of rigid Spears, and Helmets throng'd, and Shields
6.85: The banded Powers of Satan hasting on
6.86: With furious expedition; for they weend
6.87: That self same day by fight, or by surprize
6.88: To win the Mount of God, and on his Throne
6.89: To set the envier of his State, the proud
6.90: Aspirer, but thir thoughts prov'd fond and vain
6.91: In the mid way: though strange to us it seemd
6.92: At first, that Angel should with Angel warr,
6.93: And in fierce hosting meet, who wont to meet
6.94: So oft in Festivals of joy and love
6.95: Unanimous, as sons of one great Sire
6.96: Hymning th' Eternal Father: but the shout
6.97: Of Battel now began, and rushing sound
6.98: Of onset ended soon each milder thought.
6.99: High in the midst exalted as a God
6.100: Th' Apostat in his Sun-bright Chariot sate
6.102: With Flaming Cherubim, and golden Shields;
6.103: Then lighted from his gorgeous Throne, for now
6.104: 'Twixt Host and Host but narrow space was left,
6.105: A dreadful interval, and Front to Front
6.107: Of hideous length: before the cloudie Van,
6.108: On the rough edge of battel ere it joyn'd,
6.109: Satan with vast and haughtie strides advanc't,
6.110: Came towring, armd in Adamant and Gold;
6.111: Abdiel that sight endur'd not, where he stood
6.112: Among the mightiest, bent on highest deeds,
6.113: And thus his own undaunted heart explores.
6.114: O Heav'n! that such resemblance of the Highest
6.115: Should yet remain, where faith and realtie
6.116: Remain not; wherfore should not strength & might
6.117: There fail where Vertue fails, or weakest prove
6.118: Where boldest; though to sight unconquerable?
6.119: His puissance, trusting in th' Almightie's aide,
6.120: I mean to try, whose Reason I have tri'd
6.121: Unsound and false; nor is it aught but just,
6.122: That he who in debate of Truth hath won,
6.123: Should win in Arms, in both disputes alike
6.124: Victor; though brutish that contest and foule,
6.125: When Reason hath to deal with force, yet so
6.126: Most reason is that Reason overcome.
6.127: So pondering, and from his armed Peers
6.128: Forth stepping opposite, half way he met
6.129: His daring foe, at this prevention more
6.130: Incens't, and thus securely him defi'd.
6.131: Proud, art thou met? thy hope was to have reacht
6.132: The highth of thy aspiring unoppos'd,
6.133: The Throne of God unguarded, and his side
6.134: Abandond at the terror of thy Power
6.135: Or potent tongue; fool, not to think how vain
6.136: Against th' Omnipotent to rise in Arms;
6.137: Who out of smallest things could without end
6.138: Have rais'd incessant Armies to defeat
6.139: Thy folly; or with solitarie hand
6.140: Reaching beyond all limit, at one blow
6.141: Unaided could have finisht thee, and whelmd
6.142: Thy Legions under darkness; but thou seest
6.143: All are not of thy Train; there be who Faith
6.144: Prefer, and Pietie to God, though then
6.145: To thee not visible, when I alone
6.146: Seemd in thy World erroneous to dissent
6.147: From all: my Sect thou seest, now learn too late
6.148: How few somtimes may know, when thousands err.
6.149: Whom the grand foe with scornful eye askance
6.150: Thus answerd. Ill for thee, but in wisht houre
6.151: Of my revenge, first sought for thou returnst
6.152: From flight, seditious Angel, to receave
6.153: Thy merited reward, the first assay
6.154: Of this right hand provok't, since first that tongue
6.156: A third part of the Gods, in Synod met
6.157: Thir Deities to assert, who while they feel
6.158: Vigour Divine within them, can allow
6.159: Omnipotence to none. But well thou comst
6.160: Before thy fellows, ambitious to win
6.161: From me som Plume, that thy success may show
6.162: Destruction to the rest: this pause between
6.163: (Unanswerd least thou boast) to let thee know;
6.164: At first I thought that Libertie and Heav'n
6.165: To heav'nly Soules had bin all one; but now
6.166: I see that most through sloth had rather serve,
6.167: Ministring Spirits, traind up in Feast and Song;
6.168: Such hast thou arm'd, the Minstrelsie of Heav'n,
6.170: As both thir deeds compar'd this day shall prove.
6.171: To whom in brief thus Abdiel stern repli'd.
6.172: Apostat, still thou errst, nor end wilt find
6.173: Of erring, from the path of truth remote:
6.174: Unjustly thou deprav'st it with the name
6.175: Of Servitude to serve whom God ordains,
6.176: Or Nature; God and Nature bid the same,
6.177: When he who rules is worthiest, and excells
6.178: Them whom he governs. This is servitude,
6.179: To serve th' unwise, or him who hath rebelld
6.180: Against his worthier, as thine now serve thee,
6.181: Thy self not free, but to thy self enthrall'd;
6.182: Yet leudly dar'st our ministring upbraid.
6.183: Reign thou in Hell thy Kingdom, let mee serve
6.184: In Heav'n God ever blessed, and his Divine
6.185: Behests obey, worthiest to be obey'd,
6.186: Yet Chains in Hell, not Realms expect: mean while
6.187: From mee returnd, as erst thou saidst, from flight,
6.188: This greeting on thy impious Crest receive.
6.189: So saying, a noble stroke he lifted high,
6.190: Which hung not, but so swift with tempest fell
6.191: On the proud Crest of Satan, that no sight,
6.192: Nor motion of swift thought, less could his Shield
6.193: Such ruin intercept: ten paces huge
6.194: He back recoild; the tenth on bended knee
6.195: His massie Spear upstaid; as if on Earth
6.196: Winds under ground or waters forcing way
6.197: Sidelong, had push't a Mountain from his seat
6.198: Half sunk with all his Pines. Amazement seis'd
6.199: The Rebel Thrones, but greater rage to see
6.200: Thus foil'd thir mightiest, ours joy filld, and shout,
6.201: Presage of Victorie and fierce desire
6.202: Of Battel: whereat Michael bid sound
6.203: Th' Arch-Angel trumpet; through the vast of Heav'n
6.204: It sounded, and the faithful Armies rung
6.205: Hosanna to the Highest: nor stood at gaze
6.206: The adverse Legions, nor less hideous joyn'd
6.207: The horrid shock: now storming furie rose,
6.208: And clamour such as heard in Heav'n till now
6.209: Was never, Arms on Armour clashing bray'd
6.210: Horrible discord, and the madding Wheeles
6.211: Of brazen Chariots rag'd; dire was the noise
6.212: Of conflict; over head the dismal hiss
6.213: Of fiery Darts in flaming volies flew,
6.214: And flying vaulted either Host with fire.
6.215: So under fierie Cope together rush'd
6.216: Both Battels maine, with ruinous assault
6.218: Resounded, and had Earth bin then, all Earth
6.219: Had to her Center shook. What wonder? when
6.220: Millions of fierce encountring Angels fought
6.221: On either side, the least of whom could weild
6.222: These Elements, and arm him with the force
6.223: Of all thir Regions: how much more of Power
6.224: Armie against Armie numberless to raise
6.226: Though not destroy, thir happie Native seat;
6.227: Had not th' Eternal King Omnipotent
6.228: From his strong hold of Heav'n high over-rul'd
6.229: And limited thir might; though numberd such
6.230: As each divided Legion might have seemd
6.231: A numerous Host, in strength each armed hand
6.232: A Legion; led in fight, yet Leader seemd
6.233: Each Warriour single as in Chief, expert
6.234: When to advance, or stand, or turn the sway
6.235: Of Battel, open when, and when to close
6.236: The ridges of grim Warr; no thought of flight,
6.237: None of retreat, no unbecoming deed
6.238: That argu'd fear; each on himself reli'd,
6.239: As onely in his arm the moment lay
6.240: Of victorie; deeds of eternal fame
6.241: Were don, but infinite: for wide was spred
6.242: That Warr and various; somtimes on firm ground
6.243: A standing fight, then soaring on main wing
6.244: Tormented all the Air; all Air seemd then
6.245: Conflicting Fire: long time in eeven scale
6.246: The Battel hung; till Satan, who that day
6.247: Prodigious power had shewn, and met in Armes
6.248: No equal, raunging through the dire attack
6.249: Of fighting Seraphim confus'd, at length
6.250: Saw where the Sword of Michael smote, and fell'd
6.251: Squadrons at once, with huge two-handed sway
6.252: Brandisht aloft the horrid edge came down
6.253: Wide wasting; such destruction to withstand
6.254: He hasted, and oppos'd the rockie Orb
6.255: Of tenfold Adamant, his ample Shield
6.256: A vast circumference: At his approach
6.257: The great Arch-Angel from his warlike toile
6.258: Surceas'd, and glad as hoping here to end
6.259: Intestine War in Heav'n, the arch foe subdu'd
6.260: Or Captive drag'd in Chains, with hostile frown
6.261: And visage all enflam'd first thus began.
6.262: Author of evil, unknown till thy revolt,
6.263: Unnam'd in Heav'n, now plenteous, as thou seest
6.264: These Acts of hateful strife, hateful to all,
6.265: Though heaviest by just measure on thy self
6.266: And thy adherents: how hast thou disturb'd
6.267: Heav'ns blessed peace, and into Nature brought
6.269: Of thy Rebellion? how hast thou instill'd
6.270: Thy malice into thousands, once upright
6.271: And faithful, now prov'd false. But think not here
6.272: To trouble Holy Rest; Heav'n casts thee out
6.273: From all her Confines. Heav'n the seat of bliss
6.274: Brooks not the works of violence and Warr.
6.275: Hence then, and evil go with thee along
6.276: Thy ofspring, to the place of evil, Hell,
6.277: Thou and thy wicked crew; there mingle broiles,
6.278: Ere this avenging Sword begin thy doome,
6.279: Or som more sudden vengeance wing'd from God
6.281: So spake the Prince of Angels; to whom thus
6.282: The Adversarie. Nor think thou with wind
6.283: Of airie threats to aw whom yet with deeds
6.284: Thou canst not. Hast thou turnd the least of these
6.285: To flight, or if to fall, but that they rise
6.286: Unvanquisht, easier to transact with mee
6.287: That thou shouldst hope, imperious, & with threats
6.288: To chase me hence? erre not that so shall end
6.289: The strife which thou call'st evil, but wee style
6.290: The strife of Glorie: which we mean to win,
6.291: Or turn this Heav'n it self into the Hell
6.292: Thou fablest, here however to dwell free,
6.293: If not to reign: mean while thy utmost force,
6.294: And join him nam'd Almightie to thy aid,
6.295: I flie not, but have sought thee farr and nigh.
6.296: They ended parle, and both addrest for fight
6.297: Unspeakable; for who, though with the tongue
6.298: Of Angels, can relate, or to what things
6.299: Liken on Earth conspicuous, that may lift
6.301: Of Godlike Power: for likest Gods they seemd,
6.302: Stood they or mov'd, in stature, motion, arms
6.303: Fit to decide the Empire of great Heav'n.
6.304: Now wav'd thir fierie Swords, and in the Aire
6.305: Made horrid Circles; two broad Suns thir Shields
6.307: In horror; from each hand with speed retir'd
6.308: Where erst was thickest fight, th' Angelic throng,

6.346: In Entrailes, Heart or Head, Liver or Reines,

6.349: Receive, no more then can the fluid Aire:
6.350: All Heart they live, all Head, all Eye, all Eare,
6.351: All Intellect, all Sense, and as they please,
6.352: They Limb themselves, and colour, shape or size

6.541: Sad resolution and secure: let each
