6.808: Vengeance is his, or whose he sole appoints;
6.809: Number to this dayes work is not ordain'd
6.810: Nor multitude, stand onely and behold
6.811: Gods indignation on these Godless pourd
6.812: By mee; not you but mee they have despis'd,
6.813: Yet envied; against mee is all thir rage,
6.814: Because the Father, t' whom in Heav'n supream
6.815: Kingdom and Power and Glorie appertains,
6.816: Hath honourd me according to his will.
6.817: Therefore to mee thir doom he hath assig'n'd;
6.818: That they may have thir wish, to trie with mee
6.819: In Battel which the stronger proves, they all,
6.820: Or I alone against them, since by strength
6.821: They measure all, of other excellence
6.822: Not emulous, nor care who them excells;
6.823: Nor other strife with them do I voutsafe.
6.824: So spake the Son, and into terrour chang'd
6.825: His count'nance too severe to be beheld
6.826: And full of wrauth bent on his Enemies.
6.827: At once the Four spred out thir Starrie wings
6.828: With dreadful shade contiguous, and the Orbes
6.829: Of his fierce Chariot rowld, as with the sound
6.830: Of torrent Floods, or of a numerous Host.
6.831: Hee on his impious Foes right onward drove,
6.832: Gloomie as Night; under his burning Wheeles
6.834: All but the Throne it self of God. Full soon
6.835: Among them he arriv'd; in his right hand
6.836: Grasping ten thousand Thunders, which he sent
6.837: Before him, such as in thir Soules infix'd
6.838: Plagues; they astonisht all resistance lost,
6.839: All courage; down thir idle weapons drop'd;
6.840: O're Shields and Helmes, and helmed heads he rode
6.841: Of Thrones and mighty Seraphim prostrate,
6.842: That wish'd the Mountains now might be again
6.843: Thrown on them as a shelter from his ire.
6.844: Nor less on either side tempestuous fell
6.845: His arrows, from the fourfold-visag'd Foure,
6.846: Distinct with eyes, and from the living Wheels,
6.847: Distinct alike with multitude of eyes,
6.848: One Spirit in them rul'd, and every eye
6.849: Glar'd lightning, and shot forth pernicious fire
6.850: Among th' accurst, that witherd all thir strength,
6.851: And of thir wonted vigour left them draind,
6.853: Yet half his strength he put not forth, but check'd
6.854: His Thunder in mid Volie, for he meant
6.855: Not to destroy, but root them out of Heav'n:
6.856: The overthrown he rais'd, and as a Heard
6.857: Of Goats or timerous flock together throngd
6.858: Drove them before him Thunder-struck, pursu'd
6.859: With terrors and with furies to the bounds
6.860: And Chrystall wall of Heav'n, which op'ning wide,
6.861: Rowld inward, and a spacious Gap disclos'd
6.862: Into the wastful Deep; the monstrous sight
6.863: Strook them with horror backward, but far worse
6.864: Urg'd them behind; headlong themselvs they threw
6.865: Down from the verge of Heav'n, Eternal wrauth
6.866: Burnt after them to the bottomless pit.
6.867: Hell heard th' unsufferable noise, Hell saw
6.868: Heav'n ruining from Heav'n and would have fled
6.869: Affrighted; but strict Fate had cast too deep
6.870: Her dark foundations, and too fast had bound.
6.871: Nine dayes they fell; confounded Chaos roard,
6.872: And felt tenfold confusion in thir fall
6.873: Through his wilde Anarchie, so huge a rout
6.874: Incumberd him with ruin: Hell at last
6.875: Yawning receavd them whole, and on them clos'd,
6.876: Hell thir fit habitation fraught with fire
6.877: Unquenchable, the house of woe and paine.
6.878: Disburd'nd Heav'n rejoic'd, and soon repaird
6.879: Her mural breach, returning whence it rowld.
6.880: Sole Victor from th' expulsion of his Foes
6.882: To meet him all his Saints, who silent stood
6.883: Eye witnesses of his Almightie Acts,
6.884: With Jubilie advanc'd; and as they went,
6.885: Shaded with branching Palme, each order bright,
6.886: Sung Triumph, and him sung Victorious King,
6.887: Son, Heire, and Lord, to him Dominion giv'n,
6.888: Worthiest to Reign: he celebrated rode
6.889: Triumphant through mid Heav'n, into the Courts
6.890: And Temple of his mightie Father Thron'd
6.891: On high; who into Glorie him receav'd,
6.892: Where now he sits at the right hand of bliss.
6.893: Thus measuring things in Heav'n by things on Earth
6.894: At thy request, and that thou maist beware
6.895: By what is past, to thee I have reveal'd
6.896: What might have else to human Race bin hid;
6.897: The discord which befel, and Warr in Heav'n
6.898: Among th' Angelic Powers, and the deep fall
6.899: Of those too high aspiring, who rebelld
6.900: With Satan, hee who envies now thy state,
6.901: Who now is plotting how he may seduce
6.902: Thee also from obedience, that with him
6.903: Bereavd of happiness thou maist partake
6.905: Which would be all his solace and revenge,
6.906: As a despite don against the most High,
6.907: Thee once to gaine Companion of his woe.
6.908: But list'n not to his Temptations, warne
6.909: Thy weaker; let it profit thee to have heard
6.911: Of disobedience; firm they might have stood,
6.912: Yet fell; remember, and fear to transgress.

7.0:
*The Argument*
Raphael at the request of Adam relates how and wherefore this world was first created; that God, after the expelling of Satan and his Angels out of Heaven, declar'd his pleasure to create another World and other Creatures to dwell therein; sends his Son with Glory and attendance of Angels to perform the work of Creation in six dayes: the Angels celebrate with Hymns the performance thereof, and his reascention into Heaven.
7.1: Descend from Heav'n Urania, by that name
7.2: If rightly thou art call'd, whose Voice divine
7.3: Following, above th' Olympian Hill I soare,
7.4: Above the flight of Pegasean wing.
7.5: The meaning, not the Name I call: for thou
7.6: Nor of the Muses nine, nor on the top
7.7: Of old Olympus dwell'st, but Heav'nlie borne,
7.8: Before the Hills appeerd, or Fountain flow'd,
7.9: Thou with Eternal wisdom didst converse,
7.10: Wisdom thy Sister, and with her didst play
7.11: In presence of th' Almightie Father, pleas'd
7.12: With thy Celestial Song. Up led by thee
7.13: Into the Heav'n of Heav'ns I have presum'd,
7.14: An Earthlie Guest, and drawn Empyreal Aire,
7.15: Thy tempring; with like safetie guided down
7.16: Return me to my Native Element:
7.17: Least from this flying Steed unrein'd, (as once
7.18: Bellerophon, though from a lower Clime)
7.19: Dismounted, on th' Aleian Field I fall
7.20: Erroneous, there to wander and forlorne.
7.21: Half yet remaines unsung, but narrower bound
7.23: Standing on Earth, not rapt above the Pole,
7.24: More safe I Sing with mortal voice, unchang'd
7.25: To hoarce or mute, though fall'n on evil dayes,
7.26: On evil dayes though fall'n, and evil tongues;
7.27: In darkness, and with dangers compast round,
7.28: And solitude; yet not alone, while thou
7.29: Visit'st my slumbers Nightly, or when Morn
7.30: Purples the East: still govern thou my Song,
7.31: Urania, and fit audience find, though few.
7.32: But drive farr off the barbarous dissonance
7.33: Of Bacchus and his Revellers, the Race
7.34: Of that wilde Rout that tore the Thracian Bard
7.35: In Rhodope, where Woods and Rocks had Eares
7.36: To rapture, till the savage clamor dround
7.37: Both Harp and Voice; nor could the Muse defend
7.38: Her Son. So fail not thou, who thee implores:
7.39: For thou art Heav'nlie, shee an empty dreame.
7.40: Say Goddess, what ensu'd when Raphael,
7.42: Adam by dire example to beware
7.43: Apostasie, by what befell in Heaven
7.44: To those Apostates, least the like befall
7.45: In Paradise to Adam or his Race,
7.46: Charg'd not to touch the interdicted Tree,
7.47: If they transgress, and slight that sole command,
7.48: So easily obeyd amid the choice
7.49: Of all tasts else to please thir appetite,
7.50: Though wandring. He with his consorted Eve
7.51: The storie heard attentive, and was fill'd
7.52: With admiration, and deep Muse to heare
7.53: Of things so high and strange, things to thir thought
7.54: So unimaginable as hate in Heav'n,
7.55: And Warr so neer the Peace of God in bliss
7.56: With such confusion: but the evil soon
7.57: Driv'n back redounded as a flood on those
7.58: From whom it sprung, impossible to mix
7.59: With Blessedness. Whence Adam soon repeal'd
7.60: The doubts that in his heart arose: and now
7.61: Led on, yet sinless, with desire to know
7.62: What neerer might concern him, how this World
7.63: Of Heav'n and Earth conspicuous first began,
7.64: When, and whereof created, for what cause,
7.65: What within Eden or without was done
7.66: Before his memorie, as one whose drouth
7.67: Yet scarce allay'd still eyes the current streame,
7.68: Whose liquid murmur heard new thirst excites,
7.69: Proceeded thus to ask his Heav'nly Guest.
7.70: Great things, and full of wonder in our eares,
7.71: Farr differing from this World, thou hast reveal'd
7.73: Down from the Empyrean to forewarne
7.74: Us timely of what might else have bin our loss,
7.75: Unknown, which human knowledg could not reach:
7.76: For which to the infinitly Good we owe
7.78: Receave with solemne purpose to observe
7.79: Immutably his sovran will, the end
7.80: Of what we are. But since thou hast voutsaf't
7.81: Gently for our instruction to impart
7.82: Things above Earthly thought, which yet concernd
7.83: Our knowing, as to highest wisdom seemd,
7.84: Deign to descend now lower, and relate
7.85: What may no less perhaps availe us known,
7.86: How first began this Heav'n which we behold
7.87: Distant so high, with moving Fires adornd
7.88: Innumerable, and this which yeelds or fills
7.89: All space, the ambient Aire wide interfus'd
7.90: Imbracing round this florid Earth, what cause
7.91: Mov'd the Creator in his holy Rest
7.92: Through all Eternitie so late to build
7.93: In Chaos, and the work begun, how soon
7.94: Absolv'd, if unforbid thou maist unfould
7.95: What wee, not to explore the secrets aske
7.96: Of his Eternal Empire, but the more
7.97: To magnifie his works, the more we know.
7.98: And the great Light of Day yet wants to run
7.99: Much of his Race though steep, suspens in Heav'n
7.100: Held by thy voice, thy potent voice he heares,
7.101: And longer will delay to heare thee tell
7.102: His Generation, and the rising Birth
7.103: Of Nature from the unapparent Deep:
7.104: Or if the Starr of Eevning and the Moon
7.105: Haste to thy audience, Night with her will bring
7.106: Silence, and Sleep listning to thee will watch,
7.107: Or we can bid his absence, till thy Song
7.108: End, and dismiss thee ere the Morning shine.
7.109: Thus Adam his illustrous Guest besought:
7.110: And thus the Godlike Angel answerd milde.
7.111: This also thy request with caution askt
7.112: Obtaine: though to recount Almightie works
7.113: What words or tongue of Seraph can suffice,
7.114: Or heart of man suffice to comprehend?
7.115: Yet what thou canst attain, which best may serve
7.116: To glorifie the Maker, and inferr
7.117: Thee also happier, shall not be withheld
7.118: Thy hearing, such Commission from above
7.119: I have receav'd, to answer thy desire
7.120: Of knowledge within bounds; beyond abstain
7.121: To ask, nor let thine own inventions hope
7.122: Things not reveal'd, which th' invisible King,
7.123: Onely Omniscient, hath supprest in Night,
7.124: To none communicable in Earth or Heaven:
7.125: Anough is left besides to search and know.
7.126: But Knowledge is as food, and needs no less
7.127: Her Temperance over Appetite, to know
7.128: In measure what the mind may well contain,
7.129: Oppresses else with Surfet, and soon turns
7.130: Wisdom to Folly, as Nourishment to Winde.
7.131: Know then, that after Lucifer from Heav'n
7.132: (So call him, brighter once amidst the Host
7.133: Of Angels, then that Starr the Starrs among)
7.134: Fell with his flaming Legions through the Deep
7.135: Into his place, and the great Son returnd
7.136: Victorious with his Saints, th' Omnipotent
7.137: Eternal Father from his Throne beheld
7.138: Thir multitude, and to his Son thus spake.
7.139: At least our envious Foe hath fail'd, who thought
7.140: All like himself rebellious, by whose aid
7.141: This inaccessible high strength, the seat
7.143: He trusted to have seis'd, and into fraud
7.144: Drew many, whom thir place knows here no more;
7.145: Yet farr the greater part have kept, I see,
7.146: Thir station, Heav'n yet populous retaines
7.147: Number sufficient to possess her Realmes
7.148: Though wide, and this high Temple to frequent
7.149: With Ministeries due and solemn Rites:
7.150: But least his heart exalt him in the harme
7.151: Already done, to have dispeopl'd Heav'n,
7.152: My damage fondly deem'd, I can repaire
7.153: That detriment, if such it be to lose
7.154: Self-lost, and in a moment will create
7.155: Another World, out of one man a Race
7.156: Of men innumerable, there to dwell,
7.157: Not here, till by degrees of merit rais'd
7.158: They open to themselves at length the way
7.159: Up hither, under long obedience tri'd,
7.160: And Earth be chang'd to Heavn, & Heav'n to Earth,
7.161: One Kingdom, Joy and Union without end.
7.162: Mean while inhabit laxe, ye Powers of Heav'n,
7.163: And thou my Word, begotten Son, by thee
7.164: This I perform, speak thou, and be it don:
7.165: My overshadowing Spirit and might with thee
7.166: I send along, ride forth, and bid the Deep
7.167: Within appointed bounds be Heav'n and Earth,
7.168: Boundless the Deep, because I am who fill
7.170: Though I uncircumscrib'd my self retire,
7.171: And put not forth my goodness, which is free
7.172: To act or not, Necessitie and Chance
7.173: Approach not mee, and what I will is Fate.
7.174: So spake th' Almightie, and to what he spake
7.175: His Word, the Filial Godhead, gave effect.
7.176: Immediate are the Acts of God, more swift
7.177: Then time or motion, but to human ears
7.178: Cannot without process of speech be told,
7.179: So told as earthly notion can receave.
7.180: Great triumph and rejoycing was in Heav'n
7.181: When such was heard declar'd the Almightie's will;
7.182: Glorie they sung to the most High, good will
7.183: To future men, and in thir dwellings peace:
7.184: Glorie to him whose just avenging ire
7.185: Had driven out th' ungodly from his sight
7.186: And th' habitations of the just; to him
7.187: Glorie and praise, whose wisdom had ordain'd
7.188: Good out of evil to create, in stead
7.189: Of Spirits maligne a better Race to bring
7.190: Into thir vacant room, and thence diffuse
7.191: His good to Worlds and Ages infinite.
7.192: So sang the Hierarchies: Mean while the Son
7.193: On his great Expedition now appeer'd,
7.194: Girt with Omnipotence, with Radiance crown'd
7.195: Of Majestie Divine, Sapience and Love
7.196: Immense, and all his Father in him shon.
7.197: About his Chariot numberless were pour'd
7.198: Cherub and Seraph, Potentates and Thrones,
7.199: And Vertues, winged Spirits, and Chariots wing'd,
7.200: From the Armoury of God, where stand of old
7.201: Myriads between two brazen Mountains lodg'd
7.202: Against a solemn day, harnest at hand,
7.203: Celestial Equipage; and now came forth
7.204: Spontaneous, for within them Spirit livd,
7.205: Attendant on thir Lord: Heav'n op'nd wide
7.206: Her ever during Gates, Harmonious sound
7.207: On golden Hinges moving, to let forth
7.208: The King of Glorie in his powerful Word
7.209: And Spirit coming to create new Worlds.
7.210: On heav'nly ground they stood, and from the shore
7.211: They view'd the vast immeasurable Abyss
7.212: Outrageous as a Sea, dark, wasteful, wilde,
7.213: Up from the bottom turn'd by furious windes
7.214: And surging waves, as Mountains to assault
7.215: Heav'ns highth, and with the Center mix the Pole.
7.216: Silence, ye troubl'd waves, and thou Deep, peace,
7.217: Said then th' Omnific Word, your discord end:
7.218: Nor staid, but on the Wings of Cherubim
7.220: Farr into Chaos, and the World unborn;
7.221: For Chaos heard his voice: him all his Traine
7.222: Follow'd in bright procession to behold
7.223: Creation, and the wonders of his might.
7.224: Then staid the fervid Wheeles, and in his hand
7.225: He took the golden Compasses, prepar'd
7.226: In Gods Eternal store, to circumscribe
7.227: This Universe, and all created things:
7.228: One foot he center'd, and the other turn'd
7.229: Round through the vast profunditie obscure,
7.230: And said, thus farr extend, thus farr thy bounds,
7.231: This be thy just Circumference, O World.
7.232: Thus God the Heav'n created, thus the Earth,
7.233: Matter unform'd and void: Darkness profound
7.234: Cover'd th' Abyss: but on the watrie calme
7.235: His brooding wings the Spirit of God outspred,
7.236: And vital vertue infus'd, and vital warmth
7.237: Throughout the fluid Mass, but downward purg'd
7.238: The black tartareous cold infernal dregs
7.239: Adverse to life: then founded, then conglob'd
7.240: Like things to like, the rest to several place
7.241: Disparted, and between spun out the Air,
7.242: And Earth self-ballanc't on her Center hung.
7.243: Let ther be Light, said God, and forthwith Light
7.244: Ethereal, first of things, quintessence pure
7.245: Sprung from the Deep, and from her Native East
7.246: To journie through the airie gloom began,
7.247: Sphear'd in a radiant Cloud, for yet the Sun
7.248: Was not; shee in a cloudie Tabernacle
7.249: Sojourn'd the while. God saw the Light was good;
7.250: And light from darkness by the Hemisphere
7.251: Divided: Light the Day, and Darkness Night
7.252: He nam'd. Thus was the first Day Eev'n and Morn:
7.254: By the Celestial Quires, when Orient Light
7.255: Exhaling first from Darkness they beheld;
7.256: Birth-day of Heav'n and Earth; with joy and shout
7.257: The hollow Universal Orb they fill'd,
7.258: And touch't thir Golden Harps, & hymning prais'd
7.259: God and his works, Creatour him they sung,
7.260: Both when first Eevning was, and when first Morn.
7.261: Again, God said, let ther be Firmament
7.262: Amid the Waters, and let it divide
7.263: The Waters from the Waters: and God made
7.264: The Firmament, expanse of liquid, pure,
7.266: In circuit to the uttermost convex
7.267: Of this great Round: partition firm and sure,
7.268: The Waters underneath from those above
7.269: Dividing: for as Earth, so hee the World
7.270: Built on circumfluous Waters calme, in wide
7.271: Crystallin Ocean, and the loud misrule
7.272: Of Chaos farr remov'd, least fierce extreames
7.273: Contiguous might distemper the whole frame:
7.274: And Heav'n he nam'd the Firmament: So Eev'n
7.275: And Morning Chorus sung the second Day.
7.276: The Earth was form'd, but in the Womb as yet
7.278: Appeer'd not: over all the face of Earth
7.279: Main Ocean flow'd, not idle, but with warme
7.280: Prolific humour soft'ning all her Globe,
7.281: Fermented the great Mother to conceave,
7.282: Satiate with genial moisture, when God said
7.283: Be gather'd now ye Waters under Heav'n
7.284: Into one place, and let dry Land appeer.
7.286: Emergent, and thir broad bare backs upheave
7.287: Into the Clouds, thir tops ascend the Skie:
7.288: So high as heav'd the tumid Hills, so low
7.289: Down sunk a hollow bottom broad and deep,
7.290: Capacious bed of Waters: thither they
7.292: As drops on dust conglobing from the drie;
7.293: Part rise in crystal Wall, or ridge direct,
7.294: For haste; such flight the great command impress'd
7.295: On the swift flouds: as Armies at the call
7.296: Of Trumpet (for of Armies thou hast heard)
7.297: Troop to thir Standard, so the watrie throng,
7.298: Wave rowling after Wave, where way they found,
7.299: If steep, with torrent rapture, if through Plaine,
7.300: Soft-ebbing; nor withstood them Rock or Hill,
7.301: But they, or under ground, or circuit wide
7.302: With Serpent errour wandring, found thir way,
7.303: And on the washie Oose deep Channels wore;
7.304: Easie, e're God had bid the ground be drie,
7.305: All but within those banks, where Rivers now
7.306: Stream, and perpetual draw thir humid traine.
7.307: The dry Land, Earth, and the great receptacle
7.308: Of congregated Waters he call'd Seas:
7.309: And saw that it was good, and said, Let th' Earth
7.310: Put forth the verdant Grass, Herb yeilding Seed,
7.311: And Fruit Tree yeilding Fruit after her kind;
7.312: Whose Seed is in her self upon the Earth.
7.313: He scarce had said, when the bare Earth, till then
7.315: Brought forth the tender Grass, whose verdure clad
7.316: Her Universal Face with pleasant green,
7.317: Then Herbs of every leaf, that sudden flour'd
7.318: Op'ning thir various colours, and made gay
7.319: Her bosom smelling sweet: and these scarce blown,
7.320: Forth flourish't thick the clustring Vine, forth crept
7.321: The smelling Gourd, up stood the cornie Reed
7.322: Embattell'd in her field: add the humble Shrub,
7.323: And Bush with frizl'd hair implicit: last
7.324: Rose as in Dance the stately Trees, and spred
7.325: Thir branches hung with copious Fruit; or gemm'd
7.326: Thir Blossoms: with high Woods the Hills were crownd,
7.327: With tufts the vallies & each fountain side,
7.328: With borders long the Rivers. That Earth now
7.329: Seemd like to Heav'n, a seat where Gods might dwell,
7.330: Or wander with delight, and love to haunt
7.331: Her sacred shades: though God had yet not rain'd
7.332: Upon the Earth, and man to till the ground
7.333: None was, but from the Earth a dewie Mist
7.334: Went up and waterd all the ground, and each
7.335: Plant of the field, which e're it was in the Earth
7.336: God made, and every Herb, before it grew
7.337: On the green stemm; God saw that it was good:
7.338: So Eev'n and Morn recorded the Third Day.
7.339: Again th' Almightie spake: Let there be Lights
7.340: High in th' expanse of Heaven to divide
7.341: The Day from Night; and let them be for Signes,
7.342: For Seasons, and for Dayes, and circling Years,
7.343: And let them be for Lights as I ordaine
7.344: Thir Office in the Firmament of Heav'n
7.345: To give Light on the Earth; and it was so.
7.346: And God made two great Lights, great for thir use
7.347: To Man, the greater to have rule by Day,
7.348: The less by Night alterne: and made the Starrs,
7.349: And set them in the Firmament of Heav'n
7.350: To illuminate the Earth, and rule the Day
7.351: In thir vicissitude, and rule the Night,
7.352: And Light from Darkness to divide. God saw,
7.353: Surveying his great Work, that it was good:
7.354: For of Celestial Bodies first the Sun
7.355: A mightie Spheare he fram'd, unlightsom first,
7.356: Though of Ethereal Mould: then form'd the Moon
7.357: Globose, and everie magnitude of Starrs,
7.358: And sowd with Starrs the Heav'n thick as a field:
7.359: Of Light by farr the greater part he took,
7.360: Transplanted from her cloudie Shrine, and plac'd
7.361: In the Suns Orb, made porous to receive
7.362: And drink the liquid Light, firm to retaine
7.363: Her gather'd beams, great Palace now of Light.
7.364: Hither as to thir Fountain other Starrs
7.365: Repairing, in thir gold'n Urns draw Light,
7.366: And hence the Morning Planet guilds his horns;
7.367: By tincture or reflection they augment
7.368: Thir small peculiar, though from human sight
7.369: So farr remote, with diminution seen.
7.370: First in his East the glorious Lamp was seen,
7.371: Regent of Day, and all th' Horizon round
7.372: Invested with bright Rayes, jocond to run
7.373: His Longitude through Heav'ns high rode: the gray
7.374: Dawn, and the Pleiades before him danc'd
7.375: Shedding sweet influence: less bright the Moon,
7.376: But opposite in leveld West was set
7.377: His mirror, with full face borrowing her Light
7.378: From him, for other light she needed none
7.379: In that aspect, and still that distance keepes
7.380: Till night, then in the East her turn she shines,
7.381: Revolvd on Heav'ns great Axle, and her Reign
7.382: With thousand lesser Lights dividual holds,
7.383: With thousand thousand Starres, that then appeer'd
7.384: Spangling the Hemisphere: then first adornd
7.385: With thir bright Luminaries that Set and Rose,
7.386: Glad Eevning & glad Morn crownd the fourth day.
7.387: And God said, let the Waters generate
7.388: Reptil with Spawn abundant, living Soule:
7.389: And let Fowle flie above the Earth, with wings
7.390: Displayd on the op'n Firmament of Heav'n.
7.391: And God created the great Whales, and each
7.392: Soul living, each that crept, which plenteously
7.393: The waters generated by thir kindes,
7.394: And every Bird of wing after his kinde;
7.395: And saw that it was good, and bless'd them, saying,
7.396: Be fruitful, multiply, and in the Seas
7.397: And Lakes and running Streams the waters fill;
7.398: And let the Fowle be multiply'd on the Earth.
7.399: Forthwith the Sounds and Seas, each Creek & Bay
7.400: With Frie innumerable swarme, and Shoales
7.401: Of Fish that with thir Finns & shining Scales
7.402: Glide under the green Wave, in Sculles that oft
7.403: Bank the mid Sea: part single or with mate
7.404: Graze the Sea weed thir pasture, & through Groves
7.405: Of Coral stray, or sporting with quick glance
7.406: Show to the Sun thir wav'd coats dropt with Gold,
7.407: Or in thir Pearlie shells at ease, attend
7.408: Moist nutriment, or under Rocks thir food
7.409: In jointed Armour watch: on smooth the Seale,
7.410: And bended Dolphins play: part huge of bulk
7.411: Wallowing unweildie, enormous in thir Gate
7.413: Hugest of living Creatures, on the Deep
7.414: Stretcht like a Promontorie sleeps or swimmes,
7.415: And seems a moving Land, and at his Gilles
7.416: Draws in, and at his Trunck spouts out a Sea.
7.417: Mean while the tepid Caves, and Fens and shoares
7.418: Thir Brood as numerous hatch, from the Egg that soon
7.419: Bursting with kindly rupture forth disclos'd
7.420: Thir callow young, but featherd soon and fledge
7.421: They summ'd thir Penns, and soaring th' air sublime
7.422: With clang despis'd the ground, under a cloud
7.423: In prospect; there the Eagle and the Stork
7.424: On Cliffs and Cedar tops thir Eyries build:
7.425: Part loosly wing the Region, part more wise
7.426: In common, rang'd in figure wedge thir way,
7.427: Intelligent of seasons, and set forth
7.428: Thir Aierie Caravan high over Sea's
7.429: Flying, and over Lands with mutual wing
7.430: Easing thir flight; so stears the prudent Crane
7.431: Her annual Voiage, born on Windes; the Aire
7.432: Floats, as they pass, fann'd with unnumber'd plumes:
7.433: From Branch to Branch the smaller Birds with song
7.434: Solac'd the Woods, and spred thir painted wings
7.435: Till Ev'n, nor then the solemn Nightingal
7.436: Ceas'd warbling, but all night tun'd her soft layes:
7.437: Others on Silver Lakes and Rivers Bath'd
7.438: Thir downie Brest; the Swan with Arched neck
7.439: Between her white wings mantling proudly, Rowes
7.440: Her state with Oarie feet: yet oft they quit
7.441: The Dank, and rising on stiff Pennons, towre
7.442: The mid Aereal Skie: Others on ground
7.443: Walk'd firm; the crested Cock whose clarion sounds
7.444: The silent hours, and th' other whose gay Traine
7.445: Adorns him, colour'd with the Florid hue
7.446: Of Rainbows and Starrie Eyes. The Waters thus
7.447: With Fish replenisht, and the Aire with Fowle,
7.448: Ev'ning and Morn solemniz'd the Fift day.
7.449: The Sixt, and of Creation last arose
7.450: With Eevning Harps and Mattin, when God said,
7.451: Let th' Earth bring forth Fowle living in her kinde,
7.452: Cattel and Creeping things, and Beast of the Earth,
7.453: Each in their kinde. The Earth obey'd, and strait
7.454: Op'ning her fertil Woomb teem'd at a Birth
7.456: Limb'd and full grown: out of the ground up-rose
7.457: As from his Laire the wilde Beast where he wonns
7.458: In Forrest wilde, in Thicket, Brake, or Den;
7.459: Among the Trees in Pairs they rose, they walk'd:
7.460: The Cattel in the Fields and Meddowes green:
7.461: Those rare and solitarie, these in flocks
7.462: Pasturing at once, and in broad Herds upsprung:
7.463: The grassie Clods now Calv'd, now half appeer'd
7.464: The Tawnie Lion, pawing to get free
7.465: His hinder parts, then springs as broke from Bonds,
7.466: And Rampant shakes his Brinded main; the Ounce,
7.467: The Libbard, and the Tyger, as the Moale
7.468: Rising, the crumbl'd Earth above them threw
7.469: In Hillocks; the swift Stag from under ground
7.470: Bore up his branching head: scarse from his mould
7.471: Behemoth biggest born of Earth upheav'd
7.472: His vastness: Fleec't the Flocks and bleating rose,
7.473: As Plants: ambiguous between Sea and Land
7.474: The River Horse and scalie Crocodile.
7.475: At once came forth whatever creeps the ground,
7.476: Insect or Worme; those wav'd thir limber fans
7.477: For wings, and smallest Lineaments exact
7.478: In all the Liveries dect of Summers pride
7.479: With spots of Gold and Purple, azure and green:
7.480: These as a line thir long dimension drew,
7.481: Streaking the ground with sinuous trace; not all
7.482: Minims of Nature; some of Serpent kinde
7.483: Wondrous in length and corpulence involv'd
7.484: Thir Snakie foulds, and added wings. First crept
7.486: Of future, in small room large heart enclos'd,
7.488: Hereafter, join'd in her popular Tribes
7.490: The Femal Bee that feeds her Husband Drone
7.491: Deliciously, and builds her waxen Cells
7.492: With Honey stor'd: the rest are numberless,
7.493: And thou thir Natures know'st, and gav'st them Names,
7.494: Needlest to thee repeated; nor unknown
7.495: The Serpent suttl'st Beast of all the field,
7.496: Of huge extent somtimes, with brazen Eyes
7.497: And hairie Main terrific, though to thee
7.498: Not noxious, but obedient at thy call.
7.499: Now Heav'n in all her Glorie shon, and rowld
7.500: Her motions, as the great first-Movers hand
7.501: First wheeld thir course; Earth in her rich attire
7.502: Consummate lovly smil'd; Aire, Water, Earth,
7.503: By Fowl, Fish, Beast, was flown, was swum, was walkt
7.504: Frequent; and of the Sixt day yet remain'd;
7.505: There wanted yet the Master work, the end
7.506: Of all yet don; a Creature who not prone
7.507: And Brute as other Creatures, but endu'd
7.508: With Sanctitie of Reason, might erect
7.509: His Stature, and upright with Front serene
7.510: Govern the rest, self-knowing, and from thence
7.512: But grateful to acknowledge whence his good
7.513: Descends, thither with heart and voice and eyes
7.515: And worship God Supream, who made him chief
7.516: Of all his works: therefore the Omnipotent
7.517: Eternal Father (For where is not hee
7.518: Present) thus to his Son audibly spake.
7.519: Let us make now Man in our image, Man
7.520: In our similitude, and let them rule
7.521: Over the Fish and Fowle of Sea and Aire,
7.522: Beast of the Field, and over all the Earth,
7.523: And every creeping thing that creeps the ground.
7.524: This said, he formd thee, Adam, thee O Man
7.525: Dust of the ground, and in thy nostrils breath'd
7.526: The breath of Life; in his own Image hee
7.527: Created thee, in the Image of God
7.528: Express, and thou becam'st a living Soul.
7.529: Male he created thee, but thy consort
7.530: Femal for Race; then bless'd Mankinde, and said,
7.531: Be fruitful, multiplie, and fill the Earth,
7.532: Subdue it, and throughout Dominion hold
7.533: Over Fish of the Sea, and Fowle of the Aire,
7.534: And every living thing that moves on the Earth.
7.535: Wherever thus created, for no place
7.536: Is yet distinct by name, thence, as thou know'st
7.537: He brought thee into this delicious Grove,
7.538: This Garden, planted with the Trees of God,
7.539: Delectable both to behold and taste;
7.540: And freely all thir pleasant fruit for food
7.541: Gave thee, all sorts are here that all th' Earth yeelds,
7.542: Varietie without end; but of the Tree
7.543: Which tasted works knowledge of Good and Evil,
7.544: Thou mai'st not; in the day thou eat'st, thou di'st;
7.545: Death is the penaltie impos'd, beware,
7.546: And govern well thy appetite, least sin
7.547: Surprise thee, and her black attendant Death.
7.548: Here finish'd hee, and all that he had made
7.549: View'd, and behold all was entirely good;
7.550: So Ev'n and Morn accomplish'd the Sixt day:
7.551: Yet not till the Creator from his work
7.553: Up to the Heav'n of Heav'ns his high abode,
7.554: Thence to behold this new created World
7.555: Th' addition of his Empire, how it shew'd
7.556: In prospect from his Throne, how good, how faire,
7.557: Answering his great Idea. Up he rode
7.558: Followd with acclamation and the sound
7.559: Symphonious of ten thousand Harpes that tun'd
7.560: Angelic harmonies: the Earth, the Aire
7.562: The Heav'ns and all the Constellations rung,
7.563: The Planets in thir stations list'ning stood,
7.564: While the bright Pomp ascended jubilant.
7.565: Open, ye everlasting Gates, they sung,
7.566: Open, ye Heav'ns, your living dores; let in
7.567: The great Creator from his work returnd
7.568: Magnificent, his Six days work, a World;
7.569: Open, and henceforth oft; for God will deigne
7.570: To visit oft the dwellings of just Men
7.572: Thither will send his winged Messengers
7.573: On errands of supernal Grace. So sung
7.574: The glorious Train ascending: He through Heav'n,
7.575: That open'd wide her blazing Portals, led
7.576: To Gods Eternal house direct the way,
7.577: A broad and ample rode, whose dust is Gold
7.578: And pavement Starrs, as Starrs to thee appeer,
7.579: Seen in the Galaxie, that Milkie way
7.580: Which nightly as a circling Zone thou seest
7.581: Pouderd with Starrs. And now on Earth the Seaventh
7.582: Eev'ning arose in Eden, for the Sun
7.583: Was set, and twilight from the East came on,
7.584: Forerunning Night; when at the holy mount
7.585: Of Heav'ns high-seated top, th' Impereal Throne
7.586: Of Godhead, fixt for ever firm and sure,
7.587: The Filial Power arriv'd, and sate him down
7.588: With his great Father (for he also went
7.590: Hath Omnipresence) and the work ordain'd,
7.591: Author and end of all things, and from work
7.592: Now resting, bless'd and hallowd the Seav'nth day,
7.593: As resting on that day from all his work,
7.594: But not in silence holy kept; the Harp
7.595: Had work and rested not, the solemn Pipe,
7.596: And Dulcimer, all Organs of sweet stop,
7.597: All sounds on Fret by String or Golden Wire
7.598: Temper'd soft Tunings, intermixt with Voice
7.599: Choral or Unison: of incense Clouds
7.600: Fuming from Golden Censers hid the Mount.
7.601: Creation and the Six dayes acts they sung,
7.602: Great are thy works, Jehovah, infinite
7.603: Thy power; what thought can measure thee or tongue
7.604: Relate thee; greater now in thy return
7.605: Then from the Giant Angels; thee that day
7.606: Thy Thunders magnifi'd; but to create
7.607: Is greater then created to destroy.
7.608: Who can impair thee, mighty King, or bound
7.609: Thy Empire? easily the proud attempt
7.610: Of Spirits apostat and thir Counsels vaine
7.611: Thou hast repeld, while impiously they thought
7.612: Thee to diminish, and from thee withdraw
7.613: The number of thy worshippers. Who seekes
7.614: To lessen thee, against his purpose serves
7.615: To manifest the more thy might: his evil
7.616: Thou usest, and from thence creat'st more good.
7.617: Witness this new-made World, another Heav'n
7.618: From Heaven Gate not farr, founded in view
7.619: On the cleer Hyaline, the Glassie Sea;
7.620: Of amplitude almost immense, with Starr's
7.621: Numerous, and every Starr perhaps a World
7.622: Of destind habitation; but thou know'st
7.623: Thir seasons: among these the seat of men,
7.624: Earth with her nether Ocean circumfus'd,
7.625: Thir pleasant dwelling place. Thrice happie men,
7.626: And sons of men, whom God hath thus advanc't,
7.627: Created in his Image, there to dwell
7.628: And worship him, and in reward to rule
7.629: Over his Works, on Earth, in Sea, or Air,
7.630: And multiply a Race of Worshippers
7.631: Holy and just: thrice happie if they know
7.633: So sung they, and the Empyrean rung,
7.634: With Halleluiahs: Thus was Sabbath kept.
7.635: And thy request think now fulfill'd, that ask'd
7.636: How first this World and face of things began,
7.637: And what before thy memorie was don
7.639: Informd by thee might know; if else thou seekst
7.640: Aught, not surpassing human measure, say.

8.0:
*The Argument*
Adam inquires concerning celestial Motions, is doubtfully answer'd and exhorted to search rather things more worthy of knowledg: Adam assents, and still desirous to detain Raphael, relates to him what he remember'd since his own Creation, his placing in Paradise, his talk with God concerning solitude and fit society, his first meeting and Nuptials with Eve, his discourse with the Angel thereupon; who after admonitions repeated departs.
8.1: [THE Angel ended, and in Adams Eare
8.2: So Charming left his voice, that he a while
8.3: Thought him still speaking, still stood fixt to hear;
8.4: Then as new wak't thus gratefully repli'd.]
8.5: What thanks sufficient, or what recompence
8.6: Equal have I to render thee, Divine
8.7: Hystorian, who thus largely hast allayd
8.8: The thirst I had of knowledge, and voutsaf't
8.10: Things else by me unsearchable, now heard
8.11: With wonder, but delight, and, as is due,
8.12: With glorie attributed to the high
8.13: Creator; some thing yet of doubt remaines,
8.14: Which onely thy solution can resolve.
8.15: When I behold this goodly Frame, this World
8.16: Of Heav'n and Earth consisting, and compute,
8.17: Thir magnitudes, this Earth a spot, a graine,
8.18: An Atom, with the Firmament compar'd
8.19: And all her numberd Starrs, that seem to rowle
8.21: Thir distance argues and thir swift return
8.23: Round this opacous Earth, this punctual spot,
8.24: One day and night; in all thir vast survey
8.25: Useless besides, reasoning I oft admire,
8.26: How Nature wise and frugal could commit
8.28: So many nobler Bodies to create,
8.29: Greater so manifold to this one use,
8.30: For aught appeers, and on thir Orbs impose
8.31: Such restless revolution day by day
8.33: That better might with farr less compass move,
8.34: Serv'd by more noble then her self, attaines
8.35: Her end without least motion, and receaves,
8.36: As Tribute such a sumless journey brought
8.37: Of incorporeal speed, her warmth and light;
8.38: Speed, to describe whose swiftness Number failes.
8.39: So spake our Sire, and by his count'nance seemd
8.40: Entring on studious thoughts abstruse, which Eve
8.41: Perceaving where she sat retir'd in sight,
8.42: With lowliness Majestic from her seat,
8.43: And Grace that won who saw to wish her stay,
8.44: Rose, and went forth among her Fruits and Flours,
8.45: To visit how they prosper'd, bud and bloom,
8.46: Her Nurserie; they at her coming sprung
8.47: And toucht by her fair tendance gladlier grew.
8.48: Yet went she not, as not with such discourse
8.49: Delighted, or not capable her eare
8.50: Of what was high: such pleasure she reserv'd,
8.52: Her Husband the Relater she preferr'd
8.53: Before the Angel, and of him to ask
8.54: Chose rather; hee, she knew would intermix
8.55: Grateful digressions, and solve high dispute
8.56: With conjugal Caresses, from his Lip
8.57: Not Words alone pleas'd her. O when meet now
8.58: Such pairs, in Love and mutual Honour joyn'd?
8.59: With Goddess-like demeanour forth she went;
8.60: Not unattended, for on her as Queen
8.61: A pomp of winning Graces waited still,
8.62: And from about her shot Darts of desire
8.63: Into all Eyes to wish her still in sight.
8.64: And Raphael now to Adam's doubt propos'd
8.66: To ask or search I blame thee not, for Heav'n
8.67: Is as the Book of God before thee set,
8.68: Wherein to read his wondrous Works, and learne
8.69: His Seasons, Hours, or Days, or Months, or Yeares:
8.70: This to attain, whether Heav'n move or Earth,
8.71: Imports not, if thou reck'n right, the rest
8.72: From Man or Angel the great Architect
8.73: Did wisely to conceal, and not divulge
8.74: His secrets to be scann'd by them who ought
8.75: Rather admire; or if they list to try
8.76: Conjecture, he his Fabric of the Heav'ns
8.77: Hath left to thir disputes, perhaps to move
8.78: His laughter at thir quaint Opinions wide
8.79: Hereafter, when they come to model Heav'n
8.80: And calculate the Starrs, how they will weild
8.81: The mightie frame, how build, unbuild, contrive
8.82: To save appeerances, how gird the Sphear
8.83: With Centric and Eccentric scribl'd o're,
8.84: Cycle and Epicycle, Orb in Orb:
8.85: Alreadie by thy reasoning this I guess,
8.86: Who art to lead thy ofspring, and supposest
8.87: That Bodies bright and greater should not serve
8.88: The less not bright, nor Heav'n such journies run,
8.89: Earth sitting still, when she alone receaves
8.90: The benefit: consider first, that Great
8.91: Or Bright inferrs not Excellence: the Earth
8.92: Though, in comparison of Heav'n, so small,
8.93: Nor glistering, may of solid good containe
8.94: More plenty then the Sun that barren shines,
8.95: Whose vertue on it self workes no effect,
8.96: But in the fruitful Earth; there first receavd
8.97: His beams, unactive else, thir vigor find.
8.98: Yet not to Earth are those bright Luminaries
8.99: Officious, but to thee Earths habitant.
8.100: And for the Heav'ns wide Circuit, let it speak
8.101: The Makers high magnificence, who built
8.102: So spacious, and his Line stretcht out so farr;
8.103: That Man may know he dwells not in his own;
8.104: An Edifice too large for him to fill,
8.105: Lodg'd in a small partition, and the rest
8.106: Ordain'd for uses to his Lord best known.
8.107: The swiftness of those Circles attribute,
8.109: That to corporeal substances could adde
8.110: Speed almost Spiritual; mee thou thinkst not slow,
8.111: Who since the Morning hour set out from Heav'n
8.112: Where God resides, and ere mid-day arriv'd
8.114: By Numbers that have name. But this I urge,
8.115: Admitting Motion in the Heav'ns, to shew
8.116: Invalid that which thee to doubt it mov'd;
8.117: Not that I so affirm, though so it seem
8.118: To thee who hast thy dwelling here on Earth.
8.119: God to remove his wayes from human sense,
8.120: Plac'd Heav'n from Earth so farr, that earthly sight,
8.121: If it presume, might erre in things too high,
8.122: And no advantage gaine. What if the Sun
8.123: Be Center to the World, and other Starrs
8.124: By his attractive vertue and thir own
8.125: Incited, dance about him various rounds?
8.126: Thir wandring course now high, now low, then hid,
8.128: In six thou seest, and what if sev'nth to these
8.129: The Planet Earth, so stedfast though she seem,
8.131: Which else to several Sphears thou must ascribe,
8.133: Or save the Sun his labour, and that swift
8.135: Invisible else above all Starrs, the Wheele
8.136: Of Day and Night; which needs not thy beleefe,
8.137: If Earth industrious of her self fetch Day
8.138: Travelling East, and with her part averse
8.139: From the Suns beam meet Night, her other part
8.140: Still luminous by his ray. What if that light
8.141: Sent from her through the wide transpicuous aire,
8.142: To the terrestrial Moon be as a Starr
8.143: Enlightning her by Day, as she by Night
8.144: This Earth? reciprocal, if Land be there,
8.145: Feilds and Inhabitants: Her spots thou seest
8.146: As Clouds, and Clouds may rain, and Rain produce
8.147: Fruits in her soft'nd Soile, for some to eate
8.148: Allotted there; and other Suns perhaps
8.149: With thir attendant Moons thou wilt descrie
8.151: Which two great Sexes animate the World,
8.152: Stor'd in each Orb perhaps with some that live.
8.153: For such vast room in Nature unpossest
8.154: By living Soule, desert and desolate,
8.155: Onely to shine, yet scarce to contribute
8.156: Each Orb a glimps of Light, conveyd so farr
8.157: Down to this habitable, which returnes
8.158: Light back to them, is obvious to dispute.
8.159: But whether thus these things, or whether not,
8.160: Whether the Sun predominant in Heav'n
8.161: Rise on the Earth, or Earth rise on the Sun,
8.162: Hee from the East his flaming rode begin,
8.163: Or Shee from West her silent course advance
8.164: With inoffensive pace that spinning sleeps
8.165: On her soft Axle, while she paces Eev'n,
8.166: And bears thee soft with the smooth Air along,
8.167: Sollicit not thy thoughts with matters hid,
8.168: Leave them to God above, him serve and feare;
8.169: Of other Creatures, as him pleases best,
8.170: Wherever plac't, let him dispose: joy thou
8.171: In what he gives to thee, this Paradise
8.172: And thy faire Eve; Heav'n is for thee too high
8.173: To know what passes there; be lowlie wise:
8.174: Think onely what concernes thee and thy being;
8.175: Dream not of other Worlds, what Creatures there
8.176: Live, in what state, condition or degree,
8.177: Contented that thus farr hath been reveal'd
8.178: Not of Earth onely but of highest Heav'n.
8.179: To whom thus Adam cleerd of doubt, repli'd.
8.180: How fully hast thou satisfi'd mee, pure
8.182: And freed from intricacies, taught to live,
8.183: The easiest way, nor with perplexing thoughts
8.184: To interrupt the sweet of Life, from which
8.185: God hath bid dwell farr off all anxious cares,
8.186: And not molest us, unless we our selves
8.187: Seek them with wandring thoughts, and notions vaine.
8.188: But apt the Mind or Fancie is to roave
8.189: Uncheckt, and of her roaving is no end;
8.190: Till warn'd, or by experience taught, she learne,
8.191: That not to know at large of things remote
8.192: From use, obscure and suttle, but to know
8.193: That which before us lies in daily life,
8.194: Is the prime Wisdom, what is more, is fume,
8.196: And renders us in things that most concerne
8.197: Unpractis'd, unprepar'd, and still to seek.
8.198: Therefore from this high pitch let us descend
8.199: A lower flight, and speak of things at hand
8.200: Useful, whence haply mention may arise
8.201: Of somthing not unseasonable to ask
8.202: By sufferance, and thy wonted favour deign'd.
8.203: Thee I have heard relating what was don
8.204: Ere my remembrance: now hear mee relate
8.205: My Storie, which perhaps thou hast not heard;
8.206: And Day is yet not spent; till then thou seest
8.207: How suttly to detaine thee I devise,
8.208: Inviting thee to hear while I relate,
8.209: Fond, were it not in hope of thy reply:
8.210: For while I sit with thee, I seem in Heav'n,
8.211: And sweeter thy discourse is to my eare
8.212: Then Fruits of Palm-tree pleasantest to thirst
8.213: And hunger both, from labour, at the houre
8.214: Of sweet repast; they satiate, and soon fill,
8.215: Though pleasant, but thy words with Grace Divine
8.216: Imbu'd, bring to thir sweetness no satietie.
8.217: To whom thus Raphael answer'd heav'nly meek.
8.218: Nor are thy lips ungraceful, Sire of men,
8.219: Nor tongue ineloquent; for God on thee
8.220: Abundantly his gifts hath also pour'd,
8.221: Inward and outward both, his image faire:
8.222: Speaking or mute all comliness and grace
8.223: Attends thee, and each word, each motion formes.
8.224: Nor less think wee in Heav'n of thee on Earth
8.225: Then of our fellow servant, and inquire
8.226: Gladly into the wayes of God with Man:
8.227: For God we see hath honour'd thee, and set
8.228: On Man his equal Love: say therefore on;
8.229: For I that Day was absent, as befell,
8.230: Bound on a voyage uncouth and obscure,
8.231: Farr on excursion toward the Gates of Hell;
8.232: Squar'd in full Legion (such command we had)
8.233: To see that none thence issu'd forth a spie,
8.234: Or enemie, while God was in his work,
8.235: Least hee incenst at such eruption bold,
8.236: Destruction with Creation might have mixt.
8.237: Not that they durst without his leave attempt,
8.238: But us he sends upon his high behests
8.239: For state, as Sovran King, and to enure
8.240: Our prompt obedience. Fast we found, fast shut
8.241: The dismal Gates, and barricado'd strong;
8.242: But long ere our approaching heard within
8.243: Noise, other then the sound of Dance or Song,
8.244: Torment, and lowd lament, and furious rage.
8.245: Glad we return'd up to the coasts of Light
8.246: Ere Sabbath Eev'ning: so we had in charge.
8.247: But thy relation now; for I attend,
8.248: Pleas'd with thy words no less then thou with mine.
8.249: So spake the Godlike Power, and thus our Sire.
8.250: For Man to tell how human Life began
8.251: Is hard; for who himself beginning knew?
8.252: Desire with thee still longer to converse
8.253: Induc'd me. As new wak't from soundest sleep
8.254: Soft on the flourie herb I found me laid
8.255: In Balmie Sweat, which with his Beames the Sun
8.256: Soon dri'd, and on the reaking moisture fed.
8.257: Strait toward Heav'n my wondring Eyes I turnd,
8.258: And gaz'd a while the ample Skie, till rais'd
8.259: By quick instinctive motion up I sprung,
8.261: Stood on my feet; about me round I saw
8.262: Hill, Dale, and shadie Woods, and sunnie Plaines,
8.263: And liquid Lapse of murmuring Streams; by these,
8.264: Creatures that livd, and movd, and walk'd, or flew,
8.265: Birds on the branches warbling; all things smil'd,
8.266: With fragrance and with joy my heart oreflow'd.
8.267: My self I then perus'd, and Limb by Limb
8.268: Survey'd, and sometimes went, and sometimes ran
8.269: With supple joints, as lively vigour led:
8.270: But who I was, or where, or from what cause,
8.271: Knew not; to speak I tri'd, and forthwith spake,
8.272: My Tongue obey'd and readily could name
8.273: What e're I saw. Thou Sun, said I, faire Light,
8.274: And thou enlight'nd Earth, so fresh and gay,
8.275: Ye Hills and Dales, ye Rivers, Woods, and Plaines,
8.276: And ye that live and move, fair Creatures, tell,
8.277: Tell, if ye saw, how came I thus, how here?
8.278: Not of my self; by some great Maker then,
8.279: In goodness and in power praeeminent;
8.280: Tell me, how may I know him, how adore,
8.281: From whom I have that thus I move and live,
8.282: And feel that I am happier then I know.
8.283: While thus I call'd, and stray'd I knew not whither,
8.284: From where I first drew Aire, and first beheld
8.285: This happie Light, when answer none return'd,
8.286: On a green shadie Bank profuse of Flours
8.287: Pensive I sate me down; there gentle sleep
8.288: First found me, and with soft oppression seis'd
8.289: My droused sense, untroubl'd, though I thought
8.290: I then was passing to my former state
8.292: When suddenly stood at my Head a dream,
8.294: My Fancy to believe I yet had being,
8.295: And livd: One came, methought, of shape Divine,
8.296: And said, thy Mansion wants thee, Adam, rise,
8.297: First Man, of Men innumerable ordain'd
8.298: First Father, call'd by thee I come thy Guide
8.299: To the Garden of bliss, thy seat prepar'd.
8.300: So saying, by the hand he took me rais'd,
8.301: And over Fields and Waters, as in Aire
8.302: Smooth sliding without step, last led me up
8.303: A woodie Mountain; whose high top was plaine,
8.304: A Circuit wide, enclos'd, with goodliest Trees
8.305: Planted, with Walks, and Bowers, that what I saw
8.306: Of Earth before scarse pleasant seemd. Each Tree
8.307: Load'n with fairest Fruit, that hung to the Eye
8.308: Tempting, stirr'd in me sudden appetite
8.309: To pluck and eate; whereat I wak'd, and found
8.310: Before mine Eyes all real, as the dream
8.311: Had lively shadowd: Here had new begun
8.312: My wandring, had not hee who was my Guide
8.313: Up hither, from among the Trees appeer'd,
8.314: Presence Divine. Rejoycing, but with aw
8.315: In adoration at his feet I fell
8.316: Submiss: he rear'd me, & Whom thou soughtst I am,
8.317: Said mildely, Author of all this thou seest
8.318: Above, or round about thee or beneath.
8.319: This Paradise I give thee, count it thine
8.320: To Till and keep, and of the Fruit to eate:
8.321: Of every Tree that in the Garden growes
8.322: Eate freely with glad heart; fear here no dearth:
8.323: But of the Tree whose operation brings
8.324: Knowledg of good and ill, which I have set
8.325: The Pledge of thy Obedience and thy Faith,
8.326: Amid the Garden by the Tree of Life,
8.327: Remember what I warne thee, shun to taste,
8.328: And shun the bitter consequence: for know,
8.329: The day thou eat'st thereof, my sole command
8.331: From that day mortal, and this happie State
8.332: Shalt loose, expell'd from hence into a World
8.333: Of woe and sorrow. Sternly he pronounc'd
8.335: Yet dreadful in mine eare, though in my choice
8.336: Not to incur; but soon his cleer aspect
8.337: Return'd and gratious purpose thus renew'd.
8.338: Not onely these fair bounds, but all the Earth
8.339: To thee and to thy Race I give; as Lords
8.340: Possess it, and all things that therein live,
8.341: Or live in Sea, or Aire, Beast, Fish, and Fowle.
8.342: In signe whereof each Bird and Beast behold
8.343: After thir kindes; I bring them to receave
8.344: From thee thir Names, and pay thee fealtie
8.345: With low subjection; understand the same
8.346: Of Fish within thir watry residence,
8.347: Not hither summond, since they cannot change
8.348: Thir Element to draw the thinner Aire.
8.349: As thus he spake, each Bird and Beast behold
8.350: Approaching two and two, These cowring low
8.351: With blandishment, each Bird stoop'd on his wing.
8.352: I nam'd them, as they pass'd, and understood
8.353: Thir Nature, with such knowledg God endu'd
8.354: My sudden apprehension: but in these
8.355: I found not what me thought I wanted still;
8.356: And to the Heav'nly vision thus presum'd.
8.357: O by what Name, for thou above all these,
8.358: Above mankinde, or aught then mankinde higher,
8.359: Surpassest farr my naming, how may I
8.360: Adore thee, Author of this Universe,
8.361: And all this good to man, for whose well being
8.362: So amply, and with hands so liberal
8.363: Thou hast provided all things: but with mee
8.364: I see not who partakes. In solitude
8.365: What happiness, who can enjoy alone,
8.366: Or all enjoying, what contentment find?
8.367: Thus I presumptuous; and the vision bright,
8.368: As with a smile more bright'nd, thus repli'd.
8.369: What call'st thou solitude, is not the Earth
8.370: With various living creatures, and the Aire
8.371: Replenisht, and all these at thy command
8.372: To come and play before thee, know'st thou not
8.373: Thir language and thir wayes, they also know,
8.374: And reason not contemptibly; with these
8.375: Find pastime, and beare rule; thy Realm is large.
8.376: So spake the Universal Lord, and seem'd
8.377: So ordering. I with leave of speech implor'd,
8.379: Let not my words offend thee, Heav'nly Power,
8.380: My Maker, be propitious while I speak.
8.381: Hast thou not made me here thy substitute,
8.382: And these inferiour farr beneath me set?
8.384: Can sort, what harmonie or true delight?
8.385: Which must be mutual, in proportion due
8.386: Giv'n and receiv'd; but in disparitie
8.387: The one intense, the other still remiss
8.388: Cannot well suite with either, but soon prove
8.389: Tedious alike: Of fellowship I speak
8.390: Such as I seek, fit to participate
8.391: All rational delight, wherein the brute
8.392: Cannot be human consort; they rejoyce
8.393: Each with thir kinde, Lion with Lioness;
8.394: So fitly them in pairs thou hast combin'd;
8.395: Much less can Bird with Beast, or Fish with Fowle
8.396: So well converse, nor with the Ox the Ape;
8.397: Wors then can Man with Beast, and least of all.
8.398: Whereto th' Almighty answer'd, not displeas'd.
8.399: A nice and suttle happiness I see
8.400: Thou to thy self proposest, in the choice
8.401: Of thy Associates, Adam, and wilt taste
8.402: No pleasure, though in pleasure, solitarie.
8.403: What thinkst thou then of mee, and this my State,
8.404: Seem I to thee sufficiently possest
8.405: Of happiness, or not? who am alone
8.406: From all Eternitie, for none I know
8.407: Second to mee or like, equal much less.
8.408: How have I then with whom to hold converse
8.409: Save with the Creatures which I made, and those
8.411: Beneath what other Creatures are to thee?
8.412: He ceas'd, I lowly answer'd. To attaine
8.413: The highth and depth of thy Eternal wayes
8.414: All human thoughts come short, Supream of things;
8.415: Thou in thy self art perfet, and in thee
8.416: Is no deficience found; not so is Man,
8.417: But in degree, the cause of his desire
8.418: By conversation with his like to help,
8.419: Or solace his defects. No need that thou
8.421: And through all numbers absolute, though One;
8.422: But Man by number is to manifest
8.424: Like of his like, his Image multipli'd,
8.427: Thou in thy secresie although alone,
8.428: Best with thy self accompanied, seek'st not
8.430: Canst raise thy Creature to what highth thou wilt
8.432: I by conversing cannot these erect
8.433: From prone, nor in thir wayes complacence find.
8.434: Thus I embold'nd spake, and freedom us'd
8.435: Permissive, and acceptance found, which gain'd
8.436: This answer from the gratious voice Divine.
8.437: Thus farr to try thee, Adam, I was pleas'd,
8.438: And finde thee knowing not of Beasts alone,
8.439: Which thou hast rightly nam'd, but of thy self,
8.440: Expressing well the spirit within thee free,
8.441: My Image, not imparted to the Brute,
8.442: Whose fellowship therefore unmeet for thee
8.443: Good reason was thou freely shouldst dislike,
8.444: And be so minded still; I, ere thou spak'st,
8.445: Knew it not good for Man to be alone,
8.446: And no such companie as then thou saw'st
8.447: Intended thee, for trial onely brought,
8.448: To see how thou could'st judge of fit and meet:
8.449: What next I bring shall please thee, be assur'd,
8.450: Thy likeness, thy fit help, thy other self,
8.451: Thy wish, exactly to thy hearts desire.
8.452: Hee ended, or I heard no more, for now
8.453: My earthly by his Heav'nly overpowerd,
8.454: Which it had long stood under, streind to the highth
8.456: As with an object that excels the sense,
8.457: Dazl'd and spent, sunk down, and sought repair
8.458: Of sleep, which instantly fell on me, call'd
8.459: By Nature as in aide, and clos'd mine eyes.
8.460: Mine eyes he clos'd, but op'n left the Cell
8.461: Of Fancie my internal sight, by which
8.462: Abstract as in a transe methought I saw,
8.463: Though sleeping, where I lay, and saw the shape
8.464: Still glorious before whom awake I stood;
8.465: Who stooping op'nd my left side, and took
8.466: From thence a Rib, with cordial spirits warme,
8.467: And Life-blood streaming fresh; wide was the wound,
8.468: But suddenly with flesh fill'd up & heal'd:
8.469: The Rib he formd and fashond with his hands;
8.470: Under his forming hands a Creature grew,
8.471: Manlike, but different sex, so lovly faire,
8.472: That what seemd fair in all the World, seemd now
8.473: Mean, or in her summd up, in her containd
8.474: And in her looks, which from that time infus'd
8.475: Sweetness into my heart, unfelt before,
8.476: And into all things from her Aire inspir'd
8.477: The spirit of love and amorous delight.
8.478: She disappeerd, and left me dark, I wak'd
8.479: To find her, or for ever to deplore
8.480: Her loss, and other pleasures all abjure:
8.481: When out of hope, behold her, not farr off,
8.482: Such as I saw her in my dream, adornd
8.483: With what all Earth or Heaven could bestow
8.484: To make her amiable: On she came,
8.485: Led by her Heav'nly Maker, though unseen,
8.486: And guided by his voice, nor uninformd
8.487: Of nuptial Sanctitie and marriage Rites:
8.488: Grace was in all her steps, Heav'n in her Eye,
8.489: In every gesture dignitie and love.
8.490: I overjoyd could not forbear aloud.
8.491: This turn hath made amends; thou hast fulfill'd
8.492: Thy words, Creator bounteous and benigne,
8.493: Giver of all things faire, but fairest this
8.494: Of all thy gifts, nor enviest. I now see
8.495: Bone of my Bone, Flesh of my Flesh, my Self
8.496: Before me; Woman is her Name, of Man
8.497: Extracted; for this cause he shall forgoe
8.498: Father and Mother, and to his Wife adhere;
8.499: And they shall be one Flesh, one Heart, one Soule.
8.500: She heard me thus, and though divinely brought,
8.502: Her vertue and the conscience of her worth,
8.503: That would be woo'd, and not unsought be won,
8.504: Not obvious, not obtrusive, but retir'd,
8.505: The more desirable, or to say all,
8.506: Nature her self, though pure of sinful thought,
8.507: Wrought in her so, that seeing me, she turn'd;
8.508: I follow'd her, she what was Honour knew,
8.510: My pleaded reason. To the Nuptial Bowre
8.511: I led her blushing like the Morn: all Heav'n,
8.512: And happie Constellations on that houre
8.513: Shed thir selectest influence; the Earth
8.514: Gave sign of gratulation, and each Hill;
8.515: Joyous the Birds; fresh Gales and gentle Aires
8.516: Whisper'd it to the Woods, and from thir wings
8.517: Flung Rose, flung Odours from the spicie Shrub,
8.518: Disporting, till the amorous Bird of Night
8.519: Sung Spousal, and bid haste the Eevning Starr
8.520: On his Hill top, to light the bridal Lamp.
8.521: Thus I have told thee all my State, and brought
8.522: My Storie to the sum of earthly bliss
8.523: Which I enjoy, and must confess to find
8.524: In all things else delight indeed, but such
8.525: As us'd or not, works in the mind no change,
8.527: I mean of Taste, Sight, Smell, Herbs, Fruits, & Flours,
8.528: Walks, and the melodie of Birds; but here
8.530: Transported touch; here passion first I felt,
8.531: Commotion strange, in all enjoyments else
8.532: Superiour and unmov'd, here onely weake
8.533: Against the charm of Beauties powerful glance.
8.534: Or Nature faild in mee, and left some part
8.535: Not proof enough such Object to sustain,
8.536: Or from my side subducting, took perhaps
8.537: More then enough; at least on her bestow'd
8.538: Too much of Ornament, in outward shew
8.540: For well I understand in the prime end
8.541: Of Nature her th' inferiour, in the mind
8.542: And inward Faculties, which most excell,
8.543: In outward also her resembling less
8.544: His Image who made both, and less expressing
8.545: The character of that Dominion giv'n
8.546: O're other Creatures; yet when I approach
8.547: Her loveliness, so absolute she seems
8.548: And in her self compleat, so well to know
8.549: Her own, that what she wills to do or say,
8.551: All higher knowledge in her presence falls
8.552: Degraded, Wisdom in discourse with her
8.553: Looses discount'nanc't, and like folly shewes;
8.554: Authoritie and Reason on her waite,
8.555: As one intended first, not after made
8.557: Greatness of mind and nobleness thir seat
8.558: Build in her loveliest, and create an awe
8.559: About her, as a guard Angelic plac't.
8.560: To whom the Angel with contracted brow.
8.561: Accuse not Nature, she hath don her part;
8.562: Do thou but thine, and be not diffident
8.563: Of Wisdom, she deserts thee not, if thou
8.564: Dismiss not her, when most thou needst her nigh,
8.566: Less excellent, as thou thy self perceav'st.
8.567: For what admir'st thou, what transports thee so,
8.568: An outside? fair no doubt, and worthy well
8.569: Thy cherishing, thy honouring, and thy love,
8.570: Not thy subjection: weigh with her thy self;
8.571: Then value: Oft times nothing profits more
8.572: Then self-esteem, grounded on just and right
8.573: Well manag'd; of that skill the more thou know'st,
8.574: The more she will acknowledge thee her Head,
8.575: And to realities yeild all her shows;
8.576: Made so adorn for thy delight the more,
8.577: So awful, that with honour thou maist love
8.578: Thy mate, who sees when thou art seen least wise.
8.579: But if the sense of touch whereby mankind
8.580: Is propagated seem such dear delight
8.581: Beyond all other, think the same voutsaf't
8.582: To Cattel and each Beast; which would not be
8.583: To them made common & divulg'd, if aught
8.584: Therein enjoy'd were worthy to subdue
8.585: The Soule of Man, or passion in him move.
8.586: What higher in her societie thou findst
8.588: In loving thou dost well, in passion not,
8.589: Wherein true Love consists not; love refines
8.590: The thoughts, and heart enlarges, hath his seat
8.591: In Reason, and is judicious, is the scale
8.592: By which to heav'nly Love thou maist ascend,
8.593: Not sunk in carnal pleasure, for which cause
8.594: Among the Beasts no Mate for thee was found.
8.595: To whom thus half abash't Adam repli'd.
8.596: Neither her out-side formd so fair, nor aught
8.597: In procreation common to all kindes
8.598: (Though higher of the genial Bed by far,
8.599: And with mysterious reverence I deem)
8.600: So much delights me, as those graceful acts,
8.601: Those thousand decencies that daily flow
8.602: From all her words and actions, mixt with Love
8.603: And sweet compliance, which declare unfeign'd
8.604: Union of Mind, or in us both one Soule;
8.605: Harmonie to behold in wedded pair
8.606: More grateful then harmonious sound to the eare.
8.607: Yet these subject not; I to thee disclose
8.608: What inward thence I feel, not therefore foild,
8.609: Who meet with various objects, from the sense
8.611: Approve the best, and follow what I approve.
8.612: To love thou blam'st me not, for love thou saist
8.613: Leads up to Heav'n, is both the way and guide;
8.614: Bear with me then, if lawful what I ask;
8.615: Love not the heav'nly Spirits, and how thir Love
8.616: Express they, by looks onely, or do they mix
8.618: To whom the Angel with a smile that glow'd
8.619: Celestial rosie red, Loves proper hue,
8.620: Answer'd. Let it suffice thee that thou know'st
8.621: Us happie, and without Love no happiness.
8.622: Whatever pure thou in the body enjoy'st
8.623: (And pure thou wert created) we enjoy
8.624: In eminence, and obstacle find none
8.625: Of membrane, joynt, or limb, exclusive barrs:
8.626: Easier then Air with Air, if Spirits embrace,
8.627: Total they mix, Union of Pure with Pure
8.629: As Flesh to mix with Flesh, or Soul with Soul.
8.630: But I can now no more; the parting Sun
8.631: Beyond the Earths green Cape and verdant Isles
8.632: Hesperean sets, my Signal to depart.
8.633: Be strong, live happie, and love, but first of all
8.634: Him whom to love is to obey, and keep
8.635: His great command; take heed least Passion sway
8.636: Thy Judgement to do aught, which else free Will
8.637: Would not admit; thine and of all thy Sons
8.638: The weal or woe in thee is plac't; beware.
8.639: I in thy persevering shall rejoyce,
8.640: And all the Blest: stand fast; to stand or fall
8.641: Free in thine own Arbitrement it lies.
8.642: Perfet within, no outward aid require;
8.643: And all temptation to transgress repel.
8.644: So saying, he arose; whom Adam thus
8.645: Follow'd with benediction. Since to part,
8.647: Sent from whose sovran goodness I adore.
8.648: Gentle to me and affable hath been
8.649: Thy condescension, and shall be honour'd ever
8.650: With grateful Memorie: thou to mankind
8.651: Be good and friendly still, and oft return.
8.652: So parted they, the Angel up to Heav'n
8.653: From the thick shade, and Adam to his Bowre.

9.0:
*The Argument*
Satan having compast the Earth, with meditated guile returns as a mist by Night into Paradise, enters into the Serpent sleeping. Adam and Eve in the Morning go forth to thir labours, which Eve proposes to divide in several places, each labouring apart: Adam consents not, alledging the danger, lest that Enemy, of whom they were forewarn'd, should attempt her found alone: Eve loath to be thought not circumspect or firm enough, urges her going apart, the rather desirous to make tryal of her strength; Adam at last yields: The Serpent finds her alone; his subtle approach, first gazing, then speaking with much flattery extolling Eve above all other Creatures. Eve wondring to hear the Serpent speak, asks how he attain'd to human speech and such understanding not till now; the Serpent answers, that by tasting of a certain Tree in the Garden he attain'd both to Speech and Reason, till then void of both: Eve requires him to bring her to that Tree, and finds it to be the Tree of Knowledge forbidden: The Serpent now grown bolder, with many wiles and arguments induces her at length to eat; she pleas'd with the taste deliberates awhile whether to impart thereof to Adam or not, at last brings him of the Fruit, relates what persuaded her to eat thereof: Adam at first amaz'd, but perceiving her lost, resolves through vehemence of love to perish with her; and extenuating the trespass, eats also of the Fruit: The effects thereof in them both; they seek to cover thir nakedness; then fall to variance and accusation of one another.
9.1: No more of talk where God or Angel Guest
9.2: With Man, as with his Friend, familiar us'd
9.3: To sit indulgent, and with him partake
9.4: Rural repast, permitting him the while
9.5: Venial discourse unblam'd: I now must change
9.6: Those Notes to Tragic; foul distrust, and breach
9.7: Disloyal on the part of Man, revolt
9.8: And disobedience: On the part of Heav'n
9.10: Anger and just rebuke, and judgement giv'n,
9.11: That brought into this World a world of woe,
9.12: Sinne and her shadow Death, and Miserie
9.13: Deaths Harbinger: Sad task, yet argument
9.14: Not less but more Heroic then the wrauth
9.15: Of stern Achilles on his Foe pursu'd
9.16: Thrice Fugitive about Troy Wall; or rage
9.18: Or Neptun's ire or Juno's, that so long
9.19: Perplex'd the Greek and Cytherea's Son;
9.20: If answerable style I can obtaine
9.21: Of my Celestial Patroness, who deignes
9.23: And dictates to me slumbring, or inspires
9.25: Since first this subject for Heroic Song
9.26: Pleas'd me long choosing, and beginning late;
9.27: Not sedulous by Nature to indite
9.29: Heroic deem'd, chief maistrie to dissect
9.30: With long and tedious havoc fabl'd Knights
9.31: In Battels feign'd; the better fortitude
9.33: Unsung; or to describe Races and Games,
9.36: Bases and tinsel Trappings, gorgious Knights
9.37: At Joust and Torneament; then marshal'd Feast
9.38: Serv'd up in Hall with Sewers, and Seneshals;
9.39: The skill of Artifice or Office mean,
9.40: Not that which justly gives Heroic name
9.41: To Person or to Poem. Mee of these
9.42: Nor skilld nor studious, higher Argument
9.43: Remaines, sufficient of it self to raise
9.44: That name, unless an age too late, or cold
9.45: Climat, or Years damp my intended wing
9.46: Deprest, and much they may, if all be mine,
9.47: Not Hers who brings it nightly to my Ear.
9.48: The Sun was sunk, and after him the Starr
9.49: Of Hesperus, whose Office is to bring
9.50: Twilight upon the Earth, short Arbiter
9.51: Twixt Day and Night, and now from end to end
9.52: Nights Hemisphere had veild the Horizon round:
9.53: When Satan who late fled before the threats
9.54: Of Gabriel out of Eden, now improv'd
9.55: In meditated fraud and malice, bent
9.56: On mans destruction, maugre what might hap
9.57: Of heavier on himself, fearless return'd.
9.58: By Night he fled, and at Midnight return'd
9.59: From compassing the Earth, cautious of day,
9.60: Since Uriel Regent of the Sun descri'd
9.61: His entrance, and forewarnd the Cherubim
9.62: That kept thir watch; thence full of anguish driv'n,
9.63: The space of seven continu'd Nights he rode
9.64: With darkness, thrice the Equinoctial Line
9.65: He circl'd, four times cross'd the Carr of Night
9.66: From Pole to Pole, traversing each Colure;
9.67: On the eighth return'd, and on the Coast averse
9.68: From entrance or Cherubic Watch, by stealth
9.69: Found unsuspected way. There was a place,
9.70: Now not, though Sin, not Time, first wraught the change,
9.71: Where Tigris at the foot of Paradise
9.72: Into a Gulf shot under ground, till part
9.73: Rose up a Fountain by the Tree of Life;
9.74: In with the River sunk, and with it rose
9.75: Satan involv'd in rising Mist, then sought
9.76: Where to lie hid; Sea he had searcht and Land
9.77: From Eden over Pontus, and the Poole
9.78: Maeotis, up beyond the River Ob;
9.79: Downward as farr Antartic; and in length
9.80: West from Orantes to the Ocean barr'd
9.81: At Darien, thence to the Land where flowes
9.82: Ganges and Indus: thus the Orb he roam'd
9.83: With narrow search; and with inspection deep
9.84: Consider'd every Creature, which of all
9.85: Most opportune might serve his Wiles, and found
9.86: The Serpent suttlest Beast of all the Field.
9.88: Of thoughts revolv'd, his final sentence chose
9.89: Fit Vessel, fittest Imp of fraud, in whom
9.90: To enter, and his dark suggestions hide
9.91: From sharpest sight: for in the wilie Snake,
9.92: Whatever sleights none would suspicious mark,
9.93: As from his wit and native suttletie
9.94: Proceeding, which in other Beasts observ'd
9.95: Doubt might beget of Diabolic pow'r
9.96: Active within beyond the sense of brute.
9.97: Thus he resolv'd, but first from inward griefe
9.98: His bursting passion into plaints thus pour'd:
9.99: O Earth, how like to Heav'n, if not preferrd
9.100: More justly, Seat worthier of Gods, as built
9.101: With second thoughts, reforming what was old!
9.102: For what God after better worse would build?
9.103: Terrestrial Heav'n, danc't round by other Heav'ns
9.104: That shine, yet bear thir bright officious Lamps,
9.105: Light above Light, for thee alone, as seems,
9.106: In thee concentring all thir precious beams
9.107: Of sacred influence: As God in Heav'n
9.108: Is Center, yet extends to all, so thou
9.109: Centring receav'st from all those Orbs; in thee,
9.110: Not in themselves, all thir known vertue appeers
9.111: Productive in Herb, Plant, and nobler birth
9.112: Of Creatures animate with gradual life
9.113: Of Growth, Sense, Reason, all summ'd up in Man.
9.114: With what delight could I have walkt thee round
9.115: If I could joy in aught, sweet interchange
9.116: Of Hill and Vallie, Rivers, Woods and Plaines,
9.117: Now Land, now Sea, & Shores with Forrest crownd,
9.118: Rocks, Dens, and Caves; but I in none of these
9.119: Find place or refuge; and the more I see
9.120: Pleasures about me, so much more I feel
9.121: Torment within me, as from the hateful siege
9.122: Of contraries; all good to me becomes
9.123: Bane, and in Heav'n much worse would be my state.
9.124: But neither here seek I, no nor in Heav'n
9.125: To dwell, unless by maistring Heav'ns Supreame;
9.126: Nor hope to be my self less miserable
9.127: By what I seek, but others to make such
9.128: As I though thereby worse to me redound:
9.129: For onely in destroying I finde ease
9.130: To my relentless thoughts; and him destroyd,
9.131: Or won to what may work his utter loss,
9.132: For whom all this was made, all this will soon
9.133: Follow, as to him linkt in weal or woe,
9.134: In wo then; that destruction wide may range:
9.135: To mee shall be the glorie sole among
9.136: The infernal Powers, in one day to have marr'd
9.137: What he Almightie styl'd, six Nights and Days
9.138: Continu'd making, and who knows how long
9.139: Before had bin contriving, though perhaps
9.140: Not longer then since I in one Night freed
9.142: Th' Angelic Name, and thinner left the throng
9.143: Of his adorers: hee to be aveng'd,
9.144: And to repaire his numbers thus impair'd,
9.145: Whether such vertue spent of old now faild
9.146: More Angels to Create, if they at least
9.147: Are his Created or to spite us more,
9.148: Determin'd to advance into our room
9.149: A Creature form'd of Earth, and him endow,
9.151: With Heav'nly spoils, our spoils: What he decreed
9.152: He effected; Man he made, and for him built
9.153: Magnificent this World, and Earth his seat,
9.154: Him Lord pronounc'd, and, O indignitie!
9.155: Subjected to his service Angel wings,
9.156: And flaming Ministers to watch and tend
9.157: Thir earthlie Charge: Of these the vigilance
9.158: I dread, and to elude, thus wrapt in mist
9.159: Of midnight vapor glide obscure, and prie
9.160: In every Bush and Brake, where hap may finde
9.161: The Serpent sleeping, in whose mazie foulds
9.162: To hide me, and the dark intent I bring.
9.163: O foul descent! that I who erst contended
9.164: With Gods to sit the highest, am now constraind
9.165: Into a Beast, and mixt with bestial slime,
9.166: This essence to incarnate and imbrute,
9.167: That to the hight of Deitie aspir'd;
9.168: But what will not Ambition and Revenge
9.169: Descend to? who aspires must down as low
9.170: As high he soard, obnoxious first or last
9.171: To basest things. Revenge, at first though sweet,
9.172: Bitter ere long back on it self recoiles;
9.173: Let it; I reck not, so it light well aim'd,
9.174: Since higher I fall short, on him who next
9.175: Provokes my envie, this new Favorite
9.176: Of Heav'n, this Man of Clay, Son of despite,
9.177: Whom us the more to spite his Maker rais'd
9.178: From dust: spite then with spite is best repaid.
9.179: So saying, through each Thicket Danck or Drie,
9.180: Like a black mist low creeping, he held on
9.181: His midnight search, where soonest he might finde
9.182: The Serpent: him fast sleeping soon he found
9.183: In Labyrinth of many a round self-rowl'd,
9.184: His head the midst, well stor'd with suttle wiles:
9.185: Not yet in horrid Shade or dismal Den,
9.186: Nor nocent yet, but on the grassie Herbe
9.187: Fearless unfeard he slept: in at his Mouth
9.188: The Devil enterd, and his brutal sense,
9.189: In heart or head, possessing soon inspir'd
9.190: With act intelligential; but his sleep
9.191: Disturbd not, waiting close th' approach of Morn.
9.192: Now whenas sacred Light began to dawne
9.193: In Eden on the humid Flours, that breathd
9.194: Thir morning Incense, when all things that breath,
9.195: From th' Earths great Altar send up silent praise
9.196: To the Creator, and his Nostrils fill
9.197: With gratefull Smell, forth came the human pair
9.198: And joynd thir vocal Worship to the Quire
9.199: Of Creatures wanting voice, that done, partake
9.200: The season, prime for sweetest Sents and Aires:
9.201: Then commune how that day they best may ply
9.202: Thir growing work: for much thir work outgrew
9.203: The hands dispatch of two Gardning so wide.
9.204: And Eve first to her Husband thus began.
9.205: Adam, well may we labour still to dress
9.206: This Garden, still to tend Plant, Herb and Flour.
9.207: Our pleasant task enjoyn'd, but till more hands
9.208: Aid us, the work under our labour grows,
9.209: Luxurious by restraint; what we by day
9.210: Lop overgrown, or prune, or prop, or bind,
9.211: One night or two with wanton growth derides
9.212: Tending to wilde. Thou therefore now advise
9.213: Or hear what to my mind first thoughts present,
9.214: Let us divide our labours, thou where choice
9.215: Leads thee, or where most needs, whether to wind
9.216: The Woodbine round this Arbour, or direct
9.217: The clasping Ivie where to climb, while I
9.218: In yonder Spring of Roses intermixt
9.219: With Myrtle, find what to redress till Noon:
9.220: For while so near each other thus all day
9.221: Our task we choose, what wonder if so near
9.222: Looks intervene and smiles, or object new
9.223: Casual discourse draw on, which intermits
9.224: Our dayes work brought to little, though begun
9.225: Early, and th' hour of Supper comes unearn'd.
9.226: To whom mild answer Adam thus return'd.
9.227: Sole Eve, Associate sole, to me beyond
9.228: Compare above all living Creatures deare,
9.229: Well hast thou motion'd, wel thy thoughts imployd
9.230: How we might best fulfill the work which here
9.231: God hath assign'd us, nor of me shalt pass
9.232: Unprais'd: for nothing lovelier can be found
9.233: In woman, then to studie houshold good,
9.234: And good workes in her Husband to promote.
9.235: Yet not so strictly hath our Lord impos'd
9.236: Labour, as to debarr us when we need
9.237: Refreshment, whether food, or talk between,
9.238: Food of the mind, or this sweet intercourse
9.239: Of looks and smiles, for smiles from Reason flow,
9.240: To brute deni'd, and are of Love the food,
