9.241: Love not the lowest end of human life.
9.242: For not to irksom toile, but to delight
9.243: He made us, and delight to Reason joyn'd.
9.244: These paths and Bowers doubt not but our joynt hands
9.245: Will keep from Wilderness with ease, as wide
9.246: As we need walk, till younger hands ere long
9.247: Assist us: But if much converse perhaps
9.248: Thee satiate, to short absence I could yeild.
9.249: For solitude somtimes is best societie,
9.250: And short retirement urges sweet returne.
9.251: But other doubt possesses me, least harm
9.252: Befall thee sever'd from me; for thou knowst
9.253: What hath bin warn'd us, what malicious Foe
9.254: Envying our happiness, and of his own
9.255: Despairing, seeks to work us woe and shame
9.256: By sly assault; and somwhere nigh at hand
9.257: Watches, no doubt, with greedy hope to find
9.258: His wish and best advantage, us asunder,
9.259: Hopeless to circumvent us joynd, where each
9.260: To other speedie aide might lend at need;
9.261: Whether his first design be to withdraw
9.262: Our fealtie from God, or to disturb
9.263: Conjugal Love, then which perhaps no bliss
9.264: Enjoy'd by us excites his envie more;
9.265: Or this, or worse, leave not the faithful side
9.266: That gave thee being, stil shades thee and protects.
9.267: The Wife, where danger or dishonour lurks,
9.268: Safest and seemliest by her Husband staies,
9.269: Who guards her, or with her the worst endures.
9.270: To whom the Virgin Majestie of Eve,
9.271: As one who loves, and some unkindness meets,
9.272: With sweet austeer composure thus reply'd.
9.273: Ofspring of Heav'n and Earth, and all Earths Lord,
9.274: That such an enemie we have, who seeks
9.275: Our ruin, both by thee informd I learne,
9.276: And from the parting Angel over-heard
9.277: As in a shadie nook I stood behind,
9.278: Just then returnd at shut of Evening Flours.
9.279: But that thou shouldst my firmness therefore doubt
9.280: To God or thee, because we have a foe
9.281: May tempt it, I expected not to hear.
9.282: His violence thou fearst not, being such,
9.283: As wee, not capable of death or paine,
9.284: Can either not receave, or can repell.
9.285: His fraud is then thy fear, which plain inferrs
9.286: Thy equal fear that my firm Faith and Love
9.287: Can by his fraud be shak'n or seduc't;
9.288: Thoughts, which how found they harbour in thy Brest,
9.289: Adam, misthought of her to thee so dear?
9.290: To whom with healing words Adam reply'd.
9.291: Daughter of God and Man, immortal Eve,
9.292: For such thou art, from sin and blame entire:
9.293: Not diffident of thee do I dissuade
9.294: Thy absence from my sight, but to avoid
9.295: Th' attempt it self, intended by our Foe.
9.296: For hee who tempts, though in vain, at least asperses
9.297: The tempted with dishonour foul, suppos'd
9.298: Not incorruptible of Faith, not prooff
9.299: Against temptation: thou thy self with scorne
9.300: And anger wouldst resent the offer'd wrong,
9.301: Though ineffectual found: misdeem not then,
9.302: If such affront I labour to avert
9.303: From thee alone, which on us both at once
9.304: The Enemie, though bold, will hardly dare,
9.305: Or daring, first on mee th' assault shall light.
9.306: Nor thou his malice and false guile contemn;
9.307: Suttle he needs must be, who could seduce
9.308: Angels, nor think superfluous others aid.
9.309: I from the influence of thy looks receave
9.310: Access in every Vertue, in thy sight
9.311: More wise, more watchful, stronger, if need were
9.312: Of outward strength; while shame, thou looking on,
9.313: Shame to be overcome or over-reacht
9.314: Would utmost vigor raise, and rais'd unite.
9.315: Why shouldst not thou like sense within thee feel
9.316: When I am present, and thy trial choose
9.317: With me, best witness of thy Vertue tri'd.
9.318: So spake domestick Adam in his care
9.319: And Matrimonial Love, but Eve, who thought
9.320: Less attributed to her Faith sincere,
9.321: Thus her reply with accent sweet renewd.
9.322: If this be our condition, thus to dwell
9.323: In narrow circuit strait'nd by a Foe,
9.324: Suttle or violent, we not endu'd
9.325: Single with like defence, wherever met,
9.326: How are we happie, still in fear of harm?
9.327: But harm precedes not sin: onely our Foe
9.328: Tempting affronts us with his foul esteem
9.329: Of our integritie: his foul esteeme
9.330: Sticks no dishonor on our Front, but turns
9.331: Foul on himself; then wherfore shund or feard
9.332: By us? who rather double honour gaine
9.333: From his surmise prov'd false, finde peace within,
9.334: Favour from Heav'n, our witness from th' event.
9.335: And what is Faith, Love, Vertue unassaid
9.337: Let us not then suspect our happie State
9.338: Left so imperfet by the Maker wise,
9.339: As not secure to single or combin'd.
9.340: Fraile is our happiness, if this be so,
9.341: And Eden were no Eden thus expos'd.
9.342: To whom thus Adam fervently repli'd.
9.343: O Woman, best are all things as the will
9.344: Of God ordaind them, his creating hand
9.346: Of all that he Created, much less Man,
9.347: Or ought that might his happie State secure,
9.348: Secure from outward force; within himself
9.349: The danger lies, yet lies within his power:
9.350: Against his will he can receave no harme.
9.351: But God left free the Will, for what obeyes
9.352: Reason, is free, and Reason he made right,
9.353: But bid her well beware, and still erect,
9.354: Least by some faire appeering good surpris'd
9.355: She dictate false, and missinforme the Will
9.356: To do what God expresly hath forbid.
9.357: Not then mistrust, but tender love enjoynes,
9.358: That I should mind thee oft, and mind thou me.
9.359: Firm we subsist, yet possible to swerve,
9.360: Since Reason not impossibly may meet
9.361: Some specious object by the Foe subornd,
9.363: Not keeping strictest watch, as she was warnd.
9.364: Seek not temptation then, which to avoide
9.365: Were better, and most likelie if from mee
9.366: Thou sever not; Trial will come unsought.
9.367: Wouldst thou approve thy constancie, approve
9.368: First thy obedience; th' other who can know,
9.369: Not seeing thee attempted, who attest?
9.370: But if thou think, trial unsought may finde
9.371: Us both securer then thus warnd thou seemst,
9.372: Go; for thy stay, not free, absents thee more;
9.373: Go in thy native innocence, relie
9.374: On what thou hast of vertue, summon all,
9.375: For God towards thee hath done his part, do thine.
9.376: So spake the Patriarch of Mankinde, but Eve
9.377: Persisted, yet submiss, though last, repli'd.
9.378: With thy permission then, and thus forewarnd
9.379: Chiefly by what thy own last reasoning words
9.380: Touchd onely, that our trial, when least sought,
9.381: May finde us both perhaps farr less prepar'd,
9.382: The willinger I goe, nor much expect
9.383: A Foe so proud will first the weaker seek;
9.384: So bent, the more shall shame him his repulse.
9.385: Thus saying, from her Husbands hand her hand
9.386: Soft she withdrew, and like a Wood-Nymph light
9.387: Oread or Dryad, or of Delia's Traine,
9.388: Betook her to the Groves, but Delia's self
9.389: In gate surpass'd and Goddess-like deport,
9.390: Though not as shee with Bow and Quiver armd,
9.391: But with such Gardning Tools as Art yet rude,
9.392: Guiltless of fire had formd, or Angels brought,
9.393: To Pales, or Pomona, thus adornd,
9.394: Likest she seemd, Pomona when she fled
9.395: Vertumnus, or to Ceres in her Prime,
9.396: Yet Virgin of Proserpina from Jove.
9.397: Her long with ardent look his Eye pursu'd
9.398: Delighted, but desiring more her stay.
9.399: Oft he to her his charge of quick returne,
9.400: Repeated, shee to him as oft engag'd
9.401: To be returnd by Noon amid the Bowre,
9.402: And all things in best order to invite
9.404: O much deceav'd, much failing, hapless Eve,
9.405: Of thy presum'd return! event perverse!
9.406: Thou never from that houre in Paradise
9.407: Foundst either sweet repast, or sound repose;
9.408: Such ambush hid among sweet Flours and Shades
9.410: To intercept thy way, or send thee back
9.411: Despoild of Innocence, of Faith, of Bliss.
9.412: For now, and since first break of dawne the Fiend,
9.413: Meer Serpent in appearance, forth was come,
9.414: And on his Quest, where likeliest he might finde
9.415: The onely two of Mankinde, but in them
9.416: The whole included Race, his purposd prey.
9.417: In Bowre and Field he sought, where any tuft
9.418: Of Grove or Garden-Plot more pleasant lay,
9.419: Thir tendance or Plantation for delight,
9.420: By Fountain or by shadie Rivulet
9.421: He sought them both, but wish'd his hap might find
9.422: Eve separate, he wish'd, but not with hope
9.423: Of what so seldom chanc'd, when to his wish,
9.424: Beyond his hope, Eve separate he spies,
9.425: Veild in a Cloud of Fragrance, where she stood,
9.426: Half spi'd, so thick the Roses bushing round
9.427: About her glowd, oft stooping to support
9.428: Each Flour of slender stalk, whose head though gay
9.429: Carnation, Purple, Azure, or spect with Gold,
9.430: Hung drooping unsustaind, them she upstaies
9.431: Gently with Mirtle band, mindless the while,
9.432: Her self, though fairest unsupported Flour,
9.433: From her best prop so farr, and storm so nigh.
9.434: Neerer he drew, and many a walk travers'd
9.435: Of stateliest Covert, Cedar, Pine, or Palme,
9.436: Then voluble and bold, now hid, now seen
9.438: Imborderd on each Bank, the hand of Eve:
9.439: Spot more delicious then those Gardens feign'd
9.440: Or of reviv'd Adonis, or renownd
9.441: Alcinous, host of old Laertes Son,
9.442: Or that, not Mystic, where the Sapient King
9.443: Held dalliance with his faire Egyptian Spouse.
9.444: Much hee the Place admir'd, the Person more.
9.445: As one who long in populous City pent,
9.446: Where Houses thick and Sewers annoy the Aire,
9.447: Forth issuing on a Summers Morn, to breathe
9.448: Among the pleasant Villages and Farmes
9.449: Adjoynd, from each thing met conceaves delight,
9.450: The smell of Grain, or tedded Grass, or Kine,
9.451: Or Dairie, each rural sight, each rural sound;
9.452: If chance with Nymphlike step fair Virgin pass,
9.453: What pleasing seemd, for her now pleases more,
9.454: She most, and in her look summs all Delight.
9.455: Such Pleasure took the Serpent to behold
9.456: This Flourie Plat, the sweet recess of Eve
9.457: Thus earlie, thus alone; her Heav'nly forme
9.458: Angelic, but more soft, and Feminine,
9.459: Her graceful Innocence, her every Aire
9.460: Of gesture or lest action overawd
9.461: His Malice, and with rapine sweet bereav'd
9.462: His fierceness of the fierce intent it brought:
9.463: That space the Evil one abstracted stood
9.464: From his own evil, and for the time remaind
9.466: Of guile, of hate, of envie, of revenge;
9.467: But the hot Hell that alwayes in him burnes,
9.468: Though in mid Heav'n, soon ended his delight,
9.469: And tortures him now more, the more he sees
9.470: Of pleasure not for him ordain'd: then soon
9.471: Fierce hate he recollects, and all his thoughts
9.473: Thoughts, whither have he led me, with what sweet
9.475: What hither brought us, hate, not love, nor hope
9.476: Of Paradise for Hell, hope here to taste
9.477: Of pleasure, but all pleasure to destroy,
9.478: Save what is in destroying, other joy
9.479: To me is lost. Then let me not let pass
9.480: Occasion which now smiles, behold alone
9.481: The Woman, opportune to all attempts,
9.482: Her Husband, for I view far round, not nigh,
9.483: Whose higher intellectual more I shun,
9.484: And strength, of courage hautie, and of limb
9.485: Heroic built, though of terrestrial mould,
9.486: Foe not informidable, exempt from wound,
9.487: I not; so much hath Hell debas'd, and paine
9.488: Infeebl'd me, to what I was in Heav'n.
9.489: Shee fair, divinely fair, fit Love for Gods,
9.490: Not terrible, though terrour be in Love
9.491: And beautie, not approacht by stronger hate,
9.492: Hate stronger, under shew of Love well feign'd,
9.493: The way which to her ruin now I tend.
9.494: So spake the Enemie of Mankind, enclos'd
9.495: In Serpent, Inmate bad, and toward Eve
9.496: Address'd his way, not with indented wave,
9.497: Prone on the ground, as since, but on his reare,
9.498: Circular base of rising foulds, that tour'd
9.499: Fould above fould a surging Maze, his Head
9.500: Crested aloft, and Carbuncle his Eyes;
9.501: With burnisht Neck of verdant Gold, erect
9.502: Amidst his circling Spires, that on the grass
9.503: Floted redundant: pleasing was his shape,
9.504: And lovely, never since of Serpent kind
9.505: Lovelier, not those that in Illyria chang'd
9.506: Hermione and Cadmus, or the God
9.507: In Epidaurus; nor to which transformd
9.508: Ammonian Jove, or Capitoline was seen,
9.509: Hee with Olympias, this with her who bore
9.510: Scipio the highth of Rome. With tract oblique
9.511: At first, as one who sought access, but feard
9.512: To interrupt, side-long he works his way.
9.513: As when a Ship by skilful Stearsman wrought
9.514: Nigh Rivers mouth or Foreland, where the Wind
9.515: Veres oft, as oft so steers, and shifts her Saile;
9.516: So varied hee, and of his tortuous Traine
9.517: Curld many a wanton wreath in sight of Eve,
9.518: To lure her Eye; shee busied heard the sound
9.519: Of rusling Leaves, but minded not, as us'd
9.520: To such disport before her through the Field,
9.521: From every Beast, more duteous at her call,
9.522: Then at Circean call the Herd disguis'd.
9.523: Hee boulder now, uncall'd before her stood;
9.524: But as in gaze admiring: Oft he bowd
9.525: His turret Crest, and sleek enamel'd Neck,
9.526: Fawning, and lick'd the ground whereon she trod.
9.527: His gentle dumb expression turnd at length
9.528: The Eye of Eve to mark his play; he glad
9.529: Of her attention gaind, with Serpent Tongue
9.530: Organic, or impulse of vocal Air,
9.532: Wonder not, sovran Mistress, if perhaps
9.533: Thou canst, who art sole Wonder, much less arm
9.534: Thy looks, the Heav'n of mildness, with disdain,
9.535: Displeas'd that I approach thee thus, and gaze
9.536: Insatiate, I thus single; nor have feard
9.537: Thy awful brow, more awful thus retir'd.
9.538: Fairest resemblance of thy Maker faire,
9.539: Thee all things living gaze on, all things thine
9.540: By gift, and thy Celestial Beautie adore
9.541: With ravishment beheld, there best beheld
9.543: In this enclosure wild, these Beasts among,
9.544: Beholders rude, and shallow to discerne
9.545: Half what in thee is fair, one man except,
9.546: Who sees thee? (and what is one?) who shouldst be seen
9.547: A Goddess among Gods, ador'd and serv'd
9.548: By Angels numberless, thy daily Train.
9.549: So gloz'd the Tempter, and his Proem tun'd;
9.550: Into the Heart of Eve his words made way,
9.551: Though at the voice much marveling; at length
9.552: Not unamaz'd she thus in answer spake.
9.553: What may this mean? Language of Man pronounc't
9.554: By Tongue of Brute, and human sense exprest?
9.555: The first at lest of these I thought deni'd
9.556: To Beasts, whom God on their Creation-Day
9.557: Created mute to all articulat sound;
9.558: The latter I demurre, for in thir looks
9.559: Much reason, and in thir actions oft appeers.
9.560: Thee, Serpent, suttlest beast of all the field
9.561: I knew, but not with human voice endu'd;
9.562: Redouble then this miracle, and say,

9.1045: Oppress'd them, wearied with thir amorous play.
9.1046: Soon as the force of that fallacious Fruit,
9.1048: About thir spirits had plaid, and inmost powers
9.1049: Made erre, was now exhal'd, and grosser sleep
9.1050: Bred of unkindly fumes, with conscious dreams
9.1051: Encumberd, now had left them, up they rose
9.1052: As from unrest, and each the other viewing,
9.1053: Soon found thir Eyes how op'nd, and thir minds
9.1054: How dark'nd; innocence, that as a veile
9.1055: Had shadow'd them from knowing ill, was gon,
9.1057: And honour from about them, naked left
9.1058: To guiltie shame: hee cover'd, but his Robe
9.1059: Uncover'd more. So rose the Danite strong
9.1062: Shorn of his strength, They destitute and bare
9.1063: Of all thir vertue: silent, and in face
9.1064: Confounded long they sate, as struck'n mute,
9.1065: Till Adam, though not less then Eve abasht,
9.1066: At length gave utterance to these words constraind.
9.1067: O Eve, in evil hour thou didst give eare
9.1068: To that false Worm, of whomsoever taught
9.1069: To counterfet Mans voice, true in our Fall,
9.1070: False in our promis'd Rising; since our Eyes
9.1071: Op'nd we find indeed, and find we know
9.1072: Both Good and Evil, Good lost and Evil got,
9.1073: Bad Fruit of Knowledge, if this be to know,
9.1074: Which leaves us naked thus, of Honour void,
9.1075: Of Innocence, of Faith, of Puritie,
9.1076: Our wonted Ornaments now soild and staind,
9.1077: And in our Faces evident the signes
9.1078: Of foul concupiscence; whence evil store;
9.1079: Even shame, the last of evils; of the first
9.1080: Be sure then. How shall I behold the face
9.1081: Henceforth of God or Angel, earst with joy
9.1082: And rapture so oft beheld? those heav'nly shapes
9.1083: Will dazle now this earthly, with thir blaze
9.1084: Insufferably bright. O might I here
9.1085: In solitude live savage, in some glade
9.1087: To Starr or Sun-light, spread thir umbrage broad,
9.1088: And brown as Evening: Cover me ye Pines,
9.1090: Hide me, where I may never see them more.
9.1091: But let us now, as in bad plight, devise
9.1092: What best may for the present serve to hide
9.1093: The Parts of each from other, that seem most
9.1094: To shame obnoxious, and unseemliest seen,
9.1095: Some Tree whose broad smooth Leaves together sowd,
9.1096: And girded on our loyns, may cover round
9.1097: Those middle parts, that this new commer, Shame,
9.1098: There sit not, and reproach us as unclean.
9.1099: So counsel'd hee, and both together went
9.1100: Into the thickest Wood, there soon they chose
9.1101: The Figtree, not that kind for Fruit renown'd,
9.1102: But such as at this day to Indians known
9.1103: In Malabar or Decan spreds her Armes
9.1104: Braunching so broad and long, that in the ground
9.1105: The bended Twigs take root, and Daughters grow
9.1106: About the Mother Tree, a Pillard shade
9.1107: High overarch't, and echoing Walks between;
9.1108: There oft the Indian Herdsman shunning heate
9.1109: Shelters in coole, and tends his pasturing Herds
9.1110: At Loopholes cut through thickest shade: Those Leaves
9.1111: They gatherd, broad as Amazonian Targe,
9.1112: And with what skill they had, together sowd,
9.1113: To gird thir waste, vain Covering if to hide
9.1114: Thir guilt and dreaded shame; O how unlike
9.1115: To that first naked Glorie. Such of late
9.1116: Columbus found th' American so girt
9.1117: With featherd Cincture, naked else and wilde
9.1118: Among the Trees on Iles and woodie Shores.
9.1119: Thus fenc't, and as they thought, thir shame in part
9.1120: Coverd, but not at rest or ease of Mind,
9.1121: They sate them down to weep, nor onely Teares
9.1122: Raind at thir Eyes, but high Winds worse within
9.1123: Began to rise, high Passions, Anger, Hate,
9.1124: Mistrust, Suspicion, Discord, and shook sore
9.1125: Thir inward State of Mind, calme Region once
9.1126: And full of Peace, now tost and turbulent:
9.1127: For Understanding rul'd not, and the Will
9.1128: Heard not her lore, both in subjection now
9.1129: To sensual Appetite, who from beneathe
9.1131: Superior sway: From thus distemperd brest,
9.1132: Adam, estrang'd in look and alterd stile,
9.1133: Speech intermitted thus to Eve renewd.
9.1134: Would thou hadst heark'nd to my words, & stai'd
9.1135: With me, as I besought thee, when that strange
9.1136: Desire of wandring this unhappie Morn,
9.1137: I know not whence possessd thee; we had then
9.1138: Remaind still happie, not as now, despoild
9.1139: Of all our good, sham'd, naked, miserable.
9.1140: Let none henceforth seek needless cause to approve
9.1141: The Faith they owe; when earnestly they seek
9.1142: Such proof, conclude, they then begin to faile.
9.1143: To whom soon mov'd with touch of blame thus Eve.
9.1144: What words have past thy Lips, Adam severe,
9.1145: Imput'st thou that to my default, or will
9.1146: Of wandering, as thou call'st it, which who knows
9.1147: But might as ill have happ'nd thou being by,
9.1148: Or to thy self perhaps: hadst thou bin there,
9.1149: Or here th' attempt, thou couldst not have discernd
9.1150: Fraud in the Serpent, speaking as he spake;
9.1151: No ground of enmitie between us known,
9.1152: Why hee should mean me ill, or seek to harme.
9.1153: Was I to have never parted from thy side?
9.1154: As good have grown there still a liveless Rib.
9.1155: Being as I am, why didst not thou the Head
9.1156: Command me absolutely not to go,
9.1157: Going into such danger as thou saidst?
9.1158: Too facil then thou didst not much gainsay,
9.1159: Nay, didst permit, approve, and fair dismiss.
9.1160: Hadst thou bin firm and fixt in thy dissent,
9.1161: Neither had I transgress'd, nor thou with mee.
9.1162: To whom then first incenst Adam repli'd.
9.1163: Is this the Love, is the recompence
9.1164: Of mine to thee, ingrateful Eve, exprest
9.1165: Immutable when thou wert lost, not I,
9.1166: Who might have liv'd and joyd immortal bliss,
9.1167: Yet willingly chose rather Death with thee:
9.1168: And am I now upbraided, as the cause
9.1169: Of thy transgressing? not enough severe,
9.1170: It seems, in thy restraint: what could I more?
9.1171: I warn'd thee, I admonish'd thee, foretold
9.1172: The danger, and the lurking Enemie
9.1173: That lay in wait; beyond this had bin force,
9.1174: And force upon free Will hath here no place.
9.1175: But confidence then bore thee on, secure
9.1176: Either to meet no danger, or to finde
9.1177: Matter of glorious trial; and perhaps
9.1178: I also err'd in overmuch admiring
9.1179: What seemd in thee so perfet, that I thought
9.1180: No evil durst attempt thee, but I rue
9.1181: That errour now, which is become my crime,
9.1182: And thou th' accuser. Thus it shall befall
9.1183: Him who to worth in Women overtrusting
9.1184: Lets her Will rule; restraint she will not brook,
9.1185: And left to her self, if evil thence ensue,
9.1186: Shee first his weak indulgence will accuse.
9.1187: Thus they in mutual accusation spent
9.1188: The fruitless hours, but neither self-condemning
9.1189: And of thir vain contest appeer'd no end.

10.0:
*The Argument*
Mans transgression known, the Guardian Angels forsake Paradise, and return up to Heaven to approve thir vigilance, and are approv'd, God declaring that The entrance of Satan could not be by them prevented. He sends his Son to judge the Transgressors, who descends and gives Sentence accordingly; then in pity cloaths them both, and reascends. Sin and Death sitting till then at the Gates of Hell by wondrous sympathie feeling the success of Satan in this new World, and the sin by Man there committed, resolve to sit no longer confin'd in Hell, but to follow Satan thir Sire up to the place of Man:  To make the way easier from Hell to this World to and fro, they pave a broad Highway or Bridge over Chaos, according to the Track that Satan first made; then preparing for Earth, they meet him proud of his success returning to Hell; thir mutual gratulation. Satan arrives at Pandemonium, in full assembly relates with boasting his success against Man; instead of applause is entertained with a general hiss by all his audience, transform'd with himself also suddenly into Serpents, according to his doom giv'n in Paradise; then deluded with a shew of the forbidden Tree springing up before them, they greedily reaching to take of the Fruit, chew dust and bitter ashes.The proceedings of Sin and Death; God foretels the final Victory of his Son over them, and the renewing of all things; but for the present commands his Angels to make several alterations in the Heavens and Elements. Adam more and more perceiving his fall'n condition heavily bewailes, rejects the condolement of Eve; she persists and at length appeases him: then to evade the Curse likely to fall on thir Ofspring, proposes to Adam violent wayes, which he approves not, but conceiving better hope, puts her in mind of the late Promise made them, that her Seed should be reveng'd on the Serpent, and exhorts her with him to seek Peace of the offended Deity, by repentance and supplication.
10.1: Meanwhile the hainous and despightfull act
10.2: Of Satan done in Paradise, and how
10.3: Hee in the Serpent had perverted Eve,
10.4: Her Husband shee, to taste the fatall fruit,
10.5: Was known in Heav'n; for what can scape the Eye
10.6: Of God All-seeing, or deceave his Heart
10.7: Omniscient, who in all things wise and just,
10.8: Hinder'd not Satan to attempt the minde
10.9: Of Man, with strength entire, and free Will arm'd,
10.10: Complete to have discover'd and repulst
10.11: Whatever wiles of Foe or seeming Friend.
10.12: For still they knew, and ought to have still remember'd
10.13: The high Injunction not to taste that Fruit,
10.14: Whoever tempted; which they not obeying,
10.15: Incurr'd, what could they less, the penaltie,
10.16: And manifold in sin, deserv'd to fall.
10.17: Up into Heav'n from Paradise in hast
10.18: Th' Angelic Guards ascended, mute and sad
10.19: For Man, for of his state by this they knew,
10.20: Much wondring how the suttle Fiend had stoln
10.21: Entrance unseen. Soon as th' unwelcome news
10.22: From Earth arriv'd at Heaven Gate, displeas'd
10.23: All were who heard, dim sadness did not spare
10.24: That time Celestial visages, yet mixt
10.25: With pitie, violated not thir bliss.
10.27: Th' ethereal People ran, to hear and know
10.28: How all befell: they towards the Throne Supream
10.29: Accountable made haste to make appear
10.30: With righteous plea, thir utmost vigilance,
10.31: And easily approv'd; when the most High
10.32: Eternal Father from his secret Cloud,
10.33: Amidst in Thunder utter'd thus his voice.
10.34: Assembl'd Angels, and ye Powers return'd
10.35: From unsuccessful charge, be not dismaid,
10.36: Nor troubl'd at these tidings from the Earth,
10.37: Which your sincerest care could not prevent,
10.38: Foretold so lately what would come to pass,
10.39: When first this Tempter cross'd the Gulf from Hell.
10.40: I told ye then he should prevail and speed
10.41: On his bad Errand, Man should be seduc't
10.42: And flatter'd out of all, believing lies
10.43: Against his Maker; no Decree of mine
10.45: Or touch with lightest moment of impulse
10.46: His free Will, to her own inclining left
10.47: In eevn scale. But fall'n he is, and now
10.48: What rests, but that the mortal Sentence pass
10.49: On his transgression, Death denounc't that day,
10.50: Which he presumes already vain and void,
10.51: Because not yet inflicted, as he fear'd,
10.52: By some immediate stroak; but soon shall find
10.53: Forbearance no acquittance ere day end.
10.54: Justice shall not return as bountie scorn'd.
10.55: But whom send I to judge them? whom but thee
10.56: Vicegerent Son, to thee I have transferr'd
10.57: All Judgement, whether in Heav'n, or Earth; or Hell.
10.58: Easie it may be seen that I intend
10.59: Mercie collegue with Justice, sending thee
10.60: Mans Friend, his Mediator, his design'd
10.62: And destin'd Man himself to judge Man fall'n.
10.63: So spake the Father, and unfoulding bright
10.64: Toward the right hand his Glorie, on the Son
10.65: Blaz'd forth unclouded Deitie; he full
10.67: Express'd, and thus divinely answer'd milde.
10.68: Father Eternal, thine is to decree,
10.69: Mine both in Heav'n and Earth to do thy will
10.70: Supream, that thou in mee thy Son belov'd
10.71: Mayst ever rest well pleas'd. I go to judge
10.72: On Earth these thy transgressors, but thou knowst,
10.73: Whoever judg'd, the worst on mee must light,
10.74: When time shall be, for so I undertook
10.75: Before thee; and not repenting, this obtaine
10.76: Of right, that I may mitigate thir doom
10.77: On me deriv'd, yet I shall temper so
10.78: Justice with Mercie, as may illustrate most
10.79: Them fully satisfied, and thee appease.
10.80: Attendance none shall need, nor Train, where none
10.81: Are to behold the Judgement, but the judg'd,
10.82: Those two; the third best absent is condemn'd,
10.83: Convict by flight, and Rebel to all Law
10.84: Conviction to the Serpent none belongs.
10.85: Thus saying, from his radiant Seat he rose
10.86: Of high collateral glorie: him Thrones and Powers,
10.88: Accompanied to Heaven Gate, from whence
10.89: Eden and all the Coast in prospect lay.
10.90: Down he descended strait; the speed of Gods
10.91: Time counts not, though with swiftest minutes wing'd.
10.92: Now was the Sun in Western cadence low
10.93: From Noon, and gentle Aires due at thir hour
10.94: To fan the Earth now wak'd, and usher in
10.95: The Eevning coole when he from wrauth more coole
10.96: Came the mild Judge and Intercessor both
10.97: To sentence Man: the voice of God they heard
10.98: Now walking in the Garden, by soft windes
10.99: Brought to thir Ears, while day declin'd, they heard
10.100: And from his presence hid themselves among
10.101: The thickest Trees, both Man and Wife, till God
10.102: Approaching, thus to Adam call'd aloud.
10.103: Where art thou Adam, wont with joy to meet
10.104: My coming seen far off? I miss thee here,
10.105: Not pleas'd, thus entertaind with solitude,
10.106: Where obvious dutie erewhile appear'd unsaught:
10.107: Or come I less conspicuous, or what change
10.108: Absents thee, or what chance detains? Come forth.
10.109: He came, and with him Eve, more loth, though first
10.110: To offend, discount'nanc't both, and discompos'd;
10.111: Love was not in thir looks, either to God
10.112: Or to each other, but apparent guilt,
10.113: And shame, and perturbation, and despaire,
10.114: Anger, and obstinacie, and hate, and guile.
10.115: Whence Adam faultring long, thus answer'd brief.
10.116: I heard thee in the Garden, and of thy voice
10.117: Affraid, being naked, hid my self. To whom
10.118: The gracious Judge without revile repli'd.
10.119: My voice thou oft hast heard, and hast not fear'd,
10.120: But still rejoyc't, how is it now become
10.121: So dreadful to thee? that thou art naked, who
10.122: Hath told thee? hast thou eaten of the Tree
10.123: Whereof I gave thee charge thou shouldst not eat?
10.124: To whom thus Adam sore beset repli'd.
10.125: O Heav'n! in evil strait this day I stand
10.126: Before my Judge, either to undergoe
10.127: My self the total Crime, or to accuse
10.128: My other self, the partner of my life;
10.129: Whose failing, while her Faith to me remaines,
10.130: I should conceal, and not expose to blame
10.131: By my complaint; but strict necessitie
10.133: Least on my head both sin and punishment,
10.135: Devolv'd; though should I hold my peace, yet thou
10.136: Wouldst easily detect what I conceale.
10.137: This Woman whom thou mad'st to be my help,
10.138: And gav'st me as thy perfet gift, so good,
10.139: So fit, so acceptable, so Divine,
10.140: That from her hand I could suspect no ill,
10.141: And what she did, whatever in it self,
10.142: Her doing seem'd to justifie the deed;
10.143: Shee gave me of the Tree, and I did eate.
10.144: To whom the sovran Presence thus repli'd.
10.145: Was shee thy God, that her thou didst obey
10.146: Before his voice, or was shee made thy guide,
10.147: Superior, or but equal, that to her
10.148: Thou did'st resigne thy Manhood, and the Place
10.149: Wherein God set thee above her made of thee,
10.150: And for thee, whose perfection farr excell'd
10.151: Hers in all real dignitie: Adornd
10.152: She was indeed, and lovely to attract
10.153: Thy Love, not thy Subjection, and her Gifts
10.154: Were such as under Government well seem'd,
10.155: Unseemly to beare rule, which was thy part
10.156: And person, had'st thou known thy self aright.
10.157: So having said, he thus to Eve in few:
10.158: Say Woman, what is this which thou hast done?
10.159: To whom sad Eve with shame nigh overwhelm'd,
10.160: Confessing soon, yet not before her Judge
10.161: Bold or loquacious, thus abasht repli'd.
10.162: The Serpent me beguil'd and I did eate.
10.163: Which when the Lord God heard, without delay
10.164: To Judgement he proceeded on th' accus'd
10.165: Serpent though brute, unable to transferre
10.166: The Guilt on him who made him instrument
10.167: Of mischief, and polluted from the end
10.168: Of his Creation; justly then accurst,
10.169: As vitiated in Nature: more to know
10.170: Concern'd not Man (since he no further knew)
10.171: Nor alter'd his offence; yet God at last
10.172: To Satan first in sin his doom apply'd,
10.173: Though in mysterious terms, judg'd as then best:
10.174: And on the Serpent thus his curse let fall.
10.175: Because thou hast done this, thou art accurst
10.176: Above all Cattel, each Beast of the Field;
10.177: Upon thy Belly groveling thou shalt goe,
10.178: And dust shalt eat all the days of thy Life.
10.179: Between Thee and the Woman I will put
10.180: Enmitie, and between thine and her Seed;
10.181: Her Seed shall bruise thy head, thou bruise his heel.
10.182: So spake this Oracle, then verifi'd
10.183: When Jesus son of Mary second Eve,
10.184: Saw Satan fall like Lightning down from Heav'n,
10.185: Prince of the Aire; then rising from his Grave
10.187: In open shew, and with ascention bright
10.188: Captivity led captive through the Aire,
10.189: The Realme it self of Satan long usurpt,
10.190: Whom he shall tread at last under our feet;
10.191: Eevn hee who now foretold his fatal bruise,
10.192: And to the Woman thus his Sentence turn'd.
10.193: Thy sorrow I will greatly multiplie
10.194: By thy Conception; Children thou shalt bring
10.195: In sorrow forth, and to thy Husbands will
10.196: Thine shall submit, hee over thee shall rule.
10.197: On Adam last thus judgement he pronounc'd.
10.198: Because thou hast heark'nd to the voice of thy Wife,
10.199: And eaten of the Tree concerning which
10.200: I charg'd thee, saying: Thou shalt not eate thereof,
10.201: Curs'd is the ground for thy sake, thou in sorrow
10.202: Shalt eate thereof all the days of thy Life;
10.203: Thornes also and Thistles it shall bring thee forth
10.204: Unbid, and thou shalt eate th' Herb of th' Field,
10.205: In the sweat of thy Face shalt thou eate Bread,
10.206: Till thou return unto the ground, for thou
10.207: Out of the ground wast taken, know thy Birth,
10.208: For dust thou art, and shalt to dust returne.
10.209: So judg'd he Man, both Judge and Saviour sent,
10.210: And th' instant stroke of Death denounc't that day
10.211: Remov'd farr off; then pittying how they stood
10.212: Before him naked to the aire, that now
10.213: Must suffer change, disdain'd not to begin
10.214: Thenceforth the forme of servant to assume,
10.215: As when he wash'd his servants feet, so now
10.216: As Father of his Familie he clad
10.217: Thir nakedness with Skins of Beasts, or slain,
10.218: Or as the Snake with youthful Coate repaid;
10.219: And thought not much to cloath his Enemies:
10.220: Nor hee thir outward onely with the Skins
10.221: Of Beasts, but inward nakedness, much more
10.222: Opprobrious, with his Robe of righteousness,
10.223: Araying cover'd from his Fathers sight.
10.224: To him with swift ascent he up returnd,
10.226: In glory as of old, to him appeas'd
10.227: All, though all-knowing, what had past with Man
10.229: Meanwhile ere thus was sin'd and judg'd on Earth,
10.230: Within the Gates of Hell sate Sin and Death,
10.231: In counterview within the Gates, that now
10.232: Stood open wide, belching outrageous flame
10.233: Farr into Chaos, since the Fiend pass'd through,
10.234: Sin opening, who thus now to Death began.
10.235: O Son, why sit we here each other viewing
10.236: Idlely, while Satan our great Author thrives
10.237: In other Worlds, and happier Seat provides
10.238: For us his ofspring deare? It cannot be
10.239: But that success attends him; if mishap,
10.240: Ere this he had return'd, with fury driv'n
10.241: By his Avenger, since no place like this
10.242: Can fit his punishment, or their revenge.
10.243: Methinks I feel new strength within me rise,
10.244: Wings growing, and Dominion giv'n me large
10.245: Beyond this Deep; whatever drawes me on,
10.246: Or sympathie, or som connatural force
10.247: Powerful at greatest distance to unite
10.248: With secret amity things of like kinde
10.249: By secretest conveyance. Thou my Shade
10.251: For Death from Sin no power can separate.
10.252: But least the difficultie of passing back
10.253: Stay his returne perhaps over this Gulfe
10.255: Adventrous work, yet to thy power and mine
10.256: Not unagreeable, to found a path
10.257: Over this Maine from Hell to that new World
10.258: Where Satan now prevailes, a Monument
10.259: Of merit high to all th' infernal Host,
10.260: Easing thir passage hence, for intercourse,
10.261: Or transmigration, as thir lot shall lead.
10.262: Nor can I miss the way, so strongly drawn
10.263: By this new felt attraction and instinct.
10.264: Whom thus the meager Shadow answerd soon.
10.265: Goe whither Fate and inclination strong
10.266: Leads thee, I shall not lag behinde, nor erre
10.267: The way, thou leading, such a sent I draw
10.268: Of carnage, prey innumerable, and taste
10.269: The savour of Death from all things there that live:
10.270: Nor shall I to the work thou enterprisest
10.271: Be wanting, but afford thee equal aid.
10.272: So saying, with delight he snuff'd the smell
10.273: Of mortal change on Earth. As when a flock
10.274: Of ravenous Fowl, though many a League remote,
10.275: Against the day of Battel, to a Field,
10.276: Where Armies lie encampt, come flying, lur'd
10.277: With sent of living Carcasses design'd
10.278: For death, the following day, in bloodie fight.
10.279: So sented the grim Feature, and upturn'd
10.280: His Nostril wide into the murkie Air,
10.281: Sagacious of his Quarrey from so farr.
10.282: Then Both from out Hell Gates into the waste
10.283: Wide Anarchie of Chaos damp and dark
10.284: Flew divers, & with Power (thir Power was great)
10.285: Hovering upon the Waters; what they met
10.286: Solid or slimie, as in raging Sea
10.287: Tost up and down, together crowded drove
10.288: From each side shoaling towards the mouth of Hell.
10.289: As when two Polar Winds blowing adverse
10.290: Upon the Cronian Sea, together drive
10.291: Mountains of Ice, that stop th' imagin'd way
10.292: Beyond Petsora Eastward, to the rich
10.294: Death with his Mace petrific, cold and dry,
10.295: As with a Trident smote, and fix't as firm
10.296: As Delos floating once; the rest his look
10.297: Bound with Gorgonian rigor not to move,
10.298: And with Asphaltic slime; broad as the Gate,
10.299: Deep to the Roots of Hell the gather'd beach
10.300: They fasten'd, and the Mole immense wraught on
10.301: Over the foaming deep high Archt, a Bridge
10.302: Of length prodigious joyning to the Wall
10.303: Immoveable of this now fenceless world
10.304: Forfeit to Death; from hence a passage broad,
10.305: Smooth, easie, inoffensive down to Hell.
10.306: So, if great things to small may be compar'd,
10.307: Xerxes, the Libertie of Greece to yoke,
10.308: From Susa his Memnonian Palace high
10.309: Came to the Sea, and over Hellespont
10.310: Bridging his way, Europe with Asia joyn'd,
10.311: And scourg'd with many a stroak th' indignant waves.
10.312: Now had they brought the work by wondrous Art
10.313: Pontifical, a ridge of pendent Rock
10.314: Over the vext Abyss, following the track
10.315: Of Satan, to the selfsame place where hee
10.316: First lighted from his Wing, and landed safe
10.317: From out of Chaos to the outside bare
10.318: Of this round World: with Pinns of Adamant
10.319: And Chains they made all fast, too fast they made
10.320: And durable; and now in little space
10.321: The Confines met of Empyrean Heav'n
10.322: And of this World, and on the left hand Hell
10.323: With long reach interpos'd; three sev'ral wayes
10.324: In sight, to each of these three places led.
10.325: And now thir way to Earth they had descri'd,
10.326: To Paradise first tending, when behold
10.327: Satan in likeness of an Angel bright
10.328: Betwixt the Centaure and the Scorpion stearing
10.329: His Zenith, while the Sun in Aries rose:
10.330: Disguis'd he came, but those his Children dear
10.331: Thir Parent soon discern'd, though in disguise.
10.332: Hee, after Eve seduc't, unminded slunk
10.333: Into the Wood fast by, and changing shape
10.334: To observe the sequel, saw his guileful act
10.335: By Eve, though all unweeting, seconded
10.336: Upon her Husband, saw thir shame that sought
10.337: Vain covertures; but when he saw descend
10.338: The Son of God to judge them, terrifi'd
10.339: Hee fled, not hoping to escape, but shun
10.340: The present, fearing guiltie what his wrauth
10.341: Might suddenly inflict; that past, return'd
10.342: By Night, and listning where the hapless Paire
10.343: Sate in thir sad discourse, and various plaint,
10.344: Thence gatherd his own doom, which understood
10.345: Not instant, but of future time. With joy
10.346: And tidings fraught, to Hell he now return'd,
10.347: And at the brink of Chaos, neer the foot
10.348: Of this new wondrous Pontifice, unhop't
10.349: Met who to meet him came, his Ofspring dear.
10.350: Great joy was at thir meeting, and at sight
10.351: Of that stupendious Bridge his joy encreas'd.
10.352: Long hee admiring stood, till Sin, his faire
10.353: Inchanting Daughter, thus the silence broke.
10.354: O Parent, these are thy magnific deeds,
10.355: Thy Trophies, which thou view'st as not thine own,
10.356: Thou art thir Author and prime Architect:
10.357: For I no sooner in my Heart divin'd,
10.358: My Heart, which by a secret harmonie
10.359: Still moves with thine, joyn'd in connexion sweet,
10.360: That thou on Earth hadst prosper'd, which thy looks
10.361: Now also evidence, but straight I felt
10.362: Though distant from thee Worlds between, yet felt
10.363: That I must after thee with this thy Son;
10.364: Such fatal consequence unites us three:
10.365: Hell could no longer hold us in her bounds,
10.367: Detain from following thy illustrious track.
10.368: Thou hast atchiev'd our libertie, confin'd
10.369: Within Hell Gates till now, thou us impow'rd
10.370: To fortifie thus farr, and overlay
10.371: With this portentous Bridge the dark Abyss.
10.372: Thine now is all this World, thy vertue hath won
10.373: What thy hands builded not, thy Wisdom gain'd
10.374: With odds what Warr hath lost, and fully aveng'd
10.375: Our foile in Heav'n; here thou shalt Monarch reign,
10.376: There didst not; there let him still Victor sway,
10.377: As Battel hath adjudg'd, from this new World
10.378: Retiring, by his own doom alienated,
10.379: And henceforth Monarchie with thee divide
10.380: Of all things, parted by th' Empyreal bounds,
10.381: His Quadrature, from thy Orbicular World,
10.382: Or trie thee now more dang'rous to his Throne.
10.383: Whom thus the Prince of Darkness answerd glad.
10.384: Fair Daughter, and thou Son and Grandchild both,
10.385: High proof ye now have giv'n to be the Race
10.386: Of Satan (for I glorie in the name,
10.388: Amply have merited of me, of all
10.389: Th' Infernal Empire, that so neer Heav'ns dore
10.390: Triumphal with triumphal act have met,
10.391: Mine with this glorious Work, & made one Realm
10.392: Hell and this World, one Realm, one Continent
10.393: Of easie thorough-fare. Therefore while I
10.394: Descend through Darkness, on your Rode with ease
10.395: To my associate Powers, them to acquaint
10.396: With these successes, and with them rejoyce,
10.397: You two this way, among those numerous Orbs
10.398: All yours, right down to Paradise descend;
10.399: There dwell & Reign in bliss, thence on the Earth
10.400: Dominion exercise and in the Aire,
10.401: Chiefly on Man, sole Lord of all declar'd,
10.402: Him first make sure your thrall, and lastly kill.
10.403: My Substitutes I send ye, and Create
10.404: Plenipotent on Earth, of matchless might
10.405: Issuing from mee: on your joynt vigor now
10.406: My hold of this new Kingdom all depends,
10.407: Through Sin to Death expos'd by my exploit.
10.408: If your joynt power prevaile, th' affaires of Hell
10.409: No detriment need feare, goe and be strong.
10.410: So saying he dismiss'd them, they with speed
10.411: Thir course through thickest Constellations held
10.412: Spreading thir bane; the blasted Starrs lookt wan,
10.414: Then sufferd. Th' other way Satan went down
10.415: The Causey to Hell Gate; on either side
10.417: And with rebounding surge the barrs assaild,
10.418: That scorn'd his indignation: through the Gate,
10.419: Wide open and unguarded, Satan pass'd,
10.420: And all about found desolate; for those
10.421: Appointed to sit there, had left thir charge,
10.422: Flown to the upper World; the rest were all
10.423: Farr to the inland retir'd, about the walls
10.424: Of Pandemonium, Citie and proud seate
10.425: Of Lucifer, so by allusion calld,
10.426: Of that bright Starr to Satan paragond.
10.427: There kept thir Watch the Legions, while the Grand
10.428: In Council sate, sollicitous what chance
10.429: Might intercept thir Emperour sent, so hee
10.430: Departing gave command, and they observ'd.
10.431: As when the Tartar from his Russian Foe
10.432: By Astracan over the Snowie Plaines
10.433: Retires, or Bactrian Sophi from the hornes
10.434: Of Turkish Crescent, leaves all waste beyond
10.435: The Realme of Aladule, in his retreate
10.436: To Tauris or Casbeen. So these the late
10.437: Heav'n-banisht Host, left desert utmost Hell
10.438: Many a dark League, reduc't in careful Watch
10.439: Round thir Metropolis, and now expecting
10.440: Each hour their great adventurer from the search
10.441: Of Forrein Worlds: he through the midst unmarkt,
10.443: Of lowest order, past; and from the dore
10.445: Ascended his high Throne, which under state
10.446: Of richest texture spred, at th' upper end
10.447: Was plac't in regal lustre. Down a while
10.448: He sate, and round about him saw unseen:
10.449: At last as from a Cloud his fulgent head
10.450: And shape Starr bright appeer'd, or brighter, clad
10.451: With what permissive glory since his fall
10.452: Was left him, or false glitter: All amaz'd
10.453: At that so sudden blaze the Stygian throng
10.454: Bent thir aspect, and whom they wish'd beheld,
10.455: Thir mighty Chief returnd: loud was th' acclaime:
10.456: Forth rush'd in haste the great consulting Peers,
10.457: Rais'd from thir dark Divan, and with like joy
10.458: Congratulant approach'd him, who with hand
10.459: Silence, and with these words attention won.
10.461: For in possession such, not onely of right,
10.462: I call ye and declare ye now, returnd
10.463: Successful beyond hope, to lead ye forth
10.464: Triumphant out of this infernal Pit
10.465: Abominable, accurst, the house of woe,
10.466: And Dungeon of our Tyrant: Now possess,
10.467: As Lords, a spacious World, to our native Heaven
10.468: Little inferiour, by my adventure hard
10.469: With peril great atchiev'd. Long were to tell
10.470: What I have don, what sufferd, with what paine
10.471: Voyag'd the unreal, vast, unbounded deep
10.473: By Sin and Death a broad way now is pav'd
10.474: To expedite your glorious march; but I
10.475: Toild out my uncouth passage, forc't to ride
10.476: Th' untractable Abysse, plung'd in the womb
10.477: Of unoriginal Night and Chaos wilde,
10.478: That jealous of thir secrets fiercely oppos'd
10.479: My journey strange, with clamorous uproare
10.480: Protesting Fate supreame; thence how I found
10.481: The new created World, which fame in Heav'n
10.482: Long had foretold, a Fabrick wonderful
10.484: Plac't in a Paradise, by our exile
10.485: Made happie: Him by fraud I have seduc'd
10.486: From his Creator, and the more to increase
10.487: Your wonder, with an Apple; he thereat
10.488: Offended, worth your laughter, hath giv'n up
10.489: Both his beloved Man and all his World,
10.490: To Sin and Death a prey, and so to us,
10.491: Without our hazard, labour or allarme,
10.492: To range in, and to dwell, and over Man
10.493: To rule, as over all he should have rul'd.
10.494: True is, mee also he hath judg'd, or rather
10.495: Mee not, but the brute Serpent in whose shape
10.496: Man I deceav'd: that which to mee belongs,
10.497: Is enmity, which he will put between
10.498: Mee and Mankinde; I am to bruise his heel;
10.499: His Seed, when is not set, shall bruise my head:
10.500: A World who would not purchase with a bruise,
10.501: Or much more grievous pain? Ye have th' account
10.502: Of my performance: What remaines, ye Gods,
10.503: But up and enter now into full bliss.
10.504: So having said, a while he stood, expecting
10.505: Thir universal shout and high applause
10.506: To fill his eare, when contrary he hears
10.507: On all sides, from innumerable tongues
10.508: A dismal universal hiss, the sound
10.509: Of public scorn; he wonderd, but not long
10.510: Had leasure, wondring at himself now more;
10.511: His Visage drawn he felt to sharp and spare,
10.512: His Armes clung to his Ribs, his Leggs entwining
10.513: Each other, till supplanted down he fell
10.514: A monstrous Serpent on his Belly prone,
10.515: Reluctant, but in vaine, a greater power
10.516: Now rul'd him, punisht in the shape he sin'd,
10.517: According to his doom: he would have spoke,
10.518: But hiss for hiss returnd with forked tongue
10.519: To forked tongue, for now were all transform'd
10.520: Alike, to Serpents all as accessories
10.521: To his bold Riot: dreadful was the din
10.522: Of hissing through the Hall, thick swarming now
10.523: With complicated monsters, head and taile,
10.524: Scorpion and Asp, and Amphisbaena dire,
10.525: Cerastes hornd, Hydrus, and Ellops drear,
10.526: And Dipsas (Not so thick swarm'd once the Soil
10.527: Bedropt with blood of Gorgon, or the Isle
10.528: Ophiusa) but still greatest hee the midst,
10.529: Now Dragon grown, larger then whom the Sun
10.530: Ingenderd in the Pythian Vale on slime,
10.531: Huge Python, and his Power no less he seem'd
10.532: Above the rest still to retain; they all
10.533: Him follow'd issuing forth to th' open Field,
10.534: Where all yet left of that revolted Rout
10.535: Heav'n-fall'n, in station stood or just array,
10.536: Sublime with expectation when to see
10.537: In Triumph issuing forth thir glorious Chief;
10.538: They saw, but other sight instead, a crowd
10.539: Of ugly Serpents; horror on them fell,
10.540: And horrid sympathie; for what they saw,
10.541: They felt themselvs now changing; down thir arms,
10.542: Down fell both Spear and Shield, down they as fast,
10.543: And the dire hiss renew'd, and the dire form
10.544: Catcht by Contagion, like in punishment,
10.545: As in thir crime. Thus was th' applause they meant,
10.546: Turnd to exploding hiss, triumph to shame
10.547: Cast on themselves from thir own mouths. There stood
10.548: A Grove hard by, sprung up with this thir change,
10.549: His will who reigns above, to aggravate
10.550: Thir penance, laden with fair Fruit, like that
10.551: Which grew in Paradise, the bait of Eve
10.552: Us'd by the Tempter: on that prospect strange
10.553: Thir earnest eyes they fix'd, imagining
10.554: For one forbidden Tree a multitude
10.555: Now ris'n, to work them furder woe or shame;
10.556: Yet parcht with scalding thurst and hunger fierce,
10.557: Though to delude them sent, could not abstain,
10.558: But on they rould in heaps, and up the Trees
10.559: Climbing, sat thicker then the snakie locks
10.560: That curld Megaera: greedily they pluck'd
10.561: The Frutage fair to sight, like that which grew
10.562: Neer that bituminous Lake where Sodom flam'd;
10.563: This more delusive, not the touch, but taste
10.564: Deceav'd; they fondly thinking to allay
10.565: Thir appetite with gust, instead of Fruit
10.566: Chewd bitter Ashes, which th' offended taste
10.567: With spattering noise rejected: oft they assayd,
10.568: Hunger and thirst constraining, drugd as oft,
10.569: With hatefullest disrelish writh'd thir jaws
10.570: With soot and cinders fill'd; so oft they fell
10.571: Into the same illusion, not as Man
10.572: Whom they triumph'd once lapst. Thus were they plagu'd
10.573: And worn with Famin, long and ceasless hiss,
10.574: Till thir lost shape, permitted, they resum'd,
10.575: Yearly enjoynd, some say, to undergo
10.576: This annual humbling certain number'd days,
10.577: To dash thir pride, and joy for Man seduc't.
10.579: Among the Heathen of thir purchase got,
10.580: And Fabl'd how the Serpent, whom they calld
10.582: Encroaching Eve perhaps, had first the rule
10.583: Of high Olympus, thence by Saturn driv'n
10.584: And Ops, ere yet Dictaean Jove was born.
10.585: Mean while in Paradise the hellish pair
10.586: Too soon arriv'd, Sin there in power before,
10.587: Once actual, now in body, and to dwell
10.589: Close following pace for pace, not mounted yet
10.590: On his pale Horse: to whom Sin thus began.
10.591: Second of Satan sprung, all conquering Death,
10.592: What thinkst thou of our Empire now, though earnd
10.593: With travail difficult, not better farr
10.594: Then stil at Hels dark threshold to have sate watch,
10.595: Unnam'd, undreaded, and thy self half starv'd?
10.596: Whom thus the Sin-born Monster answerd soon.
10.597: To mee, who with eternal Famin pine,
10.598: Alike is Hell, or Paradise, or Heaven,
10.599: There best, where most with ravin I may meet;
10.600: Which here, though plenteous, all too little seems
10.601: To stuff this Maw, this vast unhide-bound Corps.
10.602: To whom th' incestuous Mother thus repli'd.
10.603: Thou therefore on these Herbs, and Fruits, & Flours
10.604: Feed first, on each Beast next, and Fish, and Fowle,
10.605: No homely morsels, and whatever thing
10.606: The Sithe of Time mowes down, devour unspar'd,
10.607: Till I in Man residing through the Race,
10.608: His thoughts, his looks, words, actions all infect,
10.609: And season him thy last and sweetest prey.
10.610: This said, they both betook them several wayes,
10.611: Both to destroy, or unimmortal make
10.612: All kinds, and for destruction to mature
10.613: Sooner or later; which th' Almightie seeing,
10.614: From his transcendent Seat the Saints among,
10.615: To those bright Orders utterd thus his voice.
10.616: See with what heat these Dogs of Hell advance
10.617: To waste and havoc yonder World, which I
10.618: So fair and good created, and had still
10.619: Kept in that state, had not the folly of Man
10.620: Let in these wastful Furies, who impute
10.621: Folly to mee, so doth the Prince of Hell
10.622: And his Adherents, that with so much ease
10.623: I suffer them to enter and possess
10.624: A place so heav'nly, and conniving seem
10.626: That laugh, as if transported with some fit
10.627: Of Passion, I to them had quitted all,
10.628: At random yeilded up to their misrule;
10.629: And know not that I call'd and drew them thither
10.630: My Hell-hounds, to lick up the draff and filth
10.631: Which mans polluting Sin with taint hath shed
10.632: On what was pure, till cramm'd and gorg'd, nigh burst
10.633: With suckt and glutted offal, at one fling
10.634: Of thy victorious Arm, well-pleasing Son,
10.635: Both Sin, and Death, and yawning Grave at last
10.636: Through Chaos hurld, obstruct the mouth of Hell
10.637: For ever, and seal up his ravenous Jawes.
10.638: Then Heav'n and Earth renewd shall be made pure
10.639: To sanctitie that shall receive no staine:
10.640: Till then the Curse pronounc't on both precedes.
10.641: Hee ended, and the heav'nly Audience loud
10.642: Sung Halleluia, as the sound of Seas,
10.643: Through multitude that sung: Just are thy ways,
10.644: Righteous are thy Decrees on all thy Works;
10.645: Who can extenuate thee? Next, to the Son,
10.646: Destin'd restorer of Mankind, by whom
10.647: New Heav'n and Earth shall to the Ages rise,
10.648: Or down from Heav'n descend. Such was thir song,
10.649: While the Creator calling forth by name
10.650: His mightie Angels gave them several charge,
10.651: As sorted best with present things. The Sun
10.652: Had first his precept so to move, so shine,
10.653: As might affect the Earth with cold and heat
10.654: Scarce tollerable, and from the North to call
10.655: Decrepit Winter, from the South to bring
10.656: Solstitial summers heat. To the blanc Moone
10.657: Her office they prescrib'd, to th' other five
10.659: In Sextile, Square, and Trine, and Opposite,
10.660: Of noxious efficacie, and when to joyne
10.661: In Synod unbenigne, and taught the fixt
10.662: Thir influence malignant when to showre,
10.663: Which of them rising with the Sun, or falling,
10.664: Should prove tempestuous: To the Winds they set
10.665: Thir corners, when with bluster to confound
10.666: Sea, Aire, and Shoar, the Thunder when to rowle
10.667: With terror through the dark Aereal Hall.
10.668: Some say he bid his Angels turne ascanse
10.669: The Poles of Earth twice ten degrees and more
10.670: From the Suns Axle; they with labour push'd
10.671: Oblique the Centric Globe: Som say the Sun
10.672: Was bid turn Reines from th' Equinoctial Rode
10.673: Like distant breadth to Taurus with the Seav'n
10.674: Atlantick Sisters, and the Spartan Twins
10.675: Up to the Tropic Crab; thence down amaine
10.676: By Leo and the Virgin and the Scales,
10.677: As deep as Capricorne, to bring in change
10.678: Of Seasons to each Clime; else had the Spring
10.679: Perpetual smil'd on Earth with vernant Flours,
10.680: Equal in Days and Nights, except to those
10.681: Beyond the Polar Circles; to them Day
10.682: Had unbenighted shon, while the low Sun
10.683: To recompence his distance, in thir sight
10.684: Had rounded still th' Horizon, and not known
10.685: Or East or West, which had forbid the Snow
10.686: From cold Estotiland, and South as farr
10.687: Beneath Magellan. At that tasted Fruit
10.688: The Sun, as from Thyestean Banquet, turn'd
10.689: His course intended; else how had the World
10.690: Inhabited, though sinless, more then now,
10.691: Avoided pinching cold and scorching heate?
10.692: These changes in the Heav'ns, though slow, produc'd
10.693: Like change on Sea and Land, sideral blast,
10.694: Vapour, and Mist, and Exhalation hot,
10.695: Corrupt and Pestilent: Now from the North
10.696: Of Norumbega, and the Samoed shoar
10.697: Bursting thir brazen Dungeon, armd with ice
10.698: And snow and haile and stormie gust and flaw,
10.699: Boreas and Caecias and Argestes loud
10.700: And Thrascias rend the Woods and Seas upturn;
10.701: With adverse blast up-turns them from the South
10.702: Notus and Afer black with thundrous Clouds
10.703: From Serraliona; thwart of these as fierce
10.704: Forth rush the Levant and the Ponent Windes
10.705: Eurus and Zephir with thir lateral noise,
10.707: Outrage from liveless things; but Discord first
10.708: Daughter of Sin, among th' irrational,
10.710: Beast now with Beast gan war, & Fowle with Fowle,
10.711: And Fish with Fish; to graze the Herb all leaving,
10.712: Devourd each other; nor stood much in awe
10.713: Of Man, but fled him, or with count'nance grim
10.714: Glar'd on him passing: these were from without
10.715: The growing miseries, which Adam saw
10.716: Alreadie in part, though hid in gloomiest shade,
10.717: To sorrow abandond, but worse felt within,
10.718: And in a troubl'd Sea of passion tost,
10.719: Thus to disburd'n sought with sad complaint.
10.720: O miserable of happie! is this the end
10.721: Of this new glorious World, and mee so late
10.722: The Glory of that Glory, who now becom
10.723: Accurst of blessed, hide me from the face
10.724: Of God, whom to behold was then my highth
10.725: Of happiness: yet well, if here would end
10.726: The miserie, I deserv'd it, and would beare
10.727: My own deservings; but this will not serve;
10.728: All that I eate or drink, or shall beget,
10.729: Is propagated curse. O voice once heard
10.731: Now death to heare! for what can I encrease
10.732: Or multiplie, but curses on my head?
10.733: Who of all Ages to succeed, but feeling
10.734: The evil on him brought by me, will curse
10.735: My Head, Ill fare our Ancestor impure,
10.736: For this we may thank Adam; but his thanks
10.737: Shall be the execration; so besides
10.738: Mine own that bide upon me, all from mee
10.739: Shall with a fierce reflux on mee redound,
10.740: On mee as on thir natural center light
10.741: Heavie, though in thir place. O fleeting joyes
10.742: Of Paradise, deare bought with lasting woes!
10.743: Did I request thee, Maker, from my Clay
10.744: To mould me Man, did I sollicite thee
10.745: From darkness to promote me, or here place
10.746: In this delicious Garden? as my Will
10.747: Concurd not to my being, it were but right
10.748: And equal to reduce me to my dust,
10.749: Desirous to resigne, and render back
10.750: All I receav'd, unable to performe
10.751: Thy terms too hard, by which I was to hold
10.752: The good I sought not. To the loss of that,
10.753: Sufficient penaltie, why hast thou added
10.754: The sense of endless woes? inexplicable
10.755: Thy Justice seems; yet to say truth, too late,
10.756: I thus contest; then should have been refusd
10.757: Those terms whatever, when they were propos'd:
10.758: Thou didst accept them; wilt thou enjoy the good,
10.759: Then cavil the conditions? and though God
10.760: Made thee without thy leave, what if thy Son
10.762: Wherefore didst thou beget me? I sought it not:
10.763: Wouldst thou admit for his contempt of thee
10.764: That proud excuse? yet him not thy election,
10.766: God made thee of choice his own, and of his own
10.767: To serve him, thy reward was of his grace,
10.768: Thy punishment then justly is at his Will.
10.769: Be it so, for I submit, his doom is fair,
10.770: That dust I am, and shall to dust returne:
10.771: O welcom hour whenever! why delayes
10.772: His hand to execute what his Decree
10.773: Fixd on this day? why do I overlive,
10.774: Why am I mockt with death, and length'nd out
10.775: To deathless pain? how gladly would I meet
10.776: Mortalitie my sentence, and be Earth
10.777: Insensible, how glad would lay me down
10.778: As in my Mothers lap? there I should rest
10.779: And sleep secure; his dreadful voice no more
10.780: Would Thunder in my ears, no fear of worse
10.781: To mee and to my ofspring would torment me
10.782: With cruel expectation. Yet one doubt
10.783: Pursues me still, least all I cannot die,
10.784: Least that pure breath of Life, the Spirit of Man
10.785: Which God inspir'd, cannot together perish
10.786: With this corporeal Clod; then in the Grave,
10.787: Or in some other dismal place, who knows
10.788: But I shall die a living Death? O thought
10.789: Horrid, if true! yet why? it was but breath
10.790: Of Life that sinn'd; what dies but what had life
10.791: And sin? the Bodie properly hath neither.
10.792: All of me then shall die: let this appease
10.793: The doubt, since humane reach no further knows.
10.794: For though the Lord of all be infinite,
10.795: Is his wrauth also? be it, man is not so,
10.796: But mortal doom'd. How can he exercise
10.797: Wrath without end on Man whom Death must end?
10.798: Can he make deathless Death? that were to make
10.799: Strange contradiction, which to God himself
10.801: Of weakness, not of Power. Will he, draw out,
10.802: For angers sake, finite to infinite
10.803: In punisht man, to satisfie his rigour
10.804: Satisfi'd never; that were to extend
10.805: His Sentence beyond dust and Natures Law,
10.806: By which all Causes else according still
10.807: To the reception of thir matter act,
10.808: Not to th' extent of thir own Spheare. But say
10.809: That Death be not one stroak, as I suppos'd,
10.811: From this day onward, which I feel begun
10.812: Both in me, and without me, and so last
10.813: To perpetuitie; Ay me, that fear
10.814: Comes thundring back with dreadful revolution
10.815: On my defensless head; both Death and I
10.816: Am found Eternal, and incorporate both,
10.817: Nor I on my part single, in mee all
10.819: That I must leave ye, Sons; O were I able
10.820: To waste it all my self, and leave ye none!
10.821: So disinherited how would ye bless
10.822: Me now your Curse! Ah, why should all mankind
10.823: For one mans fault thus guiltless be condemn'd,
10.824: If guiltless? But from mee what can proceed,
10.825: But all corrupt, both Mind and Will deprav'd,
10.826: Not to do onely, but to will the same
10.827: With me? how can they acquitted stand
10.828: In sight of God? Him after all Disputes
10.829: Forc't I absolve: all my evasions vain
10.830: And reasonings, though through Mazes, lead me still
10.831: But to my own conviction: first and last
10.832: On mee, mee onely, as the sourse and spring
10.833: Of all corruption, all the blame lights due;
10.834: So might the wrauth, Fond wish! couldst thou support
10.835: That burden heavier then the Earth to bear,
10.836: Then all the world much heavier, though divided
10.837: With that bad Woman? Thus what thou desir'st,
10.838: And what thou fearst, alike destroyes all hope
10.839: Of refuge, and concludes thee miserable
10.840: Beyond all past example and future,
10.841: To Satan onely like both crime and doom.
10.842: O Conscience, into what Abyss of fears
10.843: And horrors hast thou driv'n me; out of which
10.844: I find no way, from deep to deeper plung'd!
10.845: Thus Adam to himself lamented loud
10.846: Through the still Night, not now, as ere man fell,
10.847: Wholsom and cool, and mild, but with black Air
10.848: Accompanied, with damps and dreadful gloom,
10.849: Which to his evil Conscience represented
10.850: All things with double terror: On the ground
10.851: Outstretcht he lay, on the cold ground, and oft
10.852: Curs'd his Creation, Death as oft accus'd
10.854: The day of his offence. Why comes not Death,
10.855: Said hee, with one thrice acceptable stroke
10.856: To end me? Shall Truth fail to keep her word,
10.857: Justice Divine not hast'n to be just?
10.858: But Death comes not at call, Justice Divine
10.859: Mends not her slowest pace for prayers or cries.
10.860: O Woods, O Fountains, Hillocks, Dales and Bowrs,
10.861: With other echo farr I taught your Shades
10.862: To answer, and resound farr other Song.
10.863: Whom thus afflicted when sad Eve beheld,
10.864: Desolate where she sate, approaching nigh,
10.865: Soft words to his fierce passion she assay'd:
10.866: But her with stern regard he thus repell'd.
10.867: Out of my sight, thou Serpent, that name best
10.868: Befits thee with him leagu'd, thy self as false
10.869: And hateful; nothing wants, but that thy shape,
10.870: Like his, and colour Serpentine may shew
10.871: Thy inward fraud, to warn all Creatures from thee
10.872: Henceforth; least that too heav'nly form, pretended
10.873: To hellish falshood, snare them. But for thee
10.874: I had persisted happie, had not thy pride
10.875: And wandring vanitie, when lest was safe,
10.877: Not to be trusted, longing to be seen
10.878: Though by the Devil himself, him overweening
10.879: To over-reach, but with the Serpent meeting
10.880: Fool'd and beguil'd, by him thou, I by thee,
10.881: To trust thee from my side, imagin'd wise,
10.882: Constant, mature, proof against all assaults,
10.883: And understood not all was but a shew
10.884: Rather then solid vertu, all but a Rib
10.885: Crooked by nature, bent, as now appears,
10.886: More to the part sinister from me drawn,
10.887: Well if thrown out, as supernumerarie
10.888: To my just number found. O why did God,
10.889: Creator wise, that peopl'd highest Heav'n
10.890: With Spirits Masculine, create at last
10.891: This noveltie on Earth, this fair defect
10.892: Of Nature, and not fill the World at once
10.893: With Men as Angels without Feminine,
10.894: Or find some other way to generate
10.895: Mankind? this mischief had not then befall'n,
10.896: And more that shall befall, innumerable
10.897: Disturbances on Earth through Femal snares,
10.898: And straight conjunction with this Sex: for either
10.899: He never shall find out fit Mate, but such
10.900: As some misfortune brings him, or mistake,
10.901: Or whom he wishes most shall seldom gain
10.902: Through her perverseness, but shall see her gaind
10.903: By a farr worse, or if she love, withheld
10.904: By Parents, or his happiest choice too late
10.905: Shall meet, alreadie linkt and Wedlock-bound
10.906: To a fell Adversarie, his hate or shame:
10.908: To humane life, and houshold peace confound.
10.909: He added not, and from her turn'd, but Eve
10.910: Not so repulst, with Tears that ceas'd not flowing,
10.911: And tresses all disorderd, at his feet
10.912: Fell humble, and imbracing them, besaught
10.913: His peace, and thus proceeded in her plaint.
10.914: Forsake me not thus, Adam, witness Heav'n
10.915: What love sincere, and reverence in my heart
10.916: I beare thee, and unweeting have offended,
10.918: I beg, and clasp thy knees; bereave me not,
10.919: Whereon I live, thy gentle looks, thy aid,
10.920: Thy counsel in this uttermost distress,
10.921: My onely strength and stay: forlorn of thee,
10.922: Whither shall I betake me, where subsist?
10.923: While yet we live, scarse one short hour perhaps,
10.924: Between us two let there be peace, both joyning,
10.925: As joyn'd in injuries, one enmitie
10.926: Against a Foe by doom express assign'd us,
10.927: That cruel Serpent: On me exercise not
10.928: Thy hatred for this miserie befall'n,
10.929: On me already lost, mee then thy self
10.930: More miserable; both have sin'd, but thou
10.931: Against God onely, I against God and thee,
10.932: And to the place of judgement will return,
10.933: There with my cries importune Heaven, that all
10.934: The sentence from thy head remov'd may light
10.935: On me, sole cause to thee of all this woe,
10.936: Mee mee onely just object of his ire.
10.937: She ended weeping, and her lowlie plight,
10.938: Immoveable till peace obtain'd from fault
10.939: Acknowledg'd and deplor'd, in Adam wraught
10.941: Towards her, his life so late and sole delight,
10.942: Now at his feet submissive in distress,
10.943: Creature so faire his reconcilement seeking,
10.944: His counsel whom she had displeas'd, his aide;
10.945: As one disarm'd, his anger all he lost,
10.946: And thus with peaceful words uprais'd her soon.
10.947: Unwarie, and too desirous, as before,
10.948: So now of what thou knowst not, who desir'st
10.949: The punishment all on thy self; alas,
10.950: Beare thine own first, ill able to sustaine
10.951: His full wrauth whose thou feelst as yet lest part,
10.952: And my displeasure bearst so ill. If Prayers
10.953: Could alter high Decrees, I to that place
10.954: Would speed before thee, and be louder heard,
10.955: That on my head all might be visited,
10.956: Thy frailtie and infirmer Sex forgiv'n,
10.957: To me committed and by me expos'd.
10.958: But rise, let us no more contend, nor blame
10.959: Each other, blam'd enough elsewhere, but strive
10.960: In offices of Love, how we may light'n
10.961: Each others burden in our share of woe;
10.962: Since this days Death denounc't, if ought I see,
10.963: Will prove no sudden, but a slow-pac't evill,
10.964: A long days dying to augment our paine,
10.965: And to our Seed (O hapless Seed!) deriv'd.
10.966: To whom thus Eve, recovering heart, repli'd.
10.967: Adam, by sad experiment I know
10.968: How little weight my words with thee can finde,
10.969: Found so erroneous, thence by just event
10.971: Restor'd by thee, vile as I am, to place
10.972: Of new acceptance, hopeful to regaine
10.973: Thy Love, the sole contentment of my heart,
10.974: Living or dying from thee I will not hide
10.975: What thoughts in my unquiet brest are ris'n,
10.976: Tending to som relief of our extremes,
10.977: Or end, though sharp and sad, yet tolerable,
10.978: As in our evils, and of easier choice.
10.979: If care of our descent perplex us most,
10.980: Which must be born to certain woe, devourd
10.981: By Death at last, and miserable it is
10.982: To be to others cause of misery,
10.983: Our own begotten, and of our Loines to bring
10.984: Into this cursed World a woful Race,
10.985: That after wretched Life must be at last
10.986: Food for so foule a Monster, in thy power
10.987: It lies, yet ere Conception to prevent
10.988: The Race unblest, to being yet unbegot.
10.990: So Death shall be deceav'd his glut, and with us two
10.991: Be forc'd to satisfie his Rav'nous Maw.
10.992: But if thou judge it hard and difficult,
10.994: From Loves due Rites, Nuptial embraces sweet,
10.995: And with desire to languish without hope,
10.997: With like desire, which would be miserie
10.998: And torment less then none of what we dread,
10.999: Then both our selves and Seed at once to free
10.1000: From what we fear for both, let us make short,
10.1001: Let us seek Death, or hee not found, supply
10.1002: With our own hands his Office on our selves;
10.1003: Why stand we longer shivering under feares,
10.1004: That shew no end but Death, and have the power,
10.1005: Of many wayes to die the shortest choosing,
10.1007: She ended heer, or vehement despaire
10.1008: Broke off the rest; so much of Death her thoughts
10.1009: Had entertaind, as di'd her Cheeks with pale.
10.1010: But Adam with such counsel nothing sway'd,
10.1011: To better hopes his more attentive minde
10.1012: Labouring had rais'd, and thus to Eve repli'd.
10.1013: Eve, thy contempt of life and pleasure seems
10.1014: To argue in thee somthing more sublime
10.1015: And excellent then what thy minde contemnes;
10.1017: That excellence thought in thee, and implies,
10.1018: Not thy contempt, but anguish and regret
10.1019: For loss of life and pleasure overlov'd.
10.1020: Or if thou covet death, as utmost end
10.1021: Of miserie, so thinking to evade
10.1022: The penaltie pronounc't, doubt not but God
10.1023: Hath wiselier arm'd his vengeful ire then so
10.1024: To be forestall'd; much more I fear least Death
10.1025: So snatcht will not exempt us from the paine
10.1026: We are by doom to pay; rather such acts
10.1027: Of contumacie will provoke the highest
10.1028: To make death in us live: Then let us seek
10.1030: I have in view, calling to minde with heed
10.1031: Part of our Sentence, that thy Seed shall bruise
10.1032: The Serpents head; piteous amends, unless
10.1033: Be meant, whom I conjecture, our grand Foe
10.1034: Satan, who in the Serpent hath contriv'd
10.1035: Against us this deceit: to crush his head
10.1036: Would be revenge indeed; which will be lost
10.1037: By death brought on our selves, or childless days
10.1038: Resolv'd, as thou proposest; so our Foe
10.1039: Shall scape his punishment ordain'd, and wee
10.1040: Instead shall double ours upon our heads.
10.1041: No more be mention'd then of violence
10.1042: Against our selves, and wilful barrenness,
10.1043: That cuts us off from hope, and savours onely
10.1044: Rancor and pride, impatience and despite,
10.1045: Reluctance against God and his just yoke
10.1046: Laid on our Necks. Remember with what mild
10.1047: And gracious temper he both heard and judg'd
10.1048: Without wrauth or reviling; wee expected
10.1050: Was meant by Death that day, when lo, to thee
10.1051: Pains onely in Child-bearing were foretold,
10.1052: And bringing forth, soon recompenc't with joy,
10.1053: Fruit of thy Womb: On mee the Curse aslope
10.1054: Glanc'd on the ground, with labour I must earne
10.1055: My bread; what harm? Idleness had bin worse;
10.1056: My labour will sustain me; and least Cold
10.1057: Or Heat should injure us, his timely care
10.1058: Hath unbesaught provided, and his hands
10.1059: Cloath'd us unworthie, pitying while he judg'd;
10.1060: How much more, if we pray him, will his ear
10.1061: Be open, and his heart to pitie incline,
10.1062: And teach us further by what means to shun
10.1063: Th' inclement Seasons, Rain, Ice, Hail and Snow,
10.1064: Which now the Skie with various Face begins
10.1065: To shew us in this Mountain, while the Winds
10.1066: Blow moist and keen, shattering the graceful locks
10.1067: Of these fair spreading Trees; which bids us seek
10.1068: Som better shroud, som better warmth to cherish
10.1069: Our Limbs benumm'd, ere this diurnal Starr
10.1070: Leave cold the Night, how we his gather'd beams
10.1071: Reflected, may with matter sere foment,
10.1072: Or by collision of two bodies grinde
10.1073: The Air attrite to Fire, as late the Clouds
10.1074: Justling or pusht with Winds rude in thir shock
10.1075: Tine the slant Lightning, whose thwart flame driv'n down
10.1076: Kindles the gummie bark of Firr or Pine,
10.1077: And sends a comfortable heat from farr,
10.1078: Which might supplie the Sun: such Fire to use,
10.1079: And what may else be remedie or cure
10.1080: To evils which our own misdeeds have wrought,
10.1081: Hee will instruct us praying, and of Grace
10.1082: Beseeching him, so as we need not fear
10.1083: To pass commodiously this life, sustain'd
10.1084: By him with many comforts, till we end
10.1085: In dust, our final rest and native home.
10.1086: What better can we do, then to the place
10.1087: Repairing where he judg'd us, prostrate fall
10.1088: Before him reverent, and there confess
10.1089: Humbly our faults, and pardon beg, with tears
10.1090: Watering the ground, and with our sighs the Air
10.1091: Frequenting, sent from hearts contrite, in sign
10.1092: Of sorrow unfeign'd, and humiliation meek.
10.1093: Undoubtedly he will relent and turn
10.1094: From his displeasure; in whose look serene,
10.1095: When angry most he seem'd and most severe,
10.1096: What else but favor, grace, and mercie shon?
10.1097: So spake our Father penitent, nor Eve
10.1098: Felt less remorse: they forthwith to the place
10.1099: Repairing where he judg'd them prostrate fell
10.1100: Before him reverent, and both confess'd
10.1101: Humbly thir faults, and pardon beg'd, with tears
10.1102: Watering the ground, and with thir sighs the Air
10.1103: Frequenting, sent from hearts contrite, in sign
10.1104: Of sorrow unfeign'd, and humiliation meek.

11.0:
*The Argument*
The Son of God presents to his Father the Prayers of our first Parents now repenting, and intercedes for them: God accepts them, but declares that they must no longer abide in Paradise; sends Michael with a Band of Cherubim to dispossess them; but first to reveal to Adam future things: Michaels coming down, Adam shews to Eve certain ominous signs; he discerns Michaels approach, goes out to meet him: the Angel denounces thir departure.  Eve's Lamentation. Adam pleads, but submits: The Angel leads him up to a high Hill, sets before him in a vision what shall happ'n till the Flood.
11.1: Thus they in lowliest plight repentant stood
11.2: Praying, for from the Mercie-seat above
11.4: The stonie from thir hearts, and made new flesh
11.5: Regenerat grow instead, that sighs now breath'd
11.6: Unutterable, which the Spirit of prayer
11.7: Inspir'd, and wing'd for Heav'n with speedier flight
11.8: Then loudest Oratorie: yet thir port
11.9: Not of mean suiters, nor important less
11.10: Seem'd thir Petition, then when th' ancient Pair
11.11: In Fables old, less ancient yet then these,
11.12: Deucalion and chaste Pyrrha to restore
11.13: The Race of Mankind drownd, before the Shrine
11.14: Of Themis stood devout. To Heav'n thir prayers
11.15: Flew up, nor missed the way, by envious windes
11.16: Blow'n vagabond or frustrate: in they passd
11.17: Dimentionless through Heav'nly dores; then clad
