11.18: With incense, where the Golden Altar fum'd,
11.19: By thir great Intercessor, came in sight
11.20: Before the Fathers Throne: Them the glad Son
11.22: See Father, what first fruits on Earth are sprung
11.23: From thy implanted Grace in Man, these Sighs
11.24: And Prayers, which in this Golden Censer, mixt
11.25: With Incense, I thy Priest before thee bring,
11.26: Fruits of more pleasing savour from thy seed
11.27: Sow'n with contrition in his heart, then those
11.28: Which his own hand manuring all the Trees
11.29: Of Paradise could have produc't, ere fall'n
11.30: From innocence. Now therefore bend thine eare
11.31: To supplication, heare his sighs though mute;
11.32: Unskilful with what words to pray, let mee
11.33: Interpret for him, mee his Advocate
11.34: And propitiation, all his works on mee
11.35: Good or not good ingraft, my Merit those
11.36: Shall perfet, and for these my Death shall pay.
11.37: Accept me, and in mee from these receave
11.38: The smell of peace toward Mankinde, let him live
11.39: Before thee reconcil'd, at least his days
11.40: Numberd, though sad, till Death, his doom (which I
11.41: To mitigate thus plead, not to reverse)
11.42: To better life shall yeeld him, where with mee
11.43: All my redeemd may dwell in joy and bliss,
11.44: Made one with me as I with thee am one.
11.45: To whom the Father, without Cloud, serene.
11.46: All thy request for Man, accepted Son,
11.47: Obtain, all thy request was my Decree:
11.48: But longer in that Paradise to dwell,
11.49: The Law I gave to Nature him forbids:
11.50: Those pure immortal Elements that know
11.51: No gross, no unharmoneous mixture foule,
11.52: Eject him tainted now, and purge him off
11.53: As a distemper, gross to aire as gross,
11.54: And mortal food, as may dispose him best
11.55: For dissolution wrought by Sin, that first
11.56: Distemperd all things, and of incorrupt
11.57: Corrupted. I at first with two fair gifts
11.60: This other serv'd but to eternize woe;
11.61: Till I provided Death; so Death becomes
11.62: His final remedie, and after Life
11.63: Tri'd in sharp tribulation, and refin'd
11.64: By Faith and faithful works, to second Life,
11.65: Wak't in the renovation of the just,
11.66: Resignes him up with Heav'n and Earth renewd.
11.67: But let us call to Synod all the Blest
11.68: Through Heav'ns wide bounds; from them I will not hide
11.69: My judgments, how with Mankind I proceed,
11.70: As how with peccant Angels late they saw;
11.71: And in thir state, though firm, stood more confirmd.
11.72: He ended, and the Son gave signal high
11.73: To the bright Minister that watchd, hee blew
11.74: His Trumpet, heard in Oreb since perhaps
11.75: When God descended, and perhaps once more
11.76: To sound at general Doom. Th' Angelic blast
11.77: Filld all the Regions: from thir blissful Bowrs
11.78: Of Amarantin Shade, Fountain or Spring,
11.79: By the waters of Life, where ere they sate
11.80: In fellowships of joy: the Sons of Light
11.81: Hasted, resorting to the Summons high,
11.82: And took thir Seats; till from his Throne supream
11.83: Th' Almighty thus pronounced his sovran Will.
11.84: O Sons, like one of us Man is become
11.85: To know both Good and Evil, since his taste
11.86: Of that defended Fruit; but let him boast
11.87: His knowledge of Good lost, and Evil got,
11.88: Happier, had it suffic'd him to have known
11.89: Good by it self, and Evil not at all.
11.90: He sorrows now, repents, and prayes contrite,
11.91: My motions in him, longer then they move,
11.92: His heart I know, how variable and vain
11.93: Self-left. Least therefore his now bolder hand
11.94: Reach also of the Tree of Life, and eat,
11.95: And live for ever, dream at least to live
11.96: Forever, to remove him I decree,
11.97: And send him from the Garden forth to Till
11.98: The Ground whence he was taken, fitter soile.
11.99: Michael, this my behest have thou in charge,
11.100: Take to thee from among the Cherubim
11.101: Thy choice of flaming Warriours, least the Fiend
11.102: Or in behalf of Man, or to invade
11.103: Vacant possession som new trouble raise:
11.104: Hast thee, and from the Paradise of God
11.105: Without remorse drive out the sinful Pair,
11.106: From hallowd ground th' unholie, and denounce
11.107: To them and to thir Progenie from thence
11.108: Perpetual banishment. Yet least they faint
11.109: At the sad Sentence rigorously urg'd,
11.110: For I behold them soft'nd and with tears
11.111: Bewailing thir excess, all terror hide.
11.112: If patiently thy bidding they obey,
11.114: To Adam what shall come in future dayes,
11.115: As I shall thee enlighten, intermix
11.116: My Cov'nant in the Womans seed renewd;
11.117: So send them forth, though sorrowing, yet in peace:
11.118: And on the East side of the Garden place,
11.119: Where entrance up from Eden easiest climbes,
11.120: Cherubic watch, and of a Sword the flame
11.121: Wide waving, all approach farr off to fright,
11.122: And guard all passage to the Tree of Life:
11.124: To Spirits foule, and all my Trees thir prey,
11.125: With whose stol'n Fruit Man once more to delude.
11.126: He ceas'd; and th' Archangelic Power prepar'd
11.127: For swift descent, with him the Cohort bright
11.128: Of watchful Cherubim; four faces each
11.129: Had, like a double Janus, all thir shape
11.130: Spangl'd with eyes more numerous then those
11.131: Of Argus, and more wakeful then to drouze,
11.132: Charm'd with Arcadian Pipe, the Pastoral Reed
11.133: Of Hermes, or his opiate Rod. Meanwhile
11.134: To resalute the World with sacred Light
11.135: Leucothea wak'd, and with fresh dews imbalmd
11.136: The Earth, when Adam and first Matron Eve
11.137: Had ended now thir Orisons, and found,
11.138: Strength added from above, new hope to spring
11.139: Out of despaire, joy, but with fear yet linkt;
11.140: Which thus to Eve his welcome words renewd.
11.141: Eve, easily may Faith admit, that all
11.142: The good which we enjoy, from Heav'n descends
11.143: But that from us ought should ascend to Heav'n
11.144: So prevalent as to concerne the mind
11.145: Of God high blest, or to incline his will,
11.146: Hard to belief may seem; yet this will Prayer,
11.147: Or one short sigh of humane breath, up-borne
11.148: Ev'n to the Seat of God. For since I saught
11.149: By Prayer th' offended Deitie to appease,
11.150: Kneel'd and before him humbl'd all my heart,
11.151: Methought I saw him placable and mild,
11.152: Bending his eare; perswasion in me grew
11.153: That I was heard with favour; peace returnd
11.154: Home to my brest, and to my memorie
11.155: His promise, that thy Seed shall bruise our Foe;
11.156: Which then not minded in dismay, yet now
11.157: Assures me that the bitterness of death
11.158: Is past, and we shall live. Whence Haile to thee,
11.159: Eve rightly call'd, Mother of all Mankind,
11.160: Mother of all things living, since by thee
11.161: Man is to live, and all things live for Man.
11.162: To whom thus Eve with sad demeanour meek.
11.163: Ill worthie I such title should belong
11.164: To me transgressour, who for thee ordaind
11.165: A help, became thy snare; to mee reproach
11.166: Rather belongs, distrust and all dispraise:
11.167: But infinite in pardon was my Judge,
11.168: That I who first brought Death on all, am grac't
11.169: The sourse of life; next favourable thou,
11.170: Who highly thus to entitle me voutsaf't,
11.171: Farr other name deserving. But the Field
11.172: To labour calls us now with sweat impos'd,
11.173: Though after sleepless Night; for see the Morn,
11.174: All unconcern'd with our unrest, begins
11.175: Her rosie progress smiling; let us forth,
11.176: I never from thy side henceforth to stray,
11.177: Wherere our days work lies, though now enjoind
11.178: Laborious, till day droop; while here we dwell,
11.179: What can be toilsom in these pleasant Walkes?
11.180: Here let us live, though in fall'n state, content.
11.181: So spake, so wish'd much-humbl'd Eve, but Fate
11.182: Subscrib'd not; Nature first gave Signs, imprest
11.183: On Bird, Beast, Aire, Aire suddenly eclips'd
11.184: After short blush of Morn; nigh in her sight
11.185: The Bird of Jove, stoopt from his aerie tour,
11.186: Two Birds of gayest plume before him drove:
11.187: Down from a Hill the Beast that reigns in Woods,
11.188: First Hunter then, pursu'd a gentle brace,
11.189: Goodliest of all the Forrest, Hart and Hinde;
11.190: Direct to th' Eastern Gate was bent thir flight.
11.191: Adam observ'd, and with his Eye the chase
11.192: Pursuing, not unmov'd to Eve thus spake.
11.193: O Eve, some furder change awaits us nigh,
11.194: Which Heav'n by these mute signs in Nature shews
11.195: Forerunners of his purpose, or to warn
11.196: Us haply too secure of our discharge
11.197: From penaltie, because from death releast
11.198: Some days; how long, and what till then our life,
11.199: Who knows, or more then this, that we are dust,
11.200: And thither must return and be no more.
11.201: Why else this double object in our sight
11.202: Of flight pursu'd in th' Air and ore the ground
11.203: One way the self-same hour? why in the East
11.204: Darkness ere Dayes mid-course, and Morning light
11.205: More orient in yon Western Cloud that draws
11.206: O're the blew Firmament a radiant white,
11.207: And slow descends, with somthing heav'nly fraught.
11.208: He err'd not, for by this the heav'nly Bands
11.209: Down from a Skie of Jasper lighted now
11.210: In Paradise, and on a Hill made alt,
11.211: A glorious Apparition, had not doubt
11.212: And carnal fear that day dimm'd Adams eye.
11.213: Not that more glorious, when the Angels met
11.214: Jacob in Mahanaim, where he saw
11.215: The field Pavilion'd with his Guardians bright;
11.216: Nor that which on the flaming Mount appeerd
11.217: In Dothan, cover'd with a Camp of Fire,
11.218: Against the Syrian King, who to surprize
11.219: One man, Assassin-like had levied Warr,
11.221: In thir bright stand, there left his Powers to seise
11.222: Possession of the Garden; hee alone,
11.223: To finde where Adam shelterd, took his way,
11.224: Not unperceav'd of Adam, who to Eve,
11.225: While the great Visitant approachd, thus spake.
11.226: Eve, now expect great tidings, which perhaps
11.227: Of us will soon determin, or impose
11.228: New Laws to be observ'd; for I descrie
11.229: From yonder blazing Cloud that veils the Hill
11.230: One of the heav'nly Host, and by his Gate
11.231: None of the meanest, some great Potentate
11.232: Or of the Thrones above, such Majestie
11.233: Invests him coming; yet not terrible,
11.234: That I should fear, nor sociably mild,
11.235: As Raphael, that I should much confide,
11.236: But solemn and sublime, whom not to offend,
11.237: With reverence I must meet, and thou retire.
11.238: He ended; and th' Arch-Angel soon drew nigh,
11.239: Not in his shape Celestial, but as Man
11.240: Clad to meet Man; over his lucid Armes
11.241: A militarie Vest of purple flowd
11.242: Livelier then Meliboean, or the graine
11.243: Of Sarra, worn by Kings and Hero's old
11.244: In time of Truce; Iris had dipt the wooff;
11.245: His starrie Helme unbuckl'd shew'd him prime
11.246: In Manhood where Youth ended; by his side
11.247: As in a glistering Zodiac hung the Sword,
11.248: Satans dire dread, and in his hand the Spear.
11.249: Adam bowd low, hee Kingly from his State
11.250: Inclin'd not, but his coming thus declar'd.
11.251: Adam, Heav'ns high behest no Preface needs:
11.252: Sufficient that thy Prayers are heard, and Death,
11.253: Then due by sentence when thou didst transgress,
11.254: Defeated of his seisure many dayes
11.255: Giv'n thee of Grace, wherein thou may'st repent,
11.256: And one bad act with many deeds well done
11.257: Mayst cover: well may then thy Lord appeas'd
11.258: Redeem thee quite from Deaths rapacious claimes;
11.259: But longer in this Paradise to dwell
11.260: Permits not; to remove thee I am come,
11.261: And send thee from the Garden forth to till
11.262: The ground whence thou wast tak'n, fitter Soile.
11.263: He added not, for Adam at the newes
11.264: Heart-strook with chilling gripe of sorrow stood,
11.265: That all his senses bound; Eve, who unseen
11.266: Yet all had heard, with audible lament
11.267: Discover'd soon the place of her retire.
11.268: O unexpected stroke, worse then of Death!
11.269: Must I thus leave thee Paradise? thus leave
11.270: Thee Native Soile, these happie Walks and Shades,
11.271: Fit haunt of Gods? where I had hope to spend,
11.272: Quiet though sad, the respit of that day
11.273: That must be mortal to us both. O flours,
11.274: That never will in other Climate grow,
11.275: My early visitation, and my last
11.276: At Eev'n, which I bred up with tender hand
11.277: From the first op'ning bud, and gave ye Names,
11.278: Who now shall reare ye to the Sun, or ranke
11.279: Your Tribes, and water from th' ambrosial Fount?
11.280: Thee lastly nuptial Bowre, by mee adornd
11.281: With what to sight or smell was sweet; from thee
11.282: How shall I part, and whither wander down
11.283: Into a lower World, to this obscure
11.284: And wilde, how shall we breath in other Aire
11.285: Less pure, accustomd to immortal Fruits?
11.286: Whom thus the Angel interrupted milde.
11.287: Lament not Eve, but patiently resigne
11.288: What justly thou hast lost; nor set thy heart,
11.289: Thus over fond, on that which is not thine;
11.290: Thy going is not lonely, with thee goes
11.291: Thy Husband, him to follow thou art bound;
11.292: Where he abides, think there thy native soile.
11.293: Adam by this from the cold sudden damp
11.294: Recovering, and his scatterd spirits returnd,
11.295: To Michael thus his humble words addressd.
11.296: Celestial, whether among the Thrones, or nam'd
11.297: Of them the Highest, for such of shape may seem
11.298: Prince above Princes, gently hast thou tould
11.299: Thy message, which might else in telling wound,
11.300: And in performing end us; what besides
11.301: Of sorrow and dejection and despair
11.302: Our frailtie can sustain, thy tidings bring,
11.303: Departure from this happy place, our sweet
11.305: Familiar to our eyes, all places else
11.307: Nor knowing us nor known: and if by prayer
11.308: Incessant I could hope to change the will
11.309: Of him who all things can, I would not cease
11.310: To wearie him with my assiduous cries:
11.311: But prayer against his absolute Decree
11.312: No more availes then breath against the winde,
11.313: Blown stifling back on him that breaths it forth:
11.314: Therefore to his great bidding I submit.
11.315: This most afflicts me, that departing hence,
11.316: As from his face I shall be hid, deprivd
11.317: His blessed count'nance; here I could frequent,
11.318: With worship, place by place where he voutsaf'd
11.319: Presence Divine, and to my Sons relate;
11.320: On this Mount he appeerd, under this Tree
11.321: Stood visible, among these Pines his voice
11.322: I heard, here with him at this Fountain talk'd:
11.323: So many grateful Altars I would reare
11.324: Of grassie Terfe, and pile up every Stone
11.325: Of lustre from the brook, in memorie,
11.326: Or monument to Ages, and thereon
11.327: Offer sweet smelling Gumms & Fruits and Flours:
11.328: In yonder nether World where shall I seek
11.329: His bright appearances, or footstep trace?
11.330: For though I fled him angrie, yet recall'd
11.331: To life prolongd and promisd Race, I now
11.332: Gladly behold though but his utmost skirts
11.333: Of glory, and farr off his steps adore.
11.334: To whom thus Michael with regard benigne.
11.335: Adam, thou know'st Heav'n his, and all the Earth
11.336: Not this Rock onely; his Omnipresence fills
11.337: Land, Sea, and Aire, and every kinde that lives,
11.338: Fomented by his virtual power and warmd:
11.339: All th' Earth he gave thee to possess and rule,
11.340: No despicable gift; surmise not then
11.341: His presence to these narrow bounds confin'd
11.342: Of Paradise or Eden: this had been
11.343: Perhaps thy Capital Seate, from whence had spred
11.344: All generations, and had hither come
11.345: From all the ends of th' Earth, to celebrate
11.346: And reverence thee thir great Progenitor.
11.347: But this praeeminence thou hast lost, brought down
11.348: To dwell on eeven ground now with thy Sons:
11.349: Yet doubt not but in Vallie and in Plaine
11.350: God is as here, and will be found alike
11.351: Present, and of his presence many a signe
11.352: Still following thee, still compassing thee round
11.353: With goodness and paternal Love, his Face
11.354: Express, and of his steps the track Divine.
11.355: Which that thou mayst beleeve, and be confirmd,
11.356: Ere thou from hence depart, know I am sent
11.357: To shew thee what shall come in future dayes
11.358: To thee and to thy Ofspring; good with bad
11.359: Expect to hear, supernal Grace contending
11.360: With sinfulness of Men; thereby to learn
11.361: True patience, and to temper joy with fear
11.363: By moderation either state to beare,
11.364: Prosperous or adverse: so shalt thou lead
11.365: Safest thy life, and best prepar'd endure
11.366: Thy mortal passage when it comes. Ascend
11.367: This Hill; let Eve (for I have drencht her eyes)
11.368: Here sleep below while thou to foresight wak'st,
11.369: As once thou slepst, while Shee to life was formd.
11.370: To whom thus Adam gratefully repli'd.
11.371: Ascend, I follow thee, safe Guide, the path
11.372: Thou lead'st me, and to the hand of Heav'n submit,
11.373: However chast'ning, to the evil turne
11.374: My obvious breast, arming to overcom
11.375: By suffering, and earne rest from labour won,
11.376: If so I may attain. So both ascend
11.377: In the Visions of God: It was a Hill
11.378: Of Paradise the highest, from whose top
11.379: The Hemisphere of Earth in cleerest Ken
11.380: Stretcht out to amplest reach of prospect lay.
11.381: Not higher that Hill nor wider looking round,
11.382: Whereon for different cause the Tempter set
11.383: Our second Adam in the Wilderness,
11.384: To shew him all Earths Kingdomes and thir Glory.
11.385: His Eye might there command wherever stood
11.386: City of old or modern Fame, the Seat
11.387: Of mightiest Empire, from the destind Walls
11.388: Of Cambalu, seat of Cathaian Can
11.389: And Samarchand by Oxus, Temirs Throne,
11.390: To Paquin of Sinaean Kings, and thence
11.391: To Agra and Lahor of great Mogul
11.392: Down to the golden Chersonese, or where
11.393: The Persian in Ecbatan sate, or since
11.394: In Hispahan, or where the Russian Ksar
11.395: In Mosco, or the Sultan in Bizance,
11.396: Turchestan-born; nor could his eye not ken
11.397: Th' Empire of Negus to his utmost Port
11.398: Ercoco and the less Maritine Kings
11.400: And Sofala thought Ophir, to the Realme
11.401: Of Congo, and Angola fardest South;
11.402: Or thence from Niger Flood to Atlas Mount
11.403: The Kingdoms of Almansor, Fez, and Sus,
11.405: On Europe thence, and where Rome was to sway
11.406: The World: in Spirit perhaps he also saw
11.407: Rich Mexico the seat of Motezume,
11.408: And Cusco in Peru, the richer seat
11.410: Guiana, whose great Citie Geryons Sons
11.411: Call El Dorado: but to nobler sights
11.412: Michael from Adams eyes the Filme remov'd
11.413: Which that false Fruit that promis'd clearer sight
11.414: Had bred; then purg'd with Euphrasie and Rue
11.415: The visual Nerve, for he had much to see;
11.416: And from the Well of Life three drops instill'd.
11.417: So deep the power of these Ingredients pierc'd,
11.418: Eevn to the inmost seat of mental sight,
11.419: That Adam now enforc't to close his eyes,
11.420: Sunk down and all his Spirits became intranst:
11.421: But him the gentle Angel by the hand
11.422: Soon rais'd, and his attention thus recall'd.
11.423: Adam, now ope thine eyes, and first behold
11.424: Th' effects which thy original crime hath wrought
11.425: In some to spring from thee, who never touch'd
11.426: Th' excepted Tree, nor with the Snake conspir'd,
11.427: Nor sinn'd thy sin, yet from that sin derive
11.428: Corruption to bring forth more violent deeds.
11.429: His eyes he op'nd, and beheld a field,
11.430: Part arable and tilth, whereon were Sheaves
11.431: New reapt, the other part sheep-walks and foulds;
11.432: Ith' midst an Altar as the Land-mark stood
11.433: Rustic, of grassie sord; thither anon
11.434: A sweatie Reaper from his Tillage brought
11.435: First Fruits, the green Eare, and the yellow Sheaf,
11.436: Uncull'd, as came to hand; a Shepherd next
11.437: More meek came with the Firstlings of his Flock
11.438: Choicest and best; then sacrificing, laid
11.439: The Inwards and thir Fat, with Incense strew'd,
11.440: On the cleft Wood, and all due Rites perform'd.
11.441: His Offring soon propitious Fire from Heav'n
11.442: Consum'd with nimble glance, and grateful steame;
11.443: The others not, for his was not sincere;
11.444: Whereat hee inlie rag'd, and as they talk'd,
11.445: Smote him into the Midriff with a stone
11.446: That beat out life; he fell, and deadly pale
11.447: Groand out his Soul with gushing bloud effus'd.
11.448: Much at that sight was Adam in his heart
11.449: Dismai'd, and thus in haste to th' Angel cri'd.
11.450: O Teacher, some great mischief hath befall'n
11.451: To that meek man, who well had sacrific'd;
11.452: Is Pietie thus and pure Devotion paid?
11.453: T' whom Michael thus, hee also mov'd, repli'd.
11.454: These two are Brethren, Adam, and to come
11.455: Out of thy loyns; th' unjust the just hath slain,
11.456: For envie that his Brothers Offering found
11.457: From Heav'n acceptance; but the bloodie Fact
11.458: Will be aveng'd, and th' others Faith approv'd
11.459: Loose no reward, though here thou see him die,
11.460: Rowling in dust and gore. To which our Sire.
11.461: Alas, both for the deed and for the cause!
11.462: But have I now seen Death? Is this the way
11.463: I must return to native dust? O sight
11.464: Of terrour, foul and ugly to behold,
11.465: Horrid to think, how horrible to feel!
11.466: To whom thus Michael. Death thou hast seen
11.467: In his first shape on man; but many shapes
11.468: Of Death, and many are the wayes that lead
11.469: To his grim Cave, all dismal; yet to sense
11.470: More terrible at th' entrance then within.
11.471: Some, as thou saw'st, by violent stroke shall die,
11.472: By Fire, Flood, Famin, by Intemperance more
11.473: In Meats and Drinks, which on the Earth shal bring
11.474: Diseases dire, of which a monstrous crew
11.475: Before thee shall appear; that thou mayst know
11.476: What miserie th' inabstinence of Eve
11.477: Shall bring on men. Immediately a place
11.478: Before his eyes appeard, sad, noysom, dark,
11.479: A Lazar-house it seemd, wherein were laid
11.480: Numbers of all diseas'd, all maladies
11.481: Of gastly Spasm, or racking torture, qualmes
11.482: Of heart-sick Agonie, all feavorous kinds,
11.484: Intestin Stone and Ulcer, Colic pangs,
11.485: Dropsies, and Asthma's, and Joint-racking Rheums.
11.486: Dire was the tossing, deep the groans, despair
11.487: Tended the sick busiest from Couch to Couch;
11.488: And over them triumphant Death his Dart
11.489: Shook, but delaid to strike, though oft invok't
11.490: With vows, as thir chief good, and final hope.
11.491: Sight so deform what heart of Rock could long
11.492: Drie-ey'd behold? Adam could not, but wept,
11.493: Though not of Woman born; compassion quell'd
11.494: His best of Man, and gave him up to tears
11.495: A space, till firmer thoughts restraind excess,
11.496: And scarce recovering words his plaint renew'd.
11.497: O miserable Mankind, to what fall
11.498: Degraded, to what wretched state reserv'd?
11.499: Better end heer unborn. Why is life giv'n
11.500: To be thus wrested from us? rather why
11.501: Obtruded on us thus? who if we knew
11.502: What we receive, would either not accept
11.503: Life offer'd, or soon beg to lay it down,
11.504: Glad to be so dismist in peace. Can thus
11.505: Th' Image of God in man created once
11.506: So goodly and erect, though faultie since,
11.507: To such unsightly sufferings be debas't
11.508: Under inhuman pains? Why should not Man,
11.510: In part, from such deformities be free,
11.511: And for his Makers Image sake exempt?
11.512: Thir Makers Image, answerd Michael, then
11.513: Forsook them, when themselves they villifi'd
11.514: To serve ungovern'd appetite, and took
11.515: His Image whom they serv'd, a brutish vice,
11.516: Inductive mainly to the sin of Eve.
11.517: Therefore so abject is thir punishment,
11.518: Disfiguring not Gods likeness, but thir own,
11.519: Or if his likeness, by themselves defac't
11.520: While they pervert pure Natures healthful rules
11.521: To loathsom sickness, worthily, since they
11.522: Gods Image did not reverence in themselves.
11.523: I yeild it just, said Adam, and submit.
11.524: But is there yet no other way, besides
11.525: These painful passages, how we may come
11.526: To Death, and mix with our connatural dust?
11.527: There is, said Michael, if thou well observe
11.528: The rule of not too much, by temperance taught
11.529: In what thou eatst and drinkst, seeking from thence
11.531: Till many years over thy head return:
11.532: So maist thou live, till like ripe Fruit thou drop
11.533: Into thy Mothers lap, or be with ease
11.534: Gatherd, not harshly pluckt, for death mature:
11.535: This is old age; but then thou must outlive
11.536: Thy youth, thy strength, thy beauty, which will change
11.537: To witherd weak & gray; thy Senses then
11.538: Obtuse, all taste of pleasure must forgoe,
11.539: To what thou hast, and for the Aire of youth
11.540: Hopeful and cheerful, in thy blood will reigne
11.541: A melancholly damp of cold and dry
11.542: To waigh thy spirits down, and last consume
11.543: The Balme of Life. To whom our Ancestor.
11.544: Henceforth I flie not Death, nor would prolong
11.545: Life much, bent rather how I may be quit
11.546: Fairest and easiest of this combrous charge,
11.547: Which I must keep till my appointed day
11.548: Of rendring up, Michael to him repli'd.
11.549: Nor love thy Life, nor hate; but what thou livst
11.550: Live well, how long or short permit to Heav'n:
11.551: And now prepare thee for another sight.
11.552: He lookd and saw a spacious Plaine, whereon
11.553: Were Tents of various hue; by some were herds
11.554: Of Cattel grazing: others, whence the sound
11.555: Of Instruments that made melodious chime
11.556: Was heard, of Harp and Organ; and who moovd
11.557: Thir stops and chords was seen: his volant touch
11.558: Instinct through all proportions low and high
11.559: Fled and pursu'd transverse the resonant fugue.
11.560: In other part stood one who at the Forge
11.561: Labouring, two massie clods of Iron and Brass
11.562: Had melted (whether found where casual fire
11.563: Had wasted woods on Mountain or in Vale,
11.564: Down to the veins of Earth, thence gliding hot
11.565: To som Caves mouth, or whether washt by stream
11.566: From underground) the liquid Ore he dreind
11.567: Into fit moulds prepar'd; from which he formd
11.568: First his own Tooles; then, what might else be wrought
11.569: Fusile or grav'n in mettle. After these,
11.570: But on the hether side a different sort
11.571: From the high neighbouring Hills, which was thir Seat,
11.572: Down to the Plain descended: by thir guise
11.573: Just men they seemd, and all thir study bent
11.574: To worship God aright, and know his works
11.575: Not hid, nor those things lost which might preserve
11.576: Freedom and Peace to men: they on the Plain
11.577: Long had not walkt, when from the Tents behold
11.578: A Beavie of fair Women, richly gay
11.579: In Gems and wanton dress; to the Harp they sung
11.580: Soft amorous Ditties, and in dance came on:
11.581: The Men though grave, ey'd them, and let thir eyes
11.582: Rove without rein, till in the amorous Net
11.583: Fast caught, they lik'd, and each his liking chose;
11.584: And now of love they treat till th' Eevning Star
11.585: Loves Harbinger appeerd; then all in heat
11.586: They light the Nuptial Torch, and bid invoke
11.587: Hymen, then first to marriage Rites invok't;
11.588: With Feast and Musick all the Tents resound.
11.589: Such happy interview and fair event
11.590: Of love & youth not lost, Songs, Garlands, Flours,
11.591: And charming Symphonies attach'd the heart
11.592: Of Adam, soon enclin'd to admit delight,
11.593: The bent of Nature; which he thus express'd.
11.594: True opener of mine eyes, prime Angel blest,
11.595: Much better seems this Vision, and more hope
11.596: Of peaceful dayes portends, then those two past;
11.597: Those were of hate and death, or pain much worse,
11.598: Here Nature seems fulfilld in all her ends.
11.599: To whom thus Michael. Judg not what is best
11.600: By pleasure, though to Nature seeming meet,
11.601: Created, as thou art, to nobler end
11.603: Those Tents thou sawst so pleasant, were the Tents
11.604: Of wickedness, wherein shall dwell his Race
11.605: Who slew his Brother; studious they appere
11.606: Of Arts that polish Life, Inventers rare,
11.607: Unmindful of thir Maker, though his Spirit
11.608: Taught them, but they his gifts acknowledg'd none.
11.609: Yet they a beauteous ofspring shall beget;
11.610: For that fair femal Troop thou sawst, that seemd
11.611: Of Goddesses, so blithe, so smooth, so gay,
11.612: Yet empty of all good wherein consists
11.613: Womans domestic honour and chief praise;
11.614: Bred onely and completed to the taste
11.615: Of lustful appetence, to sing, to dance,
11.616: To dress, and troule the Tongue, and roule the Eye.
11.617: To these that sober Race of Men, whose lives
11.618: Religious titl'd them the Sons of God,
11.619: Shall yeild up all thir vertue, all thir fame
11.620: Ignobly, to the trains and to the smiles
11.621: Of these fair Atheists, and now swim in joy,
11.622: (Erelong to swim at larg) and laugh; for which
11.623: The world erelong a world of tears must weepe.
11.624: To whom thus Adam of short joy bereft.
11.625: O pittie and shame, that they who to live well
11.626: Enterd so faire, should turn aside to tread
11.627: Paths indirect, or in the mid way faint!
11.628: But still I see the tenor of Mans woe
11.629: Holds on the same, from Woman to begin.
11.630: From Mans effeminate slackness it begins,
11.631: Said th' Angel, who should better hold his place
11.632: By wisdome, and superiour gifts receavd.
11.633: But now prepare thee for another Scene.
11.634: He lookd and saw wide Territorie spred
11.635: Before him, Towns, and rural works between,
11.636: Cities of Men with lofty Gates and Towrs,
11.637: Concours in Arms, fierce Faces threatning Warr,
11.638: Giants of mightie Bone, and bould emprise;
11.639: Part wield thir Arms, part courb the foaming Steed,
11.640: Single or in Array of Battel rang'd
11.641: Both Horse and Foot, nor idely mustring stood;
11.642: One way a Band select from forage drives
11.643: A herd of Beeves, faire Oxen and faire Kine
11.644: From a fat Meddow ground; or fleecy Flock,
11.645: Ewes and thir bleating Lambs over the Plaine,
11.646: Thir Bootie; scarce with Life the Shepherds flye,
11.647: But call in aide, which tacks a bloody Fray;
11.648: With cruel Tournament the Squadrons joine;
11.649: Where Cattel pastur'd late, now scatterd lies
11.650: With Carcasses and Arms th' ensanguind Field
11.651: Deserted: Others to a Citie strong
11.652: Lay Siege, encampt; by Batterie, Scale, and Mine,
11.653: Assaulting; others from the Wall defend
11.654: With Dart and Jav'lin, Stones and sulfurous Fire;
11.655: On each hand slaughter and gigantic deeds.
11.656: In other part the scepter'd Haralds call
11.657: To Council in the Citie Gates: anon
11.658: Grey-headed men and grave, with Warriours mixt,
11.659: Assemble, and Harangues are heard, but soon
11.660: In factious opposition, till at last
11.661: Of middle Age one rising, eminent
11.662: In wise deport, spake much of Right and Wrong,
11.663: Of Justice, of Religion, Truth and Peace,
11.664: And Judgement from above: him old and young
11.665: Exploded, and had seiz'd with violent hands,
11.666: Had not a Cloud descending snatch'd him thence
11.667: Unseen amid the throng: so violence
11.669: Through all the Plain, and refuge none was found.
11.670: Adam was all in tears, and to his guide
11.671: Lamenting turnd full sad; O what are these,
11.672: Deaths Ministers, not Men, who thus deal Death
11.674: Ten thousand fould the sin of him who slew
11.675: His Brother; for of whom such massacher
11.676: Make they but of thir Brethren, men of men?
11.677: But who was that Just Man, whom had not Heav'n
11.678: Rescu'd, had in his Righteousness bin lost?
11.679: To whom thus Michael; These are the product
11.680: Of those ill-mated Marriages thou saw'st;
11.681: Where good with bad were matcht, who of themselves
11.682: Abhor to joyn; and by imprudence mixt,
11.683: Produce prodigious Births of bodie or mind.
11.684: Such were these Giants, men of high renown;
11.685: For in those dayes Might onely shall be admir'd,
11.686: And Valour and Heroic Vertu call'd;
11.687: To overcome in Battel, and subdue
11.688: Nations, and bring home spoils with infinite
11.689: Man-slaughter, shall be held the highest pitch
11.690: Of human Glorie, and for Glorie done
11.691: Of triumph, to be styl'd great Conquerours,
11.692: Patrons of Mankind, Gods, and Sons of Gods,
11.693: Destroyers rightlier call'd and Plagues of men.
11.694: Thus Fame shall be achiev'd, renown on Earth,
11.695: And what most merits fame in silence hid.
11.696: But hee the seventh from thee, whom thou beheldst
11.697: The onely righteous in a World perverse,
11.698: And therefore hated, therefore so beset
11.699: With Foes for daring single to be just,
11.700: And utter odious Truth, that God would come
11.701: To judge them with his Saints: Him the most High
11.702: Rapt in a balmie Cloud with winged Steeds
11.703: Did, as thou sawst, receave, to walk with God
11.704: High in Salvation and the Climes of bliss,
11.705: Exempt from Death; to shew thee what reward
11.706: Awaits the good, the rest what punishment;
11.707: Which now direct thine eyes and soon behold.
11.708: He look'd, & saw the face of things quite chang'd;
11.709: The brazen Throat of Warr had ceast to roar,
11.710: All now was turn'd to jollitie and game,
11.711: To luxurie and riot, feast and dance,
11.713: Rape or Adulterie, where passing faire
11.714: Allurd them; thence from Cups to civil Broiles.
11.715: At length a Reverend Sire among them came,
11.716: And of thir doings great dislike declar'd,
11.717: And testifi'd against thir wayes; hee oft
11.719: Triumphs or Festivals, and to them preachd
11.720: Conversion and Repentance, as to Souls
11.722: But all in vain: which when he saw, he ceas'd
11.723: Contending, and remov'd his Tents farr off;
11.724: Then from the Mountain hewing Timber tall,
11.725: Began to build a Vessel of huge bulk,
11.726: Measur'd by Cubit, length, & breadth, and highth,
11.727: Smeard round with Pitch, and in the side a dore
11.728: Contriv'd, and of provisions laid in large
11.729: For Man and Beast: when loe a wonder strange!
11.730: Of everie Beast, and Bird, and Insect small
11.731: Came seavens, and pairs, and enterd in, as taught
11.732: Thir order; last the Sire, and his three Sons
11.733: With thir four Wives, and God made fast the dore.
11.734: Meanwhile the Southwind rose, & with black wings
11.735: Wide hovering, all the Clouds together drove
11.736: From under Heav'n; the Hills to their supplie
11.737: Vapour, and Exhalation dusk and moist,
11.738: Sent up amain; and now the thick'nd Skie
11.739: Like a dark Ceeling stood; down rush'd the Rain
11.740: Impetuous, and continu'd till the Earth
11.741: No more was seen; the floating Vessel swum
11.742: Uplifted; and secure with beaked prow
11.743: Rode tilting o're the Waves, all dwellings else
11.744: Flood overwhelmd, and them with all thir pomp
11.745: Deep under water rould; Sea cover'd Sea,
11.746: Sea without shoar; and in thir Palaces
11.747: Where luxurie late reign'd, Sea-monsters whelp'd
11.748: And stabl'd; of Mankind, so numerous late,
11.749: All left, in one small bottom swum imbark't.
11.750: How didst thou grieve then, Adam, to behold
11.751: The end of all thy Ofspring, end so sad,
11.753: Of tears and sorrow a Floud thee also drown'd,
11.754: And sunk thee as thy Sons; till gently reard
11.755: By th' Angel, on thy feet thou stoodst at last,
11.756: Though comfortless, as when a Father mourns
11.757: His Childern, all in view destroyd at once;
11.758: And scarce to th' Angel utterdst thus thy plaint.
11.759: O Visions ill foreseen! better had I
11.760: Liv'd ignorant of future, so had borne
11.761: My part of evil onely, each dayes lot
11.762: Anough to bear; those now, that were dispenst
11.763: The burd'n of many Ages, on me light
11.764: At once, by my foreknowledge gaining Birth
11.765: Abortive, to torment me ere thir being,
11.766: With thought that they must be. Let no man seek
11.767: Henceforth to be foretold what shall befall
11.768: Him or his Childern, evil he may be sure,
11.769: Which neither his foreknowing can prevent,
11.770: And hee the future evil shall no less
11.771: In apprehension then in substance feel
11.772: Grievous to bear: but that care now is past,
11.773: Man is not whom to warne: those few escap't
11.774: Famin and anguish will at last consume
11.775: Wandring that watrie Desert: I had hope
11.776: When violence was ceas't, and Warr on Earth,
11.777: All would have then gon well, peace would have crownd
11.778: With length of happy days the race of man;
11.779: But I was farr deceav'd; for now I see
11.780: Peace to corrupt no less then Warr to waste.
11.781: How comes it thus? unfould, Celestial Guide,
11.782: And whether here the Race of man will end.
11.783: To whom thus Michael. Those whom last thou sawst
11.784: In triumph and luxurious wealth, are they
11.785: First seen in acts of prowess eminent
11.786: And great exploits, but of true vertu void;
11.787: Who having spilt much blood, and don much waste
11.789: Fame in the World, high titles, and rich prey,
11.790: Shall change thir course to pleasure, ease, and sloth,
11.791: Surfet, and lust, till wantonness and pride
11.792: Raise out of friendship hostil deeds in Peace.
11.793: The conquerd also, and enslav'd by Warr
11.794: Shall with thir freedom lost all vertu loose
11.795: And feare of God, from whom thir pietie feign'd
11.796: In sharp contest of Battel found no aide
11.797: Against invaders; therefore coold in zeale
11.798: Thenceforth shall practice how to live secure,
11.799: Worldlie or dissolute, on what thir Lords
11.800: Shall leave them to enjoy; for th' Earth shall bear
11.801: More then anough, that temperance may be tri'd:
11.802: So all shall turn degenerate, all deprav'd,
11.803: Justice and Temperance, Truth and Faith forgot;
11.804: One Man except, the onely Son of light
11.805: In a dark Age, against example good,
11.806: Against allurement, custom, and a World
11.807: Offended; fearless of reproach and scorn,
11.808: Or violence, hee of thir wicked wayes
11.809: Shall them admonish, and before them set
11.810: The paths of righteousness, how much more safe,
11.811: And full of peace, denouncing wrauth to come
11.812: On thir impenitence; and shall returne
11.813: Of them derided, but of God observd
11.814: The one just Man alive; by his command
11.815: Shall build a wondrous Ark, as thou beheldst,
11.816: To save himself and houshold from amidst
11.817: A World devote to universal rack.
11.818: No sooner hee with them of Man and Beast
11.819: Select for life shall in the Ark be lodg'd,
11.820: And shelterd round, but all the Cataracts
11.821: Of Heav'n set open on the Earth shall powre
11.822: Raine day and night, all fountaines of the Deep
11.823: Broke up, shall heave the Ocean to usurp
11.824: Beyond all bounds, till inundation rise
11.825: Above the highest Hills: then shall this Mount
11.826: Of Paradise by might of Waves be moovd
11.827: Out of his place, pushd by the horned floud,
11.828: With all his verdure spoil'd, and Trees adrift
11.829: Down the great River to the op'ning Gulf,
11.830: And there take root an Iland salt and bare,
11.831: The haunt of Seales and Orcs, and Sea-mews clang.
11.832: To teach thee that God attributes to place
11.833: No sanctitie, if none be thither brought
11.834: By Men who there frequent, or therein dwell.
11.835: And now what further shall ensue, behold.
11.836: He lookd, and saw the Ark hull on the floud,
11.837: Which now abated, for the Clouds were fled,
11.838: Drivn by a keen North-winde, that blowing drie
11.839: Wrinkl'd the face of Deluge, as decai'd;
11.840: And the cleer Sun on his wide watrie Glass
11.841: Gaz'd hot, and of the fresh Wave largely drew,
11.842: As after thirst, which made thir flowing shrink
11.843: From standing lake to tripping ebbe, that stole
11.844: With soft foot towards the deep, who now had stopt
11.845: His Sluces, as the Heav'n his windows shut.
11.846: The Ark no more now flotes, but seems on ground
11.847: Fast on the top of som high mountain fixt.
11.848: And now the tops of Hills as Rocks appeer;
11.849: With clamor thence the rapid Currents drive
11.850: Towards the retreating Sea thir furious tyde.
11.851: Forthwith from out the Arke a Raven flies,
11.852: And after him, the surer messenger,
11.853: A Dove sent forth once and agen to spie
11.854: Green Tree or ground whereon his foot may light;
11.855: The second time returning, in his Bill
11.856: An Olive leafe he brings, pacific signe:
11.857: Anon drie ground appeers, and from his Arke
11.858: The ancient Sire descends with all his Train;
11.859: Then with uplifted hands, and eyes devout,
11.860: Grateful to Heav'n, over his head beholds
11.861: A dewie Cloud, and in the Cloud a Bow
11.862: Conspicuous with three lifted colours gay,
11.863: Betok'ning peace from God, and Cov'nant new.
11.864: Whereat the heart of Adam erst so sad
11.865: Greatly rejoyc'd, and thus his joy broke forth.
11.866: O thou that future things canst represent
11.867: As present, Heav'nly instructer, I revive
11.868: At this last sight, assur'd that Man shall live
11.869: With all the Creatures, and thir seed preserve.
11.870: Farr less I now lament for one whole World
11.871: Of wicked Sons destroyd, then I rejoyce
11.872: For one Man found so perfet and so just,
11.873: That God voutsafes to raise another World
11.874: From him, and all his anger to forget.
11.875: But say, what mean those colourd streaks in Heavn,
11.876: Distended as the Brow of God appeas'd,
11.877: Or serve they as a flourie verge to binde
11.878: The fluid skirts of that same watrie Cloud,
11.879: Least it again dissolve and showr the Earth?
11.880: To whom th' Archangel. Dextrously thou aim'st;
11.881: So willingly doth God remit his Ire,
11.882: Though late repenting him of Man deprav'd,
11.883: Griev'd at his heart, when looking down he saw
11.884: The whole Earth fill'd with violence, and all flesh
11.885: Corrupting each thir way; yet those remoov'd,
11.886: Such grace shall one just Man find in his sight,
11.887: That he relents, not to blot out mankind,
11.888: And makes a Covenant never to destroy
11.889: The Earth again by flood, nor let the Sea
11.890: Surpass his bounds, nor Rain to drown the World
11.891: With Man therein or Beast; but when he brings
11.892: Over the Earth a Cloud, will therein set
11.893: His triple-colour'd Bow, whereon to look
11.894: And call to mind his Cov'nant: Day and Night,
11.895: Seed time and Harvest, Heat and hoary Frost
11.896: Shall hold thir course, till fire purge all things new,
11.897: Both Heav'n and Earth, wherein the just shall dwell.

12.0:
*The Argument*
The Angel Michael continues from the Flood to relate what shall succeed; then, in the mention of Abraham, comes by degrees to explain who that Seed of the Woman shall be, which was promised Adam and Eve in the Fall; his Incarnation, Death, Resurrection, and Ascention; the state of the Church till his second Coming. Adam greatly satisfied and recomforted by these Relations and Promises descends the Hill with Michael; wakens Eve, who all this while had slept, but with gentle dreams compos'd to quietness of mind and submission. Michael in either hand leads them out of Paradise, the fiery Sword waving behind them, and the Cherubim taking thir Stations to guard the Place.
12.1: [As one who in his journey bates at Noone
12.2: Though bent on speed, so heer the Archangel' paus'd
12.3: Betwixt the world destroy'd and world restor'd,
12.4: If Adam aught perhaps might interpose;
12.5: Then with transition sweet new Speech resumes]
12.6: Thus thou hast seen one World begin and end;
12.7: And Man as from a second stock proceed.
12.8: Much thou hast yet to see, but I perceave
12.9: Thy mortal sight to faile; objects divine
12.10: Must needs impaire and wearie human sense:
12.11: Henceforth what is to com I will relate,
12.12: Thou therefore give due audience, and attend.
12.13: This second sours of Men, while yet but few,
12.14: And while the dread of judgement past remains
12.15: Fresh in thir mindes, fearing the Deitie,
12.16: With some regard to what is just and right
12.17: Shall lead thir lives, and multiplie apace,
12.18: Labouring the soile, and reaping plenteous crop,
12.19: Corn wine and oyle; and from the herd or flock,
12.20: Oft sacrificing Bullock, Lamb, or Kid,
12.21: With large Wine-offerings pour'd, and sacred Feast
12.22: Shal spend thir dayes in joy unblam'd, and dwell
12.23: Long time in peace by Families and Tribes
12.24: Under paternal rule; till one shall rise
12.25: Of proud ambitious heart, who not content
12.28: Over his brethren, and quite dispossess
12.29: Concord and law of Nature from the Earth;
12.30: Hunting (and Men not Beasts shall be his game)
12.31: With Warr and hostile snare such as refuse
12.33: A mightie Hunter thence he shall be styl'd
12.34: Before the Lord, as in despite of Heav'n,
12.35: Or from Heav'n claming second Sovrantie;
12.36: And from Rebellion shall derive his name,
12.37: Though of Rebellion others he accuse.
12.38: Hee with a crew, whom like Ambition joyns
12.39: With him or under him to tyrannize,
12.40: Marching from Eden towards the West, shall finde
12.41: The Plain, wherein a black bituminous gurge
12.42: Boiles out from under ground, the mouth of Hell;
12.43: Of Brick, and of that stuff they cast to build
12.44: A Citie & Towre, whose top may reach to Heav'n;
12.45: And get themselves a name, least far disperst
12.46: In foraign Lands thir memorie be lost,
12.47: Regardless whether good or evil fame.
12.48: But God who oft descends to visit men
12.49: Unseen, and through thir habitations walks
12.50: To mark thir doings, them beholding soon,
12.51: Comes down to see thir Citie, ere the Tower
12.52: Obstruct Heav'n Towrs, and in derision sets
12.53: Upon thir Tongues a various Spirit to rase
12.54: Quite out thir Native Language, and instead
12.55: To sow a jangling noise of words unknown:
12.56: Forthwith a hideous gabble rises loud
12.57: Among the Builders; each to other calls
12.58: Not understood, till hoarse, and all in rage,
12.59: As mockt they storm; great laughter was in Heav'n
12.60: And looking down, to see the hubbub strange
12.61: And hear the din; thus was the building left
12.62: Ridiculous, and the work Confusion nam'd.
12.64: O execrable Son so to aspire
12.65: Above his Brethren, to himself affirming
12.66: Authoritie usurpt, from God not giv'n:
12.67: He gave us onely over Beast, Fish, Fowl
12.68: Dominion absolute; that right we hold
12.69: By his donation; but Man over men
12.70: He made not Lord; such title to himself
12.71: Reserving, human left from human free.
12.72: But this Usurper his encroachment proud
12.73: Stayes not on Man; to God his Tower intends
12.74: Siege and defiance: Wretched man! what food
12.75: Will he convey up thither to sustain
12.76: Himself and his rash Armie, where thin Aire
12.77: Above the Clouds will pine his entrails gross,
12.78: And famish him of Breath, if not of Bread?
12.79: To whom thus Michael. Justly thou abhorr'st
12.80: That Son, who on the quiet state of men
12.81: Such trouble brought, affecting to subdue
12.83: Since thy original lapse, true Libertie
12.84: Is lost, which alwayes with right Reason dwells
12.85: Twinn'd, and from her hath no dividual being:
12.86: Reason in man obscur'd, or not obeyd,
12.88: And upstart Passions catch the Government
12.89: From Reason, and to servitude reduce
12.90: Man till then free. Therefore since hee permits
12.91: Within himself unworthie Powers to reign
12.92: Over free Reason, God in Judgement just
12.93: Subjects him from without to violent Lords;
12.95: His outward freedom: Tyrannie must be,
12.96: Though to the Tyrant thereby no excuse.
12.97: Yet somtimes Nations will decline so low
12.98: From vertue, which is reason, that no wrong,
12.99: But Justice, and some fatal curse annext
12.100: Deprives them of thir outward libertie,
12.101: Thir inward lost: Witness th' irreverent Son
12.102: Of him who built the Ark, who for the shame
12.103: Don to his Father, heard this heavie curse,
12.104: Servant Of Servants, on his vitious Race.
12.105: Thus will this latter, as the former World,
12.106: Still tend from bad to worse, till God at last
12.108: His presence from among them, and avert
12.109: His holy Eyes; resolving from thenceforth
12.110: To leave them to thir own polluted wayes;
12.111: And one peculiar Nation to select
12.112: From all the rest, of whom to be invok'd,
12.113: A Nation from one faithful man to spring:
12.114: Him on this side Euphrates yet residing,
12.115: Bred up in Idol-worship; O that men
12.116: (Canst thou believe?) should be so stupid grown,
12.117: While yet the Patriark liv'd, who scap'd the Flood,
12.118: As to forsake the living God, and fall
12.119: To-worship thir own work in Wood and Stone
12.120: For Gods! yet him God the most High voutsafes
12.121: To call by Vision from his Fathers house,
12.122: His kindred and false Gods, into a Land
12.123: Which he will shew him, and from him will raise
12.124: A mightie Nation, and upon him showre
12.125: His benediction so, that in his Seed
12.126: All Nations shall be blest; hee straight obeys,
12.127: Not knowing to what Land, yet firm believes:
12.128: I see him, but thou canst not, with what Faith
12.129: He leaves his Gods, his Friends, and native Soile
12.130: Ur of Chaldaea, passing now the Ford
12.131: To Haran, after him a cumbrous Train
12.132: Of Herds and Flocks, and numerous servitude;
12.133: Not wandring poor, but trusting all his wealth
12.134: With God, who call'd him, in a land unknown.
12.135: Canaan he now attains, I see his Tents
12.136: Pitcht about Sechem, and the neighbouring Plaine
12.137: Of Moreb; there by promise he receaves
12.138: Gift to his Progenie of all that Land;
12.139: From Hamath Northward to the Desert South
12.140: (Things by thir names I call, though yet unnam'd)
12.141: From Hermon East to the great Western Sea,
12.142: Mount Hermon, yonder Sea, each place behold
12.143: In prospect, as I point them; on the shoare
12.144: Mount Carmel; here the double-founted stream
12.145: Jordan, true limit Eastward; but his Sons
12.146: Shall dwell to Senir, that long ridge of Hills.
12.147: This ponder, that all Nations of the Earth
12.148: Shall in his Seed be blessed; by that Seed
12.149: Is meant thy great deliverer, who shall bruise
12.150: The Serpents head; whereof to thee anon
12.151: Plainlier shall be reveald. This Patriarch blest,
12.152: Whom Faithful Abraham due time shall call,
12.153: A Son, and of his Son a Grand-childe leaves,
12.154: Like him in faith, in wisdom, and renown;
12.155: The Grandchilde with twelve Sons increast, departs
12.156: From Canaan, to a Land hereafter call'd
12.157: Egypt, divided by the River Nile;
12.158: See where it flows, disgorging at seaven mouthes
12.159: Into the Sea: to sojourn in that Land
12.160: He comes invited by a yonger Son
12.161: In time of dearth, a Son whose worthy deeds
12.162: Raise him to be the second in that Realme
12.163: Of Pharao: there he dies, and leaves his Race
12.164: Growing into a Nation, and now grown
12.165: Suspected to a sequent King, who seeks
12.166: To stop thir overgrowth, as inmate guests
12.167: Too numerous; whence of guests he makes them slaves
12.168: Inhospitably, and kills thir infant Males:
12.169: Till by two brethren (those two brethren call
12.170: Moses and Aaron) sent from God to claime
12.171: His people from enthralment, they return
12.172: With glory and spoile back to thir promis'd Land.
12.173: But first the lawless Tyrant, who denies
12.174: To know thir God, or message to regard,
12.175: Must be compelld by Signes and Judgements dire;
12.176: To blood unshed the Rivers must be turnd,
12.177: Frogs, Lice and Flies must all his Palace fill
12.178: With loath'd intrusion, and fill all the land;
12.179: His Cattel must of Rot and Murren die,
12.180: Botches and blaines must all his flesh imboss,
12.181: And all his people; Thunder mixt with Haile,
12.182: Haile mixt with fire must rend th' Egyptian Skie
12.183: And wheel on th' Earth, devouring where it rouls;
12.184: What it devours not, Herb, or Fruit, or Graine,
12.185: A darksom Cloud of Locusts swarming down
12.186: Must eat, and on the ground leave nothing green:
12.187: Darkness must overshadow all his bounds,
12.188: Palpable darkness, and blot out three dayes;
12.189: Last with one midnight stroke all the first-born
12.190: Of Egypt must lie dead. Thus with ten wounds
12.191: This River-dragon tam'd at length submits
12.192: To let his sojourners depart, and oft
12.193: Humbles his stubborn heart, but still as Ice
12.194: More hard'nd after thaw, till in his rage
12.195: Pursuing whom he late dismissd, the Sea
12.196: Swallows him with his Host, but them lets pass
12.197: As on drie land between two christal walls,
12.198: Aw'd by the rod of Moses so to stand
12.199: Divided, till his rescu'd gain thir shoar:
12.200: Such wondrous power God to his Saint will lend,
12.201: Though present in his Angel, who shall goe
12.202: Before them in a Cloud, and Pillar of Fire,
12.203: To guide them in thir journey, and remove
12.204: Behinde them, while th' obdurat King pursues:
12.205: All night he will pursue, but his approach
12.206: Darkness defends between till morning Watch;
12.207: Then through the Firey Pillar and the Cloud
12.208: God looking forth will trouble all his Host
12.209: And craze thir Chariot wheels: when by command
12.210: Moses once more his potent Rod extends
12.211: Over the Sea; the Sea his Rod obeys;
12.212: On thir imbattelld ranks the Waves return,
12.213: And overwhelm thir Warr: the Race elect
12.214: Safe towards Canaan from the shoar advance
12.215: Through the wilde Desert, not the readiest way,
12.216: Least entring on the Canaanite allarmd
12.217: Warr terrifie them inexpert, and feare
12.218: Return them back to Egypt, choosing rather
12.219: Inglorious life with servitude; for life
12.220: To noble and ignoble is more sweet
12.221: Untraind in Armes, where rashness leads not on.
12.222: This also shall they gain by thir delay
12.223: In the wide Wilderness, there they shall found
12.224: Thir government, and thir great Senate choose
12.225: Through the twelve Tribes, to rule by Laws ordaind:
12.226: God from the Mount of Sinai, whose gray top
12.227: Shall tremble, he descending, will himself
12.228: In Thunder Lightning and loud Trumpets sound
12.229: Ordaine them Lawes; part such as appertaine
12.230: To civil Justice, part religious Rites
12.231: Of sacrifice, informing them, by types
12.232: And shadowes, of that destind Seed to bruise
12.233: The Serpent, by what meanes he shall achieve
12.234: Mankinds deliverance. But the voice of God
12.235: To mortal eare is dreadful; they beseech
12.236: That Moses might report to them his will,
12.237: And terror cease; he grants them thir desire,
12.238: Instructed that to God is no access
12.239: Without Mediator, whose high Office now
12.240: Moses in figure beares, to introduce
12.241: One greater, of whose day he shall foretell,
12.242: And all the Prophets in thir Age the times
12.243: Of great Messiah shall sing. Thus Laws and Rites
12.244: Establisht, such delight hath God in Men
12.245: Obedient to his will, that he voutsafes
12.246: Among them to set up his Tabernacle,
12.247: The holy One with mortal Men to dwell:
12.248: By his prescript a Sanctuary is fram'd
12.249: Of Cedar, overlaid with Gold, therein
12.250: An Ark, and in the Ark his Testimony,
12.251: The Records of his Cov'nant, over these
12.252: A Mercie-seat of Gold between the wings
12.253: Of two bright Cherubim, before him burn
12.254: Seaven Lamps as in a Zodiac representing
12.255: The Heav'nly fires; over the Tent a Cloud
12.256: Shall rest by Day, a fierie gleame by Night,
12.257: Save when they journie, and at length they come,
12.258: Conducted by his Angel to the Land
12.259: Promisd to Abraham and his Seed: the rest
12.260: Were long to tell, how many Battels fought,
12.261: How many Kings destroyd, and Kingdoms won,
12.262: Or how the Sun shall in mid Heav'n stand still
12.263: A day entire, and Nights due course adjourne,
12.264: Mans voice commanding, Sun in Gibeon stand,
12.265: And thou Moon in the vale of Aialon,
12.266: Till Israel overcome; so call the third
12.267: From Abraham, Son of Isaac, and from him
12.268: His whole descent, who thus shall Canaan win.
12.269: Here Adam interpos'd. O sent from Heav'n,
12.270: Enlightner of my darkness, gracious things
12.271: Thou hast reveald, those chiefly which concerne
12.272: Just Abraham and his Seed: now first I finde
12.273: Mine eyes true op'ning, and my heart much eas'd,
12.274: Erwhile perplext with thoughts what would becom
12.275: Of mee and all Mankind; but now I see
12.276: His day, in whom all Nations shall be blest,
12.277: Favour unmerited by me, who sought
12.279: This yet I apprehend not, why to those
12.280: Among whom God will deigne to dwell on Earth
12.281: So many and so various Laws are giv'n;
12.282: So many Laws argue so many sins
12.283: Among them; how can God with such reside?
12.284: To whom thus Michael. Doubt not but that sin
12.285: Will reign among them, as of thee begot;
12.286: And therefore was Law given them to evince
12.287: Thir natural pravitie, by stirring up
12.288: Sin against Law to fight; that when they see
12.289: Law can discover sin, but not remove,
12.290: Save by those shadowie expiations weak,
12.291: The bloud of Bulls and Goats, they may conclude
12.292: Some bloud more precious must be paid for Man,
12.293: Just for unjust, that in such righteousness
12.294: To them by Faith imputed, they may finde
12.296: Of Conscience, which the Law by Ceremonies
12.297: Cannot appease, nor Man the moral part
12.298: Perform, and not performing cannot live.
12.299: So Law appears imperfet, and but giv'n
12.300: With purpose to resign them in full time
12.301: Up to a better Cov'nant, disciplin'd
12.302: From shadowie Types to Truth, from Flesh to Spirit,
12.303: From imposition of strict Laws, to free
12.304: Acceptance of large Grace, from servil fear
12.305: To filial, works of Law to works of Faith.
12.306: And therefore shall not Moses, though of God
12.307: Highly belov'd, being but the Minister
12.308: Of Law, his people into Canaan lead;
12.309: But Joshua whom the Gentiles Jesus call,
12.310: His Name and Office bearing, who shall quell
12.311: The adversarie Serpent, and bring back
12.312: Through the worlds wilderness long wanderd man
12.313: Safe to eternal Paradise of rest.
12.314: Meanwhile they in thir earthly Canaan plac't
12.315: Long time shall dwell and prosper, but when sins
12.317: Provoking God to raise them enemies:
12.318: From whom as oft he saves them penitent
12.319: By Judges first, then under Kings; of whom
12.320: The second, both for pietie renownd
12.321: And puissant deeds, a promise shall receive
12.323: For ever shall endure; the like shall sing
12.324: All Prophecie, That of the Royal Stock
12.325: Of David (so I name this King) shall rise
12.326: A Son, the Womans Seed to thee foretold,
12.327: Foretold to Abraham, as in whom shall trust
12.328: All Nations, and to Kings foretold, of Kings
12.329: The last, for of his Reign shall be no end.
12.330: But first a long succession must ensue,
12.331: And his next Son for Wealth and Wisdom fam'd,
12.332: The clouded Ark of God till then in Tents
12.333: Wandring, shall in a glorious Temple enshrine.
12.334: Such follow him, as shall be registerd
12.335: Part good, part bad, of bad the longer scrowle,
12.336: Whose foul Idolatries, and other faults
12.337: Heapt to the popular summe, will so incense
12.338: God, as to leave them, and expose thir Land,
12.339: Thir Citie, his Temple, and his holy Ark
12.340: With all his sacred things, a scorn and prey
12.341: To that proud Citie, whose high Walls thou saw'st
12.342: Left in confusion, Babylon thence call'd.
12.343: There in captivitie he lets them dwell
12.344: The space of seventie years, then brings them back,
12.345: Remembring mercie, and his Cov'nant sworn
12.346: To David, stablisht as the dayes of Heav'n.
12.347: Returnd from Babylon by leave of Kings
12.348: Thir Lords, whom God dispos'd, the house of God
12.349: They first re-edifie, and for a while
12.350: In mean estate live moderate, till grown
12.351: In wealth and multitude, factious they grow;
12.352: But first among the Priests dissension springs,
12.353: Men who attend the Altar, and should most
12.354: Endeavour Peace: thir strife pollution brings
12.355: Upon the Temple it self: at last they seise
12.356: The Scepter, and regard not Davids Sons,
12.357: Then loose it to a stranger, that the true
12.358: Anointed King Messiah might be born
12.359: Barr'd of his right; yet at his Birth a Starr
12.360: Unseen before in Heav'n proclaims him com,
12.361: And guides the Eastern Sages, who enquire
12.362: His place, to offer Incense, Myrrh, and Gold;
12.363: His place of birth a solemn Angel tells
12.364: To simple Shepherds, keeping watch by night;
12.365: They gladly thither haste, and by a Quire
12.366: Of squadrond Angels hear his Carol sung.
12.367: A Virgin is his Mother, but his Sire
12.368: The Power of the most High; he shall ascend
12.369: The Throne hereditarie, and bound his Reign
12.370: With earths wide bounds, his glory with the Heav'ns.
12.371: He ceas'd, discerning Adam with such joy
12.372: Surcharg'd, as had like grief bin dew'd in tears,
12.373: Without the vent of words, which these he breathd.
12.374: O Prophet of glad tidings, finisher
12.375: Of utmost hope! now clear I understand
12.376: What oft my steddiest thoughts have searcht in vain,
12.377: Why our great expectation should be call'd
12.378: The seed of Woman: Virgin Mother, Haile,
12.379: High in the love of Heav'n, yet from my Loynes
12.380: Thou shalt proceed, and from thy Womb the Son
12.381: Of God most High; So God with man unites.
12.382: Needs must the Serpent now his capital bruise
12.383: Expect with mortal paine: say where and when
12.384: Thir fight, what stroke shall bruise the Victors heel.
12.385: To whom thus Michael. Dream not of thir fight,
12.386: As of a Duel, or the local wounds
12.387: Of head or heel: not therefore joynes the Son
12.388: Manhood to God-head, with more strength to foil
12.389: Thy enemie; nor so is overcome
12.390: Satan, whose fall from Heav'n, a deadlier bruise,
12.391: Disabl'd not to give thee thy deaths wound:
12.392: Which hee, who comes thy Saviour, shall recure,
12.393: Not by destroying Satan, but his works
12.394: In thee and in thy Seed: nor can this be,
12.395: But by fulfilling that which thou didst want,
12.396: Obedience to the Law of God, impos'd
12.397: On penaltie of death, and suffering death,
12.398: The penaltie to thy transgression due,
12.399: And due to theirs which out of thine will grow:
12.400: So onely can high Justice rest appaid.
12.401: The Law of God exact he shall fulfill
12.402: Both by obedience and by love, though love
12.403: Alone fulfill the Law; thy punishment
12.404: He shall endure by coming in the Flesh
12.405: To a reproachful life and cursed death,
12.406: Proclaiming Life to all who shall believe
12.407: In his redemption, and that his obedience
12.408: Imputed becomes theirs by Faith, his merits
12.409: To save them, not thir own, though legal works.
12.410: For this he shall live hated, be blasphem'd,
12.411: Seis'd on by force, judg'd, and to death condemnd
12.412: A shameful and accurst, naild to the Cross
12.413: By his own Nation, slaine for bringing Life;
12.414: But to the Cross he nailes thy Enemies,
12.415: The Law that is against thee, and the sins
12.416: Of all mankinde, with him there crucifi'd,
12.417: Never to hurt them more who rightly trust
12.418: In this his satisfaction; so he dies,
12.419: But soon revives, Death over him no power
12.420: Shall long usurp; ere the third dawning light
12.421: Returne, the Starres of Morn shall see him rise
12.422: Out of his grave, fresh as the dawning light,
12.423: Thy ransom paid, which Man from death redeems,
12.424: His death for Man, as many as offerd Life
12.425: Neglect not, and the benefit imbrace
12.426: By Faith not void of works: this God-like act
12.427: Annuls thy doom, the death thou shouldst have dy'd,
12.428: In sin for ever lost from life; this act
12.429: Shall bruise the head of Satan, crush his strength
12.430: Defeating Sin and Death, his two maine armes,
12.431: And fix farr deeper in his head thir stings
12.432: Then temporal death shall bruise the Victors heel,
12.433: Or theirs whom he redeems, a death like sleep,
12.434: A gentle wafting to immortal Life.
12.435: Nor after resurrection shall he stay
12.436: Longer on Earth then certaine times to appeer
12.437: To his Disciples, Men who in his Life
12.438: Still follow'd him; to them shall leave in charge
12.439: To teach all nations what of him they learn'd
12.440: And his Salvation, them who shall beleeve
12.441: Baptizing in the profluent streame, the signe
12.442: Of washing them from guilt of sin to Life
12.443: Pure, and in mind prepar'd, if so befall,
12.444: For death, like that which the redeemer dy'd.
12.445: All Nations they shall teach; for from that day
12.446: Not onely to the Sons of Abrahams Loines
12.447: Salvation shall be Preacht, but to the Sons
12.448: Of Abrahams Faith wherever through the world;
12.449: So in his seed all Nations shall be blest.
12.450: Then to the Heav'n of Heav'ns he shall ascend
12.451: With victory, triumphing through the aire
12.452: Over his foes and thine; there shall surprise
12.453: The Serpent, Prince of aire, and drag in Chaines
12.454: Through all his realme, & there confounded leave;
12.455: Then enter into glory, and resume
12.456: His Seat at Gods right hand, exalted high
12.457: Above all names in Heav'n; and thence shall come,
12.458: When this worlds dissolution shall be ripe,
12.459: With glory and power to judge both quick & dead,
12.460: To judge th' unfaithful dead, but to reward
12.461: His faithful, and receave them into bliss,
12.462: Whether in Heav'n or Earth, for then the Earth
12.463: Shall all be Paradise, far happier place
12.464: Then this of Eden, and far happier daies.
12.465: So spake th' Archangel Michael, then paus'd,
12.466: As at the Worlds great period; and our Sire
12.467: Replete with joy and wonder thus repli'd.
12.469: That all this good of evil shall produce,
12.470: And evil turn to good; more wonderful
12.471: Then that which by creation first brought forth
12.472: Light out of darkness! full of doubt I stand,
12.473: Whether I should repent me now of sin
12.474: By mee done and occasiond, or rejoyce
12.475: Much more, that much more good thereof shall spring,
12.476: To God more glory, more good will to Men
12.477: From God, and over wrauth grace shall abound.
12.478: But say, if our deliverer up to Heav'n
12.479: Must reascend, what will betide the few
12.480: His faithful, left among th' unfaithful herd,
12.481: The enemies of truth; who then shall guide
12.482: His people, who defend? will they not deale
12.483: Wors with his followers then with him they dealt?
12.484: Be sure they will, said th' Angel; but from Heav'n
12.485: Hee to his own a Comforter will send,
12.486: The promise of the Father, who shall dwell
12.487: His Spirit within them, and the Law of Faith
12.488: Working through love, upon thir hearts shall write,
12.489: To guide them in all truth, and also arme
12.490: With spiritual Armour, able to resist
12.491: Satans assaults, and quench his fierie darts
12.492: What Man can do against them, not affraid,
12.493: Though to the death, against such cruelties
12.495: And oft supported so as shall amaze
12.496: Thir proudest persecuters: for the Spirit
12.497: Powrd first on his Apostles, whom he sends
12.498: To evangelize the Nations, then on all
12.499: Baptiz'd, shall them with wondrous gifts endue
12.500: To speak all Tongues, and do all Miracles,
12.501: As did thir Lord before them. Thus they win
12.502: Great numbers of each Nation to receave
12.503: With joy the tidings brought from Heav'n: at length
12.504: Thir Ministry perform'd, and race well run,
12.505: Thir doctrine and thir story written left,
12.506: They die; but in thir room, as they forewarne,
12.507: Wolves shall succeed for teachers, grievous Wolves,
12.508: Who all the sacred mysteries of Heav'n
12.509: To thir own vile advantages shall turne
12.510: Of lucre and ambition, and the truth
12.512: Left onely in those written Records pure,
12.513: Though not but by the Spirit understood.
12.514: Then shall they seek to avail themselves of names,
12.515: Places and titles, and with these to joine
12.516: Secular power, though feigning still to act
12.518: The Spirit of God, promisd alike and giv'n
12.519: To all Beleevers; and from that pretense,
12.520: Spiritual Lawes by carnal power shall force
12.521: On every conscience; Laws which none shall finde
12.522: Left them inrould, or what the Spirit within
12.523: Shall on the heart engrave. What will they then
12.524: But force the Spirit of Grace it self, and binde
12.525: His consort Libertie; what, but unbuild
12.526: His living Temples, built by Faith to stand,
12.527: Thir own Faith not anothers: for on Earth
12.528: Who against Faith and Conscience can be heard
12.531: On all who in the worship persevere
12.532: Of Spirit and Truth; the rest, farr greater part,
12.533: Will deem in outward Rites and specious formes
12.535: Bestuck with slandrous darts, and works of Faith
12.536: Rarely be found: so shall the World goe on,
12.537: To good malignant, to bad men benigne,
12.538: Under her own waight groaning, till the day
12.539: Appeer of respiration to the just,
12.540: And vengeance to the wicked, at return
12.541: Of him so lately promis'd to thy aid,
12.542: The Womans seed, obscurely then foretold,
12.543: Now amplier known thy Saviour and thy Lord,
12.544: Last in the Clouds from Heav'n to be reveald
12.545: In glory of the Father, to dissolve
12.546: Satan with his perverted World, then raise
12.547: From the conflagrant mass, purg'd and refin'd,
12.548: New Heav'ns, new Earth, Ages of endless date
12.549: Founded in righteousness and peace and love,
12.550: To bring forth fruits Joy and eternal Bliss.
12.551: He ended; and thus Adam last reply'd.
12.552: How soon hath thy prediction, Seer blest,
12.553: Measur'd this transient World, the Race of time,
12.554: Till time stand fixt: beyond is all abyss,
12.555: Eternitie, whose end no eye can reach.
12.556: Greatly instructed I shall hence depart,
12.557: Greatly in peace of thought, and have my fill
12.558: Of knowledge, what this vessel can containe;
12.559: Beyond which was my folly to aspire.
12.560: Henceforth I learne, that to obey is best,
12.561: And love with feare the onely God, to walk
12.562: As in his presence, ever to observe
12.563: His providence, and on him sole depend,
12.564: Merciful over all his works, with good
12.565: Still overcoming evil, and by small
12.566: Accomplishing great things, by things deemd weak
12.567: Subverting worldly strong, and worldly wise
12.568: By simply meek; that suffering for Truths sake
12.570: And to the faithful Death the Gate of Life;
12.571: Taught this by his example whom I now
12.573: To whom thus also th' Angel last repli'd:
12.574: This having learnt, thou hast attaind the summe
12.575: Of wisdom; hope no higher, though all the Starrs
12.576: Thou knewst by name, and all th' ethereal Powers,
12.577: All secrets of the deep, all Natures works,
12.578: Or works of God in Heav'n, Air, Earth, or Sea,
12.579: And all the riches of this World enjoydst,
12.580: And all the rule, one Empire; onely add
12.581: Deeds to thy knowledge answerable, add Faith,
12.582: Add Vertue, Patience, Temperance, add Love,
12.583: By name to come call'd Charitie, the soul
12.584: Of all the rest: then wilt thou not be loath
12.585: To leave this Paradise, but shalt possess
12.586: A Paradise within thee, happier farr.
12.587: Let us descend now therefore from this top
12.588: Of Speculation; for the hour precise
12.589: Exacts our parting hence; and see the Guards,
12.590: By mee encampt on yonder Hill, expect
12.591: Thir motion, at whose Front a flaming Sword,
12.592: In signal of remove, waves fiercely round;
12.593: We may no longer stay: go, waken Eve;
12.594: Her also I with gentle Dreams have calm'd
12.595: Portending good, and all her spirits compos'd
12.596: To meek submission: thou at season fit
12.597: Let her with thee partake what thou hast heard,
12.598: Chiefly what may concern her Faith to know,
12.599: The great deliverance by her Seed to come
12.600: (For by the Womans Seed) on all Mankind.
12.601: That ye may live, which will be many dayes,
12.602: Both in one Faith unanimous though sad,
12.603: With cause for evils past, yet much more cheer'd
12.604: With meditation on the happie end.
12.605: He ended, and they both descend the Hill;
12.606: Descended, Adam to the Bowre where Eve
12.607: Lay sleeping ran before, but found her wak't;
12.608: And thus with words not sad she him receav'd.
12.609: Whence thou returnst, & whither wentst, I know;
12.610: For God is also in sleep, and Dreams advise,
12.611: Which he hath sent propitious, some great good
12.612: Presaging, since with sorrow and hearts distress
12.613: Wearied I fell asleep: but now lead on;
12.614: In mee is no delay; with thee to goe,
12.615: Is to stay here; without thee here to stay,
12.616: Is to go hence unwilling; thou to mee
12.617: Art all things under Heav'n, all places thou,
12.618: Who for my wilful crime art banisht hence.
12.620: I carry hence; though all by mee is lost,
12.621: Such favour I unworthie am voutsaft,
12.622: By mee the Promis'd Seed shall all restore.
12.623: So spake our Mother Eve, and Adam heard
12.624: Well pleas'd, but answer'd not; for now too nigh
12.625: Th' Archangel stood, and from the other Hill
12.626: To thir fixt Station, all in bright array
12.627: The Cherubim descended; on the ground
12.629: Ris'n from a River o're the marish glides,
12.630: And gathers ground fast at the Labourers heel
12.631: Homeward returning. High in Front advanc't,
12.632: The brandisht Sword of God before them blaz'd
12.633: Fierce as a Comet; which with torrid heat,
12.634: And vapour as the Libyan Air adust,
12.635: Began to parch that temperate Clime; whereat
12.636: In either hand the hastning Angel caught
12.637: Our lingring Parents, and to th' Eastern Gate
12.638: Let them direct, and down the Cliff as fast
12.639: To the subjected Plaine; then disappeer'd.
12.640: They looking back, all th' Eastern side beheld
12.641: Of Paradise, so late thir happie seat,
12.642: Wav'd over by that flaming Brand, the Gate
12.643: With dreadful Faces throng'd and fierie Armes:
12.644: Som natural tears they drop'd, but wip'd them soon;
12.645: The World was all before them, where to choose
12.646: Thir place of rest, and Providence thir guide:
12.647: They hand in hand with wandring steps and slow,
12.648: Through Eden took thir solitarie way.

1.1: I WHO e're while the happy Garden sung,
1.2: By one mans disobedience lost, now sing
1.4: By one mans firm obedience fully tri'd
1.5: Through all temptation, and the Tempter foil'd
1.6: In all his wiles, defeated and repuls't,
1.7: And Eden rais'd in the wast Wilderness.
1.8: Thou Spirit who ledst this glorious Eremite
1.9: Into the Desert, his Victorious Field
1.10: Against the Spiritual Foe, and broughtst him thence
1.11: By proof the undoubted Son of God, inspire,
1.12: As thou art wont, my prompted Song else mute,
1.13: And bear through highth or depth of natures bounds
1.14: With prosperous wing full summ'd to tell of deeds
1.15: Above Heroic, though in secret done,
1.16: And unrecorded left through many an Age,
1.17: Worthy t' have not remain'd so long unsung.
1.18: Now had the great Proclaimer with a voice
1.19: More awful then the sound of Trumpet, cri'd
1.20: Repentance, and Heavens Kingdom nigh at hand
1.21: To all Baptiz'd: to his great Baptism flock'd
1.22: With aw the Regions round, and with them came
1.23: From Nazareth the Son of Joseph deem'd
1.24: To the flood Jordan, came as then obscure,
1.25: Unmarkt, unknown; but him the Baptist soon
1.26: Descri'd, divinely warn'd, and witness bore
1.27: As to his worthier, and would have resign'd
1.28: To him his Heavenly Office, nor was long
1.29: His witness unconfirm'd: on him baptiz'd
1.30: Heaven open'd, and in likeness of a Dove
1.31: The Spirit descended, while the Fathers voice
1.32: From Heav'n pronounc'd him his beloved Son
1.33: That heard the Adversary, who roving still
1.34: About the world, at that assembly fam'd
1.35: Would not be last, and with the voice divine
1.36: Nigh Thunder-struck, th' exalted man, to whom
1.37: Such high attest was giv'n, a while survey'd
1.38: With wonder, then with envy fraught and rage
1.39: Flies to his place, nor rests, but in mid air
1.40: To Councel summons all his mighty Peers,
1.41: Within thick Clouds and dark ten-fold involv'd,
1.42: A gloomy Consistory; and them amidst
1.43: With looks agast and sad he thus bespake.
1.44: O ancient Powers of Air and this wide world,
1.45: For much more willingly I mention Air,
1.46: This our old Conquest, then remember Hell
1.47: Our hated habitation; well ye know
1.48: How many Ages, as the years of men,
1.49: This Universe we have possest, and rul'd
1.50: In manner at our will th' affairs of Earth,
1.51: Since Adam and his facil consort Eve
1.52: Lost Paradise deceiv'd by me, though since
1.53: With dread attending when that fatal wound
1.54: Shall be inflicted by the Seed of Eve
1.55: Upon my head, long the decrees of Heav'n
1.56: Delay, for longest time to him is short;
1.57: And now too soon for us the circling hours
1.58: This dreaded time have compast, wherein we
1.59: Must bide the stroak of that long threatn'd wound,
1.60: At least if so we can, and by the head
1.61: Broken be not intended all our power
1.62: To be infring'd, our freedom and our being
1.63: In this fair Empire won of Earth and Air;
1.64: For this ill news I bring, the Womans seed
1.65: Destin'd to this, is late of woman born,
1.66: His birth to our just fear gave no small cause,
1.67: But his growth now to youths full flowr, displaying
1.68: All vertue, grace and wisdom to atchieve
1.69: Things highest, greatest, multiplies my fear.
1.70: Before him a great Prophet, to proclaim
1.71: His coming is sent Harbinger, who all
1.72: Invites, and in the Consecrated stream
1.73: Pretends to wash off sin and fit them so
1.74: Purified to receive him pure, or rather
