1.75: To do him honour as their King; all come,
1.76: And he himself among them was baptiz'd,
1.77: Not thence to be more pure, but to receive
1.78: The testimony of Heaven, that who he is
1.79: Thenceforth the Nations may not doubt; I saw
1.80: The Prophet do him reverence, on him rising
1.81: Out of the water, Heav'n above the Clouds
1.82: Unfold her Crystal Dores, thence on his head
1.83: A perfect Dove descend, what e're it meant
1.84: And out of Heav'n the Sov'raign voice I heard,
1.85: This is my Son belov'd, in him am pleas'd.
1.86: His Mother then is mortal, but his Sire,
1.87: He who obtains the Monarchy of Heav'n,
1.88: And what will he not do to advance his Son?
1.89: His first-begot we know, and sore have felt,
1.90: When his fierce thunder drove us to the deep;
1.91: Who this is we must learn, for man he seems
1.92: In all his lineaments, though in his face
1.93: The glimpses of his Fathers glory shine.
1.94: Ye see our danger on the utmost edge
1.95: Of hazard, which admits no long debate,
1.96: But must with something sudden be oppos'd,
1.97: Not force, but well couch't fraud, well woven snares,
1.98: E're in the head of Nations he appear
1.99: Their King, their Leader, and Supream on Earth.
1.100: I, when no other durst, sole undertook
1.101: The dismal expedition to find out
1.102: And ruine Adam, and the exploit perform'd
1.104: Will waft me; and the way found prosperous once
1.105: Induces best to hope of like success.
1.106: He ended, and his words impression left
1.107: Of much amazement to th' infernal Crew,
1.108: Distracted and surpriz'd with deep dismay
1.109: At these sad tidings; but no time was then
1.110: For long indulgence to their fears or grief:
1.111: Unanimous they all commit the care
1.112: And management of this main enterprize
1.113: To him their great Dictator, whose attempt
1.114: At first against mankind so well had thriv'd
1.115: In Adam's overthrow, and led thir march
1.116: From Hell's deep-vaulted Den to dwell in light,
1.117: Regents and Potentates, and Kings, yea gods
1.118: Of many a pleasant Realm and Province wide.
1.119: So to the Coast of Jordan he directs
1.120: His easie steps; girded with snaky wiles,
1.121: Where he might likeliest find this new-declar'd,
1.122: This man of men, attested Son of God,
1.123: Temptation and all guile on him to try;
1.124: So to subvert whom he suspected rais'd
1.125: To end his Raign on Earth so long enjoy'd:
1.127: The purpos'd Counsel pre-ordain'd and fixt
1.128: Of the most High, who in full frequence bright
1.129: Of Angels, thus to Gabriel smiling spake.
1.130: Gabriel this day by proof thou shalt behold,
1.131: Thou and all Angels conversant on Earth
1.132: With man or mens affairs, how I begin
1.133: To verifie that solemn message late,
1.134: On which I sent thee to the Virgin pure
1.135: In Galilee, that she should bear a Son
1.136: Great in Renown, and call'd the Son of God;
1.137: Then toldst her doubting how these things could be
1.138: To her a Virgin, that on her should come
1.139: The Holy Ghost, and the power of the highest
1.140: O're-shadow her: this man born and now up-grown,
1.141: To shew him worthy of his birth divine
1.142: And high prediction, henceforth I expose
1.143: To Satan; let him tempt and now assay
1.144: His utmost subtilty, because he boasts
1.145: And vaunts of his great cunning to the throng
1.146: Of his Apostasie; he might have learnt
1.147: Less over-weening, since he fail'd in Job,
1.149: Whate're his cruel malice could invent.
1.150: He now shall know I can produce a man
1.151: Of female Seed, far abler to resist
1.152: All his sollicitations, and at length
1.153: All his vast force, and drive him back to Hell,
1.154: Winning by Conquest what the first man lost
1.155: By fallacy surpriz'd.  But first I mean
1.156: To exercise him in the Wilderness,
1.157: There he shall first lay down the rudiments
1.158: Of his great warfare, e're I send him forth
1.159: To conquer Sin and Death the two grand foes,
1.161: His weakness shall o'recome Satanic strength
1.162: And all the world, and mass of sinful flesh;
1.163: That all the Angels and Aetherial Powers,
1.164: They now, and men hereafter may discern,
1.165: From what consummate vertue I have chose
1.166: This perfect Man, by merit call'd my Son,
1.167: To earn Salvation for the Sons of men.
1.168: So spake the Eternal Father, and all Heaven
1.169: Admiring stood a space, then into Hymns
1.170: Burst forth, and in Celestial measures mov'd,
1.171: Circling the Throne and Singing, while the hand
1.172: Sung with the voice, and this the argument.
1.173: Victory and Triumph to the Son of God
1.174: Now entring his great duel, not of arms,
1.175: But to vanquish by wisdom hellish wiles.
1.176: The Father knows the Son; therefore secure
1.177: Ventures his filial Vertue, though untri'd,
1.178: Against whate're may tempt, whate're seduce,
1.180: Be frustrate all ye stratagems of Hell,
1.181: And devilish machinations come to nought.
1.182: So they in Heav'n their Odes and Vigils tun'd:
1.183: Mean while the Son of God, who yet some days
1.184: Lodg'd in Bethabara where John baptiz'd,
1.185: Musing and much revolving in his brest,
1.186: How best the mighty work he might begin
1.187: Of Saviour to mankind, and which way first
1.188: Publish his God-like office now mature,
1.189: One day forth walk'd alone, the Spirit leading;
1.190: And his deep thoughts, the better to converse
1.191: With solitude, till far from track of men,
1.192: Thought following thought, and step by step led on,
1.193: He entred now the bordering Desert wild,
1.194: And with dark shades and rocks environ'd round,
1.196: O what a multitude of thoughts at once
1.197: Awakn'd in me swarm, while I consider
1.198: What from within I feel my self and hear
1.199: What from without comes often to my ears,
1.200: Ill sorting with my present state compar'd.
1.201: When I was yet a child, no childish play
1.202: To me was pleasing, all my mind was set
1.203: Serious to learn and know, and thence to do
1.204: What might be publick good; my self I thought
1.205: Born to that end, born to promote all truth,
1.206: All righteous things: therefore above my years,
1.207: The Law of God I read, and found it sweet,
1.208: Made it my whole delight, and in it grew
1.209: To such perfection, that e're yet my age
1.210: Had measur'd twice six years, at our great Feast
1.211: I went into the Temple, there to hear
1.212: The Teachers of our Law, and to propose
1.213: What might improve my knowledge or their own;
1.214: And was admir'd by all, yet this not all
1.215: To which my Spirit aspir'd, victorious deeds
1.216: Flam'd in my heart, heroic acts, one while
1.217: To rescue Israel from the Roman yoke,
1.218: Thence to subdue and quell o're all the earth
1.219: Brute violence and proud Tyrannick pow'r,
1.220: Till truth were freed, and equity restor'd:
1.221: Yet held it more humane, more heavenly first
1.222: By winning words to conquer willing hearts,
1.223: And make perswasion do the work of fear;
1.224: At least to try, and teach the erring Soul
1.226: Misled: the stubborn only to subdue.
1.227: These growing thoughts my Mother soon perceiving
1.228: By words at times cast forth inly rejoyc'd,
1.229: And said to me apart, high are thy thoughts
1.230: O Son, but nourish them and let them soar
1.231: To what highth sacred vertue and true worth
1.232: Can raise them, though above example high;
1.233: By matchless Deeds express thy matchless Sire.
1.234: For know, thou art no Son of mortal man,
1.235: Though men esteem thee low of Parentage,
1.236: Thy Father is the Eternal King, who rules
1.237: All Heaven and Earth, Angels and Sons of men,
1.238: A messenger from God fore-told thy birth
1.239: Conceiv'd in me a Virgin, he fore-told
1.240: Thou shouldst be great and sit on David's Throne.
1.241: And of thy Kingdom there should be no end.
1.242: At thy Nativity a glorious Quire
1.243: Of Angels in the fields of Bethlehem sung
1.244: To Shepherds watching at their folds by night,
1.245: And told them the Messiah now was born,
1.246: Where they might see him, and to thee they came;
1.247: Directed to the Manger where thou lais't,
1.248: For in the Inn was left no better room:
1.249: A Star, not seen before in Heaven appearing
1.250: Guided the Wise Men thither from the East,
1.251: To honour thee with Incense, Myrrh, and Gold,
1.252: By whose bright course led on they found the place,
1.253: Affirming it thy Star new grav'n in Heaven,
1.254: By which they knew thee King of Israel born.
1.255: Just Simeon and Prophetic Anna, warn'd
1.256: By Vision, found thee in the Temple, and spake
1.257: Before the Altar and the vested Priest,
1.258: Like things of thee to all that present stood.
1.259: This having heard, strait I again revolv'd
1.260: The Law and Prophets, searching what was writ
1.261: Concerning the Messiah, to our Scribes
1.262: Known partly, and soon found of whom they spake
1.263: I am; this chiefly, that my way must lie
1.264: Through many a hard assay even to the death,
1.265: E're I the promis'd Kingdom can attain,
1.266: Or work redemption for mankind, whose sins
1.267: Full weight must be transferr'd upon my head.
1.268: Yet neither thus disheartn'd or dismay'd,
1.269: The time prefixt I waited, when behold
1.270: The Baptist, (of whose birth I oft had heard,
1.271: Not knew by sight) now come, who was to come
1.272: Before Messiah and his way prepare.
1.273: I as all others to his Baptism came,
1.274: Which I believ'd was from above; but he
1.275: Strait knew me, and with loudest voice proclaim'd
1.276: Me him (for it was shew'n him so from Heaven)
1.277: Me him whose Harbinger he was; and first
1.278: Refus'd on me his Baptism to confer,
1.279: As much his greater, and was hardly won;
1.280: But as I rose out of the laving stream,
1.281: Heaven open'd her eternal doors, from whence
1.282: The Spirit descended on me like a Dove,
1.283: And last the sum of all, my Father's voice,
1.284: Audibly heard from Heav'n, pronounc'd me his,
1.285: Me his beloved Son, in whom alone
1.286: He was well pleas'd; by which I knew the time
1.287: Now full, that I no more should live obscure,
1.288: But openly begin, as best becomes
1.289: The Authority which I deriv'd from Heaven.
1.290: And now by some strong motion I am led
1.291: Into this wilderness, to what intent
1.292: I learn not yet, perhaps I need not know;
1.293: For what concerns my knowledge God reveals.
1.294: So spake our Morning Star then in his rise,
1.295: And looking round on every side beheld
1.296: A pathless Desert, dusk with horrid shades;
1.297: The way he came not having mark'd, return
1.298: Was difficult, by humane steps untrod;
1.299: And he still on was led, but with such thoughts
1.300: Accompanied of things past and to come
1.301: Lodg'd in his brest, as well might recommend
1.303: Full forty days he pass'd, whether on hill
1.304: Sometimes, anon in shady vale, each night
1.305: Under the covert of some ancient Oak,
1.306: Or Cedar, to defend him from the dew,
1.307: Or harbour'd in one Cave, is not reveal'd;
1.308: Nor tasted humane food, nor hunger felt
1.309: Till those days ended, hunger'd then at last
1.310: Among wild Beasts: they at his sight grew mild,
1.311: Nor sleeping him nor waking harm'd, his walk
1.312: The fiery Serpent fled, and noxious Worm,
1.313: The Lion and fierce Tiger glar'd aloof.
1.314: But now an aged man in Rural weeds,
1.315: Following, as seem'd, the quest of some stray Ewe,
1.316: Or wither'd sticks to gather; which might serve
1.317: Against a Winters day when winds blow keen,
1.318: To warm him wet return'd from field at Eve,
1.319: He saw approach, who first with curious eye
1.320: Perus'd him, then with words thus utt'red spake.
1.321: Sir, what ill chance hath brought thee to this place
1.322: So far from path or road of men, who pass
1.323: In Troop or Caravan, for single  none
1.324: Durst ever, who return'd, and dropt not here
1.325: His Carcass,  pin'd with hunger and with droughth?
1.326: I ask the rather and the more admire,
1.327: For that to me thou seem'st the man, whom late
1.328: Our new baptizing Prophet at the Ford
1.329: Of Jordan honour'd so, and call'd thee Son
1.330: Of God: I saw and heard, for we sometimes
1.331: Who dwell this wild, constrain'd by want, come forth
1.332: To Town or Village nigh (nighest is far)
1.333: Where ought we hear, and curious are to hear,
1.334: What happ'ns new; Fame also finds us out.
1.335: To whom the Son of God.  Who brought me hither
1.336: Will bring me hence, no other Guide I seek,
1.337: By Miracle he may, reply'd the Swain,
1.338: What other way I see not, for we here
1.339: Live on tough roots and stubs, to thirst inur'd
1.340: More then the Camel, and to drink go far,
1.341: Men to much misery and hardship born;
1.342: But if thou be the Son of God, Command
1.343: That out of these hard stones be made thee bread;
1.344: So shalt thou save thy self and us relieve
1.345: With Food, whereof we wretched seldom taste.
1.346: He ended, and the Son of God reply'd.
1.347: Think'st thou such force in Bread? is it not written
1.348: (For I discern thee other then thou seem'st)
1.349: Man lives not by Bread only, but each Word
1.350: Proceeding from the mouth of God; who fed
1.351: Our Fathers here with Manna; in the Mount
1.352: Moses was forty days, nor eat nor drank,
1.353: And forty days Eliah without food
1.354: Wandred this barren waste, the same I now:
1.355: Why dost thou then suggest to me distrust,
1.356: Knowing who I am, as I know who thou art?
1.357: Whom thus answer'd th' Arch Fiend now undisguis'd.
1.358: 'Tis true, I am that Spirit unfortunate,
1.359: Who leagu'd with millions more in rash revolt
1.360: Kept not my happy Station, but was driv'n
1.361: With them from bliss to the bottomless deep,
1.362: Vet to that hideous place not so confin'd
1.363: By rigour unconniving, but that oft
1.364: Leaving my dolorous Prison I enjoy
1.365: Large liberty to round this Globe of Earth,
1.366: Or range in th' Air, nor from the Heav'n of Heav'ns
1.367: Hath he excluded my resort sometimes.
1.368: I came among the Sons of God, when he
1.369: Gave up into my hands Uzzean Job
1.370: To prove him, and illustrate his high worth;
1.371: And when to all his Angels he propos'd
1.372: To draw the proud King Ahab into fraud
1.373: That he might fall in Ramoth, they demurring,
1.374: I undertook that office, and the tongues
1.375: Of all his flattering Prophets glibb'd with lyes
1.376: To his destruction, as I had in charge.
1.377: For what he bids I do; though I have lost
1.378: Much lustre of my native brightness, lost
1.379: To be belov'd of God, I have not lost
1.380: To love, at least contemplate and admire
1.381: What I see excellent in good, or fair,
1.382: Or vertuous, I should so have lost all sense.
1.383: What can be then less in me then desire
1.384: To see thee and approach thee, whom I know
1.385: Declar'd the Son of God, to hear attent
1.386: Thy wisdom, and behold thy God-like deeds?
1.387: Men generally think me much a foe
1.388: To all mankind: why should I? they to me
1.389: Never did wrong or violence, by them
1.390: I lost not what I lost, rather by them
1.391: I gain'd what I have gain'd, and with them dwell
1.392: Copartner in these Regions of the World,
1.393: If not disposer; lend them oft my aid,
1.394: Oft my advice by presages and signs,
1.395: And answers, oracles, portents and dreams,
1.396: Whereby they may direct their future life.
1.397: Envy they say excites me, thus to gain
1.398: Companions of my misery and wo.
1.399: At first it may be; but long since with wo
1.400: Nearer acquainted, now I feel by proof,
1.401: That fellowship in pain divides not smart,
1.402: Nor lightens aught each mans peculiar load.
1.403: Small consolation then, were Man adjoyn'd:
1.404: This wounds me most (what can it less) that Man,
1.405: Man fall'n shall be restor'd, I never more.
1.406: To whom our Saviour sternly thus reply'd.
1.407: Deservedly thou griev'st, compos'd of lyes
1.408: From the beginning, and in lies wilt end;
1.409: Who boast'st release from Hell, and leave to come
1.410: Into the Heav'n of Heavens; thou com'st indeed,
1.411: As a poor miserable captive thrall,
1.412: Comes to the place where he before had sat
1.413: Among the Prime in Splendour, now depos'd,
1.415: A spectacle of ruin or of scorn
1.416: To all the Host of Heaven; the happy place
1.417: Imparts to thee no happiness, no joy,
1.419: Lost bliss, to thee no more communicable,
1.420: So never more in Hell then when in Heaven.
1.421: But thou art serviceable to Heaven's King.
1.422: Wilt thou impute to obedience what thy fear
1.423: Extorts, or pleasure to do ill excites?
1.424: What but thy malice mov'd thee to misdeem
1.425: Of righteous Job, then cruelly to afflict him
1.426: With all inflictions, but his patience won?
1.427: The other service was thy chosen task,
1.428: To be a lyer in four hundred mouths;
1.429: For lying is thy sustenance, thy food.
1.430: Yet thou pretend'st to truth; all Oracles
1.431: By thee are giv'n, and what confest more true
1.432: Among the Nations? that hath been thy craft,
1.433: By mixing somewhat true to vent more lyes.
1.434: But what have been thy answers, what but dark
1.435: Ambiguous and with double sense deluding,
1.436: Which they who ask'd have seldom understood,
1.437: And not well understood as good not known?
1.438: Who ever by consulting at thy shrine
1.439: Return'd the wiser, or the more instruct
1.440: To flye or follow what concern'd him most,
1.441: And run not sooner to his fatal snare?
1.442: For God hath justly giv'n the Nations up
1.443: To thy Delusions; justly, since they fell
1.444: Idolatrous, but when his purpose is
1.445: Among them to declare his Providence
1.446: To thee not known, whence hast thou then thy truth,
1.447: But from him or his Angels President
1.448: In every Province, who themselves disdaining
1.449: To approach thy Temples, give thee in command
1.450: What to the smallest tittle thou shalt say
1.451: To thy Adorers; thou with trembling fear,
1.452: Or like a Fawning Parasite obey'st;
1.453: Then to thy self ascrib'st the truth fore-told.
1.454: But this thy glory shall be soon retrench'd;
1.455: No more shalt thou by oracling abuse
1.456: The Gentiles; henceforth Oracles are ceast,
1.457: And thou no more with Pomp and Sacrifice
1.458: Shalt be enquir'd at Delphos or elsewhere,
1.459: At least in vain, for they shall find thee mute.
1.460: God hath now sent his living Oracle
1.461: Into the World, to teach his final will,
1.462: And sends his Spirit of Truth henceforth to dwell
1.463: In pious Hearts, an inward Oracle
1.464: To all truth requisite for men to know.
1.465: So spake our Saviour; but the subtle Fiend,
1.466: Though inly stung with anger and disdain,
1.467: Dissembl'd, and this answer smooth return'd.
1.468: Sharply thou hast insisted on rebuke,
1.469: And urg'd me hard with doings, which not will
1.470: But misery hath rested from me; where
1.471: Easily canst thou find one miserable,
1.472: And not inforc'd oft-times to part from truth;
1.473: If it may stand him more in stead to lye,
1.474: Say and unsay, feign, flatter, or abjure?
1.475: But thou art plac't above me, thou art Lord;
1.476: From thee I can and must submiss endure
1.477: Check or reproof, and glad to scape so quit.
1.478: Hard are the ways of truth, and rough to walk,
1.479: Smooth on the tongue discourst, pleasing to th' ear,
1.480: And tuneable as Silvan Pipe or Song;
1.481: What wonder then if I delight to hear
1.482: Her dictates from thy mouth? most men admire
1.483: Vertue, who follow not her lore: permit me
1.484: To hear thee when I come (since no man comes)
1.485: And talk at least, though I despair to attain.
1.486: Thy Father, who is holy, wise and pure,
1.487: Suffers the Hypocrite or Atheous Priest
1.488: To tread his Sacred Courts, and minister
1.489: About his Altar, handling holy things,
1.490: Praying or vowing, and vouchsaf'd his voice
1.491: To Balaam reprobate, a Prophet yet
1.492: Inspir'd; disdain not such access to me.
1.493: To whom our Saviour with unalter'd brow
1.494: Thy coming hither, though I know thy scope,
1.495: I bid not or forbid; do as thou find'st
1.496: Permission from above; thou canst not more.
1.497: He added not; and Satan bowing low
1.499: Into thin Air diffus'd: for now began
1.500: Night with her sullen wing to double-shade
1.501: The Desert Fowls in thir clay nests were couch't;
1.502: And now wild Beasts came forth the woods to roam.

2.1: MEAN while the new-baptiz'd, who yet remain'd
2.2: At Jordan with the Baptist, and had seen
2.3: Him whom they heard so late expresly call'd
2.4: Jesus Messiah Son of God declar'd,
2.5: And on that high Authority had believ'd,
2.6: And with him talkt, and with him lodg'd, I mean
2.7: Andrew and Simon, famous after known
2.8: With others though in Holy Writ not nam'd,
2.9: Now missing him thir joy so lately found,
2.10: So lately found, and so abruptly gone,
2.11: Began to doubt, and doubted many days,
2.12: And as the days increas'd, increas'd thir doubt:
2.13: Sometimes they thought he might be only shewn,
2.14: And for a time caught up to God, as once
2.15: Moses was in the Mount, and missing long;
2.16: And the great Thisbite who on fiery wheels
2.17: Rode up to Heaven, yet once again to come.
2.18: Therefore as those young Prophets then with care
2.19: Sought lost Eliah, so in each place these
2.21: The City of Palms, Aenon, and Salem Old,
2.22: Machaerus and each Town or City wall'd
2.23: On this side the broad lake Genezaret
2.24: Or in Perea, but return'd in vain.
2.25: Then on the bank of Jordan, by a Creek:
2.26: Where winds with Reeds, and Osiers whisp'ring play
2.27: Plain Fishermen, no greater men them call,
2.28: Close in a Cottage low together got
2.29: Thir unexpected loss and plaints out breath'd.
2.30: Alas from what high hope to what relapse
2.31: Unlook'd for are we fall'n, our eyes beheld
2.32: Messiah certainly now come, so long
2.33: Expected of our Fathers; we have heard
2.34: His words, his wisdom full of grace and truth,
2.35: Now, now, for sure, deliverance is at hand,
2.36: The Kingdom shall to Israel be restor'd:
2.37: Thus we rejoyc'd, but soon our joy is turn'd
2.39: For whither is he gone, what accident
2.40: Hath rapt him from us? will he now retire
2.43: Send thy Messiah forth, the time is come;
2.44: Behold the Kings of the Earth how they oppress
2.45: Thy chosen, to what highth thir pow'r unjust
2.46: They have exalted, and behind them cast
2.47: All fear of thee, arise and vindicate
2.48: Thy Glory, free thy people from thir yoke,
2.49: But let us wait; thus far he hath perform'd,
2.50: Sent his Anointed, and to us reveal'd him,
2.51: By his great Prophet, pointed at and shown,
2.52: In publick, and  with him we have convers'd;
2.53: Let us be glad of this, and all our fears
2.54: Lay on his Providence; he will not fail
2.55: Nor will withdraw him now, nor will recall,
2.56: Mock us with his blest sight, then snatch him hence,
2.57: Soon we shall see our hope, our joy return.
2.58: Thus they out of their plaints new hope resume
2.59: To find whom at the first they found unsought:
2.60: But to his Mother Mary, when she saw
2.61: Others return'd from Baptism, not her Son,
2.62: Nor left at Jordan, tydings of him none;
2.63: Within her brest, though calm; her brest though pure,
2.64: Motherly cares and fears got head, and rais'd
2.65: Some troubl'd thoughts, which she in sighs thus clad.
2.66: O what avails me now that honour high
2.67: To have conceiv'd of God, or that salute
2.68: Hale highly favour'd, among women blest;
2.69: While I to sorrows am no less advanc't,
2.70: And fears as eminent, above the lot
2.71: Of other women, by the birth I bore,
2.72: In such a season born when scarce a Shed
2.73: Could be obtain'd to shelter him or me
2.74: From the bleak air; a Stable was our warmth,
2.75: A Manger his, yet soon enforc't to flye
2.76: Thence into Egypt, till the Murd'rous King
2.77: Were dead, who sought his life, and missing fill'd
2.78: With Infant blood the streets of Bethlehem;
2.79: From Egypt home return'd, in Nazareth
2.80: Hath been our dwelling many years, his life
2.82: Little suspicious to any King; but now
2.83: Full grown to Man, acknowledg'd, as I hear,
2.84: By John the Baptist, and in publick shown,
2.85: Son own'd from Heaven by his Father's voice;
2.86: I  look't for some great change; to Honour? no,
2.87: But trouble, as old Simeon plain foretold,
2.88: That to the fall and rising he should be
2.89: Of  Many in Israel, and to a sign
2.90: Spoken against, that through my very Soul
2.91: A sword shall pierce, this is my favour'd lot,
2.93: Afflicted I may be, it seems, and blest;
2.94: I will not argue that, nor will repine.
2.95: But where delays he now? some great intent
2.96: Conceals him: when twelve years he scarce had seen,
2.97: I lost him, but so found, as well I saw
2.98: He could not lose himself; but went about
2.99: His Father's business; what he meant I mus'd,
2.100: Since understand; much more his absence now
2.101: Thus long to some great purpose he obscures.
2.102: But I to wait with patience am inur'd;
2.103: My heart hath been a store-house long of things
2.104: And sayings laid up, portending strange events.
2.105: Thus Mary pondering oft, and oft to mind
2.107: Since first her Salutation heard, with thoughts
2.109: The while her Son tracing the Desert wild,
2.110: Sole but with holiest Meditations fed,
2.111: Into himself descended, and at once
2.112: All his great work to come before him set;
2.113: How to begin, how to accomplish best
2.114: His end of being on Earth, and mission high:
2.115: For Satan with slye preface to return
2.116: Had left him vacant, and with speed was gon
2.117: Up to the middle Region of thick Air,
2.118: Where all his Potentates in Council sate;
2.119: There without sign of boast, or sign of joy,
2.120: Sollicitous and blank he thus began.
2.121: Princes, Heavens antient Sons, Aethereal Thrones,
2.122: Demonian Spirits now, from the Element
2.123: Each of his reign allotted, rightlier call'd,
2.124: Powers of Fire, Air, Water, and Earth beneath,
2.125: So may we hold our place and these mild seats
2.126: Without new trouble; such an Enemy
2.127: Is ris'n to invade us, who no less
2.128: Threat'ns then our expulsion down to Hell;
2.129: I, as I undertook, and with the vote
2.130: Consenting in full frequence was impowr'd,
2.131: Have found him, view'd him, tasted him, but find
2.132: Far other labour to be undergon
2.133: Then when I dealt with Adam first of Men,
2.134: Though Adam by his Wives allurement fell,
2.135: However to this Man inferior far,
2.136: If he be Man by Mothers side at least,
2.137: With more then humane gifts from Heav'n adorn'd,
2.139: And amplitude of mind to greatest Deeds.
2.140: Therefore I am return'd, lest confidence
2.141: Of my success with Eve in Paradise
2.143: Of like succeeding here; I summon all
2.144: Rather to be in readiness, with hand
2.145: Or counsel to assist; lest I who erst
2.146: Thought none my equal, now be over-match'd.
2.147: So spake the old Serpent doubting, and from all
2.148: With clamour was assur'd thir utmost aid
2.149: At his command; when from amidst them rose
2.150: Belial the dissolutest Spirit that fell
2.152: The fleshliest Incubus, and thus advis'd.
2.153: Set women in his eye and in his walk,
2.154: Among daughters of men the fairest found;
2.155: Many are in each Region passing fair
2.156: As the noon Skie; more like to Goddesses
2.157: Then Mortal Creatures, graceful and discreet,
2.158: Expert in amorous Arts, enchanting tongues
2.160: And sweet allay'd, yet terrible to approach,
2.161: Skill'd to retire, and in retiring draw
2.162: Hearts after them tangl'd in Amorous Nets.
2.163: Such object hath the power to soft'n and tame
2.164: Severest temper, smooth the rugged'st brow,
2.165: Enerve, and with voluptuous hope dissolve,
2.166: Draw out with credulous desire, and lead
2.167: At will the manliest, resolutest brest,
2.168: As the Magnetic hardest Iron draws.
2.169: Women, when nothing else, beguil'd the heart
2.170: Of wisest Solomon, and made him build,
2.171: And made him bow to the Gods of his Wives.
2.172: To whom quick answer Satan thus return'd
2.173: Belial in much uneven scale thou weigh'st
2.174: All others by thy self; because of old
2.175: Thou thy self doat'st on womankind, admiring
2.176: Thir shape, thir colour, and attractive grace,
2.177: None are, thou think'st, but taken with such toys.
2.178: Before the Flood thou with thy lusty Crew,
2.179: False titl'd Sons of God, roaming the Earth
2.180: Cast wanton eyes on the daughters of men,
2.181: And coupl'd with them, and begot a race.
2.182: Have we not seen, or by relation heard,
2.183: In Courts and Regal Chambers how thou lurk'st,
2.184: In Wood or Grove by mossie Fountain side,
2.185: In Valley or Green Meadow to way-lay
2.189: Too long, then lay'st thy scapes on names ador'd,
2.191: Satyr, or Fawn, or Silvan? But these haunts
2.192: Delight not all; among the Sons of Men,
2.193: How many have with a smile made small account
2.194: Of beauty and her lures, easily scorn'd
2.195: All her assaults, on worthier things intent?
2.197: A youth, how all the Beauties of the East
2.198: He slightly view'd, and slightly over-pass'd;
2.199: How hee sirnam'd of Africa dismiss'd
2.200: In his prime youth the fair Iberian maid.
2.201: For Solomon he liv'd at ease, and full
2.202: Of honour, wealth, high fare, aim'd not beyond
2.203: Higher design then to enjoy his State;
2.204: Thence to the bait of Women lay expos'd;
2.205: But he whom we attempt is wiser far
2.206: Then Solomon, of more exalted mind,
2.207: Made and set wholly on the accomplishment
2.208: Of greatest things; what woman will you find,
2.209: Though of this Age the wonder and the fame,
2.210: On whom his leisure will vouchsafe an eye
2.211: Of fond desire? or should she confident,
2.212: As sitting Queen ador'd on Beauties Throne,
2.213: Descend with all her winning charms begirt
2.214: To enamour, as the Zone of Venus once
2.215: Wrought that effect on Jove, so Fables tell;
2.216: How would one look from his Majestick brow
2.217: Seated as on the top of Vertues hill,
2.218: Discount'nance her despis'd, and put to rout
2.219: All her array; her female pride deject,
2.220: Or turn to reverent awe? for Beauty stands
2.221: In the admiration only of weak minds
2.222: Led captive; cease to admire, and all her Plumes
2.223: Fall flat and shrink into a trivial toy,
2.224: At every sudden slighting quite abasht:
2.225: Therefore with manlier objects we must try
2.226: His constancy, with such as have more shew
2.227: Of worth, of honour, glory, and popular praise;
2.228: Rocks whereon greatest men have oftest wreck'd;
2.229: Or that which only seems to satisfie
2.230: Lawful desires of Nature, not beyond;
2.231: And now I know he hungers where no food
2.232: Is to be found, in the wide Wilderness;
2.233: The rest commit to me, I shall let pass
2.234: No advantage, and his strength as oft assay.
2.235: He ceas'd, and heard thir grant in loud acclaim;
2.236: Then forthwith to him takes a chosen band
2.237: Of Spirits likest to himself in guile
2.238: To be at hand, and at his beck appear,
2.239: If cause were to unfold some active Scene
2.240: Of various persons each to know his part;
2.241: Then to the Desert takes with these his flight;
2.242: Where still from shade to shade the Son of God
2.243: After forty days fasting had remain'd,
2.244: Now hungring first, and to himself thus said.
2.245: Where will this end? four times ten days I have pass'd
2.246: Wandring this woody maze, and humane food
2.247: Nor tasted, nor had appetite: that Fast
2.248: To Vertue I impute not, or count part
2.249: Of what I suffer here; if Nature need not,
2.250: Or God support Nature without repast
2.251: Though needing, what praise is it to endure?
2.252: But now I feel I hunger, which declares,
2.253: Nature hath need of what she asks; yet God
2.254: Can satisfie that need some other way,
2.255: Though hunger still remain: so it remain
2.256: Without this bodies wasting, I content me,
2.257: And from the sting of Famine fear no harm,
2.258: Nor mind it, fed with better thoughts that feed
2.259: Mee hungring more to do my Fathers will.
2.260: It was the hour of night, when thus the Son
2.261: Commun'd in silent walk, then laid him down
2.263: Of Trees thick interwoven; there he slept,
2.264: And dream'd, as appetite is wont to dream,
2.265: Of meats and drinks, Natures refreshment sweet;
2.266: Him thought, he by the Brook of Cherith stood
2.267: And saw the Ravens with thir horny beaks
2.268: Food to Elijah bringing Even and Morn,
2.269: Though ravenous, taught to abstain from what they brought:
2.270: He saw the Prophet also how he fled
2.271: Into the Desert, and how there he slept
2.272: Under a Juniper; then how awakt,
2.273: He found his Supper on the coals prepar'd,
2.274: And by the Angel was bid rise and eat,
2.275: And eat the second time after repose,
2.276: The strength whereof suffic'd him forty days;
2.277: Sometimes that with Elijah he partook,
2.278: Or as a guest with Daniel at his pulse.
2.279: Thus wore out night, and now the Herald Lark
2.280: Left his ground-nest, high towring to descry
2.281: The morns approach, and greet her with his Song:
2.282: As lightly from his grassy Couch up rose
2.283: Our Saviour, and found all was but a dream,
2.284: Fasting he went to sleep, and fasting wak'd.
2.285: Up to a hill anon his steps he rear'd,
2.286: From whose high top to ken the prospect round,
2.287: If Cottage were in view, Sheep-cote or Herd;
2.288: But Cottage, Herd or Sheep-cote none he saw,
2.289: Only in a bottom saw a pleasant Grove,
2.290: With chaunt of tuneful Birds resounding loud;
2.291: Thither he bent his way, determin'd there
2.292: To rest at noon, and entr'd soon the shade
2.293: High rooft and walks beneath, and alleys brown
2.294: That open'd in the midst a woody Scene,
2.295: Natures own work it seem'd (Nature taught Art)
2.296: And to a Superstitious eye the haunt
2.297: Of Wood-Gods and Wood-Nymphs; he view'd it round,
2.298: When suddenly a man before him stood,
2.299: Not rustic as before, but seemlier clad,
2.300: As one in City, or Court, or Palace bred,
2.301: And with fair speech these words to him address'd.
2.302: With granted leave officious I return,
2.303: But much more wonder that the Son of God
2.304: In this wild solitude so long should bide
2.305: Of all things destitute, and well I know,
2.306: Not without hunger.  Others of some note,
2.307: As story tells, have trod this Wilderness;
2.308: The Fugitive Bond-woman with her Son
2.309: Out cast Nebaioth, yet found he relief
2.310: By a providing Angel; all the race
2.311: Of Israel here had famish'd, had not God
2.312: Rain'd from Heaven Manna, and that Prophet bold
2.313: Native of Thebes wandring here was fed
2.314: Twice by a voice inviting him to eat.
2.315: Of thee these forty days none hath regard,
2.316: Forty and more deserted here indeed.
2.317: To whom thus Jesus; what conclud'st thou hence?
2.318: They all had need, I as thou seest have none.
2.319: How hast thou hunger then?  Satan reply'd,
2.320: Tell me if Food were now before thee set,
2.321: Would'st thou not eat?  Thereafter as I like
2.322: The giver, answer'd Jesus. Why should that
2.323: Cause thy refusal, said the subtle Fiend,
2.324: Hast thou not right to all Created things,
2.325: Owe not all Creatures by just right to thee
2.326: Duty and Service, nor to stay till bid,
2.327: But tender all their power? nor mention I
2.328: Meats by the Law unclean, or offer'd first
2.329: To Idols, those young Daniel could refuse;
2.330: Nor proffer'd by an Enemy, though who
2.331: Would scruple that, with want opprest? behold
2.332: Nature asham'd, or better to express,
2.333: Troubl'd that thou should'st hunger, hath purvey'd
2.334: From all the Elements her choicest store
2.335: To treat thee as beseems, and as her Lord
2.336: With honour, only deign to sit and eat.
2.337: He spake no dream, for as his words had end,
2.338: Our Saviour lifting up his eyes beheld
2.339: In ample space under the broadest shade
2.340: A Table richly spred, in regal mode,
2.341: With dishes pil'd, and meats of noblest sort
2.342: And savour, Beasts of chase, or Fowl of game,
2.343: In pastry built, or from the spit, or boyl'd,
2.344: Gris-amber-steam'd; all Fish from Sea or Shore,
2.345: Freshet, or purling Brook, of shell or fin,
2.346: And exquisitest name, for which was drain'd
2.347: Pontus and Lucrine Bay, and Afric Coast.
2.348: Alas how simple, to these Cates compar'd,
2.349: Was that crude Apple that diverted Eve!
2.350: And at a stately side-board by the wine
2.351: That fragrant smell diffus'd, in order stood
2.352: Tall stripling youths rich clad, of fairer hew
2.353: Then Ganymed or Hylas, distant more
2.354: Under the Trees now trip'd, now solemn stood
2.355: Nymphs of Diana's train, and Naiades
2.356: With fruits and flowers from Amalthea's horn,
2.357: And Ladies of th' Hesperides, that seem'd
2.358: Fairer then feign'd of old, or fabl'd since
2.359: Of Fairy Damsels met in Forest wide
2.360: By Knights of Logres, or of Lyones,
2.362: And all the while Harmonious Airs were heard
2.363: Of chiming strings, or charming pipes and winds
2.364: Of gentlest gale Arabian odors fann'd
2.365: From their soft wings, and flora's earliest smells.
2.366: Such was the Splendour, and the Tempter now
2.368: What doubts the Son of God to sit and eat?
2.369: These are not Fruits forbidden, no interdict
2.370: Defends the touching of these viands pure,
2.371: Thir taste no knowledge works, at least of evil,
2.372: But life preserves, destroys life's enemy,
2.374: All these are Spirits of Air, and Woods, and Springs,
2.375: Thy gentle Ministers, who come to pay
2.376: Thee homage, and acknowledge thee thir Lord:
2.377: What doubt'st thou Son of God? sit down and eat.
2.378: To whom thus Jesus temperately reply'd:
2.379: Said'st thou not that to all things I had right?
2.380: And who withholds my pow'r that right to use?
2.381: Shall I receive by gift what of my own,
2.382: When and where likes me best, I can command?
2.383: I can at will, doubt not, as soon as thou,
2.384: Command a Table in this Wilderness,
2.385: And call swift flights of Angels ministrant
2.386: Array'd in Glory on my cup to attend:
2.387: Why shouldst thou then obtrude this diligence,
2.388: In vain, where no acceptance it can find,
2.389: And with my hunger what hast thou to do?
2.391: And count thy specious gifts no gifts but guiles.
2.392: To whom thus answer'd Satan malecontent:
2.393: That I have also power to give thou seest,
2.394: If of that pow'r I bring thee voluntary
2.395: What I might have bestow'd on whom I pleas'd.
2.396: And rather opportunely in this place
2.397: Chose to impart to thy apparent need,
2.398: Why shouldst thou not accept it? but I see
2.399: What I can do or offer is suspect;
2.400: Of these things others quickly will dispose
2.401: Whose pains have earn'd the far fet spoil.  With that
2.402: Both Table and Provision vanish'd quite
2.403: With sound of Harpies wings, and Talons heard;
2.404: Only the importune Tempter still remain'd,
2.405: And with these words his temptation pursu'd.
2.406: By hunger, that each other Creature tames,
2.407: Thou art not to be harm'd, therefore not mov'd;
2.409: For no allurement yields to appetite,
2.410: And all thy heart is set on high designs,
2.411: High actions: but wherewith to be atchiev'd?
2.412: Great acts require great means of enterprise,
2.413: Thou art unknown, unfriended, low of birth,
2.414: A Carpenter thy Father known, thy self
2.415: Bred up in poverty and streights at home;
2.416: Lost in a Desert here and hunger-bit:
2.417: Which way or from what hope dost thou aspire
2.419: What Followers, what Retinue canst thou gain,
2.420: Or at thy heels the dizzy Multitude,
2.421: Longer then thou canst feed them on thy cost?
2.422: Money brings Honour, Friends, Conquest, and Realms;
2.424: And his Son Herod plac'd on Juda's Throne;
2.425: (Thy throne) but gold that got him puissant friends?
2.426: Therefore, if at great things thou wouldst arrive,
2.427: Get Riches first, get Wealth, and Treasure heap,
2.428: Not difficult, if thou hearken to me,
2.429: Riches are mine, Fortune is in my hand;
2.430: They whom I favour thrive in wealth amain,
2.431: While Virtue, Valour, Wisdom sit in want.
2.432: To whom thus Jesus patiently reply'd;
2.433: Yet Wealth without these three is impotent,
2.434: To gain dominion or to keep it gain'd.
2.435: Witness those antient Empires of the Earth,
2.436: In highth of all thir flowing wealth dissolv'd:
2.437: But men endu'd with these have oft attain'd
2.438: In lowest poverty to highest deeds;
2.439: Gideon and Jephtha, and the Shepherd lad,
2.440: Whose off-spring on the Throne of Juda sat
2.441: So many Ages, and shall yet regain
2.442: That seat, and reign in Israel without end.
2.443: Among the Heathen, (for throughout the World
2.444: To me is not unknown what hath been done
2.445: Worthy of Memorial) canst thou not remember
2.447: For I esteem those names of men so poor
2.448: Who could do mighty things, and could contemn
2.449: Riches though offer'd from the hand of Kings.
2.450: And what in me seems wanting, but that I
2.451: May also in this poverty as soon
2.452: Accomplish what they did, perhaps and more?
2.453: Extol not Riches then, the toyl of Fools
2.454: The wise mans cumbrance if not snare, more apt
2.455: To slacken Virtue, and abate her edge,
2.456: Then prompt her to do aught may merit praise.
2.457: What if with like aversion I reject
2.458: Riches and Realms; yet not for that a Crown,
2.459: Golden in shew, is but a wreath of thorns,
2.460: Brings dangers, troubles, cares, and sleepless nights
2.461: To him who wears the Regal Diadem,
2.462: When on his shoulders each mans burden lies;
2.463: For therein stands the office of a King,
2.464: His Honour, Vertue, Merit and chief Praise,
2.465: That for the Publick all this weight he bears.
2.466: Yet he who reigns within himself, and rules
2.467: Passions, Desires, and Fears, is more a King;
2.468: Which every wise and vertuous man attains:
2.469: And who attains not, ill aspires to rule
2.470: Cities of men, or head-strong Multitudes,
2.472: Or lawless passions in him which he serves.
2.473: But to guide Nations in the way of truth
2.474: By saving Doctrine, and from errour lead
2.475: To know, and knowing worship God aright,
2.476: Is yet more Kingly, this attracts the Soul,
2.477: Governs the inner man, the nobler part,
2.478: That other o're the body only reigns,
2.479: And oft by force, which to a generous mind
2.480: So reigning can be no sincere delight.
2.481: Besides to give a Kingdom hath been thought
2.482: Greater and nobler done, and to lay down
2.483: Far more magnanimous, then to assume.
2.484: Riches are needless then, both for themselves,
2.485: And for thy reason why they should be sought,
2.486: To gain a Scepter, oftest better miss't.

3.1: So spake the Son of God, and Satan stood
3.2: A while as mute confounded what to say,
3.3: What to reply, confuted and convinc't
3.4: Of his weak arguing, and fallacious drift;
3.5: At length collecting all his Serpent wiles,
3.6: With soothing words renew'd, him thus accosts.
3.7: I see thou know'st what is of use to know,
3.8: What best to say canst say, to do canst do;
3.9: Thy actions to thy words accord, thy words
3.10: To thy large heart give utterance due, thy heart
3.11: Conteins of good, wise, just, the perfect shape.
3.12: Should Kings and Nations from thy mouth consult,
3.13: Thy Counsel would be as the Oracle
3.14: Urim and Thummin, those oraculous gems
3.15: On Aaron's breast: or tongue of Seers old
3.16: Infallible; or wert thou sought to deeds
3.17: That might require th' array of war, thy skill
3.18: Of conduct would be such, that all the world
3.19: Could not sustain thy Prowess, or subsist
3.20: In battel, though against thy few in arms.
3.21: These God-like Vertues wherefore dost thou hide?
3.22: Affecting private life, or more obscure
3.24: All Earth her wonder at thy acts, thy self
3.25: The fame and glory, glory the reward
3.26: That sole excites to high attempts the flame
3.27: Of most erected Spirits, most temper'd pure
3.28: Aetherial, who all pleasures else despise,
3.29: All treasures and all gain esteem as dross,
3.30: And dignities and powers all but the highest?
3.31: Thy years are ripe, and over-ripe, the Son
3.32: Of Macedonian Philip had e're these
3.33: Won Asia and the Throne of Cyrus held
3.34: At his dispose, young Scipio had brought down
3.35: The Carthaginian pride, young Pompey quell'd
3.36: The Pontic King and in triumph had rode.
3.37: Yet years, and to ripe years judgment mature,
3.38: Quench not the thirst of glory, but augment.
3.39: Great Julius, whom now all the world admires,
3.40: The more he grew in years, the more inflam'd
3.41: With glory, wept that he had liv'd so long
3.42: Inglorious: but thou yet art not too late.
3.43: To whom our Saviour calmly thus reply'd.
3.44: Thou neither dost perswade me to seek wealth
3.45: For Empires sake, nor Empire to affect
3.46: For glories sake by all thy argument.
3.47: For what is glory but the blaze of fame,
3.48: The peoples praise, if always praise unmixt?
3.49: And what the people but a herd confus'd,
3.51: Things vulgar, & well weigh'd, scarce worth the praise,
3.52: They praise and they admire they know not what;
3.53: And know not whom, but as one leads the other;
3.54: And what delight to be by such extoll'd,
3.55: To live upon thir tongues and be thir talk,
3.56: Of whom to be disprais'd were no small praise?
3.57: His lot who dares be singularly good.
3.58: Th' intelligent among them and the wise
3.59: Are few; and glory scarce of few is rais'd.
3.60: This is true glory and renown, when God
3.61: Looking on the Earth, with approbation marks
3.62: The just man, and divulges him through Heaven
3.63: To all his Angels, who with true applause
3.64: Recount his praises; thus he did to Job,
3.65: When to extend his fame through Heaven & Earth,
3.66: As thou to thy reproach mayst well remember,
3.67: He ask'd thee, hast thou seen my servant Job?
3.68: Famous he was in Heaven, on Earth less known;
3.69: Where glory is false glory, attributed
3.70: To things not glorious, men not worthy of fame.
3.71: They err who count it glorious to subdue
3.72: By Conquest far and wide, to over-run
3.73: Large Countries, and in field great Battels win,
3.74: Great Cities by assault: what do these Worthies,
3.75: But rob and spoil, burn, slaughter, and enslave
3.77: Made Captive, yet deserving freedom more
3.78: Then those thir Conquerours, who leave behind
3.79: Nothing but ruin wheresoe're they rove,
3.80: And all the flourishing works of peace destroy,
3.81: Then swell with pride, and must be titl'd Gods,
3.83: Worship't with Temple, Priest and Sacrifice;
3.84: One is the Son of Jove, of Mars the other,
3.85: Till Conquerour Death discover them scarce men,
3.86: Rowling in brutish vices, and deform'd,
3.87: Violent or shameful death thir due reward.
3.88: But if there be in glory aught of good,
3.89: It may by means far different be attain'd
3.91: By deeds of peace, by wisdom eminent,
3.92: By patience, temperance; I mention still
3.93: Him whom thy wrongs with Saintly patience born,
3.94: Made famous in a Land and times obscure;
3.95: Who names not now with honour patient Job?
3.97: By what he taught and suffer'd for so doing,
3.98: For truths sake suffering death unjust, lives now
3.99: Equal in fame to proudest Conquerours.
3.100: Yet if for fame and glory aught be done,
3.101: Aught suffer'd; if young African for fame
3.102: His wasted Country freed from Punic rage,
3.103: The deed becomes unprais'd, the man at least,
3.104: And loses, though but verbal, his reward.
3.105: Shall I seek glory then, as vain men seek
3.106: Oft not deserv'd?  I seek not mine, but his
3.107: Who sent me, and thereby witness whence I am.
3.108: To whom the Tempter murmuring thus reply'd.
3.109: Think not so slight of glory; therein least,
3.110: Resembling thy great Father: he seeks glory,
3.111: And for his glory all things made, all things
3.112: Orders and governs, nor content in Heaven
3.113: By all his Angels glorifi'd, requires
3.114: Glory from men, from all men good or bad,
3.115: Wise or unwise, no difference, no exemption;
3.116: Above all Sacrifice, or hallow'd gift
3.117: Glory he requires, and glory he receives
3.118: Promiscuous from all Nations, Jew, or Greek,
3.119: Or Barbarous, nor exception hath declar'd;
3.120: From us his foes pronounc't glory he exacts.
3.121: To whom our Saviour fervently reply'd.
3.122: And reason; since his word all things produc'd,
3.123: Though chiefly not for glory as prime end,
3.124: But to shew forth his goodness, and impart
3.125: His good communicable to every soul
3.126: Freely; of whom what could he less expect
3.127: Then glory and benediction, that is thanks,
3.129: From them who could return him nothing else,
3.130: And not returning that would likeliest render
3.133: For so much good, so much beneficence.
3.134: But why should man seek glory? who of his own
3.135: Hath nothing, and to whom nothing belongs
3.137: Who for so many benefits receiv'd
3.138: Turn'd recreant to God, ingrate and false,
3.139: And so of all true good himself despoil'd,
3.140: Yet, sacrilegious, to himself would take
3.141: That which to God alone of right belongs;
3.142: Yet so much bounty is in God, such grace,
3.143: That who advance his glory, not thir own,
3.144: Them he himself to glory will advance.
3.145: So spake the Son of God; and here again
3.146: Satan had not to answer, but stood struck
3.147: With guilt of his own sin, for he himself
3.148: Insatiable of glory had lost all,
3.149: Yet of another Plea bethought him soon.
3.150: Of glory as thou wilt, said he, so deem,
3.151: Worth or not worth the seeking, let it pass:
3.152: But to a Kingdom thou art born, ordain'd
3.153: To sit upon thy Father David's Throne;
3.154: By Mother's side thy Father, though thy right
3.155: Be now in powerful hands, that will not part
3.156: Easily from possession won with arms;
3.157: Judaea now and all the promis'd land
3.158: Reduc't a Province under Roman yoke,
3.159: Obeys Tiberius; nor is always rul'd
3.160: With temperate sway; oft have they violated
3.161: The Temple, oft the Law with foul affronts,
3.163: Antiochus: and think'st thou to regain
3.164: Thy right by sitting still or thus retiring?
3.165: So did not Machabeus: he indeed
3.166: Retir'd unto the Desert, but with arms;
3.167: And o're a mighty King so oft prevail'd,
3.168: That by strong hand his Family obtain'd,
3.169: Though Priests, the Crown, and David's Throne usurp'd,
3.170: With Modin and her Suburbs once content.
3.171: If Kingdom move thee not, let move thee Zeal,
3.172: And Duty; Zeal and Duty are not slow;
3.173: But on Occasions forelock watchful wait.
3.174: They themselves rather are occasion best,
3.175: Zeal of thy Fathers house, Duty to free
3.176: Thy Country from her Heathen servitude;
3.177: So shalt thou best fullfil, best verifie
3.178: The Prophets old, who sung thy endless raign,
3.179: The happier raign the sooner it begins,
3.180: Raign then; what canst thou better do the while?
3.181: To whom our saviour answer thus return'd.
3.182: All things are best fullfil'd in thir due time,
3.183: And time there is for all things, Truth hath said:
3.184: If of my raign Prophetic Writ hath told
3.185: That it shall never end, so when begin
3.186: The Father in his purpose hath decreed,
3.187: He in whose hand all times and seasons roul.
3.188: What if he hath decreed that I shall first
3.189: Be try'd in humble state, and things adverse,
3.191: Contempts, and scorns, and snares, and violence,
3.193: Without distrust or doubt, that he may know
3.194: What I can suffer, how obey? who best
3.195: Can suffer, best can do; best reign, who first
3.196: Well hath obey'd; just tryal e're I merit
3.197: My exaltation without change or end.
3.198: But what concerns it thee when I begin
3.199: My everlasting Kingdom, why art thou
3.201: Know'st thou not that my rising is thy fall,
3.202: And my promotion will be thy destruction?
3.203: To whom the Tempter inly rackt reply'd.
3.204: Let that come when it comes; all hope is lost
3.205: Of my reception into grace; what worse?
3.206: For where no hope is left, is left no fear;
3.207: If there be worse, the expectation more
3.208: Of worse torments me then the feeling can.
3.209: I would be at the worst; worst is my Port.
3.210: My harbour and my ultimate repose,
3.211: The end I would attain, my final good.
3.212: My error was my error, and my crime
3.213: My crime; whatever for it self condemn'd
3.214: And will alike be punish'd; whether thou
3.215: Raign or raign not; though to that gentle brow
3.216: Willingly I could flye, and hope thy raign,
3.217: From that placid aspect and meek regard,
3.218: Rather then aggravate my evil state,
3.219: Would stand between me and thy Fathers ire,
3.220: (Whose ire I dread more then the fire of Hell,)
3.221: A shelter and a kind of shading cool
3.223: If I then to the worst that can be hast,
3.224: Why move thy feet so slow to what is best,
3.225: Happiest both to thy self and all the world,
3.226: That thou who worthiest art should'st be thir King?
3.227: Perhaps thou linger'st in deep thoughts detain d
3.228: Of the enterprize so hazardous and high;
3.229: No wonder, for though in thee be united
3.230: What of perfection can in man be found,
3.231: Or human nature can receive, consider
3.232: Thy life hath yet been private, most part spent
3.233: At home, scarce view'd the Gallilean Towns
3.234: And once a year Jerusalem, few days
3.235: Short sojourn; and what thence could'st thou observe?
3.236: The world thou hast not seen, much less her glory,
3.237: Empires, and Monarchs, and thir radiant Courts
3.238: Best school of best experience, quickest in sight
3.239: In all things that to greatest actions lead.
3.240: The wisest, unexperienc't, will be ever
3.241: Timorous and loth, with novice modesty,
3.242: (As he who seeking Asses found a Kingdom)
3.244: But I will bring thee where thou soon shalt quit
3.245: Those rudiments, and see before thine eyes
3.246: The Monarchies of the Earth, thir pomp and state,
3.248: Thee, of thy self so apt, in regal Arts,
3.249: And regal Mysteries; that thou may'st know
3.250: How best their opposition to withstand.
3.251: With that (such power was giv'n him then) he took
3.252: The Son of God up to a Mountain high.
3.253: It was a Mountain at whose verdant feet
3.254: A spatious plain out strech't in circuit wide
3.255: Lay pleasant; from his side two rivers flow'd,
3.256: Th' one winding, the other strait and left between
3.257: Fair Champain with less rivers interveind,
3.258: Then meeting joyn'd thir tribute to the Sea:
3.259: Fertil of corn the glebe, of oyl and wine,
3.260: With herds the pastures throng'd, with flocks the hills,
3.261: Huge Cities and high towr'd, that well might seem
3.262: The seats of mightiest Monarchs, and so large
3.263: The Prospect was, that here and there was room
3.264: For barren desert fountainless and dry.
3.265: To this high mountain top the Tempter brought
3.266: Our Saviour, and new train of words began.
3.267: Well have we speeded, and o're hill and dale,
3.268: Forest and field, and flood, Temples and Towers
3.269: Cut shorter many a league; here thou behold'st
3.270: Assyria and her Empires antient bounds,
3.271: Araxes and the Caspian lake, thence on
3.272: As far as Indus East, Euphrates West,
3.273: And oft beyond; to South the Persian Bay,
3.275: Here Ninevee, of length within her wall
3.276: Several days journey, built by Ninus old,
3.277: Of that first golden Monarchy the seat,
3.278: And seat of Salmanassar, whose success
3.279: Israel in long captivity still mourns;
3.280: There Babylon the wonder of all tongues,
3.281: As antient, but rebuilt by him who twice
3.282: Judah and all thy Father David's house
3.283: Led captive, and Jerusalem laid waste,
3.284: Till Cyrus set them free; Persepolis
3.285: His City there thou seest, and Bactra there;
3.286: Ecbatana her structure vast there shews,
3.288: There Susa by Choaspes, amber stream,
3.289: The drink of none but Kings; of later fame
3.290: Built by Emathian, or by Parthian hands,
3.291: The great Seleucia, Nisibis, and there
3.293: Turning with easie eye thou may'st behold.
3.294: All these the Parthian, now some Ages past,
3.295: By great Arsaces led, who founded first
3.296: That Empire, under his dominion holds
3.297: From the luxurious Kings of Antioch won.
3.298: And just in time thou com'st to have a view
3.299: Of his great power; for now the Parthian King
3.300: In Ctesiphon hath gather'd all his Host
3.301: Against the Scythian, whose incursions wild
3.302: Have wasted Sogdiana; to her aid
3.303: He marches now in hast; see, though from far,
3.304: His thousands, in what martial equipage
3.305: They issue forth, Steel Bows, and Shafts their arms
3.306: Of equal dread in flight, or in pursuit;
3.307: All Horsemen, in which fight they most excel;
3.308: See how in warlike muster they appear,
3.309: In Rhombs and wedges, and half moons, and wings.
3.310: He look't and saw what numbers numberless
3.311: The City gates out powr'd, light armed Troops
3.312: In coats of Mail and military pride;
3.313: In Mail thir horses clad, yet fleet and strong,
3.314: Prauncing their riders bore, the flower and choice
3.315: Of many Provinces from bound to bound;
3.317: And Margiana to the Hyrcanian cliffs
3.318: Of Caucasus, and dark Iberian dales,
3.319: From Atropatia and the neighbouring plains
3.320: Of Adiabene, Media, and the South
3.322: He saw them in thir forms of battell rang'd,
3.323: How quick they wheel'd, and flying behind them shot
3.324: Sharp sleet of arrowie showers against the face
3.325: Of thir pursuers, and overcame by flight;
3.326: The field all iron cast a gleaming brown,
3.327: Nor wanted clouds of foot, nor on each horn,
3.328: Cuirassiers all in steel for standing fight;
3.329: Chariots or Elephants endorst with Towers
3.330: Of Archers, nor of labouring Pioners
3.331: A multitude with Spades and Axes arm'd
3.332: To lay hills plain, fell woods, or valleys fill,
3.333: Or where plain was raise hill, or over-lay
3.334: With bridges rivers proud, as with a yoke;
3.335: Mules after these, Camels and Dromedaries,
3.336: And Waggons fraught with Utensils of war.
3.337: Such forces met not, nor so wide a camp,
3.338: When Agrican with all his Northern powers
3.340: The City of Gallaphrone, from thence to win
3.341: The fairest of her Sex Angelica
3.342: His daughter, sought by many Prowest Knights,
3.343: Both Paynim, and the Peers of Charlemane.
3.344: Such and so numerous was thir Chivalrie;
3.345: At sight whereof the Fiend yet more presum'd,
3.346: And to our Saviour thus his words renew'd.
3.347: That thou may'st know I seek not to engage
3.348: Thy Vertue, and not every way secure
3.349: On no slight grounds thy safety; hear, and mark
3.350: To what end I have brought thee hither and shewn
3.351: All this fair sight; thy Kingdom though foretold
3.352: By Prophet or by Angel, unless thou
3.353: Endeavour, as thy Father David did,
3.354: Thou never shalt obtain; prediction still
3.355: In all things, and all men, supposes means,
3.356: Without means us'd, what it predicts revokes.
3.357: But say thou wer't possess'd of David's Throne
3.358: By free consent of all, none opposite,
3.359: Samaritan or Jew; how could'st thou hope
3.360: Long to enjoy it quiet and secure,
3.362: Roman and Parthian? therefore one of these
3.363: Thou must make sure thy own, the Parthian first
3.364: By my advice, as nearer and of late
3.365: Found able by invasion to annoy
3.366: Thy country, and captive lead away her Kings
3.368: Maugre the Roman: it shall be my task
3.369: To render thee the Parthian at dispose;
3.370: Chuse which thou wilt by conquest or by league
3.371: By him thou shalt regain, without him not,
3.372: That which alone can truly reinstall thee
3.373: In David's royal seat, his true Successour,
3.374: Deliverance of thy brethren, those ten Tribes
3.375: Whose off-spring in his Territory yet serve
3.376: In Habor, and among the Medes dispers't,
3.377: Ten Sons of Jacob, two of Joseph lost
3.378: Thus long from Israel; serving as of old
3.379: Thir Fathers in the land of Egypt serv'd,
3.380: This offer sets before thee to deliver.
3.381: These if from servitude thou shalt restore
3.382: To thir inheritance, then, nor till then,
3.383: Thou on the Throne of David in full glory,
3.384: From Egypt to Euphrates and beyond
3.385: Shalt raign, and Rome or Caesar not need fear.
3.386: To whom our Saviour answer'd thus unmov'd.
3.387: Much ostentation vain of fleshly arm,
3.388: And fragile arms, much instrument of war
3.389: Long in preparing, soon to nothing brought,
3.390: Before mine eyes thou hast set; and in my ear
3.391: Vented much policy, and projects deep
3.392: Of enemies, of aids, battels and leagues,
3.393: Plausible to the world, to me worth naught.
3.394: Means I must use thou say'st, prediction else
3.395: Will unpredict and fail me of the Throne:
3.396: My time I told thee, (and that time for thee
3.397: Were better farthest off) is not yet come;
3.398: When that comes think not thou to find me slack
3.399: On my part aught endeavouring, or to need
3.400: Thy politic maxims, or that cumbersome
3.401: Luggage of war there shewn me, argument
3.402: Of human weakness rather then of strength.
3.403: My brethren, as thou call'st them; those Ten Tribes
3.404: I must deliver, if I mean to raign
3.405: David's true heir, and his full Scepter sway
3.406: To just extent over all Israel's Sons;
3.407: But whence to thee this zeal, where was it then
3.408: For Israel or for David, or his Throne,
3.409: When thou stood'st up his Tempter to the pride
3.410: Of numbring Israel which cost the lives
3.411: Of threescore and ten thousand Israelites
3.412: By three days Pestilence? such was thy zeal
3.413: To Israel then, the same that now to me.
3.414: As for those captive Tribes, themselves were they
3.415: Who wrought their own captivity, fell off
3.416: From God to worship Calves, the Deities
3.417: Of Egypt, Baal next and Ashtaroth,
3.418: And all the Idolatries of Heathen round,
3.419: Besides thir other worse then heathenish crimes;
3.420: Nor in the land of their captivity
3.422: The God of their fore-fathers; but so dy'd
3.423: Impenitent, and left a race behind
3.425: From Gentils, but by Circumcision vain,
3.426: And God with Idols in their worship joyn'd.
3.427: Should I of these the liberty regard,
3.428: Who freed, as to their antient Patrimony,
3.430: Headlong would follow; and to thir Gods perhaps
3.431: Of Bethel and of Dan? no, let them serve
3.432: Thir enemies, who serve Idols with God.
3.433: Yet he at length, time to himself best known,
3.434: Remembring Abraham by some wond'rous call
3.435: May bring them back repentant and sincere,
3.436: And at their passing cleave the Assyrian flood,
3.437: While to their native land with joy they hast,
3.438: As the Red Sea and Jordan once he cleft,
3.439: When to the promis'd land thir Fathers pass'd;
3.440: To his due time and providence I leave them.
3.441: So spake Israel's true King, and to the Fiend
3.442: Made answer meet, that made void all his wiles.
3.443: So fares it when with truth falshood contends.

4.1: PERPLEX'D and troubl'd at his bad success
4.2: The Tempter stood, nor had what to reply,
4.3: Discover'd in his fraud, thrown from his hope,
4.4: So oft, and the perswasive Rhetoric
4.5: That sleek't his tongue, and won so much on Eve,
4.6: So little here, nay lost; but Eve was Eve,
4.7: This far his over-match, who self deceiv'd
4.8: And rash, before-hand had no better weigh'd
4.9: The strength he was to cope with, or his own:
4.10: But as a man who had been matchless held
4.11: In cunning, over-reach't where least he thought,
4.12: To salve his credit, and for very spight
4.13: Still will be tempting him who foyls him still,
4.14: And never cease, though to his shame the more;
4.15: Or as a swarm of flies in vintage time,
4.16: About the wine-press where sweet moust is powr'd,
4.17: Beat off; returns as oft with humming sound;
4.18: Or surging waves against a solid rock,
4.19: Though all to shivers dash't, the assault renew,
4.20: Vain battry, and in froth or bubbles end:
4.21: So Satan, whom repulse upon repulse
4.22: Met ever; and to shameful silence brought,
4.23: Yet gives not o're though desperate of success,
4.25: He brought our Saviour to the western side
4.26: Of that high mountain, whence he might behold
4.27: Another plain, long but in bredth not wide;
4.28: Wash'd by the Southern Sea, and on the North
4.29: To equal length back'd with a ridge of hills
4.30: That screen'd the fruits of the earth and seats of men
4.31: From cold Septentrion blasts, thence in the midst
4.32: Divided by a river, of whose banks
4.33: On each side an Imperial City stood,
4.34: With Towers and Temples proudly elevate
4.35: On seven small Hills, with Palaces adorn'd,
4.37: Statues and Trophees, and Triumphal Arcs,
4.38: Gardens and Groves presented to his eyes,
4.39: Above the highth of Mountains interpos'd.
4.40: By what strange Parallax or Optic skill
4.41: Of vision multiplyed through air or glass
4.42: Of Telescope, were curious to enquire:
4.43: And now the Tempter thus his silence broke.
4.44: The City which thou seest no other deem
4.45: Then great and glorious Rome, Queen of the Earth
4.46: So far renown'd, and with the spoils enricht
4.47: Of Nations; there the Capitol thou seest
4.48: Above the rest lifting his stately head
4.49: On the Tarpeian rock, her Cittadel
4.51: The Imperial Palace, compass huge, and high
4.52: The Structure, skill of noblest Architects,
4.54: Turrets and Terrases, and glittering Spires.
4.55: Many a fair Edifice besides, more like
4.56: Houses of Gods (so well I have dispos'd
4.57: My Aerie Microscope) thou may'st behold
4.58: Outside and inside both, pillars and roofs
4.59: Carv'd work, the hand of fam'd Artificers
4.60: In Cedar, Marble, Ivory or Gold.
4.61: Thence to the gates cast round thine eye, and see
4.62: What conflux issuing forth, or entring in,
4.64: Hasting or on return, in robes of State;
4.65: Lictors and rods the ensigns of thir power,
4.66: Legions and Cohorts, turmes of horse and wings:
4.67: Or Embassies from Regions far remote
4.68: In various habits on the Appian road,
4.69: Or on the Aemilian, some from farthest South,
4.70: Syene, and where the shadow both way falls,
4.71: Meroe, Nilotic Isle, and more to West,
4.72: The Realm of Bocchus to the Black-moor Sea;
4.73: From the Asian Kings and Parthian among these,
4.76: Dusk faces with white silken Turbants wreath'd:
4.77: From Gallia, Gades, and the Brittish West,
4.78: Germans and Scythians, and Sarmatians North
4.79: Beyond Danubius to the Tauric Pool.
4.80: All Nations now to Rome obedience pay,
4.81: To Rome's great Emperour, whose wide domain
4.82: In ample Territory, wealth and power,
4.83: Civility of Manners, Arts, and Arms,
4.84: And long Renown thou justly may'st prefer
4.85: Before the Parthian; these two Thrones except,
4.86: The rest are barbarous, and scarce worth the sight,
4.87: Shar'd among petty Kings too far remov'd;
4.88: These having shewn thee, I have shewn thee all
4.89: The Kingdoms of the world, and all thir glory.
4.90: This Emperour hath no Son, and now is old,
4.91: Old, and lascivious, and from Rome retir'd
4.92: To Capreae an Island small but strong
4.93: On the Campanian shore, with purpose there
4.94: His horrid lusts in private to enjoy,
4.96: All publick cares, and yet of him suspicious,
4.97: Hated of all, and hating; with what ease
4.98: Indu'd with Regal Vertues as thou art,
4.100: Might'st thou expel this monster from his Throne
4.101: Now made a stye, and in his place ascending
4.102: A victor people free from servile yoke?
4.103: And with my help thou may'st; to me the power
4.104: Is given, and by that right I give it thee.
4.105: Aim therefore at no less then all the world,
4.106: Aim at the highest, without the highest attain'd
4.107: Will be for thee no sitting, or not long
4.108: On Davids Throne, be propheci'd what will,
4.109: To whom the Son of God unmov'd reply'd.
4.110: Nor doth this grandeur and majestic show
4.112: More then of arms before, allure mine eye,
4.113: Much less my mind; though thou should'st add to tell
4.114: Thir sumptuous gluttonies, and gorgeous feasts
4.115: On Cittron tables or Atlantic stone;
4.116: (For I have also heard, perhaps have read)
4.117: Their wines of Setia, Cales, and Falerne,
4.118: Chios and Creet, and how they quaff in Gold,
4.119: Crystal and Myrrhine cups imboss'd with Gems
4.120: And studs of Pearl, to me should'st tell who thirst
4.121: And hunger still: then Embassies thou shew'st
4.122: From Nations far and nigh; what honour that,
4.123: But tedious wast of time to sit and hear
4.124: So many hollow complements and lies,
4.125: Outlandish flatteries? then proceed'st to talk
4.126: Of the Emperour, how easily subdu'd,
4.127: How gloriously; I shall, thou say'st, expel
4.128: A brutish monster: what if I withal
4.129: Expel a Devil who first made him such?
4.130: Let his tormenter Conscience find him out,
4.131: For him I was not sent, nor yet to free
4.132: That people victor once, now vile and base,
4.133: Deservedly made vassal, who once just,
4.134: Frugal, and mild, and temperate, conquer'd well,
4.135: But govern ill the Nations under yoke,
4.137: By lust and rapine; first ambitious grown
4.139: Then cruel, by thir sports to blood enur'd
4.140: Of fighting beasts, and men to beasts expos'd,
4.141: Luxurious by thir wealth, and greedier still,
4.142: And from the daily Scene effeminate.
4.143: What wise and valiant man would seek to free
4.144: These thus degenerate, by themselves enslav'd,
4.145: Or could of inward slaves make outward free?
4.146: Know therefore when my season comes to sit
4.147: On David's Throne, it shall be like a tree
4.148: Spreading and over-shadowing all the Earth,
4.149: Or as a stone that shall to pieces dash
4.150: All Monarchies besides throughout the world,
4.151: And of my Kingdom there shall be no end:
4.152: Means there shall be to this, but what the means,
4.153: Is not for thee to know, nor me to tell.
4.154: To whom the Tempter impudent repli'd.
4.155: I see all offers made by me how slight
4.156: Thou valu'st, because offer'd, and reject'st:
4.157: Nothing will please the difficult and nice,
4.158: Or nothing more then still to contradict:
4.159: On the other side know also thou, that I
4.160: On what I offer set as high esteem,
4.161: Nor what I part with mean to give for naught;
4.162: All these which in a moment thou behold'st,
4.163: The Kingdoms of the world to thee I give;
4.164: For giv'n to me, I give to whom I please,
4.165: No trifle; yet with this reserve, not else,
4.166: On this condition, if thou wilt fall down,
4.167: And worship me as thy superior Lord,
4.168: Easily done, and hold them all of me;
4.169: For what can less so great a gift deserve?
4.170: Whom thus our Saviour answer'd with disdain.
4.171: I never lik'd thy talk, thy offers less,
4.172: Now both abhor, since thou hast dar'd to utter
4.174: But I endure the time, till which expir'd,
4.175: Thou hast permission on me.  It is written
4.176: The first of all Commandments, Thou shalt worship
4.177: The Lord thy God, and only him shalt serve;
4.178: And dar'st thou to the Son of God propound
4.179: To worship thee accurst, now more accurst
4.180: For this attempt bolder then that on Eve,
4.181: And more blasphemous? which expect to rue.
4.182: The Kingdoms of the world to thee were giv'n,
4.183: Permitted rather, and by thee usurp't,
4.184: Other donation none thou canst produce:
4.185: If given, by whom but by the King of Kings,
4.186: God over all supreme? if giv'n to thee,
4.187: By thee how fairly is the Giver now
4.188: Repaid? But gratitude in thee is lost
4.189: Long since.  Wert thou so void of fear or shame,
4.190: As offer them to me the Son of God,
4.191: To me my own, on such abhorred pact,
4.192: That I fall down and worship thee as God?
4.193: Get thee behind me; plain thou now appear'st
4.194: That Evil one, Satan for ever damn'd.
4.195: To whom the Fiend with fear abasht reply'd.
4.196: Be not so sore offended, Son of God;
4.197: Though Sons of God both Angels are and Men,
4.198: If I to try whether in higher sort
4.199: Then these thou bear'st that title, have propos'd
4.200: What both from Men and Angels I receive,
4.201: Tetrarchs of fire, air, flood, and on the earth
4.202: Nations besides from all the quarter'd winds,
4.203: God of this world invok't and world beneath;
4.204: Who then thou art, whose coming is foretold
4.205: To me so fatal, me it most concerns.
4.206: The tryal hath indamag'd thee no way,
4.207: Rather more honour left and more esteem;
4.208: Me naught advantag'd, missing what I aim'd.
4.209: Therefore let pass, as they are transitory,
4.210: The Kingdoms of this world; I shall no more
4.211: Advise thee, gain them as thou canst, or not.
4.212: And thou thy self seem'st otherwise inclin'd
4.213: Then to a worldly Crown, addicted more
4.215: As by that early action may be judg'd,
4.216: When slipping from thy Mothers eye thou went'st
4.217: Alone into the Temple; there was found
4.219: On points and questions fitting Moses Chair,
4.220: Teaching not taught; the childhood shews the man,
4.221: As morning shews the day.  Be famous then
4.222: By wisdom; as thy Empire must extend,
4.223: So let extend thy mind o're all the world,
4.224: In knowledge, all things in it comprehend,
4.225: All knowledge is not couch't in Moses Law,
4.226: The Pentateuch or what the Prophets wrote,
4.227: The Gentiles also know, and write, and teach
4.228: To admiration, led by Natures light;
4.229: And with the Gentiles much thou must converse,
4.230: Ruling them by perswasion as thou mean'st,
4.231: Without thir learning how wilt thou with them,
4.232: Or they with thee hold conversation meet?
4.233: How wilt thou reason with them, how refute
4.235: Error by his own arms is best evinc't.
4.236: Look once more e're we leave this specular Mount
4.237: Westward, much nearer by Southwest, behold
4.238: Where on the Aegean shore a City stands
4.239: Built nobly, pure the air, and light the soil,
4.240: Athens the eye of Greece, Mother of Arts
4.241: And Eloquence, native to famous wits
4.242: Or hospitable, in her sweet recess,
4.243: City or Suburban, studious walks and shades;
4.244: See there the Olive Grove of Academe,
4.245: Plato's retirement, where the Attic Bird
4.246: Trills her thick-warbl'd notes the summer long,
4.247: There flowrie hill Hymettus with the sound
4.248: Of Bees industrious murmur oft invites
4.249: To studious musing; there Ilissus rouls
4.250: His whispering stream; within the walls then view
4.251: The schools of antient Sages; his who bred
4.252: Great Alexander to subdue the world,
4.253: Lyceum there, and painted Stoa next:
4.254: There thou shalt hear and learn the secret power
4.255: Of harmony in tones and numbers hit
4.256: By voice or hand, and various-measur'd verse,
4.257: Aeolian charms and Dorian Lyric Odes,
4.258: And his who gave them breath, but higher sung,
4.260: Whose Poem Phoebus challeng'd for his own.
4.261: Thence what the lofty grave Tragoedians taught
4.262: In Chorus or Iambic, teachers best
4.263: Of moral prudence, with delight receiv'd
4.264: In brief sententious precepts, while they treat
4.265: Of fate, and chance, and change in human life;
4.266: High actions, and high passions best describing;
4.267: Thence to the famous Orators repair,
4.269: Wielded at will that fierce Democratie,
4.270: Shook the Arsenal and fulmin'd over Greece,
4.272: To sage Philosophy next lend thine ear,
4.273: From Heaven descended to the low-rooft house
4.274: Of Socrates, see there his Tenement,
4.275: Whom well inspir'd the Oracle pronounc'd
4.276: Wisest of men; from whose mouth issu'd forth
4.277: Mellifluous streams that water'd all the schools
4.278: Of Academics old and new, with those
4.281: These here revolve, or, as thou lik'st, at home,
4.282: Till time mature thee to a Kingdom's waight;
4.283: These rules will render thee a King compleat
4.284: Within thy self, much more with Empire joyn'd.
4.285: To whom our Saviour sagely thus repli'd.
4.286: Think not but that I know these things, or think
4.287: I know them not; not therefore am I short
4.288: Of knowing what I aught: he who receives
4.289: Light from above, from the fountain of light,
4.290: No other doctrine needs, though granted true;
4.291: But these are false, or little else but dreams,
4.292: Conjectures, fancies, built on nothing firm.
4.293: The first and wisest of them all profess'd
4.294: To know this only, that he nothing knew;
4.295: The next to fabling fell and smooth conceits,
4.296: A third sort doubted all things, though plain sence;
4.298: But vertue joyn'd with riches and long life,
4.299: In corporal pleasure he, and careless ease,
4.300: The Stoic last in Philosophic pride,
4.301: By him call'd vertue; and his vertuous man,
4.302: Wise, perfect in himself, and all possessing
4.303: Equal to God, oft shames not to prefer,
4.304: As fearing God nor man, contemning all
4.305: Wealth, pleasure, pain or torment, death and life,
4.306: Which when he lists, he leaves, or boasts he can,
4.307: For all his tedious talk is but vain boast,
4.308: Or subtle shifts conviction to evade.
4.309: Alas what can they teach, and not mislead;
4.310: Ignorant of themselves, of God much more,
4.311: And how the world began, and how man fell
4.312: Degraded by himself, on grace depending?
4.313: Much of the Soul they talk, but all awrie,
4.314: And in themselves seek vertue, and to themselves
4.315: All glory arrogate, to God give none,
4.316: Rather accuse him under usual names,
4.317: Fortune and Fate, as one regardless quite
4.318: Of mortal things.  Who therefore seeks in these
4.319: True wisdom, finds her not, or by delusion
4.320: Far worse, her false resemblance only meets,
4.321: An empty cloud.  However many books
4.322: Wise men have said are wearisom; who reads
4.323: Incessantly, and to his reading brings not
4.324: A spirit and judgment equal or superior,
4.325: (And what he brings, what needs he elsewhere seek)
4.327: Deep verst in books and shallow in himself;
4.329: And trifles for choice matters, worth a spunge;
4.330: As Children gathering pibles on the shore.
4.331: Or if I would delight my private hours
4.332: With Music or with Poem, where so soon
4.333: As in our native Language can I find
4.334: That solace?  All our Law and Story strew'd
4.335: With Hymns, our Psalms with artful terms inscrib'd,
4.336: Our Hebrew Songs and Harps in Babylon,
4.337: That pleas'd so well our Victors ear, declare
4.338: That rather Greece from us these Arts deriv'd;
4.339: Ill imitated, while they loudest sing
4.340: The vices of thir Deities, and thir own
4.341: In Fable, Hymn, or Song, so personating
4.342: Thir Gods ridiculous, and themselves past shame.
4.343: Remove their swelling Epithetes thick laid
4.344: As varnish on a Harlots cheek, the rest,
4.345: Thin sown with aught of profit or delight,
4.346: Will far be found unworthy to compare
4.347: With Sion's songs, to all true tasts excelling,
4.348: Where God is prais'd aright, and Godlike men,
4.349: The Holiest of Holies, and his Saints;
4.350: Such are from God inspir'd, not such from thee;
