4.351: Unless where moral vertue is express't
4.352: By light of Nature not in all quite lost.
4.353: Thir Orators thou then extoll'st, as those
4.354: The top of Eloquence, Statists indeed,
4.355: And lovers of thir Country, as may seem;
4.356: But herein to our Prophets far beneath,
4.357: As men divinely taught, and better teaching
4.358: The solid rules of Civil Government
4.360: Then all the Oratory of Greece and Rome.
4.361: In them is plainest taught, and easiest learnt,
4.362: What makes a Nation happy, and keeps it so,
4.363: What ruins Kingdoms, and lays Cities flat;
4.364: These only with our Law best form a King.
4.365: So spake the Son of God; but Satan now
4.366: Quite at a loss, for all his darts were spent,
4.367: Thus to our Saviour with stern brow reply'd.
4.368: Since neither wealth, nor honour, arms nor arts,
4.369: Kingdom nor Empire pleases thee, nor aught
4.370: By me propos'd in life contemplative,
4.371: Or active, tended on by glory, or fame,
4.372: What dost thou in this World? the Wilderness
4.373: For thee is fittest place, I found thee there,
4.374: And thither will return thee, yet remember
4.375: What I foretell thee, soon thou shalt have cause
4.376: To wish thou never hadst rejected thus
4.377: Nicely or cautiously my offer'd aid,
4.378: Which would have set thee in short time with ease
4.379: On David's Throne; or Throne of all the world,
4.380: Now at full age, fulness of time, thy season,
4.381: When Prophesies of thee are best fullfill'd.
4.382: Now contrary, if I read aught in Heaven,
4.383: Or Heav'n write aught of Fate, by what the Stars
4.385: In thir conjunction met, give me to spell,
4.388: Violence and stripes, and lastly cruel death,
4.389: A Kingdom they portend thee, but what Kingdom,
4.390: Real or Allegoric I discern not,
4.391: Nor when, eternal sure, as without end,
4.392: Without beginning; for no date prefixt
4.393: Directs me in the Starry Rubric set.
4.394: So saying he took (for still he knew his power
4.395: Not yet expir'd) and to the Wilderness
4.396: Brought back the Son of God, and left him there,
4.397: Feigning to disappear.  Darkness now rose,
4.398: As day-light sunk, and brought in lowring night
4.400: Privation meer of light and absent day.
4.401: Our Saviour meek and with untroubl'd mind
4.402: After his aerie jaunt, though hurried sore,
4.403: Hungry and cold betook him to his rest,
4.404: Wherever, under some concourse of shades
4.405: Whose branching arms thick intertwind might shield
4.406: From dews and damps of night his shelter'd head,
4.407: But shelter'd slept in vain, for at his head
4.408: The Tempter watch'd, and soon with ugly dreams
4.409: Disturb'd his sleep; and either Tropic now
4.410: 'Gan thunder, and both ends of Heav'n, the Clouds
4.411: From many a horrid rift abortive pour'd
4.412: Fierce rain with lightning mixt, water with fire
4.413: In ruine reconcil'd: nor slept the winds
4.414: Within thir stony caves, but rush'd abroad
4.415: From the four hinges of the world, and fell
4.416: On the vext Wilderness, whose tallest Pines,
4.417: Though rooted deep as high, and sturdiest Oaks
4.418: Bow'd thir Stiff necks, loaden with stormy blasts,
4.419: Or torn up sheer: ill wast thou shrouded then,
4.420: O patient Son of God, yet only stoodst
4.421: Unshaken; nor yet staid the terror there,
4.422: Infernal Ghosts, and Hellish Furies, round
4.423: Environ'd thee, some howl'd, some yell'd, some shriek'd,
4.424: Some bent at thee thir fiery darts, while thou
4.425: Sat'st unappall'd in calm and sinless peace.
4.426: Thus pass'd the night so foul till morning fair
4.427: Came forth with Pilgrim steps in amice gray;
4.428: Who with her radiant finger still'd the roar
4.429: Of thunder, chas'd the clouds, and laid the winds,
4.430: And grisly Spectres, which the Fiend had rais'd
4.431: To tempt the Son of God with terrors dire.
4.432: And now the Sun with more effectual beams
4.433: Had chear'd the face of Earth, and dry'd the wet
4.434: From drooping plant, or dropping tree; the birds
4.435: Who all things now behold more fresh and green,
4.436: After a night of storm so ruinous,
4.437: Clear'd up their choicest notes in bush and spray
4.438: To gratulate the sweet return of morn;
4.439: Nor yet amidst this joy and brightest morn
4.440: Was absent, after all his mischief done,
4.441: The Prince of darkness, glad would also seem
4.442: Of this fair change, and to our Saviour came,
4.443: Yet with no new device, they all were spent,
4.444: Rather by this his last affront resolv'd,
4.445: Desperate of better course, to vent his rage,
4.446: And mad despight to be so oft repell'd.
4.447: Him walking on a Sunny hill he found,
4.448: Back'd on the North and West by a thick wood,
4.449: Out of the wood he starts in wonted shape;
4.450: And in a careless mood thus to him said.
4.451: Fair morning yet betides thee Son of God,
4.452: After a dismal night; I heard the rack
4.453: As Earth and Skie would mingle; but my self
4.454: Was distant; and these flaws, though mortals fear them
4.455: As dangerous to the pillard frame of Heaven,
4.456: Or to the Earths dark basis underneath,
4.457: Are to the main as inconsiderable,
4.458: And harmless, if not wholsom, as a sneeze
4.459: To mans less universe, and soon are gone;
4.460: Yet as being oft times noxious where they light
4.461: On man, beast, plant, wastful and turbulent,
4.462: Like turbulencies in the affairs of men,
4.463: Over whose heads they rore, and seem to point,
4.464: They oft fore-signifie and threaten ill:
4.465: This Tempest at this Desert most was bent;
4.466: Of men at thee, for only thou here dwell'st.
4.467: Did I not tell thee, if thou didst reject
4.468: The perfet season offer'd with my aid
4.469: To win thy destin'd seat, but wilt prolong
4.470: All to the push of Fate, persue thy way
4.471: Of gaining David's Throne no man knows when,
4.472: For both the when and how is no where told,
4.473: Thou shalt be what thou art ordain'd, no doubt;
4.474: For Angels have proclaim'd it, but concealing
4.475: The time and means: each act is rightliest done,
4.476: Not when it must, but when it may be best.
4.477: If thou observe not this, be sure to find,
4.478: What I foretold thee, many a hard assay
4.479: Of dangers, and adversities and pains,
4.480: E're thou of Israel's Scepter get fast hold;
4.481: Whereof this ominous night that clos'd thee round,
4.483: May warn thee, as a sure fore-going sign.
4.484: So talk'd he, while the Son of God went on
4.485: And staid not, but in brief him answer'd thus.
4.486: Mee worse then wet thou find'st not; other harm
4.487: Those terrors which thou speak'st of did me none;
4.488: I never fear'd they could, though noising loud
4.489: And threatning nigh; what they can do as signs
4.490: Betok'ning, or ill boding, I contemn
4.491: As false portents, not sent from God, but thee;
4.492: Who knowing I shall raign past thy preventing.
4.493: Obtrud'st thy offer'd aid, that I accepting
4.494: At least might seem to hold all power of thee,
4.495: Ambitious spirit, and wouldst be thought my God,
4.496: And storm'st refus'd, thinking to terrifie
4.497: Mee to thy will; desist, thou art discern'd
4.498: And toil'st in vain, nor me in vain molest.
4.499: To whom the Fiend now swoln with rage reply'd:
4.500: Then hear, O Son of David, Virgin-born;
4.501: For Son of God to me is yet in doubt,
4.502: Of the Messiah I have heard foretold
4.503: By all the Prophets; of thy birth at length
4.504: Announc't by Gabriel with the first I knew,
4.505: And of the Angelic Song in Bethlehem field,
4.506: On thy birth-night, that sung thee Saviour born.
4.507: From that time seldom have I ceas'd to eye
4.508: Thy infancy, thy childhood, and thy youth,
4.509: Thy manhood last, though yet in private bred;
4.510: Till at the Ford of Jordan whither all
4.511: Flock'd to the Baptist, I among the rest,
4.512: Though not to be Baptiz'd, by voice from Heav'n
4.513: Heard thee pronounc'd the Son of God belov'd.
4.514: Thenceforth I thought thee worth my nearer view
4.515: And narrower Scrutiny, that I might learn
4.516: In what degree or meaning thou art call'd
4.517: The Son of God, which bears no single sence;
4.518: The Son of God I also am, or was,
4.519: And if I was, I am; relation stands;
4.520: All men are Sons of God; yet thee I thought
4.521: In some respect far higher so declar'd.
4.522: Therefore I watch'd thy footsteps from that hour,
4.523: And follow'd thee still on to this wast wild;
4.524: Where by all best conjectures I collect
4.525: Thou art to be my fatal enemy.
4.526: Good reason then, if I before-hand seek
4.528: And what he is; his wisdom, power, intent,
4.529: By parl, or composition, truce, or league
4.530: To win him, or win from him what I can.
4.531: And opportunity I here have had
4.532: To try thee, sift thee, and confess have found thee
4.533: Proof against all temptation as a rock
4.534: Of Adamant, and as a Center, firm
4.535: To the utmost of meer man both wise and good,
4.536: Not more; for Honours, Riches, Kingdoms, Glory
4.537: Have been before contemn'd, and may agen:
4.538: Therefore to know what more thou art then man,
4.539: Worth naming Son of God by voice from Heav'n,
4.540: Another method I must now begin.
4.541: So saying he caught him up, and without wing
4.542: Of Hippogrif bore through the Air sublime
4.543: Over the Wilderness and o're the Plain;
4.545: The holy City lifted high her Towers,
4.546: And higher yet the glorious Temple rear'd
4.547: Her pile, far off appearing like a Mount
4.548: Of Alabaster, top't with golden Spires:
4.549: There on the highest Pinacle he set
4.550: The Son of God; and added thus in scorn:
4.551: There stand, if thou wilt stand; to stand upright
4.552: Will ask thee skill; I to thy Fathers house
4.553: Have brought thee, and highest plac't, highest is best,
4.554: Now shew thy Progeny; if not to stand,
4.555: Cast thy self down; safely if Son of God:
4.556: For it is written, He will give command
4.557: Concerning thee to his Angels, in thir hands
4.558: They shall up lift thee, lest at any time
4.559: Thou chance to dash thy foot against a stone.
4.560: To whom thus Jesus: also it is written,
4.561: Tempt not the Lord thy God, he said and stood.
4.562: But Satan smitten with amazement fell
4.563: As when Earths Son Antaeus (to compare
4.564: Small things with greatest) in Irassa strove
4.565: With Joves Alcides and oft foil'd still rose,
4.566: Receiving from his mother Earth new strength,
4.567: Fresh from his fall, and fiercer grapple joyn'd,
4.568: Throttl'd at length in the Air, expir'd and fell;
4.569: So after many a foil the Tempter proud,
4.570: Renewing fresh assaults, amidst his pride
4.571: Fell whence he stood to see his Victor fall.
4.572: And as that Theban Monster that propos'd
4.573: Her riddle, and him, who solv'd it not, devour'd;
4.574: That once found out and solv'd, for grief and spight
4.575: Cast her self headlong from th' Ismenian steep,
4.576: So strook with dread and anguish fell the Fiend,
4.577: And to his crew, that sat consulting, brought
4.578: Joyless triumphals of his hop't success,
4.580: Who durst so proudly tempt the Son of God.
4.581: So Satan fell and strait a fiery Globe
4.582: Of Angels on full sail of wing flew nigh,
4.583: Who on their plumy Vans receiv'd him soft
4.584: From his uneasie station, and upbore
4.585: As on a floating couch through the blithe Air,
4.586: Then in a flowry valley set him down
4.587: On a green bank, and set before him spred
4.588: A table of Celestial Food, Divine,
4.589: Ambrosial, Fruits fetcht from the tree of life,
4.590: And from the fount of life Ambrosial drink,
4.591: That soon refresh'd him wearied, and repair'd
4.592: What hunger, if aught hunger had impair'd,
4.593: Or thirst, and as he fed, Angelic Quires
4.594: Sung Heavenly Anthems of his victory
4.595: Over temptation, and the Tempter proud.
4.596: True Image of the Father whether thron'd
4.597: In the bosom of bliss, and light of light
4.598: Conceiving, or remote from Heaven, enshrin'd
4.599: In fleshly Tabernacle, and human form,
4.601: Habit, or state, or motion, still expressing
4.602: The Son of God, with Godlike force indu'd
4.603: Against th' Attempter of thy Fathers Throne,
4.604: And Thief of Paradise; him long of old
4.605: Thou didst debel, and down from Heav'n cast
4.606: With all his Army, now thou hast aveng'd
4.610: He never more henceforth will dare set foot
4.611: In Paradise to tempt; his snares are broke:
4.612: For though that seat of earthly bliss be fail'd,
4.613: A fairer Paradise is founded now
4.614: For Adam and his chosen Sons, whom thou
4.615: A Saviour art come down to re-install.
4.616: Where they shall dwell secure, when time shall be
4.617: Of Tempter and Temptation without fear.
4.618: But thou, Infernal Serpent, shalt not long
4.619: Rule in the Clouds; like an Autumnal Star
4.620: Or Lightning thou shalt fall from Heav'n trod down
4.621: Under his feet: for proof, e're this thou feel'st
4.622: Thy wound, yet not thy last and deadliest wound
4.623: By this repulse receiv'd, and hold'st in Hell
4.624: No triumph; in all her gates Abaddon rues
4.625: Thy bold attempt; hereafter learn with awe
4.626: To dread the Son of God: he all unarm'd
4.627: Shall chase thee with the terror of his voice
4.628: From  thy Demoniac holds, possession foul,
4.629: Thee and thy Legions, yelling they shall flye,
4.630: And beg to hide them in a herd of Swine,
4.631: Lest he command them down into the deep
4.632: Bound, and to torment sent before thir time.
4.633: Hail Son of the most High, heir of both worlds,
4.634: Queller of Satan, on thy glorious work
4.635: Now enter, and begin to save mankind.
4.636: Thus they the Son of God our Saviour meek
4.637: Sung Victor, and from Heavenly Feast refresht
4.638: Brought on his way with joy; hee unobserv'd
4.639: Home to his Mothers house private return'd.

1.1: Sam:  A little onward lend thy guiding hand
1.2: To these dark steps, a little further on;
1.3: For yonder bank hath choice of Sun or shade,
1.4: There I am wont to sit, when any chance
1.5: Relieves me from my task of servile toyl,
1.6: Daily in the common Prison else enjoyn'd me,
1.7: Where I a Prisoner chain'd, scarce freely draw
1.8: The air imprison'd also, close and damp,
1.9: Unwholsom draught: but here I feel amends,
1.10: The breath of Heav'n fresh-blowing, pure and sweet,
1.11: With day-spring born; here leave me to respire.
1.12: This day a solemn Feast the people hold
1.13: To Dagon thir Sea-Idol, and forbid
1.15: Thir Superstition yields me; hence with leave
1.16: Retiring from the popular noise, I seek
1.17: This unfrequented place to find some ease,
1.18: Ease to the body some, none to the mind
1.19: From restless thoughts, that like a deadly swarm
1.20: Of Hornets arm'd, no sooner found alone,
1.21: But rush upon me thronging, and present
1.22: Times past, what once I was, and what am now.
1.23: O wherefore was my birth from Heaven foretold
1.24: Twice by an Angel, who at last in sight
1.25: Of both my Parents all in flames ascended
1.26: From off the Altar, where an Off'ring burn'd,
1.27: As in a fiery column charioting
1.28: His Godlike presence, and from some great act
1.29: Or benefit reveal'd to Abraham's race?
1.30: Why was my breeding order'd and prescrib'd
1.31: As of a person separate to God,
1.32: Design'd for great exploits; if I must dye
1.33: Betray'd, Captiv'd, and both my Eyes put out,
1.34: Made of my Enemies the scorn and gaze;
1.35: To grind in Brazen Fetters under task
1.36: With this Heav'n-gifted strength? O glorious strength
1.37: Put to the labour of a Beast, debas't
1.38: Lower then bondslave! Promise was that I
1.39: Should Israel from Philistian yoke deliver;
1.40: Ask for this great Deliverer now, and find him
1.41: Eyeless in Gaza at the Mill with slaves,
1.42: Himself in bonds under Philistian yoke;
1.43: Yet stay, let me not rashly call in doubt
1.44: Divine Prediction; what if all foretold
1.45: Had been fulfilld but through mine own default,
1.46: Whom have I to complain of but my self?
1.47: Who this high gift of strength committed to me,
1.48: In what part lodg'd, how easily bereft me,
1.49: Under the Seal of silence could not keep,
1.50: But weakly to a woman must reveal it
1.52: O impotence of mind, in body strong!
1.53: But what is strength without a double share
1.55: Proudly secure, yet liable to fall
1.56: By weakest suttleties, not made to rule,
1.57: But to subserve where wisdom bears command.
1.58: God, when he gave me strength, to shew withal
1.59: How slight the gift was, hung it in my Hair.
1.60: But peace, I must not quarrel with the will
1.62: Happ'ly had ends above my reach to know:
1.63: Suffices that to me strength is my bane,
1.64: And proves the sourse of all my miseries;
1.65: So many, and so huge, that each apart
1.66: Would ask a life to wail, but chief of all,
1.67: O loss of sight, of thee I most complain!
1.68: Blind among enemies, O worse then chains,
1.69: Dungeon, or beggery, or decrepit age!
1.70: Light the prime work of God to me is extinct,
1.71: And all her various objects of delight
1.72: Annull'd, which might in part my grief have eas'd,
1.73: Inferiour to the vilest now become
1.74: Of man or worm; the vilest here excel me,
1.75: They creep, yet see, I dark in light expos'd
1.76: To daily fraud, contempt, abuse and wrong,
1.77: Within doors, or without, still as a fool,
1.78: In power of others, never in my own;
